Chapter 2 tours the game folder, your user data folder and the executables, so that you know where everything lives.

Chapter 2: The Install Layout

Before you change anything, you need a map. This chapter shows where the game keeps its files, which archive holds which kind of data, and how the game turns a pile of archives into one tidy tree of "virtual paths". Once you can read that tree, every later chapter becomes easier, because every instruction in this guide boils down to "put this file at this virtual path".

If you only want ARSENAL to find the game and get going, the first step of Make a mod and see it in the game is enough. This chapter is the map behind it.

What you will learn

  • What lives in the game folder and in your user data folder.
  • What each of the game's archives (paks) contains.
  • What a "virtual path" is, and why a wrong path silently does nothing.
  • The ways a path can be written inside a data file.
  • How to look inside the paks safely, and how to see which copy of a file the game uses.
  • Which program to start, and the launch options a modder needs.

1. Two folders, two jobs

The game uses two separate places on your disk.

The game folder (written <game folder> in this guide) is where Steam installed the game. It holds the executables, the archives with all original data, and the mods folder. Treat everything here except your own mod folders as read-only.

The user data folder is created inside your Documents folder, under My Games, in a folder named Men of War - Assault Squad 2. If your Documents folder is redirected to a cloud drive such as OneDrive, the real location is there, so search for the folder name if you cannot find it. It holds:

ItemWhat it is
profiles/<id>/options.setYour profile and options, including the list of active mods
profiles/<id>/keys.setYour key bindings
log/game.logThe log of the last run (overwritten on every launch)
log/minidumps/, log/oos/Crash dumps, and out-of-sync reports from multiplayer

Two files from that list matter most to a modder. options.set is how you prove which mods are really active, and game.log is where the game explains why something failed. Chapter 18 shows how to read them.

When ARSENAL starts a test match, it runs the game as a separate "instance" with its own user data folder, named like the normal one with - instance 1 added. Your own settings in the normal folder are not touched by a test run.

The parts of game.log and what they tell you are in chapter 18.

In Gates of Hell

Gates of Hell keeps its user data folder in Documents/My Games/Gates of Hell/. When the Documents folder is under OneDrive, or when the game is started with -useLocalDataFolder, it uses %LOCALAPPDATA%/Digitalmindsoft/Gates of Hell/ instead. The log names the folder it chose in a line that begins IO: Game config directory:. The log itself is log/game.log in that folder, and crash dumps go to log/minidumps/; the console variable dbg_minidumpFileLimit (5 by default) sets how many dumps are kept. ARSENAL looks for the Gates of Hell log in both places.

2. The game folder

Inside <game folder> you will find these items:

ItemRole
mowas_2.exeThe original official game program. Most existing mods were made for this one
as64.exeThe newer, 64-bit build of the program. It can run in Classic mode or with its built-in extras in Enhanced mode (chapter 3). This guide is written for it
as64/core/Files of the 64-bit build that it mounts after the original data and before every mod
as64/plus/The built-in package as64+ that switches on Enhanced mode
*_ed executablesEditor builds of the programs, used to make maps
mowas_2_workshop.exeThe tool that uploads a mod to the Steam Workshop
resource/All original data, stored in paks
mods/One subfolder per mod. Yours goes here
maps/Optional extra multiplayer map folders, each seen by the game under map/multi/<name>/ (chapter 13)
localization.pakThe original interface texts
1.patThe base game's own patch file (section 6 explains what that is)

The as64/ folders and as64.exe exist only where the 64-bit build is installed. If you have only mowas_2.exe, everything in this guide that is not about Enhanced mode still applies. The reference entries as64/core and as64+ give the exact rules for the two built-in layers.

In Gates of Hell

The Gates of Hell folder holds four items: binaries/x64/ with the programs (call_to_arms.exe, the editor call_to_arms_ed.exe, the server call_to_arms_server.exe and the Workshop uploader call_to_arms_workshop.exe), resource/ with the data, localizations/ with the interface texts (default.pak holds the default language), and mods/. There is no as64 folder, no maps folder and no localization.pak. The game works out its data folder from the folder it was started in and names it in game.log, in a line that begins IO: Game base directory:.

3. What is inside resource/

The resource folder holds a handful of paks. Each pak is a zip file whose content belongs to one area of the game. You can open any of them with a zip tool, and you can read their contents freely.

PakHolds
gamelogic.pakAlmost all editable "soft" data: set/, properties/, script/ and the shader folder shader/
entity/e1.pak, e2.pak, c1.pak, c2.pakUnits and vehicles (e2), landscape objects, weapon models, flora, effects (e1), buildings and fences (c1, c2)
interface.pakMenu pages, icons, cursors, skins, fonts
texture.pakTextures, plus the models and definitions of some units
sound.pakSound effects
music.pakMusic
map.pak and two map-pack paksSingle-player and multiplayer maps and missions
language.pakSpoken mission lines only (no text)
video.pak and a second video pakMenu and mission videos

The two paks you will touch most are gamelogic.pak (numbers, rules and scripts) and the entity paks (what units are). The map-pack and video paks are ordinary paks too. Owning or not owning a Steam DLC changes only what the menus offer, not which files are loaded.

What the folders inside the paks contain

Once the paks are overlaid, the game sees a tree with these top-level folders:

  • set/ holds weapons and ammunition (under set/stuff, mostly in files with no extension), soldier types (breed), multiplayer modes, unit rosters and armies (multiplayer), and other shared tables. Chapter 6 and the chapters after it describe these.
  • properties/ holds shared entity templates (.ext files such as the tank template), the soldier animation and behaviour helpers, and selection helpers.
  • script/multiplayer/ holds the Lua files that drive the multiplayer computer opponent. This is the only place the game uses Lua.
  • entity/ holds the entity definitions: -vehicle for vehicles, humanskin for soldiers, construction for buildings, fences and bridges, plus inventory (weapon and item models), flora, landscape, fx and particle effects.
  • interface/ holds menu pages, command-panel icons and purchase-card pictures, cursors, fonts and the text folder where localization is mounted.
  • map/multi/<map>/ holds each multiplayer map, with one mission file per game mode; map/single/ holds single-player skirmish missions.
  • sound/, texture/, music/, video/ hold what their names say.

File types at a glance

ExtensionMeaning
.defAn entity (unit, building, object)
.extAn entity template that .def files include
.setPlain data
.incA text include, or a file of macros
.miA mission
.lngInterface text
.mdl .ply .vol .mtl .anmModel, mesh, collision volume, material and animation resources
.patchA small delete and rename list (chapter 4)

Weapon and ammunition files in set/stuff usually have no extension at all. Every text file above is written in CRLF line endings and read with UTF-8 string values (chapter 5). The file formats of the binary resources are described in chapter 16.

In Gates of Hell

Gates of Hell splits its data over more paks, most of them in subfolders of resource/. At the top sit gamelogic.pak, properties.pak, shader.pak, music.pak, video.pak and the DLC paks. entity/ holds one pak per entity folder (-vehicle.pak, construction.pak, humanskin.pak, inventory.pak and others), and interface/, map/, sound/ and texture/ hold several paks each. The rule for where entries land is the same as here: a pak in resource/entity/ holds -vehicle/..., which the game sees as entity/-vehicle/.... Vehicles sit one level deeper, by nation and class: entity/-vehicle/<nation>/<class>/<unit>/. The interface texts are not in resource/ at all but in localizations/ (chapter 4).

4. The virtual path

The game does not care which pak a file came from. When it starts, it merges everything into one tree and refers to each file by its virtual path: the path of the file as seen from the resource level. A weapon file stored in gamelogic.pak as set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle has the virtual path set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle.

Three rules explain most of the game's behaviour:

  1. Case and slashes do not matter. The game lowercases every name and treats \ as /. Set\Stuff\Rifle\Example_Rifle and set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle are the same file.
  2. Same virtual path replaces, new virtual path adds. If your mod holds a file at an existing virtual path, yours wins. If it holds a path that does not exist yet, the file is added (and nothing will read it unless some other file refers to it).
  3. The extension is part of the name. A mod file music/main_theme.wav does not replace a base music/main_theme.mp3. They are different paths.

The base entity paks are rooted one level lower than a mod's entity pak would be. The original entity/e2.pak holds -vehicle/x, which the game maps to the virtual path entity/-vehicle/x. If you build your own entity.pak in your mod's resource/ folder, you must therefore store the file as entity/-vehicle/x inside it. If you store it as -vehicle/x, you create a new, unused path instead of replacing anything. This is the most common reason that a pak mod "does nothing".

If you use loose files in your mod's resource folder instead of paks, the folder structure plays the same role: mods/mymod/resource/entity/-vehicle/x has the virtual path entity/-vehicle/x. Chapter 4 goes into the details of paks, loose folders and which wins, and the reference entry file names lists the exact name rules.

In Gates of Hell

The three rules hold. Gates of Hell also lowercases every file name it reads from a data file and turns its \ into / at once, so a reference written with capitals or backslashes finds its file. A path with letters outside plain ASCII stops it with path is too long above 1023 bytes. And a name may stand for a folder: an animation or a sound can name a folder of files, and the game picks one of them. This game takes one file there and stops with Resource not found, which is why a ported unit needs its animation names changed (Bring a unit from Gates of Hell).

5. Ways to write a path inside a data file

When one data file refers to another (an include, a model, a sound), the way the path is written decides where the game looks:

Written asMeans
/properties/tank.extCounted from the resource level, so the mod overlay applies
tank.ext or sub/x.incRelative to the folder of the file that contains the reference
../x.incEach ../ climbs one folder from that file's folder
@profiles/xInside your user data folder
//xA real path counted from the game folder, outside resource/

The double-slash form bypasses the mod overlay. You will rarely need it, so avoid it in mods.

A leading slash is the safest form for includes, because it always means "from the top of the resource tree", no matter where the including file lives. A copied file that keeps a relative include looks next to its new location, so it fails if your copy sits in a different folder from the original. Note that paths in a data file are written as quoted strings. An unquoted path breaks into several pieces because / and . end a word (chapter 5). The reference entry path forms has the full rules.

Names may use ASCII letters and digits, the space, and the characters [ ] ( ) { } @ $ % ^ - + . _ ! # &. They must not start or end with a space.

In Gates of Hell

Gates of Hell adds one form: !x is counted from the game folder, like //x. This game does not know it and reads such a path in the wrong place, so change it when you bring a file over. The other forms mean the same in both games.

6. Patches in the base game

You may wonder about 1.pat in the game folder. It is a small zip that carries the base game's own patch level. Chapter 4 explains the .pat format and .patch files, because mods can use the same mechanism to delete or rename files that they do not own.

7. Looking inside paks safely

  • Read files in place. On the Editor page of the ARSENAL window (tab IDE), the Game view lists every file the game reads with your mod loaded, including the files inside paks, and marks which layer each one comes from (the game, another mod, or yours). Game files open read-only; "Copy into my mod" makes your own editable copy at the right path. "Find in files" with "Also the game's own files" ticked searches the paks too.
  • Or use a zip tool, read-only. Do not extract into the game folder. Extract into a scratch folder that you keep for reference, and search the extracted tree as text to find who uses a name. Since data files refer to each other by virtual path, a search for a file name finds every place that refers to it.
  • One copy is not the only copy. A file in one pak may be overridden by the same path in another layer: a loose file, a later mod, or the 64-bit build's own as64/core folder. The Editor page's "Which mod wins" lists every copy of the file you have open, and the command ARSENAL vfs <game folder> which set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle prints the winning source for any path. ARSENAL vfs <game folder> --mods mymod shadowed --list lists every file that a mod replaces.
  • Some units live in texture.pak. Some units keep model and definition files in texture.pak instead of an entity pak. If you cannot find a unit's .def, search both, or let the Game view find it for you.
  • Compare copies side by side. In the Editor, "Same file elsewhere" (Alt+O) opens the same game path from the game, a loaded mod or an installed mod that is not loaded, and "Side by side" (Alt+S) shows two copies next to each other. "Vanilla only" in the Game view lists only the game's own files.
  • Look inside one pak. A .pak, .pat or .zip file opens in a viewer that lists its entries with their sizes; a click opens one entry in its own viewer. Pictures, models, sounds and other binary files open in viewers too (file viewers).

Note: the game folder can be modified by game updates or by other tools. Do not use it as a baseline for comparisons that you plan to keep. Keep your own extracted copy of the original files.

In Gates of Hell

Under GoH the Editor on the IDE tab reads the Gates of Hell paks as well. Outside the window, open them with a zip tool, read-only, and extract into a folder outside the game. ARSENAL vfs "<Gates of Hell folder>" which <path> works there too: it mounts the paks in the subfolders of resource/ and prints which one supplies a path.

8. Which program to start

Start the game through Steam. The launch dialog offers Play, Editor, Safe mode and "Safe mode (no mods)". The program you want for this guide is as64.exe. Three command-line options matter to modders:

  • -no_mods starts the game with an empty mod list, which is the quickest way to tell whether a problem comes from a mod. Every mod.info in the mods folder is still read at start, so a broken one can still stop the game (reference entry -no_mods).
  • -console opens the in-game console in the 64-bit build (reference entry -console). The original mowas_2.exe has no console outside its editor build.
  • ARSENAL's Play page and ARSENAL play start the game for you with the options a test run needs, on a separate instance, and stop it again when the log is read.

How a test run fits into your work is in chapter 18 and on the page Make a mod and see it in the game.

In Gates of Hell

Gates of Hell also starts through Steam: binaries/x64/call_to_arms.exe started directly asks Steam to start it again and quits. -no_mods starts it with no mods, -safe resets the settings to a safe profile, and -showmodinfo adds to the mod list where each mod comes from ([STEAM:<id>] or [LOCAL]) and its path. When you host a Steam match, the game starts call_to_arms_server.exe in the background with your active mods; that server program writes no profile and keeps no debug logs. ARSENAL does not start Gates of Hell.

Gates of Hell: summary

The Gates of Hell notes in this book have not been tested in a running game. Check them in your own game before you depend on them.

SectionGates of HellIn a few words
1. Two folders, two jobsdiffersMy Games/Gates of Hell, or LocalAppData with OneDrive or -useLocalDataFolder
2. The game folderdiffersprograms in binaries/x64/, texts in localizations/, no as64 or maps folder
3. What is inside resource/differsmore paks in subfolders, vehicles by nation and class
4. The virtual pathdiffersnames lowercased at read, a name may stand for a folder
5. Ways to write a path inside a data filediffersextra form !x
6. Patches in the base gamesame as far as mappedthe base game's N.pat files count the same way; the install has none at the top
7. Looking inside paks safelydiffersthe Editor reads GoH paks; zip tool and ARSENAL vfs
8. Which program to startdiffersrestarts through Steam, -safe, -showmodinfo, server program for hosts

Pitfalls

  • Pak root mistakes. A mod entity pak must store entries under entity/, not at the root that the base entity paks use.
  • Case. Case never matters for paths, so you cannot use capitalization to tell two files apart. Two zip entries that differ only by case are one file; the later one wins.
  • Extra files do nothing. A file at a path nothing refers to is dead weight. After adding a file, check by name that something loads it.
  • Loose text files are ignored. The game skips loose files with the extensions .txt, .org, .msg, .scc, .temp and a few similar backup extensions when it scans a folder. The same file inside a pak is indexed. Do not keep notes in .txt files inside your resource folder and expect them to be read. The same goes for console scripts: give a script you run with exec the extension .cfg, not .txt.
  • A cloud-redirected Documents folder. The user data folder may not be where the plain path says. Search for it by name.
  • Reading the game folder as a baseline. See the note above.

Next

Chapter 3 opens the mods folder: how mod.info works, how the game decides which mods to load, and who wins when two mods contain the same file. For unfamiliar words, see the glossary in 22-glossary.md.

Chapter 3: The Mod Folder and Load Order

A mod is a folder with a mod.info file in it. This chapter explains what goes in that file, how the game decides which mods to load and in what order, the difference between Classic and Enhanced mode, and what happens when two mods contain the same file. Get this chapter right and your mod will load reliably; get it wrong and the game will quietly ignore your work.

The short way to a working mod folder is Make a mod and see it in the game; the version lines for sharing are set in Pack and share. Every key and rule in this chapter has a full entry in Reference 1: mod.info and the mod folder.

Encoding reminder. The game's text files use CRLF (Windows) line endings. The 64-bit build reads every string value as UTF-8, in data files and .lng files alike; the original data is plain ASCII outside ; comments, and some comments still hold old cp1251 bytes that the game skips. Write UTF-8 without a byte-order mark and leave old comment bytes alone. Many editors silently change the encoding or the line endings when you save. Set your editor to keep both, and check them after every save.

What you will learn

  • How to write a correct mod.info.
  • How the game decides whether a mod is supported.
  • The difference between Classic and Enhanced mode.
  • How the active mod list works and why order matters.
  • How to find out which of two mods wins a file.
  • How to keep multiplayer players in agreement.

1. The shape of a mod folder

<game folder>/mods/mymod/
    mod.info                  required
    resource/                 loose files, same layout as the game's resource tree
    resource.pak              optional: content packed in a zip
    1.pat, 2.pat ...          optional: patch files (chapter 4)
    localization/             optional: .lng text files
    localization.pak          optional: the same, packed

Besides mod.info, only these five items are read: resource.pak, resource/, the numbered N.pat files, localization.pak and localization/. Anything else in the mod folder is ignored by the game, so it is a place for notes, working files and screenshots. If you share the mod through the Workshop, though, everything in the folder is uploaded, so keep private files out. A loose .patch file placed in the mod root is never read. Chapter 4 explains how to pack it into a .pat file.

Two important details:

  • The mod's identity is its folder name, in lowercase. The Name written inside mod.info is only a display title. If you rename the folder, the game treats it as a different mod, and any list entry that named the old folder is dropped.
  • A folder without a file named exactly mod.info is not a mod. The game skips it silently; this is what happens when a zip tool adds an extra folder level. Two folders whose names differ only by capitalization count as one name, and the second is rejected. A folder named as64+ is dropped, because that name belongs to the built-in package.

The game scans only the direct subfolders of mods, plus the built-in package and subscribed Workshop items. A mod folder anywhere else is never seen. See the reference entry mod folder, and for the files that may sit beside mod.info the entries resource.pak, N.pat and other files in the mod root.

In Gates of Hell

A Gates of Hell mod folder is read in three parts besides mod.info: the resource/ folder (with any paks inside it, each mounted where it lies), the numbered N.pat files, and the localizations/ folder with one subfolder per language code (default for the base texts). A resource.pak, localization.pak or localization/ in the mod root is skipped without a message, so a mod of this game copied over unchanged loses its packed data and its texts. Move the paks into resource/ and the texts into localizations/default/interface/text/. A mod whose language setup does not match the game's logs Localization mode used in ... does not match with default mode and still loads.

The folder name is checked too. A name with a space, a letter outside plain ASCII, or any of the signs < > + ( ) [ ] { } ! @ # $ % ^ & * - = ; : | ' " is skipped, with Warning: invalid mod folder name "<name>"! in game.log and nothing on screen. So my-mod and as64+ never load there. Use letters, digits and _; the readme of the game's own template mod asks for letters and _ only.

2. Writing mod.info

mod.info is a file in the data language of chapter 5, with one outer block {Mod ...}. Key names are not case sensitive here, and ; starts a comment. Here is a complete example for the 64-bit build:

{Mod
    {Name "My Mod"}
    {Desc "Tweaks rifle damage.\nVersion 1."}
    {MinGameVersion "3.301"}
    {Require "basemod"}
    {Delete "resource/set/stuff/junk/"}
}
KeyMeaning
NameThe title shown in the mod list. On the original game it is also the folder name the Workshop installer creates for subscribers
DescThe description. \n means a new line; a quote inside it must be written \"
MinGameVersion, MaxGameVersionThe range of game versions the mod supports, and at the same time its mode (sections 3 and 4)
RequireA mod that must also be installed and active. Repeat the key for several mods. Write "folder" or "folder:number"; only the folder name is compared
DeleteA file, or a folder prefix ending in /, to remove from the file index before this mod's own files are added. Repeatable
FileIdWritten by the Workshop uploader. Leave it alone

Three features of the file reader are worth knowing.

  • Unknown keys are skipped silently. A mistyped key does nothing and produces no message. ARSENAL modinfo (or the Check page) reports it for you.
  • A broken mod.info can stop the game. The game reads every mod.info in the mods folder at start, whether the mod is active or not, and even with -no_mods. A broken value, such as an unescaped quote inside Desc, has stopped the game from starting. Run ARSENAL modinfo <game folder>/mods to check all of them at once. Save the file as UTF-8 without a byte-order mark (or plain ASCII) with CRLF line endings; a UTF-16 file breaks it.
  • Delete here is different from the delete line in a .patch file. The mod.info form runs before your files are mounted, so it cannot remove your own files, and its path must start with resource/: a path such as "set/x" matches nothing, without any message. The patch form runs after your files and can remove anything, your own copies included (chapter 4).

In the ARSENAL window, the Share page's first step ("About my mod") writes the name, description and version lines for you, after showing what will change (Pack and share). The Quick Guided Task "I want to make a mod" asks for the title, the description and the mods it needs, and writes mod.info from your answers.

In Gates of Hell

Gates of Hell reads the same keys and two more. Its own template writes the key names in lower case ({mod, {name, {minGameVersion).

  • Tags takes one quoted string of words separated by spaces, such as {Tags "develop"}; an unquoted word is an error. The word develop lets the mod load on any game version, and no_delete hides the delete button in the game's mod list.
  • Priority takes a whole number (1 when absent) and orders mods that do not require each other (section 6).

AS2 skips both keys without a message, so a mod that relies on them loads in another order here. A broken mod.info does not stop Gates of Hell: that mod is skipped with Warning: failed to load mod <path>: <error> in game.log, and an empty one with Warning: empty mod.info file found at. FileId is read only for local mods. In the description, \n and $n both start a new line.

3. The version gate

The game compares its own version with the range in your mod. If the game version is outside the range, the mod is skipped with a warning. The rule differs between the two kinds of mod:

  • A legacy mod (MinGameVersion below 3.301) needs both MinGameVersion and MaxGameVersion. An empty or missing value makes it unsupported. The game version it is compared with is the data version, of the form 3.262.<patch>, and the comparison uses only the parts both versions have, so 3.262.1 equals 3.262 and a MaxGameVersion of 3.262 accepts every patch of 3.262. A MaxGameVersion below the game version, such as 3.100, is rejected. A MaxGameVersion lower than MinGameVersion is not reported.
  • A modern mod (MinGameVersion 3.301 or higher) passes when the program's version is at least MinGameVersion. MaxGameVersion is ignored and may be left out.

Version strings are digits and dots; other characters are ignored. The console variable dev_disableModVersionControl, when true, lets a legacy mod with an empty range load; do not ship a mod that depends on it.

In Gates of Hell

Gates of Hell compares its own version, of the form 1.xxx, with the range. Players must run the same version to join each other. Each bound is optional there: a missing MinGameVersion or MaxGameVersion leaves that side open, and a mod with neither probably loads on any version (not confirmed). The readme of the game's template mod asks for both, so set both. A range written for this game (3.x) is refused, and the log says was disabled: Unsupported game version. The tag develop (section 2) and the console variable dev_disableModVersionControl both lift the check. ARSENAL modinfo "<mod folder>" --goh --game "<Gates of Hell folder>" reads the version from your Gates of Hell and says whether the range holds it.

4. Classic mode and Enhanced mode

The 64-bit as64.exe program has a built-in extension package called as64+. When it is in the active list, the game runs in Enhanced mode. When it is not, the game runs in Classic mode. The mode decides which mods may load:

Classic modeEnhanced mode
Legacy mod (MinGameVersion below 3.301)LoadsSkipped
Modern mod (MinGameVersion 3.301 or higher)SkippedLoads
Version ruleThe data version must lie between Min and MaxThe program version must be at least Min; Max is ignored

In other words, the minimum version in your mod.info doubles as a mode label. A mod written for the original game is "legacy". A mod for the 64-bit build sets MinGameVersion to 3.301 or higher and is "modern"; that is what ARSENAL new writes. The built-in as64+ package always loads before every player mod, so any player mod can override its files, and you cannot move it above them. A mod may name as64+ in a Require line. Mode words such as "as64" or "legacy" are not folders, so a Require naming them counts as a missing mod.

Practical rules:

  • If you target the original game and Enhanced mode alike, ship two variants rather than one. ARSENAL's upgrade command and Mods > Mods > Upgrade or Port in the window turn an old mod into an AS64 copy without changing the original (see Bring an old mod up to the 64-bit build).
  • Do not leave a mod of the wrong kind in your active list. A mismatched mod is meant to be skipped, but in as64.exe a mismatched mod found in the list at startup has stopped the game with "Unable to determine fallback font" before the menu appeared, because the refusal message is written before the fonts are loaded. If the game refuses to start after you changed modes, take the mod out of the list (ARSENAL modswitch, section 5) or fix its MinGameVersion.
  • How the in-game menu switches Enhanced mode on is not described (unconfirmed). The mode follows whether as64+ is in the active list.

The reference entries as64+ and as64/core describe the two built-in layers. When a mode change goes wrong, see chapter 21.

In Gates of Hell

Gates of Hell has no Classic or Enhanced mode and no as64+ package; its version check alone decides whether a mod loads. A Require naming as64+ probably counts as a missing mod there, and a folder named as64+ is skipped for its name (section 1).

5. The active list

The game keeps the list of active mods in your profile file options.set:

{options
    {mods "as64+:0" "basemod:0" "mymod:2"}
}

Each entry is folder:number, split at the first colon. The folder part is the lowercase folder name. The comparison is exact, so a capital letter in the list never matches. The Name from mod.info is never used here.

The number is the count of patch files (1.pat, 2.pat, ...) the mod had when it was activated. It acts only as a gate: the game always mounts all the patches the mod really has, even if the list asks for fewer. If the list asks for more patches than the folder holds, the entry is skipped. After you add a .pat to an active mod, activate it again so that the number is updated. The easiest way to avoid trouble is to let the game write the list (Options, then the MODS tab, chapter 1) or to use ARSENAL modswitch, which shows the list, plans a change and writes it only with --write. It refuses a list that mixes a legacy mod with as64+, or a modern mod without it, and it refuses while the game runs, because the game rewrites options.set itself. The Play page sets the list for a test run and puts yours back afterwards.

Every time you press Apply in the MODS tab, and at every game start, the game goes through this sequence for each entry, in list order:

  1. If the folder does not exist in mods, the entry is dropped with the log line Mod '<entry>' was disabled: Not installed.
  2. If the version gate or the mode check fails, the entry is dropped with a warning.
  3. If a required mod is missing or not in the list, the entry is dropped with a warning.
  4. If the list number is larger than the patch count, the entry is dropped silently.
  5. The remaining mods are sorted so that required mods come first. A circular requirement (A requires B and B requires A) empties the whole list, with a log message that begins Dependency test error!.
  6. Each surviving mod is mounted, and the cleaned list is written back to options.set.

When the game version changes (for example after an update), the whole list is emptied and you must activate your mods again; the log says "Game version update detected". as64.exe and mowas_2.exe compare the same data version, so switching between them keeps the list. See the reference entries options.set mods and lastGameVersion.

Each Apply is a complete rebuild: the game removes all data, mounts the original game, then mounts every active mod in order. It takes about half a minute for a small mod and can take several minutes for a large one. A file you add to the mod folder while the game is running appears only after the next Apply. At the end of each Apply, game.log prints Repository: N resources, the size of the file index.

The command-line option -no_mods starts the game with no mods at all, which is the quickest way to tell whether a problem comes from a mod. How a test run activates a mod and what the log says then is in chapter 18; the button itself is the reference entry Apply.

In Gates of Hell

Gates of Hell keeps the same {mods} list in its profile. A Workshop item is named mod_<item number> there, after the item and not after its title, so renaming a published mod does not break anyone's list. The game drops a name that appears twice in the list. When it drops an entry, it writes the list back with plain folder names, without the :number part. The log shows each step: Mod: applying mods, Mod: activate mod <name> and Mod: disable mod <name>; at start it also writes Scanning mods in and Found N available mods. Whether an update of the game empties the list as this game does is not confirmed.

6. Who wins: the load order

The rule is simple and has no exceptions:

The later registration wins the whole file.

The game mounts the original data first, then the 64-bit build's own as64/core layer, then each active mod in list order. A file in a later mod replaces the same virtual path from an earlier mod or from the original game, completely. There is no merging of contents and there are no priorities. If two mods both change set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle, the one lower in the "Activated" list supplies the entire file, and the other mod's change to that file is lost. The requirement sort decides the order only between mods that require each other; among mods that do not, the order is not guaranteed, so give a mod that must come after another a Require line naming it.

Order inside one mod follows the mount sequence from chapter 4: resource.pak, then the resource folder, then the patches, then the localization pak, then the localization folder. A file never wins because it is newer or bigger; timestamps play no part. See the reference entries Override rule and Load order between mods.

What this means for you:

  • Everything you do not ship loads from the original. A small mod needs only the files it changes.
  • Put mods that change the same files in the order you intend. There is no marker in the log when one mod overrides another, so conflicts are invisible unless you look for them.
  • Prefer small, targeted files. The fewer files you replace, the fewer conflicts you cause. A copy of a whole data file also drops every entry another mod added to that file.
  • Ship each path once. Inside a single folder, when a loose file and a pak both hold the same path, the winner depends on name order in the folder listing (chapter 4, section 3). Avoid shipping the same file twice within one mod.

Tools show conflicts without you opening a single file. In the window, "Which mod wins" on the Editor page (tab IDE) lists every copy of the open file and the one the game reads. On the command line:

ARSENAL conflicts --game <game folder> --mods mymod,othermod
ARSENAL overdiff <game folder>/mods/mymod --game <game folder>

The first lists, key by key, which source wins when several mods change the same file, and warns when two mods change the same file with no Require line between them. The second lists, for each file you replace, exactly which values you changed compared with what you replaced. Use the second one before every release: it shows accidental edits.

When a file you changed seems to have no effect, chapter 21 walks through the causes.

In Gates of Hell

The rule "the later registration wins the whole file" holds in Gates of Hell too, but the order between mods is set differently. Mods that require others still come after them. Mods that do not require each other are ordered by their Priority key (section 2), lowest first, so the mod with the higher number loads later and wins. Two mods with the same Priority keep a fixed order. Each mod has only resource/, its patches and localizations/; the language folders are laid over resource/ after the mods are mounted, so a file under localizations/ probably beats the same path in any mod's resource/ (not confirmed). ARSENAL's vfs and conflicts tools take the mods in the order you give them and do not sort by Priority, so give them the order the game will use.

7. Multiplayer: everyone must match

In multiplayer the game compares the data that affects gameplay between players. A mod that adds, replaces or deletes any path under entity/, fx/, properties/, set/, sound/, map/single/, map/bonus/, map/multi/ or script/multiplayer/ is marked as affecting multiplayer, and every player in the match must have the same version of it. A mod that changes only interface/ (pictures and menus) is not compared. The content check covers the file kinds .set, .inc, .ext, .mi, .reg, .info, .def and .mdl; .lng, .dds, .ebm, .wav and Lua files are not compared and may differ between players without any warning. When players cannot join each other, check this first. ARSENAL mpsync --mod <mod folder> sorts your mod's files into compared and not compared (chapters 12 and 21; reference entry multiplayer sync folders).

In Gates of Hell

In Gates of Hell the list of active mods sent to other players is the list of mods that really mounted, each with its own version, and players must run the same game version. The game does not copy downloaded mods over mods/ when you join a match, so every player gets the session's mods from the Workshop. A host starts a separate server program (call_to_arms_server.exe) that loads the host's mod list. The start option -showmodinfo shows each mounted mod with [STEAM:<item>] or [LOCAL] and its folder, and marks with * a mod that touches the files players compare. Which folders Gates of Hell compares is not mapped, so ARSENAL mpsync does not apply there.

8. Workshop mods

The two programs handle subscribed Workshop items differently.

  • The original mowas_2.exe copies a subscribed item into mods/<Name>/, where <Name> comes from the item's own Name key. It deletes any old copy there first, adds {FileId} to the copy's mod.info, and writes a stamp file named after the item number in mods/. A local mod with the same Name as a subscribed one is overwritten at the next sync. If you publish a mod and later change its Name, the folder name on every subscriber's machine changes, and their active lists break.
  • The 64-bit as64.exe loads a subscribed item in place from Steam's download folder and does not copy it. A folder in mods/ that is an old copy of a subscribed item is ignored, with a log line saying the Workshop item is loaded instead, so a fix you make in that copy never loads.

Either way: give your development copy a different folder name from the published item, and keep notes and .git folders out of a folder you upload. See Workshop copy and Workshop upload, chapter 20 for releasing, and Pack and share for the steps in the window.

In Gates of Hell

Gates of Hell loads a subscribed item in place, like as64.exe, under the name mod_<item number>. The item must sit under Steam's workshop/content/ folder; elsewhere the log says A workshop mod outside of standard location!. Local folders are read first, so a local folder named mods/mod_<item number> loses to the Workshop item at start, and the log says Warning! Duplicate mod found [...] using second. with both paths. Deleting a mod in the game's mod list removes a local folder; for a Workshop item the files stay until Steam removes them. The game comes with its own upload program, call_to_arms_workshop.exe in binaries/x64/; ARSENAL's Share page is not shown under the Gates of Hell button.

9. A worked example

Suppose you want one mod to make rifles more accurate and another mod, by someone else, to change rifle damage, and both touch the file set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle. In the Activated list you put damagemod above accuracymod. The game mounts the original, then damagemod, then accuracymod. Because both contain that file, accuracymod's copy is the one used, and it still has the original damage numbers, so the damage change is lost. ARSENAL conflicts --game <game folder> --mods damagemod,accuracymod shows exactly this. The fix is to make a third mod, with a copy of the file that includes both changes, placed last and with Require lines naming the other two. Alternatively, move one change into a different file if the data layout allows it.

Gates of Hell: summary

The Gates of Hell notes in this book have not been tested in a running game. Check them in your own game before you depend on them.

Gates of Hell, the related game on the same engine, reads mods in a similar way. This table shows, for each section of this chapter, whether it does something different. For a unit taken from Gates of Hell, see Make a unit from Gates of Hell.

SectionGates of HellIn a few words
1. The mod folderdiffersOnly resource/, patches and localizations/ are read; spaces, non-ASCII letters and most punctuation are refused in folder names
2. mod.infodiffersExtra keys Tags and Priority; a broken file skips that mod only
3. The version gatediffersVersions 1.xxx; a bound may be missing; set both
4. Classic mode and Enhanced modediffersNo modes and no as64+
5. The active listdiffersWorkshop items named mod_<item number>; duplicates dropped
6. Who wins: the load orderdiffersPriority orders mods that do not require each other
7. Multiplayer: everyone must matchdiffersMods come from the Workshop; compared folders not mapped
8. Workshop modsdiffersLoaded in place; a local copy with the same name loses
9. A worked examplesame as far as mappedSame rule, but Priority can set the order instead of a Require line

Pitfalls

  • Wrong folder name case in options.set. Hand-edited entries must be lowercase.
  • Renamed folder. The old list entry loads nothing, and the MODS tab shows "Activated" as empty.
  • Missing version range. An empty MinGameVersion or MaxGameVersion makes a legacy mod unsupported; a mod with no version lines at all never loads.
  • Wrong mode. A modern mod in Classic mode and a legacy mod in Enhanced mode are skipped, and at startup the mismatch can stop as64.exe before the menu.
  • A broken mod.info anywhere in mods. One malformed mod.info, even of an inactive mod, can stop every launch. Run ARSENAL modinfo <game folder>/mods to check all of them.
  • A Delete path without resource/. It matches nothing and says nothing.
  • A new .pat in an active mod. Activate the mod again so that the list number matches.
  • Encoding. Saving mod.info as UTF-16 breaks it. Keep plain ASCII (or UTF-8 without a byte-order mark) with CRLF line endings, and keep .lng files in UTF-8.
  • Several mods active at once while testing. Activate only the mod under test, because the others can override your files.

Next

Chapter 4 goes inside the mod folder: loose files versus paks, how .pat and .patch files delete and rename things, and how to pack a mod for release. Words you do not know are in the glossary, 22-glossary.md.

Chapter 4: Virtual Files, Paks and Patches

Chapter 2 introduced the virtual path and chapter 3 showed how mods are ordered. This chapter looks at what happens inside one mod: how loose files and paks are combined, how a zip file becomes part of the game, and how a .pat patch can delete or rename files that your mod does not own. It ends with the tools that show you the final result and with packing a mod for release.

The short way to pack a finished mod is Pack and share. The exact rules for every item below are in Reference 1: mod.info and the mod folder.

Encoding reminder. The game's text files use CRLF (Windows) line endings. The 64-bit build reads every string value as UTF-8, in data files and .lng files alike, and identifiers must be plain ASCII. The original data is ASCII outside ; comments; some comments still hold old cp1251 bytes, which the game skips, so leave them as they are. Editors can silently change the encoding or the line endings when you save, and zip tools can do it when they "convert text files". Check both after every save and every repack.

What you will learn

  • How the game builds its single file index.
  • What a pak is and where its root is.
  • The exact order in which a mod's pieces are mounted.
  • How .pat and .patch files delete and rename files.
  • How to see which copy of a file the game uses.
  • How to pack a mod and check the result.

1. One index, last one wins

When the game loads a resource, it consults a single list: the file index. Every file the game has mounted, whether loose on disk or inside a zip, is one entry in that list under its virtual path. Adding a file whose path is already in the list throws away the older entry. There is no layering and no priority; the most recent addition wins the whole file. Removing a file deletes its entry, and nothing is left behind to show that it was ever there. See the reference entry Override rule.

Names are normalized when they enter the index. Upper case becomes lower case and a backslash becomes a forward slash. Two zip entries that differ only by case or slash direction are therefore one entry, and the later one wins. A path longer than 4096 bytes stops the game with path is too long.

A directory in the index is not a real object. It is simply the beginning of a lot of names. This is why a delete that ends with / can erase a whole folder in one line: it erases every name that starts with that text.

In Gates of Hell

The index works the same way: the last registration wins the whole file. Gates of Hell also normalizes every file name read from a data file, so "Interface\Foo" in a .def finds interface/foo; in this game, write names in lower case with forward slashes to be safe. A name with non-ASCII letters may be at most 1023 bytes there, or the game stops with path is too long. The list of entries of each pak is kept between starts and read again whenever the pak's size or time changes, so a pak you repack is picked up at the next start.

2. Paks are zip files

A pak is an ordinary zip file with the extension .pak. Entries may be stored or compressed (deflate). There is no encryption and no special header. Any zip tool can create one, and ARSENAL's packer builds them for you (section 8). When you pack your own by hand:

  • Store the entry names with forward slashes and the full virtual path, for example set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle inside a mod's resource/gamelogic.pak, or entity/-vehicle/x inside a mod's resource/entity.pak.
  • Do not wrap everything in an extra top-level folder. If the pak contains mymod/set/..., the virtual path becomes mymod/set/... and nothing is replaced.
  • Do not let the zip tool convert line endings or encoding of the text files.
  • Write correct CRC values. A wrong CRC may still load in the game, but it breaks other zip readers.
  • Zip64 archives work, so large paks are fine, but a single entry must stay below 4 GB.

Where the pak's entries land depends on the pak's own place in the tree. Each entry becomes the folder the pak sits in plus the entry name. A pak in your mod's resource/ folder puts entry a/b at the virtual path a/b. The base entity paks live one folder deeper (resource/entity/), so their entries are rooted one level lower than a mod's entity.pak. For your own mod, the rule is easy: put your paks directly in resource/, and put the full virtual path in every entry. See the reference entry pak.

Some details about how paks are read, which explain performance:

  • Small text-like entries (.def, .mdl, .inc, .set, .ext, .mi, .reg, .info, .tpl and .txt) are read into memory when the pak is mounted. Other entries are unpacked each time the game opens them. A mod with thousands of small text files therefore takes longer to apply.
  • If a zip holds the same name twice, the later entry wins.
  • Directory entries (names ending in /) are ignored. Entry names longer than 1023 bytes are cut.

To look inside a pak without unpacking it, open it in the window: the Archive viewer lists every entry of a .pak, .pat or .zip with its size and packing, and opens one entry in its own viewer (File viewers). The Editor can also save a file that lives in your mod's own pak: it rewrites that pak and keeps a restore point, so you can go back.

In Gates of Hell

Paks are zip files there too, but some details differ:

  • Every entry without a CRC value writes the warning no crc for file in package ... performance may be slowed to game.log. Write real CRC values.
  • Entries kept in memory are .reg, .def, .inc, .set, .ext, .tpl, .info, .presets, .pattern, .ammo, .fsm and .xml. They are read on first use, not when the pak is mounted. .mdl, .mi and .txt entries are read from the pak each time.
  • An entry that cannot be read stops the game with Failed to read file from pak <name>, and the message asks you to verify the game files through Steam. A mod pak that cannot be opened stops the game too.
  • The game's own paks sit in resource/ and in its subfolders, such as resource/entity/, each keyed at its own folder (chapter 2).

3. Loose files

Anything inside mods/mymod/resource/ is scanned and added to the index, folder by folder, with the same virtual path it has relative to resource/. Folders inside the scan are walked in turn, and paks found there are mounted as paks at their own place. This makes it easy to work: edit loose files while you develop, then pack them for release. See the reference entry resource/.

Not all loose files are added. The scan skips the extensions .txt, .org, .msg, .scc, .temp and three similar backup extensions, while .ply and .mtl are explicitly allowed. It also skips a file named .gitignore and folders named .git or .svn. A loose .txt file in your mod is therefore invisible to the game, even though the same file inside a pak would be indexed. If you need a loose text file the game can read, such as a console script for exec, name it .cfg.

Three warnings about loose files:

  1. A loose folder and a pak in the same folder can both hold the same path. The game does not sort the folder listing itself; it takes what the operating system returns, which on a normal Windows disk is case-insensitive name order, and the later name wins. As a result a loose folder named set beats a pak named gamelogic.pak (because set sorts after it), while a loose entity folder loses to entity.pak (because it sorts before it). This order has not been seen in play for every folder (unconfirmed). The safe habit is never to ship the same virtual path twice in one mod. See the reference entry Loose file against pak.
  2. Timestamps never decide anything. A pak that is "newer than your edits" matters only as a reminder to repack. If you have a leftover extracted copy of a file, it stays live, and it can override your freshly repacked pak.
  3. Many loose files are slow. When a match loads, the game opens every file that the multiplayer comparison covers, one at a time. A mod with tens of thousands of loose text files can take minutes longer to start a match than the same files packed in paks. Pack big trees of text files, and keep only a small set of loose fixes.

In Gates of Hell

Loose files in a mod's resource/ folder are added the same way. One cap is new: a loose file of 2 GB or more stops the game with invalid position, so keep big files in a pak or below that size. Which extensions the scan skips in Gates of Hell is not mapped.

4. The mount order inside one mod

For every active mod, the game first applies the mod.info Delete lines, then mounts these items in this exact order:

  1. resource.pak in the mod root, placed at resource/
  2. The resource/ folder, scanned recursively (any paks inside it are mounted where they are found)
  3. 1.pat, 2.pat, and so on, each placed at resource/, each with its .patch applied (section 5)
  4. localization.pak, placed at resource/interface/text/
  5. The localization/ folder, scanned into resource/interface/text/

Because each later item adds its files after the earlier ones, a loose file in resource/ should replace the same path in the mod's root resource.pak. That follows from the order, but it has not been seen in play (unconfirmed), so do not ship the same file both in resource.pak and loose: keep each path in one place. See the reference entry Mount order inside a mod.

Because patches come after the mod's own pak and folder, a patch can delete files that the mod itself brought. Because localization comes last, it can replace text files the patches did not touch. A .lng file in your localization/ folder replaces the original file of the same name completely, with no merge: keys your copy leaves out show blank or as the key (chapter 14).

The original game is mounted by the same steps from the game folder, so the game folder's own resource/ folder, paks, localization.pak and 1.pat are processed the same way. On the 64-bit build, the folder as64/core/ follows the original game and comes before every mod. Which copy wins between the language folders and the data is explained for texts in chapter 14.

In Gates of Hell

Gates of Hell mounts three items per mod, and the same three for the base game:

  1. The resource/ folder, scanned with the paks inside it
  2. 1.pat, 2.pat, and so on
  3. The localizations/ folder

A resource.pak in the mod root, a localization.pak and a localization/ folder are not read. Move the root pak into resource/ (its entries keep their full virtual paths) and the texts into localizations/<language code>/. The language folders are not mounted as they are: the files of localizations/default/ and then of the selected language are laid over resource/, so localizations/default/interface/text/x becomes interface/text/x. This probably happens after all mods are mounted, which means a file under localizations/ beats the same path in any mod's resource/ (not confirmed). The base game without its localizations/ folder stops with Failed to mount localization. Texts there are .pot, .po, .mo or .lng files (chapter 14).

5. Patches: N.pat and .patch

Sometimes you must remove or rename a file that exists in the original game. Replacing a file is not enough when the game would otherwise find the original, for example when you want a file not to exist at all. For this, the game has patch files.

A .pat file (N.pat) is a zip file, named 1.pat, 2.pat and so on, in the mod root. It is mounted like a pak at resource/, so it may also carry ordinary content files. It must also contain one .patch document: a small text file in the same data language as other game data. The game finds it by its ending: any file whose name ends in .patch will do, whatever it is called. If a .pat holds no .patch, the game stops with the error Wrong patch N.

A patch looks like this:

{Patch
    {id 1}
    {delete "set/stuff/junk/old_rifle"}
    {delete "set/stuff/junk/"}
    {remap "set/stuff/gun/a_gun" "set/stuff/gun/b_gun"}
}
ItemWhat it does
{id N}Must equal the patch's number, or the game stops with Wrong patch N version
{delete "path"}Removes the file. A path ending in / removes everything under that folder. A path that does not exist is not an error
{remap "from" "to"}Moves a file to a new path. If from does not exist, the game stops with File is not found - <from>

All paths are written relative to resource/ (no leading resource/). Backslashes are accepted. Other keys inside {Patch} are read and ignored.

Some behaviours matter:

  • The patch runs after your own pak and resource/ folder, so a delete can erase your own files as well as earlier mods' files and the original game's. A later mod can add a path again, because it mounts afterwards.
  • Files inside the same .pat are mounted before its delete lines run, so they survive unless you list them.
  • A delete leaves no marker. If something later asks for the deleted file, the game stops with File not found - resource/<path>. Only delete files you know nothing else needs, or ship a replacement.
  • Patches are applied in numeric order, and the game keeps counting only while 1.pat, 2.pat, 3.pat all exist. A gap (a 1.pat and a 3.pat without a 2.pat) stops the count at 1, and the later file is never mounted, silently.
  • A loose .patch file in the mod root is never read. Pack it into a .pat first. You may keep the editable .patch in the mod root for convenience, knowing the game ignores it, and zip it into 1.pat when you build.

The mod's patch count is the number written after the colon in the active list entry (chapter 3). After you add a new .pat to a mod that is already active, activate it again so that the list picks up the new count.

A small worked example

You want to remove a weapon, set/stuff/junk/old_rifle, from the game. In your mod folder:

  1. Create the text file 1.patch containing {Patch {id 1} {delete "set/stuff/junk/old_rifle"}}.
  2. Zip it into mods/mymod/1.pat. Put 1.patch at the top of the zip, with no folder in front of it.
  3. Activate the mod, or activate it again if it was active.

Anything that still refers to old_rifle (a unit's loadout, a roster) now fails to find it. You must change those places in the same mod, which is why the delete line is the last step of a clean removal rather than the first. ARSENAL refcheck lists the places that still refer to a name.

mod.info Delete instead of a patch

mod.info can carry a {Delete "resource/..."} line instead (chapter 3, section 2). It needs no .pat and works in the 64-bit build, but it runs before your own files are mounted, so it removes only files of the game and of earlier mods, never your own. Its path must start with resource/; without that prefix it matches nothing, without any message. See the reference entry Delete.

6. Map overlays and mission data

Two other places also feed the index, and they matter if you make maps.

  • A downloaded or local map folder (under the game's maps folder) is mounted at resource/map/multi/<name>/, after any existing files at that prefix are removed. It uses the same sequence (pak, folder, patches) as a mod.
  • A map can carry its own data overlay in a folder named mod/. When that map's mission loads, the files under it replace the matching paths under resource/ for the match. This overlay beats every active mod for that match, and it is undone when the scene closes.

Chapter 13 covers maps in detail, and the reference entries map folder and map mod overlay give the rules.

In Gates of Hell

A map folder's resource.pak is not mounted in Gates of Hell; only its resource/ folder and its patches are. A multiplayer map shipped as a resource.pak inside its folder is not read there, so put its paks inside resource/. Whether a map's mod/ overlay works there is not mapped.

7. Inspecting the effective file set

You do not have to guess which copy of a file the game will use. ARSENAL rebuilds the index the way the game does.

In the window, the Editor page (tab IDE) shows it file by file: its Game view marks every file with the layer it comes from (the game, another mod, or yours), and its "Vanilla only" switch shows the original game's files alone. "Which mod wins" (Alt+W) lists every copy of the open file with the one the game reads, "Same file elsewhere" (Alt+O) opens another copy of the same path, "Compare with vanilla" (Alt+V) shows your file beside the copy it replaces, and "Side by side" (Alt+S) shows two copies next to each other. Mods > Mods > Mod Files (with Advanced on) lists every file of your mod and which file the game really uses.

On the command line:

ARSENAL vfs <game folder> --mods othermod,mymod which set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle
ARSENAL vfs <game folder> --mods mymod shadowed --list
ARSENAL conflicts --game <game folder> --mods othermod,mymod
ARSENAL overdiff <game folder>/mods/mymod --game <game folder>

The first prints which source supplies a given path, with every copy it hides. The second lists every file your mod replaces. The third shows conflicts between mods key by key. The fourth shows, for each file you replace, exactly which values you changed, and warns when your copy of a whole file drops entries that were in the file it replaces. Together they answer almost every "why does the game not show my change?" question. The vfs tool also reports the structural mistakes in this chapter: wrongly rooted pak entries, missing .patch documents, unusual zip names and files in the mod root that the game ignores.

A useful number: at the end of every apply, the log prints Repository: N resources, where N is the size of the index. If you change a mod and the number does not change, the game did not add or remove any file (it may still have replaced one). Chapter 18 explains the rest of the log, and chapter 21 lists the usual reasons a change does not show.

In Gates of Hell

ARSENAL vfs recognises a Gates of Hell folder by its program in binaries/x64/ and mounts it the Gates of Hell way: paks in resource/ and its subfolders, patches, and the default language laid over resource/. For example ARSENAL vfs "<Gates of Hell folder>" which set/registry.reg names the pak that supplies that file. Under the Gates of Hell button the Editor reads the game the same way.

The log reads differently there. Each line starts with the time, [hh:mm:ss] . Instead of a size line per pak, game.log writes Mount package <file> with <n> entries for each pak it mounts, and Scanning mods in and Found N available mods when it looks for mods. Whether a line like Repository: N resources is written is not mapped.

8. Packing for release

While you develop, loose files are fine. For release, the usual pak layout is one pak per area, placed in the mod's resource/ folder:

Pak in the modHolds
resource/gamelogic.pakset/, properties/, script/
resource/entity.pakentity/
resource/interface.pakinterface/
resource/texture.paktexture/
resource/sound.paksound/
resource/map.pakmap/

In the window, the Share page's step "Package for friends" shows the plan first and writes the package after you confirm it. On the command line, ARSENAL packer <mod folder> --dry plans these paks from your loose files and checks them, writing nothing, and ARSENAL packer <mod folder> --out <folder> writes them. ARSENAL build <mod folder> runs every check first and packs only when the checks are clean (chapter 20).

If you use a version control system such as git, keep the loose text sources in it, ignore the finished .pak files and big binaries, and tell git not to convert line endings (* -text in .gitattributes and core.autocrlf=false) so that CRLF line endings and the old comment bytes in copied files stay byte-identical. Git does not hold your paks, so copy a pak aside before you overwrite it.

Remove any leftover loose copy of a file after you pack it. If you do not, the loose copy may be the one the game loads, and you will "fix" the pak without seeing any change.

In Gates of Hell

The same one-pak-per-area layout works, as long as every pak sits inside the mod's resource/ folder; a pak in the mod root is not read. Texts go to localizations/<language code>/, not into a localization.pak. Write real CRC values, or the log fills with no crc warnings. When you bring a unit from Gates of Hell into an AS2 mod, ARSENAL's packer refuses that mod while it still holds the files it copied from Gates of Hell, because Gates of Hell files must never be published (Make a unit from Gates of Hell). The Share page is not shown under the Gates of Hell button. For a Gates of Hell release use the game's own Workshop program (chapter 3), and see chapter 20 for the checks before a release.

Gates of Hell: summary

The Gates of Hell notes in this book have not been tested in a running game. Check them in your own game before you depend on them.

SectionGates of HellIn a few words
1. One index, last one winsdiffersSame rule; names from data files normalized; 1023-byte cap on non-ASCII names
2. Paks are zip filesdiffersWarning for a missing CRC; other file kinds kept in memory; a bad entry stops the game
3. Loose filesdiffersLoose file of 2 GB or more stops the game; skipped extensions not mapped
4. The mount order inside one moddiffersOnly resource/, patches and localizations/; language files laid over resource/
5. Patches: N.pat and .patchsame as far as mappedN.pat files are mounted as here

8. Packing for releasediffersPaks inside resource/, texts in localizations/; the game's own Workshop program

Pitfalls

  • Wrong pak root. An entry stored as -vehicle/x in a mod entity.pak does not replace entity/-vehicle/x. It adds a new, unused path.
  • Extra top-level folder in the zip. Zip the contents, not the folder that holds them.
  • The same path loose and packed. Which copy wins depends on name order in the folder; ship each path once.
  • Loose .patch. It is never read. Use a .pat.
  • Gaps in the patch numbers. Counting stops at the first missing number.
  • A .pat without a .patch, or with the wrong id. The game stops at mount.
  • Delete without replacement. The game stops with File not found - resource/... when something asks for the file.
  • Skipped extensions. Loose .txt, .org and similar files are not indexed.
  • A leftover loose copy. It can beat a freshly repacked pak.
  • Encoding. Zip tools and editors can change encoding or line endings. Keep CRLF line endings; string values are UTF-8 in data and .lng files alike; leave old cp1251 bytes inside vanilla comments as they are.

Next

Chapter 5 teaches the data language that nearly every file in this guide is written in. Terms such as "virtual path" are collected in 22-glossary.md.

Chapter 5: The SDL Data Language

Nearly every data file in the game, from a rifle to a menu page to mod.info, is written in one small language, here called SDL. It has very few rules, but the rules are strict, and the game reacts to a mistake in one of two very different ways: it stops with an error, or it quietly ignores your line. Learning which mistakes do which saves hours.

The short way to find and fix such mistakes is Check a mod, fix what the check finds, read the game log. This chapter explains the language those checks are about.

Encoding reminder. Data files use CRLF line endings. The 64-bit build reads every string value as UTF-8, in data files and .lng localization files alike; identifiers and keywords must be plain ASCII. Original data is ASCII outside ; comments, where some old cp1251 bytes remain; the game skips comments, so leave those bytes alone. An editor that silently converts the encoding or the line endings when you save can damage a file without any visible change. Check both after every save. Never save a data file as UTF-16, because the game refuses it outright.

What you will learn

  • How blocks, keys and values fit together.
  • How strings, comments, numbers and escapes work.
  • The difference between whole numbers and decimals, which is the most common cause of fatal errors.
  • How include, define and macros work.
  • What the game does with unknown keys, repeated keys and disabled blocks.
  • Which mistakes are fatal, which are silent, and how to check a file before you start the game.

1. Blocks, keys and values

An SDL file is made of blocks. A block starts with {, has a name (the key) and some content, and ends with }. The content is one or more values and further blocks.

{rifle_stats
    {damage 12}
    {name "Example Rifle"}
    {sights
        {zoom 1.5}
        {range 400}
    }
}

Here rifle_stats is the file's outer block, damage holds the whole number 12, name holds a string, and sights holds two child blocks. (This example only shows the shape; it is not a real game file.) Which keys are valid is decided by whatever reads the file, not by the language. The language only decides what is well formed.

A few details that surprise newcomers:

  • Whitespace and line breaks are free. {damage 12} and a version split over three lines mean the same.
  • The equals sign is whitespace. {damage = 12} is read as {damage 12}, and a stray = anywhere is simply ignored. Do not rely on it for readability, because some tools and humans will take it for something more.
  • Block names are not always words. Some files name an item with a string, such as {"example_unit" {cost 5}}.
  • Order often matters. The reader processes the file from top to bottom. Never sort blocks or keys alphabetically, and do not reorder lists of event handlers.

2. Comments

A semicolon starts a comment that runs to the end of the line:

{damage 12}   ; the old value was 10

This is the only comment form. A hash sign is not a comment; outside a string it is an invalid character. A semicolon inside a quoted string is just text. To remove a whole block from a file, put ; at the start of every line, because the other trick ({##, section 8) does not always remove it.

3. Words, strings and numbers

Words. An unquoted word starts with a letter or an underscore and may contain letters, digits and underscores. It ends at any other character. This is crucial: foo-bar is not one word. It is foo, a minus sign, and bar. A path such as set/stuff/x.inc is therefore not a word, and must be written as a string. Keep words plain ASCII: the bytes of a UTF-8 letter such as é or ж are not valid outside strings and comments, and they stop the reader.

Strings. Text in double quotes. A backslash always takes the next character with it, so \" does not end the string. A string may not contain a bare line break. The following escapes are decoded after reading:

WrittenBecomes
\\a single backslash
\"a double quote
\na line feed
\ra carriage return
\ta tab

Any other backslash is kept as it is, so "a\b" stays as written. There is a trap: the replacements are done one after another over the whole string, so "\\n" (which you meant as a backslash followed by n) first becomes \n and then becomes a line feed. Avoid a backslash directly before n, r, t or " unless you mean the escape.

Numbers. A whole number is digits with an optional sign, such as 12 or -3. A decimal number has a dot, such as 1.5, 0.25 or 5., and may have an exponent, such as 1e5. Note the exceptions:

  • A number must start with a digit. .5 and -.5 are not valid; write 0.5.
  • There is no suffix such as f. 1.5f is the number 1.5 followed by the word f.
  • Hexadecimal is written 0x1F and counts as a whole number. A negative hex number such as -0x10 cannot be read as one number, so avoid it.
  • A number glued to letters splits: 5abc is the number 5 followed by the word abc.

Characters that are not valid. A character such as #, ., [, < or : where a new item should start stops the reader with an error, and -, ., / and : end a word. Put such text in quotes.

In Gates of Hell

Words, strings and escapes follow the same rules. Whole numbers are 64-bit there, so a value beyond the 32-bit range is not wrapped, and a hex number keeps its hex form when the game writes it back. Numbers read from text, such as a console value or a number inside a string, follow other rules: a leading 0 means octal, so "010" is 8 and "08" is 0, and text that is not a number reads as 0. Which data fields read their numbers that way is not confirmed, so do not pad numbers with zeros in a file meant for both games.

4. Whole numbers versus decimals

This single rule causes more fatal errors than any other.

  • A field that wants a whole number accepts only a whole number. 5.0 is rejected, and so is the result of arithmetic such as (+ 100 20).
  • A field that wants a decimal number accepts both. 5 and 5.0 and (+ 100 20) all work.

When a field rejects a number, the game stops with an error that reads Integer expected!. When you are not sure which kind a field needs, copy the way the original files write it: if the original says {charge 5}, write 5; if it says {cost 5.5}, a decimal is fine. The Part III reference pages give the type of each key, for example Reference 2: entity definitions.

In multiplayer unit entries, for instance, the keys charge, level, order and icon take whole numbers, while cp, cost, score, fore and cw take decimals. So {charge 5.0} is fatal and {cost 5.0} is fine (unconfirmed in play for each of these keys).

Other value kinds you will meet:

KindHow it is written
True or false{flag 1}, {flag 0}, or the words true and false. A key written with no value, such as {flag}, means true
Names (enum)A bare word or a string, compared without regard to case. An unknown name is silently treated as "none"
PositionTwo or three numbers: {pos 10 20 0.5}
ColourA name such as red, a hex code such as FF8800 (exactly six or eight digits), or three or four decimal numbers in a string "255 128 0"
RangeEither a string "min max", or one or two bare numbers meaning a centre and a spread. The two forms mean different things, so copy the form the original uses
TimeA number of seconds in most fields. A few fields (mainly in game rules) take whole milliseconds instead
Tag listOne string of words separated by spaces, or several strings (each string is then one tag). A word starting with - removes that tag. An initial clear empties the list first. Reading a tag list again adds to it

Be careful with true-or-false: the word no, the word off and the string "false" can all be read as true. Use 0 and 1. Giving a field more values than it reads produces a warning, not a stop.

In Gates of Hell

Two value kinds behave differently:

  • Whole numbers out of range. A whole-number field given a value below -2147483648 or above 4294967295 stops the game with Integer expected!. AS2 takes such a value without a message and wraps it, so a value that loads here can be fatal there.
  • Colours. A hex colour may start with 0x before its six or eight digits. A colour that cannot be read is no longer fatal: the game writes Incorrect color definition: <text> to the log and uses opaque black. A string with spaces is read as decimal r g b or r g b a.

5. Includes

An include pulls another file's text in at that point:

(include "/properties/tank.ext")
(include "common.inc")

Round brackets mark a "control list", a directive for the reader instead of data. The path is a string. A path with a leading slash counts from the resource level and applies the mod overlay (chapter 2). A path without a leading slash is counted from the folder of the file that contains the include, and each ../ climbs one folder. Capital letters and slash direction do not matter. If the file does not exist, the game stops with a fatal error. There is no protection against a file that includes itself, directly or through other files: the reader keeps opening it until the game dies, so check your includes. The reference entries include of a template and path forms give the details.

An include can pass parameters, which section 7 explains.

6. Define and macros

A define gives a name to a piece of text:

(define "my_hit"
    {damage 12}
    {penetration 3}
)

A macro call then uses it, with the name in quotes inside round brackets:

{weapon
    ("my_hit")
}

When the game meets the call, it replaces it with the stored text, as if you had pasted it there. Facts to remember:

  • A define must appear before it is used, in the same top-level file or in a file that file included. It is not visible in a sibling file.
  • Names are exact: "Armor" and "armor" are two different names.
  • Defining the same name again replaces the earlier text silently; the last one wins.
  • The stored text is not checked when you define it. A mistake inside it shows up where the macro is used. Also, if you edit a define, you change every place that uses it.
  • A missing name stops the game with define not found.
  • A macro may call another macro. There is no guard against a macro that calls itself.

7. Macro parameters

A macro can take parameters. In the body, write a placeholder with a percent sign. In the call, supply the value:

(define "unit_cost"
    {cost %price}
    {cp %points}
)

{"example_unit"
    ("unit_cost" price(250) points(8))
}

Rules for named parameters:

  • Write price(250) with no space between the name and the bracket. price (250) is an error ('(' required).
  • A value runs to the first closing bracket, so it cannot itself contain a ). It may contain spaces, quotes and (.
  • Replacement is done on the raw text, before the text is read, so it also affects text inside strings and comments. Placeholders with longer names are replaced first (%cp before %c). Capitals matter, so %C and %c are different.
  • An unreplaced placeholder such as %price stays in the text and then produces a confusing error or a silently ignored key, so check your spelling.
  • There are no default values. Each call must supply every parameter that the body uses.

There is also a positional form: ("name" args 1 "two" 3.5). The word args must be written in lower case. The values fill the placeholders %0, %1, %2 in order.

A file can receive parameters as well. (include "file.inc" size(3)) replaces %size throughout the text of that file.

8. Conditions, arithmetic and disabled blocks

Conditions on game mode. A mod control list includes its content only when a named condition is on:

(mod "mp"
    {max_players 8}
)
(mod not "mp"
    {max_players 1}
)

The names the engine supplies include mp and coop for multiplayer, game:<map> while a mission loads, and dl_<difficulty> for scene files. Names are case-sensitive. Nesting one mod inside another stops the game with Nested mods not supported.

Arithmetic. (+ 1 2 3), (- 10 4), (* 2 3) and (/ 9 3) calculate left to right with decimals. Division by zero is not checked. The result counts as a decimal, so it works only where a decimal is accepted (section 4). Arithmetic inside arithmetic is read correctly by plain decimal fields; in other places it can be misread (unconfirmed), so compute the number yourself and write it in when you can.

Disabled blocks. If the name of a block is written with an extra #, as in {## old_unit ...}, the block is "disabled". Readers of plain scripts skip it entirely. The loaders for the registered game data (section 9) read it but mark the item disabled, and whether a disabled unit is still buyable in play is not known (unconfirmed). If you want a block really gone, remove it or comment out every line with ;. Two traps: a # glued to the name ({#old ...}) swallows the name into a tag, which is almost always a mistake, and a single # followed by a space ({# old ...}) is just an ordinary block.

In Gates of Hell

A mission in Gates of Hell sees more condition names than mp, coop and game:<map>: gametype:<type>, gameclass:<class> and training. They stay on for the whole match, not only while it loads, so a (mod "gametype:...") list in a mission file works there and does nothing here. The game's own data also tests hardcore; when that one is on is not confirmed. Disabled blocks ({##) appear in its data as well.

9. How the game reads keys
