  • More weapon kinds. Two more weapon mode tags pick their own pose sets: bolt_action and shortsmg. A rifle lying down uses pose_lie_rifle and lie_fire_rifle. Some standing and crouching long-gun poses of the 64-bit game are gone.
  • New stances and walks. There are new stance states and new walking animations, and a rifleman can fire while walking. Firing on the move uses shoot_walking_manual (under direct control) or shoot_walking_ai. Lying down there are more states, and a lying soldier treats himself with lie_self-treatment_* animations.
  • Variants. When an animation folder holds several variants, one is picked at random each time.
  • Throws are marked at 5, 10 and 20 m and the matching throw animation is used.
  • Removed. Drowning in swamps, smoking and the finger poses are gone.
  • Height steps. A dive, fall or thrown landing may cross a height step of about 4 m; the 64-bit game allows 0.3 m.
  • Firing rules. A stance tagged no-fire blocks firing, and firing in a move stance needs the item tag shoot_walking or direct control. A rocketlauncher fires only from its aiming pose.
  • Direct control. When a soldier under direct control moves, his reload, bolt and treatment animations run to their end at once, so their end events still happen.
  • Prone paths. A lying soldier finds his path with the human_prone profile if set/pather.set has one; without it nothing changes.
  • Idle. An entity effect named select_idle can choose the idle animation. Without it, only a standing soldier plays idle animations.

5. Abilities, weapon skill and veterancy

Abilities, also called perks, are defined in the files of the set/ability folder. A leveled ability lists named levels with a multiplier each, for example {level "150%" 1.5} in the health ability. A breed then picks one level in its perks:

{"health" "150%"}

Vanilla health levels run from 20% to 1000%. If a breed names a level that the ability does not have, the game logs only invalid level param "x" and quietly gives the top level. That is a silent buff of up to ten times the health, so check your spelling. Some perks take a plain number instead of a level: speed, tank, vehicle and cannon ({"speed" 0.9} makes a soldier 10 percent slower). The perk weapon_reload is read by nothing; to shorten reloads, use the veterancy key of the same name.

Weapon skill is an ability made from weapon that changes accuracy by posture and level. This is the pattern of the vanilla machine-gun skill:

{"mgun" from weapon
  {item "mgun"}
  {level "lvl_1"
    {stand {accuracy 0.25}}
    {squat {accuracy 0.50}}
    {crawl {accuracy 1.25}}
    {cover {accuracy 1.50}}
    {vehicle {accuracy 2.00}}}}

The skill works only while the item in the soldier's right hand has all the tags in item. The game picks the posture block (cover in cover, vehicle aboard a vehicle, crawl lying, squat crouching, stand otherwise); a {default} block fills all five at once. accuracy multiplies the hit rate and narrows the spread of shots; 1.0 is neutral. Vanilla data also carries an aim_range value in posture blocks, but nothing reads it.

Veterancy gives ranks. A breed's veterancy block sets the experience needed for each rank; vanilla breeds include one shared file whose thresholds for ranks 1 to 5 are 4, 8, 24, 48 and 80, and 2, 4, 12, 24 and 40 inside its multiplayer (mod "mp" ...) block. What each rank gives is set in set/ability/veterancy.set: ranks 1 to 5 add 0.15 to 0.35 to health, save 0.10 to 0.30 of reload time, and add 0, 0, 1, 1 and 2 steps to weapon skill. Only the highest rank reached applies; ranks do not add up.

In Gates of Hell

  • Weapon skill reads five numbers. A posture block takes accuracy, aim_range, recoil, zoom_recoil (while aiming down the sights) and sway, each 1 by default, and {default} copies all five to every posture. The skill then sets how much a hand weapon kicks and swings. The 64-bit game reads only accuracy and aim_range.
  • Crew skill on vehicle guns. A vehicle gun takes the best recoil and the smallest sway among the crew in its worker seats who have the matching skill.
  • New abilities. weapon_sway_control (one plain number that scales sway), Medic ({rate vet}, see section 3), Personage, Fortification, Mechanic (repair speed), Barricade and Resources. The 64-bit game has no data for them, so these perks do nothing there.
  • Veterancy has ranks 0 to 8; the 64-bit game cuts anything above 5 down to 5. On every spawn the rank is worked out again from the veterancy abilities, so a spawned soldier's rank follows his perks, not a saved score.
  • Special attack works even when the weapon is empty.
  • Kill score from a vehicle is shared among the men in the crew group's worker seats. The 64-bit game gives it by seat role name (driver, gunner, commander, loader), so with other seat names experience can go to the wrong men.

6. Breeds

A breed is a soldier template: one file under set/breed/ (multiplayer breeds are in set/breed/mp/<army>/) that gives the soldier his skin, portrait, armour, perks, veterancy and starting kit. This is the pattern of a vanilla multiplayer breed, shortened:

{breed
  {skin "ger_t2"}
  {portrait "ger_soldier2"}
  {nationality ger}
  {armors {head helmet1_ger}}
  {perks
    {"health" "150%"}
    {"speed" 0.9}
    {"rifle" lvl_3}
    {"mgun" lvl_1}}
  {veterancy
    (include "veterancy_generic.inc")
    ("veterancy_1")}
  {inventory
    {item "mp40" filled}
    {item "ammo pistol" 500}
    {item "bandage" 3}
    {in_hands 0}}}

In the inventory, each item adds stuff carrying all the given tags, with an optional count; {in_hands 0} puts the first item into his hands. Items that do not fit into his box are dropped silently, so a full box loses the last items in the list. Be careful with filled N: plain filled loads a weapon to its own capacity, but filled N also rewrites the capacity of that item for every soldier who carries it, not just this breed. Breed tags are labels for scripts and the interface; the only one the game itself acts on is kamikaze.

In Gates of Hell

A Gates of Hell breed can have two more keys: no_inventory (after hero; the soldier gets an empty box but still wears his armour) and field_icon (between portrait and icon, a picture for the interface). The 64-bit game stops on both as unknown keys, so take them out when you port a breed. Gates of Hell ranks go up to 8 (section 5).

7. Inventory and reload

A soldier's inventory is set up by the inventory extender in properties/human.ext:

{extender "inventory"
  {box {Size 6 10} {Weight 100}}
  {hand_left}
  {hand_right}
  {armor "head" {mask "head"} {bone "head"} {volumes "head"} {pierceAbsorb 30}}
  ...}

The box is a grid of cells, 6 by 10 for vanilla soldiers. Its Weight is the weight one cell can hold, not a limit on the total a soldier carries. Items take cells by their size. Stacking (several of one item in a cell, such as rounds of ammunition) works only for stuff tagged stackable; how many fit in one cell follows from the cell weight and the item's weight (unconfirmed). Besides the box, the holders are hand_right, hand_left, weapon and armor. An armor holder protects the hit volumes it names while an armour item, such as a helmet, sits in it; its pierceAbsorb (30 mm for the head, 32 mm for the body in vanilla) is how much a bullet must penetrate before it hurts the soldier (chapter 9 shows where this applies).

Reloading works on tags. A gun asks for ammunition whose tags contain the gun's filling tags (filling "ammo rifle" accepts an item tagged ammo rifle ...), and the soldier searches his own inventory first, then his squad mates'. Different filling tags never share ammunition. This is why careful tagging (chapter 6) matters: a wrong tag leaves a gun that cannot find its magazines. Reload time is the weapon's reload time less the veterancy weapon_reload bonus.

In Gates of Hell

  • Weapon list. The list of weapons a soldier can switch to holds one entry for each item in his hands and his pack. Throwables are the items tagged throwable; the 64-bit game takes any of grenade, knife, mine, dynamite, matchbox and plant. An item tagged only knife or mine drops out of the list in Gates of Hell. The same list drives the next-weapon and number keys under direct control.
  • Search order. A search by tags (a weapon to take, a grenade to throw, a mine to lay, ammunition) walks the box in the order the items were put in; the 64-bit game walks the cells row by row. With two matching items the games may pick different ones.
  • Spent launchers (one-shot rocketlauncher items) are dropped to the ground, not packed, and the soldier then takes any other weapon.
  • Preloaded guns start with a full reserve: a weapon is filled to the second number of its Filling, not one magazine.
  • Bad items. A box item whose entity cannot be found is skipped and logged instead of crashing the load. An item saved without filling reloads the right ammunition kind.
  • Stacks made by a script can be kept apart with the stack flag of the script's inventory add command.
  • Mine detectors find mines within 10 m (the 64-bit game: 5 m).

8. Crew and seats

Soldiers crew vehicles through seats: the placer block lists the seats and the boarder block the doors and boarding animations (see Reference 3 and chapter 6). A soldier takes the first free seat whose role name begins with the role he is sent to, so a "gunner" can take the seat gunner2. Seats can be grouped so that a function needs all its crew, for example a gunner and a loader. Boarding may need the vehicle to be standing still (unconfirmed). When the whole crew is ordered out at once, the vehicle stops aiming and its crew cannot be given new orders until they are out. Seated soldiers keep their health and stamina, and a dead crew member stays in his seat.

In Gates of Hell

  • Hatches. A seat can be Sealable. When its hatch closes, the man moves to a free inside seat of the same group, or stays hidden without the seat's view; when it opens he comes back. The 64-bit game rejects the key.
  • Broken seats in data or saves are ignored; a seat is broken only while its link bone is missing.
  • minworkers N on a seat group lets it work with N of its seats manned (by default all of them), so a gun with minworkers 2 and three seats keeps firing with two men. Empty seats pull a man from a free seat while the group is short.
  • Doors. A vehicle seat is left only through doors linked to it, and a door is refused as blocked less often.
  • Reservations on a seat that can no longer be taken are released, so the seat does not stay blocked for everyone.
  • Crew survive when the vehicle they sit in is removed.
  • Kill score goes to the crew group (section 5).

9. Changing soldiers and squads in the ARSENAL window

  • The Units page finds a squad or a soldier by name or id and shows its price, rank and crew in plain words. Its recipe "Bigger squad" sets how many soldiers of one type come in a squad; the price does not change by itself, so set it in "Quick change". "Add a unit (copy)" copies a squad into your mod under a new id.
  • "Describe a new unit", on the same page, can also start from a squad. A squad has no speed, armour or gun of its own there, so those words are left out; change the soldiers' breeds and weapons instead.
  • The Units page does not change a soldier's health. Change it in the breed's perks by hand, as below, or use the Quick Guided Task.
  • The Quick Guided Task has recipes for both. The soldier recipe asks, one question at a time, for the breed name, skin, armour, nationality, portrait, icon, voice, the inventory items, the health, stamina and speed perks, the tank, vehicle and cannon perks, veterancy, vision and the other perk values, and the squad the soldier joins. The squad recipe asks for the name, cost, members, charge, group, button, level, icon and bot settings. The Units page also offers a "Longer rifle range" recipe. See Use the Quick Guided Task and the Units and Balance pages.

See also: Humans reference, troubleshooting units that do not move or fire.

In Gates of Hell

The Units page and the Quick Guided Task recipes write 64-bit game data only. For Gates of Hell soldiers, ARSENAL can bring a unit across with goh unit, which ports vehicles; breeds and squads are moved by hand, taking out the keys named in sections 5 and 6. See the Gates of Hell tools.

10. Changes by hand: examples

Tougher conscripts. In your copy of the breed, raise the health perk:

{perks {"health" "200%"}}

200% is a level that exists in the vanilla health ability. A made-up level such as 130% silently gives the top level.

Faster recovery. Raise inc in the Health block. This changes every soldier if you edit properties/human.ext; to change one breed, raise its health_regeneration perk level instead. It does not stop a scripted drain.

Tired soldiers stop running sooner. In movement_limits, raise the numbers of the Fast row, for example {Fast 10 40}: running then starts at stamina 40 and stops below 10.

A leader whose kills inspire. Morale rules are fixed in the game, so you cannot change the +10 from data; use an interaction script if you need a bonus.

11. Checking your work

ARSENAL humlint <mod folder> --game <game folder>
ARSENAL keylint <mod folder>

humlint reads human definitions, breeds and abilities, and reports unknown keys in the vitality block, misspelt stamina rows, in_hands past the end of the list, filled N that changes other breeds, the inert weapon_reload perk and similar mistakes. keylint reports a perk level that the ability does not declare. Then look at the soldier in game, and read game.log for invalid level param and Unknown ability lines (chapter 18).

Gates of Hell: summary

The Gates of Hell notes in this book have not been tested in a running game. Check them in your own game before you depend on them.

SectionGates of HellIn a few words
1. The human entitydifferssoldier told by entity kind, not tags; least recognise time
2. Health, stamina and deathdiffersdamage by body part; heroes knocked out first; flash on a timer
3. Morale and self-healingdifferssame healing figures; medics heal others; morale not compared
4. Stances and animationdiffersmore weapon kinds and stances; new animation names; random variants
5. Abilities, weapon skill and veterancydiffersrecoil and sway skill; new abilities; ranks up to 8
6. Breedsdiffersno_inventory and field_icon keys
7. Inventory and reloaddiffersthrowable tag; search order; full reserve; 10 m mine detector
8. Crew and seatsdiffershatches; minworkers; own doors; crew survive
9. Changing soldiers and squads in the ARSENAL windowdiffersthe pages write 64-bit game data only
10. Changes by hand: examplesnot mapped
11. Checking your worknot mapped

Gates of Hell also has direct control and third person for soldiers, below.

Direct control and third person

In Gates of Hell the player can steer one soldier himself. There are two modes: direct control (he aims and fires with the mouse) and third person (the camera follows behind him). The key manual_mode_toggle switches between them. The 64-bit game has neither mode, and a Gates of Hell save loses its manual control when loaded there.

The camera and the rules of control come from set/tp_control.set, with the root third_person_control and the groups disabled, vehicle and human. Each entry names unit tags, can inherit another entry, and holds a clip block and camera level blocks with a maxlevel. A unit with no matching entry cannot be taken. The file's own checks log lines such as "Distance can not be greater than that for previous level", "Third Person Control entry redefinition" and "Unknown keyword". A level that names a linkbone the model does not have refuses control with "Could not find bone ... in entity ...". In multiplayer every machine looks the entry up for itself, so the file must be the same on all of them. A weapon's ThirdPersonParams block probably adds camera values for that weapon.

Under direct control:

  • More keys: squadmember1 to squadmember10, toggle_crouch, toggle_prone, special_action, next_weapon and weapon1 to weapon8. The weapon keys follow the weapon list of section 7.
  • A gun fires only at a target in range and not inside its MinRange, and not while the soldier sprints or crawls (chapter 9).
  • Firing on the move needs the tag shoot_walking_manual on the weapon; a stance tagged no-aim stops aiming.
  • Recoil and sway come from the weapon and the soldier's skill (section 5). AutoReload and ClickSound belong here too.
  • Hits from a soldier under direct control use the DamageTPC lines of the target's vitality.

Pitfalls

  • Health reaching zero does not kill by itself; a script fires {die}.
  • Bleeding has no drain of its own; it is a marker only.
  • There is no suppression system.
  • A perk level name that the ability does not have gives the top level, with only a log line.
  • The weapon_reload perk does nothing; the veterancy key of the same name works.
  • Only the highest veterancy rank applies.
  • A breed's filled N changes the capacity of that item for everyone.
  • Box Weight is a weight per cell, not a carry limit. Items that do not fit are dropped silently.
  • Stacking needs the stackable tag.
  • Most animation names are fixed in compiled code; data cannot add new kinds of motion.
  • Shared files such as human.ext change every soldier when edited.

Next: Weapons, ammo and damage.

Chapter 9: Weapons, Ammo and Damage

This is the longest technical chapter, because damage in Men of War is made of several small systems that work together: a weapon decides how a shell flies, the shell meets armour, the armour decides whether it passes, and then explosions, fire and ammunition add their own effects. We take them in the order a shell experiences them. Terms are explained as they appear and collected in the glossary.

The short ways are on Change a gun or its ammunition and Change armour and see the result. The full facts for every key are in Reference 6: Weapons and ammunition and Reference 7: Armour, volumes and damage.

What you will learn

  • The keys of a weapon and of its per-ammunition blocks.
  • How spread, accuracy and flight work.
  • How penetration is decided, step by step, with a worked example.
  • How effective armour thickness, threshold and durability work.
  • When a shell ricochets, and how blast, fragments, fire and cook-off work.
  • How damage to infantry differs from damage to vehicles.
  • How to see and test armour in the ARSENAL window, tune with worked examples, and check your work.

Work in your own mod folder, not in the game folder. Text files use CRLF line endings; the 64-bit build reads every string value as UTF-8, in data files and .lng files alike, and identifiers must be plain ASCII. Original data is ASCII outside ; comments, where some old cp1251 bytes remain; leave them as they are. Paks are zip files. Editors may silently change encoding or line endings when you save. For first principles about armour areas and volumes, read chapter 6 first. Soldiers are covered in chapter 8.

1. Weapon keys

A weapon is a stuff file under set/stuff/ (see chapter 6); a vehicle gun is a weapon_bullet that usually starts from "pattern gun". On a vehicle, weapons sit in a weaponry block made of places. This is the pattern of a vanilla tank:

{Weaponry
  {place "gun"
    {weapon "76mm_zis5" filling "ammo bullet76 ap" 1}}
  {place "mgun1"
    {type "mgun_rear"}
    {weapon "dt" filled}
    {gunner "commander"}
    {charger "commander"}}}

filling "ammo bullet76 ap" 1 means: load one round of whatever stuff has all of those tags. {weapon "dt" filled} means a full magazine. The first place in the block is the basic one. gunner and charger name the crew seats that aim and reload a place (gunner and charger by default); without that crew the place cannot be used. StationaryFiring lets a place fire only while the unit stands still. Two weapons in one place log HolderWeapon: set user ... ignored and the second is not used.

The weapon's own stuff file holds its behaviour. The keys you will touch most:

KeyMeaning
rechargeTimeSeconds to reload the magazine; for a gun that holds one shell, the time to load the next. Vehicle crews and soldiers' veterancy change it.
recoveryTimeSeconds of pause after each shot, such as a bolt cycle.
rangeTwo numbers in metres: the aim range and the longest range.
speedHow fast the projectile flies. Vanilla gun presets write half the number given to their speed macro.
gravityA multiplier on world gravity (1 when absent). Ignored for rockets.
reactiveSet for a rocket: no gravity, a slight wobble.
AimingToleranceDegrees the barrel may be off target and still fire (10 when absent; vanilla guns use 2).
calibreMillimetres, used by the overmatch rule in section 5.

The first value of range (the aim range) is more important than its name suggests. It is the distance at which the unit opens fire on its own, the scale for the damage curve and the spread function, and a guide for the AI. A longest range with no number means unlimited. Vanilla guns take their ranges from presets such as range_maximum ({range 140 150}, with shorter ranges for high explosive and APCR shells). The game reads fireSound and reloadSound as folder-style names, for example gun/85to100_cal/100mm_d10c; a wrong name gives silence, not an error.

AccuracyByMotion, written in a weapon place (vanilla tanks get it from a preset), makes accuracy worse while the unit moves or turns. It takes a speed in km/h and a factor for driving, and a turning speed in degrees per second and a factor for turning. Each factor must be at most 1; a larger one logs Accuracy must be <= 1. The live value is 1 when the unit is still and falls towards your factor as it moves; spread is divided by that value, so a lower factor means wider spread. A weapon's SpreadTolerance is compared with it, so a weapon with a tolerance may hold fire while it moves (unconfirmed).

In Gates of Hell

Gates of Hell reads more weapon keys. The 64-bit game knows none of them and stops on them with unexpected token, so a weapon brought from Gates of Hell must lose them (see Bring a unit from Gates of Hell).

KeyWhat it does in Gates of Hell
FireSoundCloseA shot sound for your own unit under direct control or in the inner view. It must have the same signal and radius as fireSound, or a warning is logged and the plain sound plays.
ClickSoundThe dry click when the weapon is empty or reloading, under direct control only.
AutoReloadOn by default. Off: a soldier under direct control does not reload by himself. The computer always reloads.
FiringTimeoutSeconds the computer waits after a shot, written value or value +-dev.
AccuracyByMotionKScales the motion penalty of AccuracyByMotion: the spread is divided by ((motion value - 1) times K + 1). 1 by default; 0 removes the penalty.
SyncedProjectilesIn a multiplayer game the server alone flies the round and the players' copies only show it.
Recoil, SwayParams, special swayThe aim kick after each shot and the slow wander of the aim under direct control.

from copies all of these. A weapon place also reads AimBone (a second bone that aims, while the shot still leaves from the foresight) and AI_In_Manual, and the weaponry block reads ManualAccuracyZoom, TpcInstantAiming, AnimatedAiming and UseLookatAiming. SequentialAim is off by default in Gates of Hell and on by default in the 64-bit game, so check how the places of a ported unit take turns to aim. Direct control itself is in chapter 8.

2. Ammunition and per-ammunition blocks

Ammunition is bullet stuff. Vanilla shells are files such as set/stuff/shell/bullet75.fg.ammo that start from "pattern fg" or from "pattern ap". The pattern gives the tag line (ammo shell fg), and the shell adds its own tags, size and a damage list of effects that happen when it explodes.

A weapon can behave differently for each kind of ammunition through parameters blocks. Vanilla guns use them for range and spread, and for a separate damage table for APCR shot (armour piercing with a hard core):

{projectileDamage 171}
("damage2" a(171) b(154) c(134) d(117) e(103))
{parameters "apcr"
  ("damage2" a(196) b(174) c(149) d(127) e(108))}

A parameters block applies when the loaded ammunition's tags contain all of the block's tags. The first matching block in file order wins. If none matches, the weapon's top-level values are used, without an error. The matching is by whole tag word: apc does not match apcbc. Two blocks with the same tags merge. A top-level key written after a parameters block also overwrites that key in every block that still had the default value, so put top-level keys first.

Only some keys may be set per ammunition: rechargeTime, recoveryTime, aimRange, maxRange, range, gravity, speed, spreading, curve, the cursor and crosshair keys, TraceFreq, bullet_view, the damage keys (projectileDamage, projectileDamageClip, projectileDamageThreshold, projectileDamageTable, healthDamage, healthDamageClip) and the ricochet keys (RicochetDamageClip, RicochetEnergyDamping, OvermatchDamping). Other keys written inside a parameters block, such as calibre, aimType, burst, DisableRicochet and ZeroingAccuracy, apply to the whole weapon, not just that ammunition. This is easy to miss.

Note that the penetration numbers (projectileDamage, projectileDamageTable, projectileDamageThreshold) belong to the weapon file, not to the ammunition file. The ammunition file has its own keys:

  • detonationThickness makes the round explode when a plate takes at least that many millimetres out of it. Without it the round never explodes on armour. Vanilla high explosive shells use 2, so any real plate or wall sets them off; rockets use 1. A round stopped this way sends no pierce event.
  • applyProjectile lets an exploding round also deal its penetrating hit (vanilla rockets use it).
  • cumulative is how far, in metres, the jet of a HEAT round (high explosive anti-tank, a shaped charge) reaches past the point of impact.
  • trace and view describe the tracer and the round seen in flight.

The weapon's calibre is worked out from its filling tag: a gun with {filling "bullet100"} has calibre 100. A weapon whose filling tag has another shape must set calibre itself, or the overmatch rule in section 5 uses the wrong number.

aimType chooses how the gun solves a shot: direct aims flat, curved lobs a shell like a mortar, and adaptive picks between the two like a howitzer. Any other word logs Unknown aim type. burst sets how many rounds a trigger pull fires (min), the burst lengths the AI uses (short, long), and whether the weapon fires without locking its aim (noaiming).

In Gates of Hell

A parameters block in Gates of Hell takes more keys, and a value written at the weapon's top level reaches every block that does not set its own:

  • MinRange (metres): the weapon fires only at targets at least that far away.
  • UnlimitedRangeTPC (on by default): under direct control the longest range does not apply; MinRange still does.
  • FiringTimeoutDistanceFactor: a table that scales the computer's pause after a shot by the distance divided by the aim range.
  • FalloffMeter and FalloffStrength (section 4), MinimumDamageModifier (the part health system in the summary), and the three overmatch tables (section 5).
  • ToplayerVignette names a screen picture for direct control; what it does is not confirmed.
  • aimType nocurve is a fourth aim type; the 64-bit game logs Unknown aim type for it.

The ammunition's tracer can differ by tag: (Trace "tag1 tag2" (Length n) (View "texture")), one look per tag. Do not name the same texture twice inside one Trace, or the rest of the block is read out of step with Block terminator expected!. The 64-bit game reads one tracer only. A dropped weapon keeps its loaded rounds in a saved mission ({Item "k98" ... 5}).

None of these keys are read by the 64-bit game; it stops on them with unexpected token. A shell brought over keeps only the keys listed in section 2. See Reference 6: Gates of Hell only.

3. Spread and accuracy

Where a round lands is a random point inside a spread circle. The circle is set by the spreading block, which takes an optional base radius and then its keys. Vanilla gun presets write it like this:

{Spreading 1
  {SpreadPower 1}}
{spreading
  {radiusTable {0 0} {50 0.33} {90 0.98} {120 1.3} {150 1.63} {250 1.95}}}
  • SpreadRadius is a base radius in metres. SpreadPower above 1 pulls more hits towards the centre. SpreadXYRatio stretches the circle along the line of fire.
  • RadiusTable is a list of {distance radius} points in metres. It beats everything else if present. Next in priority is RadiusFunction multiplied by SpreadRadius. If neither is present, the radius grows steadily with distance.
  • BurstAccuracy gives a percentage for each round in a burst; the radius is divided by it, so lower numbers make later rounds wilder.
  • ZeroingAccuracy lists factors for repeated shots from about the same spot at about the same target; the first shot is always 1, and factors below 1 tighten the spread.

Then the radius is divided by the shooter's accuracy: an aimed special shot's accuracy, or else the ManualAccuracy of the weapon block under direct control, then the motion value from AccuracyByMotion. A vehicle crew that is under strength or weak widens the result further, and a soldier's weapon skill (chapter 8) makes his shots tighter. Vanilla files wrap most of these in macros (damage2, accuracy_high, range_maximum, speed), so when you read a weapon you often find a name instead of numbers. Open the shared .presets file in the same folder to see them.

In Gates of Hell

The spread rules are the same, with two changes. A weapon with unlimited ammunition never spreads in Gates of Hell; in the 64-bit game its spread is worked out for twice the target distance or the aim range, whichever is larger. AccuracyByMotionK (section 1) can weaken or remove the motion penalty, and under direct control Recoil and SwayParams move the aim itself, on top of the spread circle.

4. Flight and hits

A round flies in small steps. At each step the game checks which entities lie on that step. Every volume whose able block allows bullets is tested, and each volume crossed gives two hits: the entry face and the exit face. All hits, including terrain, are sorted by distance and handled in order: the entry face, then the exit face of the same volume, then the next volume. The exit face is tested with its own thickness, so a round can clear the entry face and still stop inside.

Three events can reach interaction scripts (chapter 11):

  • bullet_hit happens once per entity per step, for the first volume hit, before the penetration test.
  • pierce happens only for an entry hit that passed and did not stop the round. High explosive shells never send it.
  • break_armor happens when an armour area is used up (section 6).

A failed penetration sends only bullet_hit. Scripts never see how far the round was over or under the needed penetration: a round that barely passed and one that passed with plenty to spare give the same event. That is why vanilla scripts choose their reaction from the shell's class tag (such as shell_big), not from the margin.

The side that was hit (front, side, rear, top) is stored in each face of the volume model, as chapter 6 explained; it is not worked out from the direction of the shot. The slope of the hit is worked out from the angle between the round's direction and the face: the slope factor is one divided by the cosine of that angle, never more than 10. Because the face comes from the real model triangle, your model's geometry changes the slope.

In Gates of Hell

  • Drop at long range. FalloffMeter (metres) and FalloffStrength make a round dive after it has flown that far: past the mark, its gravity grows with the square of the extra distance. With no FalloffStrength there is no extra drop, which is also how the 64-bit game behaves.
  • One hit per part per step. A part made of several volumes is hit only once per step, by its nearest volume. The 64-bit game tests every volume crossed, with an entry and an exit face each, so layered volumes of one part stop more there.
  • Distance. The damage curve is read at the hit point, not at the start of the step, so a long step gives slightly less damage than in the 64-bit game.
  • pierce happens only when the round enters a volume. A shot that starts inside a volume (point blank) sends none.
  • Own vehicle. A soldier firing from a vehicle never hits that vehicle.
  • Curved fire. A fault in the path of curved shots is fixed, so curved shells land closer to the aim point. Whether the 64-bit game has the same fault is not confirmed.
  • Multiplayer. With SyncedProjectiles (section 1) only the server's round can hit.

5. Penetration test, step by step

Here is the full path a round takes through one plate. Distances are in metres as the game counts them (the same scale as range); penetration and thickness are in millimetres of steel. The game follows the same order every time and there is no dice roll; see How penetration is worked out.

Step 1: penetration at distance. The penetration is read from the weapon's projectileDamageTable (the block that matches the ammunition, or the top-level one) at the distance flown. The table is a list of {distance penetration} points; between points the value is a straight line, and outside the first and last points it stays at that point's value. Vanilla gun tables run from 10 to 175 or 200 and end with a point at 0, so penetration falls to nothing at the end. If your table stops early on a high value, every longer shot keeps that value. If there is no table, penetration is projectileDamage times the curve named by curve (from set/ballistics.set) at the distance divided by the aim range.

That number is multiplied by the round's remaining energy, which starts at 1 and falls each time the round passes a plate or ricochets.

Step 2: thickness of the plate. The plate thickness for the side that was hit comes from the first armour area that covers the volume, if that area gives a number other than 0 for that side; otherwise from the volume's own {thickness} (chapter 6 and thickness (area)). Left and right both use the area's side value, and the bottom uses its top value.

Step 3: effective thickness. Slope makes plates thicker:

effective = ((slope - 1) * f + 1) * thickness
f = clamp( thickness / calibre * overmatchScale , 0.2 , 1.0 )

The factor f is the overmatch term. When the gun's calibre is large compared to the plate, f is small, and the slope bonus shrinks to as little as 20 percent: a big shell punches through a thin plate whatever the angle. overmatchScale comes from the gun's OvermatchDamping table by angle; the vanilla gun pattern goes up to 6 at 90 degrees. The table should reach 90 degrees, because beyond its last point the scale falls back to 1.0. Areas set to whole_wound (vanilla tracks and wheels) or ray_cast_thickness (vanilla buildings) ignore slope.

Step 4: pass test. The round passes if its penetration is at least the effective thickness. The only random parts of a hit are the spread, the ricochet chance and chances inside scripts.

Step 5: after the test. The plate takes min(effective thickness, penetration) out of the round. If that is at least the ammunition's detonationThickness, the round stops and explodes. Otherwise, after a pass, the round goes on with its energy lowered by the amount taken divided by its penetration.

Worked example. A gun with calibre 75 fires a round with penetration 100 mm at the distance of the hit. It strikes a turret plate of 80 mm at a slope factor of 1.5 (about 48 degrees off the face's normal), and the gun's OvermatchDamping gives 1.0 at that angle. Overmatch is 80 / 75 times 1.0, which is 1.07, clamped to 1.0. Effective thickness is ((1.5 - 1) times 1.0 + 1) times 80, which is 120. 100 is less than 120, so the round fails. At a flatter hit with slope 1.2, effective thickness is (0.2 times 1.0 + 1) times 80, which is 96; 100 is at least 96, so it passes. The plate takes 96 out of it, and the energy falls from 1 by 96 / 100 to 0.04, so the round has almost nothing left for anything behind the plate.

In Gates of Hell

Steps 1, 2, 4 and 5 are the same. Step 3 has more factors:

effective = overmatch * thickness * flaw * castSteel * hardness
  • Overmatch. Each ammunition block may carry one of four tables by angle, and the first one present wins: OvermatchCalibre {angle x y} gives max(1, x times (thickness / calibre) to the power y); OvermatchFixed {angle v} gives max(1, v); OvermatchSlope {angle v} gives max(1, v times the slope factor); OvermatchDamping is the rule of step 3 above, with its 0.2 to 1.0 clamp. The new three have no upper clamp: the Gates of Hell bazooka's OvermatchSlope {0 1} {60 2} {90 99} makes a grazing hit nearly impossible. Their points are kept in the order written, not sorted, so write them once and in rising angle. Angles are whole degrees.
  • Flaw. A volume's Quality word (small_flaw, medium_flaw, large_flaw) gives a factor from the angle and from thickness / calibre, never above 1. Any other word, or none, gives 1.
  • Cast steel. A volume's CastSteel cs gives min(1, cs + 0.001238 thickness - 0.0002628 calibre + 0.02706 thickness / calibre). A value of 0 or below logs Cast steel value can't be below 0!.
  • Hardness. A volume flagged HighHardness takes a factor from the calibre, thickness / calibre and a Brinell hardness by thickness from set/damage.set (vanilla: 450 up to 40 mm, 360 to 60, 340 to 80, 300 above). A thin hard plate holds well against small calibres and badly against large ones.
  • Threshold is worked out as in section 6 (two thirds of the effective thickness when nothing else is set).
  • Areas that measure thickness by casting a ray (ray_cast_thickness) start the ray just outside the volume, so their thickness can differ a little.

The 64-bit game refuses all three volume words and reads only OvermatchDamping, so a ported vehicle and its guns lose the rest. Flaw, cast steel and hardness only ever make a plate weaker, so the same plate is stronger after the port; the overmatch tables could make it stronger in Gates of Hell, and that is lost. Fire the ported unit's guns at it with the armour tools of section 11 and adjust the thickness by hand. See Bring a unit from Gates of Hell.

6. Armour thickness, threshold and durability

Whether the round passes is only half the story. The armour area can also be damaged. Each area keeps a damage total, and it is used up (breaks) when the total reaches 1.0; then the break_armor event runs.

  • Threshold is the least energy that damages the area at all. The game takes, in this order: the area's threshold {pierce {value}}; else koef times the effective thickness; else the effective thickness divided by the weapon's projectileDamageThreshold; else two thirds of the effective thickness. projectileDamageThreshold cannot be below 1; vanilla gun presets set 1.10 to 1.30 by gun size.
  • A round damages the area when its energy reaches the threshold, even if it did not pass. If the area has threshold {pierce {calibre N}}, rounds of a smaller calibre never damage it, which is how skirts and buildings ignore small arms.
  • Durability is the area's total capacity: value, else koef times the thickness, else the thickness times the material's durability from set/material.set.
  • Damage per hit is about how far the energy is above the threshold, scaled by the effective thickness and divided by the durability, with at least half the thickness counted for every damaging hit.

Vanilla tanks get their areas from the armor_tank macro in properties/tank_unarmed.ext, which gives the hull and turret {durability {pierce {koef 999}}} through its pierce_dur(999) argument. Armour-piercing rounds practically never break such an area; only blast does. So what happens to vanilla tanks after a penetration comes from interaction scripts, not from plate wear. If you want armour-piercing rounds to wear armour down, lower that number. Vanilla AS2 has only these macros for tanks (armor_light, armor_medium, armor_heavy through armor_tank, plus armor_mantlet, armor_engine and shield); there are no separate upper and lower plate macros. A unit calls one with its numbers, for example ("armor_heavy" turret(75 75 60 35) body(100 75 75 40)), in the order front, side, rear, top. Change those arguments in your copy of the unit, never the shared macro file. See Armour macros in vanilla data.

In Gates of Hell

Armour never wears in Gates of Hell. durability blocks are read but do nothing, there is no damage total, and a plate never breaks, so pierce_dur and similar settings have no effect there. The threshold is worked out as here. break_armor still runs, but only when a round passes; its value is the energy the round still has.

Parts are no longer broken by broken armour either. Instead each vehicle part has health that hits take away; see Vehicle part health in the summary. A unit ported to the 64-bit game has no part health, so what killed or crippled it in Gates of Hell must come from armour wear and its interaction scripts here.

7. Ricochet

A ricochet is considered only after a penetration fails; there is no ricochet roll before the pass test. The game takes the grazing angle, which is 90 degrees minus the angle to the face's normal (so 0 is a round skimming along the plate), and then:

  • The round does not ricochet if the gun has DisableRicochet, if it has already ricocheted twice, if the angle is past the last point of the material's chance table, if the ammunition is tagged fg or no_ricochet, if the plate's area broke on that hit, or if a random roll beats the material's chance.
  • Otherwise a new round is made, with its energy multiplied by the gun's RicochetEnergyDamping for that angle (the vanilla gun pattern: 1 up to 20 degrees, 0.8 at 30, 0.4 at 45, 0 at 60), or by a factor from the material if the gun has no table. The new round may hit something else.

The chance table lives in set/material.set (ricochet). For vanilla steel the chance is 1 up to 15 degrees of grazing, 0.6 at 30, 0.3 at 45, 0.15 at 60, and 0 at 75 and 90. A mod's own material.set replaces the whole file, so keep every vanilla material in it. A log line Invalid ricochet angle is harmless. Ground hits use the same rules with the terrain's material, unless the round is tagged fg or no_ricochet, in which case it explodes. On water, only fg rounds explode.

In Gates of Hell

Ricochet follows the same rules and values. Only the look differs: a ricochet's tracer is longer in Gates of Hell, because its length follows the speed the round keeps rather than the square of it.

8. Blast and fragments

An explosion is a blastwave effect with an energy and two radii in metres:

{damage blastwave {energy 4} {area 0.2 0.5}}
{damage add blastwave {energy 1.2} {area 4.3 7.3}}

Inside the inner radius a target takes the full energy; between the radii it falls in a straight line to nothing. The blast does not fall off with the distance the shell flew, only with the distance from the explosion. Only energy and area are valid inside the block. A plain damage blastwave replaces the first blast layer the item already has; damage add blastwave adds a layer.

The distance is measured to where the ray from the explosion enters the target volume, not to the entity's centre. Every volume whose able block allows blast is a target. Volumes are taken in order along each ray, and each takes what is left: anything behind a volume that does not break sees nothing, so walls and hills shield only if they have blast-able volumes. Blast travels at 15 m/s, so far targets are hurt a moment later.

Fragments are not simulated. A "fragment" effect is just a second, wider, weaker blast layer. Vanilla AS2 shell presets in set/stuff/shell/.presets have three macros, each called with a filler value v set by hand for the shell (("fg" args 3.5) for a 75 mm shell):

MacroLayersUsed for
fganti-tank 1.15v at 0.2 to 0.5 m; anti-personnel 1.2 at a radius that grows with vmost shells
fg_mediumthe same, with a slightly wider anti-personnel ringabout 89 to 128 mm
fg_heavyanti-tank v at 0.3 to 1.2 m; v/5 at 5.5 to 6 m; 1.2 at 8 to 16 m150 to 155 mm

Some shells add a layer of their own after the macro, as the vanilla 100 mm high explosive shell does.

Blast against armour works on five times the energy written in the data. If five times the energy is below the area's blast threshold, nothing happens. Above it, five times the energy divided by the area's blast durability is added to its damage, and the area breaks at 1.0, so repeated high explosive hits wear armour down. The value passed to break_armor is also five times the energy, while blast and blast_hit scripts see the energy as written. The scripts of vanilla tanks react to break_armor: breaking the body area can kill crew or set off ammunition, for instance.

In Gates of Hell

  • Shielding. A volume keeps at most its blast threshold of the energy and passes the rest to what lies behind it. In the 64-bit game an unbroken volume keeps all of it, so in Gates of Hell blasts reach further through soldiers and thin cover.
  • break_armor after a blast gets the threshold (the energy the volume kept), not five times the energy.
  • New events and actions for scripts: blast_wreaked (a blast got past a volume's threshold), with the actions blast_wreaked_effect, blast_hit_effect (first hit on the entity) and blast_effect (each part). Vanilla Gates of Hell hangs the blast loss of part health on blast_wreaked, for cars and trucks only (see Vehicle part health).
  • Keys. A blast layer also reads ground_interaction_radius (1 by default), which scales the ground effect where the round lands. no_ground_interaction is accepted and ignored. A second radius smaller than the first is an error.
  • Ground. The ground test runs a little above the ground at both ends, so fewer blasts are stopped by the ground by mistake.
  • Once. An item can detonate only once, and a charge lying at rest blasts along its main axis instead of straight up.

9. Fire and cook-off

A fire effect creates a hot sphere:

{damage fire {radius 4} {heating 0.5} {time 20}}

Entities inside heat up, allies at a fifth of the rate. An entity ignites when its heat passes 1.0, and how fast that happens is set by its inflammation_time (seconds, in its interaction file). An entity with no inflammation_time never ignites. Vanilla uses 0.25 s for soldiers, 20 s for vehicles, 30 s for a medium tank and 35 s for a heavy tank. Fire spreads only through new fire areas that burning things create, and fire on water ground goes out at once.

Cook-off is ammunition exploding inside a vehicle. The game adds up the blast energy of everything the vehicle carries, counting every blast layer of every item, armour-piercing rounds included; that sum is the vehicle's explosive amount. Vanilla scripts compare it with a cap per class (about 250 for light, 290 to 300 for medium and 340 to 360 for heavy tanks) to decide the odds of the ammunition going up. Two lessons follow. If you edit any blast layer of an ammunition item, the cook-off odds of every vehicle that carries it change. And if you change a vehicle's load, keep the total roughly the same. In vanilla scripts a cook-off kills the whole crew a fifth of the time and otherwise forces them out, and a full explosion can tear off the turret.

In Gates of Hell

  • Heat does not add up over a battle. A heated entity starts to cool 0.2 seconds after the last heat reaches it, so short bursts of flame do not build up to a fire as they can in the 64-bit game. It still catches fire when its heat passes 1.0, at a rate set by inflammation_time.
  • Fire that follows. A fire effect can take follow <entity id>: the fire moves with that entity and goes out when the entity is gone. The 64-bit game does not read the key.
  • Water. A fire goes out on water only when its whole sphere is below the surface, so a fire on the shore keeps burning.
  • Kill credit. Every unit, vehicles too, records who last damaged it, so a vehicle that burns out or cooks off later counts for the shooter. In the 64-bit game only soldiers keep that record.

How Gates of Hell works out cook-off is not covered in this book.

10. Damage to infantry

Soldiers take damage in two ways. A direct hit uses the weapon's healthDamage: each hit does that damage times the round's remaining energy, less the pierceAbsorb of any armour the soldier wears on that spot (never below zero), times a factor for distance. Hits closer than 5 m skip the difficulty scaling.

Blast works through scripts. In the vanilla soldier scripts, a blast layer that reaches the soldier with more than 0.59 energy deals a flat 200, 250 or 300 points (more than a soldier's health), a layer above 3.5 tears the body apart, and weaker layers only start bleeding or knock him about. On top of that, a computer-controlled soldier takes 200 times the energy as health damage; a player-controlled one takes far less, so the same shell kills computer and player soldiers at different radii. Lying and cover shrink the distance the blast sees: crouching multiplies it by 1.15, lying by 1.25, cover by 1.5, and prepared positions by 1.75 (lying) and 2.0 (cover).

In Gates of Hell

  • Damage by body part. The soldier's vitality block can hold Damage {"volume" factor} lines, one factor per hit volume (1 when a volume is not listed), DamageTPC with the same form for hits from a shooter under direct control, and DamageBlast, one factor for all blast damage. This is how a head shot is made to hurt more than an arm shot. The 64-bit game has none of these keys; remove them when you port a soldier.
  • Blast on soldiers. Every soldier, computer-controlled or not, takes blast damage from the blast_to_health_scale table in set/damage.set, times 125, times the difficulty's translate_damage. With the vanilla value 5 that is at most 562.5 per hit. The 64-bit game uses the table only for player-controlled soldiers and gives computer soldiers 200 times the energy, so blast radii against the computer change when you port.
  • set/damage.set also holds the hardness table of section 5 and the energy units (energy_per_projective 1, energy_per_health 0.025, energy_per_blastwave 5). Its projective_health_scale table is not used. Without the file the blast table is empty and blasts do no health damage, so a mod that changes it ships the whole file.
  • Cover and lying against bullets come from the difficulty settings: a damage factor and a chance to be hit at all, for a soldier in cover and for one crawling. A failed roll means no damage.
  • Difficulty settings are numbered differently, so difficulty files from Assault Squad 2 change the wrong values in Gates of Hell.
  • HEAT and soldiers. A round tagged rocketlauncher, heat, atgm or fg that hits a soldier starts no shaped charge jet, so it does not go on through him.
  • Hit effects. A short effects list is filled up with empty entries; the 64-bit game logs Throw effects not loaded instead.

11. Seeing and testing armour in the ARSENAL window

ARSENAL has three ways to look at a vehicle's armour and fire at it without starting the game: the Armor tab of the Models page (tab Models & Sim), the Shot tool in the Models page's 3D view, and the armorsim command. All three follow the rules of sections 4 to 10 and read the vehicle with your mod laid over the game. They are the penetration checker of this guide. The Armor tab and the Shot tool work for MoW:AS2 and AS64 only; under GoH the Models page shows a line in their place. The short way is on Change armour and see the result; the window itself is described in chapter 19.

The thickness table

  • The Models page has an Armor tab ("Armour: thickness, map and shot test"). Its "Thickness of each part" table shows every hit volume of a vehicle with your mod laid over the game: a number for each of the six sides, and a note saying whether the number was "set on the part itself", came "from the armour area" (and which), or has "no value: 0 mm". "Where each number comes from (file and line)" gives the file and line of every value. See The armour table on the Models page.
  • Some rows carry a flag: "not in the model, so it is never hit" (a volume in the unit's file with no shape in the model), "never hit by shells: switched off in the unit file", the ram volume ("the game uses it only for ramming and switches it off when the unit appears"), and "thickness is measured along the shell's path, the slope is not added" for areas that ignore slope (section 5).
  • Click a number to change it. The edit box asks for the "New thickness" and "Which sides" ("only the" side you clicked or "all six sides"); "Try it" shows the result first and "Change it" writes. The unit's file is copied into your mod first, and nothing is written into the game folder. A number shared with other parts says "This number is shared with other parts." and lists them; "Change all of them" changes it for every one. A number that comes from an armour area is changed in the area or in the macro call (section 6).
  • The Volumes tab of the same page sets the same thickness per side on the part itself, with its tags, part and material (chapter 6).

Who shoots, the map and the shot test

  • Under "Who shoots", "Search for a gun", pick a "Shell" the gun fires, and set a "Range" (0 to 5000 m). The page says "This shell goes through ... mm of flat armour at ... m." If the gun does not load the shell you picked, a warning says so and names the shells it does load; the shot is still fired, so you can test a shell a gun is not given in the game.
  • "What happens across the whole side" fires a grid of straight, parallel shots from one side ("Shoot from" Front, Rear, Left, Right or Top) and colours each spot by what happens there: goes through, bounces off, stops, no armour in the way, or reached by a blast. "Colour by" switches to "thickness on the slope (mm)". A line under the map says what share of the shots that hit armour go through. Point at the map to see what is there; click to shoot through that spot.
  • A click on a part in the 3D view, or on a spot of the map, runs the Shot test. It lists each plate the shell meets in order, with the part, the side, the thickness, the angle, the thickness on the slope, how many millimetres the shell can still do, and what happens: goes through, bounces off, stops in the plate, blows up in the plate, spent before it gets there, the jet does not reach, passes, nothing armoured, or misses.

Behind the armour

Under the shot test, the Behind the armour panel follows the shot past the plates: "What the shot does to the parts, the crew and the tank as a whole." It follows the game's rules and the unit's own interaction scripts (chapter 11), from your mod first and from the game where the mod changes nothing.

  • "The tank as a whole" gives the chance of each outcome and when it happens: cannot move, cannot shoot, the crew leaves, crew dead, burns, explodes, out of action. "By part of the vehicle" shows each part (hull, turret, gun, engine, tracks, wheels, fuel, ammunition, the crew and each crew member) as works, damaged, broken, destroyed, dead or off. "What happens, by cause" says which event or script line led to each result.
  • "Blasts" lists each blast that reached the vehicle with its charge, the radius of full force and the radius it reaches. "Shaped charge jet behind the armour" shows how far a HEAT jet went and what it reached. "Fire from the shell" gives the fire's radius, heat and burning time and how many seconds the unit needs in the flames to catch fire. "Tags added" lists the tags the scripts set.
  • The crew notes are part of the rules: the game itself does not hurt the crew through the vehicle's armour, neither from the shell nor from a jet, so crew losses come only from the unit's scripts. A blast hurts no crew through the vehicle either; a soldier on a seat with his own bone is a separate unit, so a blast can reach him.
  • The chances come from many repeated runs of the same shot, and the panel says how many. The flight after a ricochet is not followed. "Script words that were skipped, so the result may miss something" lists script parts the panel could not follow, and "The scripts also ask about things the shot does not say" lists questions the scripts ask that one shot cannot answer. Read both before you trust a number.
  • Options: "Keep the damage of earlier shots" fires the next shot at the damaged vehicle, and "Fresh tank" starts again. "Without the mod" runs the shot on the game's own files only, to compare. "Follow for (s)" sets how many seconds after the hit the scripts are followed (1 to 600; empty means 120). "Show every script step" lists each step. "Open" opens the file of a result in the Editor at its line; a value read from a game pak opens the copy the game loads.
  • After you change a thickness, the panel shows the result before the edit next to the new one, and lists what no longer happens.
  • A line at the end says which files were used: the open model with unsaved changes, the saved files of the mod and the game, or the game's files only.

The Shot tool in the 3D view

On the Model tab of the Models page, the Shot button sits beside Select, Move, Rotate and Scale above the 3D view. It needs the model opened for editing, because the shot uses the open model with its changes.

  • Pick the gun ("Search guns"), the "Shell" and the "Range". "Shoot from" is front, rear, left, right, top, an "Azimuth" (-360 to 360) and "Elevation" (-90 to 90), or "the camera".
  • While Shot is on, a click on the model shoots at that point. With "the camera", the shell flies along the line from the camera through the point you click. "Range" then sets only the shell's force, not where it starts. "Aim at" with a volume and Shoot sends the shell at the middle of that volume.
  • The result shows where the shell ends and what happens to the whole tank, in the same words as Behind the armour. Switches in the view show the shot result and put labels on blasts, jets and fires; "Volume names" labels the parts.
  • When you change the model, the last shot is run again and the result before the change is shown with it. With "Keep the damage of earlier shots" on, it is not run again; press "Fresh tank" first.

The same from the command line

ARSENAL armorsim table <unit>
ARSENAL armorsim shot <unit> --weapon "<gun>" --ammo "<ammo tags>" --range 500 --from 0,0
ARSENAL armorsim map <unit> --weapon "<gun>" --ammo "<ammo tags>" --range 500 --view front
ARSENAL armorsim effects <unit> --weapon "<gun>" --ammo "<ammo tags>" --range 500 --from 0,0
ARSENAL armorsim edit <unit> --volume <name> --side front --mm 60 --out <mod folder> --dry
  • table is the thickness table, shot one shot, map a whole side and effects the Behind the armour result. --from az,el gives the direction: 0 is straight from the front, 90 from the left side, and the elevation is upwards. --aim-volume <name> aims at the middle of a part.
  • effects repeats the shot 400 times by default (--samples), with a fixed --seed, and follows the scripts for 120 s (--until). --explosive <amount> and --shooter "<tags>" answer two things scripts often ask: the vehicle's explosive amount (section 9) and the tags of the shooter.
  • edit is the only one that writes; drop --dry to write, and add --shared for a number shared with other parts. --folder <mod folder> reads your mod over the game, and a mod's own paks are read too. See chapter 19.

What none of these show

They use the model's rest pose and straight shots with no gun spread, so a turret turned to the side or a shot that scatters is not seen. Single-player difficulty is not applied. The scripts are followed as written but not run by the game, so check a result that matters with a few shots in a skirmish and read game.log (section 13).

The Balance page

The Balance page shows every buy-panel unit as one row, including its gun, its penetration at 100 m, its damage and its reload time, and changes many at once. A reload change is written into the gun file, so every unit that carries the same gun changes with it. See chapter 17.

For a whole guided change of a gun, a shell or a vehicle's armour, the Quick Guided Task has recipes that ask one question at a time; see Use the Quick Guided Task.

In Gates of Hell

The armour tools of the Models page and armorsim follow the Assault Squad 2 rules only, and under the GoH button they are not available. They do not know the Gates of Hell factors of section 5, armour that never wears, or part health, so do not use them to judge a Gates of Hell unit in Gates of Hell. When ARSENAL runs for Gates of Hell, the Units sub-tab also holds the GoH unit page, with its fold Translate numbers (chapter 19); use it to bring a unit over, then test the result here with the tools above.

12. Worked tuning examples

Example 1: make a gun hit harder at long range. In your copy of the gun file, the vanilla damage2 macro writes the table {10 a} {50 b} {75 c} {100 d} {125 e} {150 0.8e} {200 0}. Give larger values for the far points, for example ("damage2" a(171) b(160) c(145) d(130) e(118)) instead of b(154) c(134) d(117) e(103). Check the result in the Balance page or with ARSENAL statsheet (section 13). Keep a last point at 0 or at a realistic value, since values beyond the last point do not drop.

Example 2: make high explosive shells less deadly to tanks. Copy set/stuff/shell/bullet75.fg.ammo into the same path in your mod and replace only the first blast layer after the macro. A plain damage blastwave replaces the first layer and leaves the anti-personnel layer alone:

{from "pattern fg"
  {tag "size_small"}
  {inventory {size 5 1}}
  ("fg" args 3.5)
  {damage blastwave {energy 3} {area 0.2 0.5}}
  {mass 12}
  {entity "shell_fg_75"}}

Do not write two plain damage blastwave lines; only the second would survive. Also remember cook-off: lowering this energy lowers the explosive amount of every vehicle that carries the shell.

Example 3: stop thin skirts being damaged by rifles. In your copy of the vehicle, after its ("shield" args 25) call, add a setting with the same area name; it merges into the area the macro made:

{armor
  {setting "shield" {threshold {pierce {calibre 20}}}}}

Rounds under 20 mm calibre no longer damage the skirts. This does not stop a round from passing; it only stops wear on the area.

13. Checking your work

ARSENAL statsheet <game folder> --mods mymod --sheet weapons,ammo,armor
ARSENAL statsheet <game folder> --mods mymod --scope mod

The first command prints tables of damage, penetration, armour and prices. The second runs only the checks on your mod's data: armour values that an area hides, parameters blocks that can never match, damage tables that do not end at 0, blast layers that a plain damage blastwave replaced, perk levels that are not declared, areas defined twice, and split parts flattened by a macro value. Single-key changes can be made with ARSENAL patch-entity and --dry-run. Then fire at the vehicle in game and read game.log. See chapter 17 for balancing and chapter 19 for the tools.

ARSENAL fix writes, in a separate patch mod, some values the way the game already reads them: a projectileDamageThreshold below 1 becomes 1, the earlier copy of a key written twice and a stray ) are emptied, and a ricochet angle row whose second angle is larger than the first gets the value the game already uses; see chapter 19. Before you trust any armour change, run the shot test and Behind the armour of section 11 on it, then confirm a few shots in a skirmish.

See also: Change a gun or its ammunition, Change armour and see the result, Check, fix and read the log, chapter 21, armour and damage surprises.

Gates of Hell: summary

The Gates of Hell notes in this book have not been tested in a running game. Check them in your own game before you depend on them.

SectionGates of HellIn a few words
1. Weapon keysdiffersrecoil, sway, AI pause, click and close sounds, synced rounds; the 64-bit game refuses them
2. Ammunition and per-ammunition blocksdiffersMinRange, unlimited range under direct control, tracers by tag
3. Spread and accuracydiffersunlimited ammunition never spreads; motion penalty can be scaled
4. Flight and hitsdifferslong-range drop; one hit per part per step
5. Penetration testdiffersfour overmatch tables; flaw, cast steel and hardness factors
6. Thickness, threshold and durabilitydiffersno armour wear; parts have health instead
7. Ricochetdifferssame rules; longer ricochet tracer
8. Blast and fragmentsdiffersvolumes keep only their threshold; new blast events
9. Fire and cook-offdiffersheat cools quickly; fire can follow a unit; cook-off not covered
10. Damage to infantrydiffersdamage by body part; one blast rule for every soldier
11. The ARSENAL windowdiffersarmour tools follow the 64-bit game only
12. Worked tuning examplesnot mappedthe examples are for the 64-bit game
13. Checking your worksame as far as mappedthe checks read the 64-bit game's rules

Vehicle part health

Gates of Hell gives every vehicle part (hull, turret, engine, gun, tracks, wheels and so on) health points. The 64-bit game has no such thing: a part there is only working, broken or destroyed.

  • set/component.set lists categories: {category "name" {hp N} {hp_broken N} {armor_damage_modifier f}}. Vanilla values include tank_light 250, tank_medium 325 and tank_heavy 400, turrets 150, 200 and 250, engines 125, 200 and 250, guns 150, 200 and 225, tracks 100, 120 and 200, and a wheel 100, with armor_damage_modifier 0.1.
  • A vehicle's perks block gives each part its numbers: {perks {component "turret" {category "turret_medium"}} {blastwave_modifier 1}}. Put {category} first, because it copies the whole record and later {health {hp N} {hp_broken N}} or {armor_damage_modifier f} lines change it. An unknown category logs Invalid component category: <name>. A part can also be matched by tag ({component tag "t" ...}), but when two tag rules match, the winner is not the first in the file, so name each part.
  • A penetrating hit takes (penetration - effective thickness) times the part's armor_damage_modifier, plus the ammunition's MinimumDamageModifier. Damage comes off hp first; at 0 the part is broken, and the rest comes off hp_broken; at 0 the part is destroyed. With hp_broken 0 a part is never destroyed by damage.
  • A part with no perk has 1 hp: the first damaging hit breaks it, and it is never destroyed.
  • A destroyed part runs the reaction destroy (the 64-bit game runs break for both states). Destroying the part body marks the vehicle destroyed, so a vehicle needs a part named body.
  • Blast takes (5 times the energy - the threshold) times the vehicle's blastwave_modifier. Vanilla Gates of Hell uses this for cars and trucks only.
  • A repair takes the part's repair time times the share of health lost.
  • The console variable dbg_damage prints each loss as hp = a -> b.
  • Saved missions keep Health, HealthBroken and RepairOrder in each part; the 64-bit game stops on those keys.

A ported vehicle loses all of this. Its toughness must come from armour, armour wear (section 6) and its interaction scripts, and the tools of section 11 show the result.

Pitfalls

  • A parameters "tags" block must match whole tag words, first match in file order; a miss silently uses the top-level values.
  • Keys such as calibre or DisableRicochet inside a parameters block apply to the whole weapon.
  • Penetration keys belong in the weapon file, not the ammunition file.
  • A damage table is held flat beyond its ends; end it with a realistic last point.
  • OvermatchDamping should reach 90 degrees.
  • A nonzero area value overrides the volume's own thickness for that side, and flattens a part split into several volumes.
  • Three numbers in an area thickness misalign the sides; write 1, 2 or 4.
  • Two plain damage blastwave lines keep only the last one.
  • A volume that cannot be hit by blast shields nothing; an unbroken one shields everything behind it.
  • Blast against computer and player soldiers differs.
  • A script block whose tag contains #, such as {##on blast, is skipped entirely.
  • The penetration margin is not available to scripts.
  • Ricochet needs a failed penetration first, and happens at most twice per round.
  • A mod's material.set replaces the whole vanilla file.
  • Editing an ammunition blast layer changes the cook-off odds of every vehicle that carries it.

Next: AI and bots.

10. AI and Bots

The short way to change what bots buy and how rich they are is on Bots: what they buy and how they play. The exact facts for every bot function, bot data name and console command are in Reference 12: Bot Lua and console, and the sensor keys are in Reference 8: Vision, effects and sound.

What you will learn

  • How a soldier or vehicle decides what to shoot, and why it sometimes refuses to shoot something obvious.
  • How the two target files (select.set and ammo.set) work, and the single most important rule about them.
  • How firing, bursts and aiming delays are controlled.
  • How infantry decide to advance, hold or retreat, and which brain properties change that.
  • What the multiplayer bot script can and cannot do, and how the ARSENAL window changes it.
  • A symptom-to-cause list for the AI problems modders hit most often.

Everything here is "soft code": data files and scripts that you can change without touching the game's program. A small part of the AI is compiled and cannot be changed, and this chapter says which part.

A reminder before you start: work in your own mod folder (for example mods/mymod/), never in the game folder. Text files use CRLF line endings; the 64-bit build reads every string value as UTF-8, in data files and .lng files alike, and identifiers must be plain ASCII. Original data is ASCII outside ; comments, where some old cp1251 bytes remain; leave them as they are. Editors can silently change encoding or line endings, so check after saving. Paks are ordinary zip files. See chapter 3 and chapter 4.

1. The decision chain

Every armed unit follows the same chain, once per think cycle:

  1. The unit's sensor collects contacts, meaning enemies it has noticed.
  2. A target selector ranks those contacts from most to least wanted.
  3. An ammo selector decides which weapon and ammunition may be used against the best-ranked target.
  4. The unit aims.
  5. The unit fires, subject to burst and tolerance rules.

Three folders of data feed this chain. The unit's own definition (its .ext file under properties/) holds the brain, the sensor and the name of its target selector. The set/target/ folder holds the target selector files and ammo.set. The set/vision/ folder holds how far and how quickly units notice things. Interaction scripts (see chapter 11) can also change how a unit fires.

You cannot add new kinds of orders, change how targets are scored internally, or change how units search for cover. Everything else in this chapter is open to you.

2. Target selection: select.set

The file set/target/select.set lists the .inc files beside it, and each of those holds one selector. A selector says: "for units that look like this, rank enemies like that". This is the vanilla selector for vehicles, set/target/tank.inc, shortened:

{selector
	{type "tank"}
	{group
		{ignore {class airborne}}
		{select {weapon "ap"}}
		{select {weapon "fg"}}
		{select {weapon "apcr"}}

		{sort {weapon "ap"} {attacking} {class tank}}
		{sort {weapon "ap"} {attacking}}
		{sort {weapon "fg"}}
		{sort time_to_aim}
	}
	{group
		{sort {class tank}}
		{sort {class armoredcar}}
		{sort {class car}}
		{sort time_to_aim}
	}
}

A selector is matched to a unit in one of two ways. {type "tank"} matches by the unit's selector name, which its definition gives with {targetSelector "tank"}. {unit "human" "bullet"} matches by tags: the unit must carry the tag human and the weapon it currently holds must carry the tag bullet. Because the match depends on the held weapon, a soldier who switches from rifle to anti-tank weapon also switches selector. The vanilla selectors are human_bullet, human_ap, human_fg, human, cannon_shell, moto, cannon_rocket, cannon_bullet, tank, tank_bullet and searchlight.

The rules that matter

  • The first matching selector wins. The game walks select.set in file order and uses the first selector that fits the unit. Order therefore matters, and putting a general selector above a specific one hides the specific one. That is why vanilla lists human_bullet, human_ap and human_fg before the general human.
  • Each unit has one ordered list. A tank does not get one ranking per weapon. The cannon and the machine gun share the same list, and each weapon takes the first enemy in that list it is allowed to hit.
  • Groups run in order and consume candidates. The first group picks the contacts it wants. The second group works on what is left, and so on.
  • A contact that no group matches is never attacked. This is the most important rule in the chapter. If every group of a selector has select lines and none of them selects tanks, units using it never fire at tanks. Nothing warns you.
  • ignore is global for later groups. A term {ignore {class airborne}} removes aircraft from the shared pool for every group after it, which is how vanilla vehicles are made to ignore planes.
  • Several {select} lines in one group mean "this or that". Terms inside a single {select} mean "this and that".
  • A group with neither select nor ignore takes everything that is left. Most vanilla soldier selectors are like that, so they can rank every contact.
  • If any contacts are inside the unit's weapon range, only those in-range contacts are considered at all.
  • Inside a group, sort lines are applied in order: contacts that satisfy the first line come first, then the next line, and ties are broken by distance (nearest first) or time_to_aim (quickest to turn toward). The sort is not stable, so exact ties come out in no guaranteed order.

Terms you can use

TermMeaning
class Xthe target's class, such as human, tank, armoredcar, car, cannon, airborne
weapon "tags"the target's weapon tags; weapon "ap" means "the target carries armour-piercing ammunition"; weapon alone means "the target is armed"
attackingthe target is shooting at us
threatingthe target has recently been a threat (the game's own spelling)
in_range Nthe target is within N metres of the shooter
invisible, out_of_rangevisibility and range tests
entity "id"one specific unit definition

Put not in front of a term to reverse it.

Worked example: riflemen who go for machine gunners first

The vanilla rifle selector, set/target/human_bullet.inc, ranks enemies within 10 metres first, then enemies shooting at the soldier, then enemy riflemen. To make riflemen prefer machine gunners after close and attacking enemies, copy the file into the same path in your mod and add one line:

{selector
	{unit "human" "bullet"}

	{group
		{sort 	{in_range 10}}
		{sort	{attacking}}
		{sort	{class human} {weapon "mgun"}}
		{sort	{class human} {weapon "bullet"}}
		{sort	{class human} {weapon}}
		{sort	{class human}}
		{sort	{threating}}
		{sort	distance}
	}
}

Your file replaces the vanilla one by path. Change one thing at a time, then read game.log as described in chapter 18.

In Gates of Hell

  • The time_to_aim sort term does nothing for vehicles: it gives every enemy the same score. A vehicle selector that relies on it as its last tie-break loses that tie-break there.
  • The threat a soldier reacts to is the nearest one he has a weapon for, and only then the nearest of any kind. A vehicle whose body part is destroyed is no longer a threat. Against a vehicle, an anti-tank soldier tries his rocket launcher before any other weapon.
  • Units tagged airborne or helicopter are not attacked while they fly. A helicopter on the ground is a normal target.

3. Ammunition choice: ammo.set

Once a target is chosen, set/target/ammo.set decides which ammunition may be used on it. It has one block per target class, each listing ammunition tags in order of preference. This is part of the vanilla block for soldiers:

{select_ammo
	{human
		{"grenade ic" {ready_for_shot}}
		{"shell fg" {ground} {ready_for_shot}}
		{"mortar fg" {ground}}
		{"hmgun"}
		{"bullet"}
		{"grenade fg"}
		{"ammo rocketlauncher" {enable_for_user 0}}
	}
}

The class names are human, car, cannon, airborne, armoredcar, light_tank and tank. Two extra blocks, human in_bush and human in_cover, are tried before the plain human block when the victim is hiding.

  • The first matching rule wins, and earlier means higher priority.
  • The game appends a catch-all with a negative priority, and a negative priority means "do not shoot this target with this ammunition". So a missing rule is a silent refusal to fire. In vanilla data there is no bullet rule for class tank, which is why rifles and machine guns do not shoot at tanks.
  • Options inside a rule include ground (aim near the target rather than at it), volume "tag" (the rule applies only while that part of the target is undamaged), ready_for_shot (a shell is already in the breech), charging (the gun is still loading), check_grenade, disable, and the switches enable_for_ai 0, enable_for_user 0 and enable_for_human_user 0.
  • {"ammo rocketlauncher" {enable_for_user 0}} against infantry means only units under AI control will use launchers on soldiers by themselves. Launchers in the player's units will not.

A related difference: a unit under player control must have its target in range to shoot, while an AI-controlled unit will also try to shoot from out of range and then move closer.

Artillery has no special AI. Guns and mortars use the same selector and ammunition rules and fire high-explosive shells at the ground near spotted infantry within their range. Bots cannot order fire missions.

In Gates of Hell

  • A rule with ground makes the unit aim at the target's position, not at one of its bones, for soldiers and vehicles alike.
  • When a gun is picked to fire at the ground, it is skipped if the target is inside the weapon's MinRange. This game has no such key, so mortars and guns there have no minimum range.
  • AI units can run out of ammunition. A weapon is empty when it has no rounds left and none are found in the unit's own or its group's inventories.

4. Firing rules

Three layers shape when a shot actually leaves the barrel.

Fire mode. The brain property fire_mode takes hold, return or open (fire at will). Units owned by a multiplayer bot are set to AI control, fire at will and zone movement. Units owned by human players are set to user control and hold position.

Aiming delay and tolerances. A soldier who acquires a target waits a random 0.3 to 1.1 seconds before aiming, scaled by difficulty. A rocket launcher is put away 8 to 14 seconds after use. A shot then waits until the gun points within AimingTolerance degrees of the target (10 when absent), then for RelaxationTime. Vehicles also wait while their SpreadTolerance is larger than the accuracy they have while moving, so a fast-moving tank holds its fire. PrepareTime is a wind-up for indirect fire on guns; 0 means none.

Bursts. The burst block of a weapon gives the short and long burst lengths, each with a spread of rounds. The vanilla machine-gun presets in set/stuff/mgun/.presets are burst_short, burst_medium and burst_long; this is burst_medium:

{burst
	{short 5 0.3}
	{long 8 0.7}
}

AI vehicle weapons always use the long burst, and you cannot pick another mode per weapon. Vanilla vehicles have no pause script between bursts.
