If machine guns in your mod set fire one burst and then fall silent for a moment, look for an interaction script on the fire event that switches the weapon off with weapon_work for a time. A player command can toggle such a script, but the AI never gives player commands, so AI vehicles keep the pause.

In Gates of Hell

  • A soldier's wait before each shot comes from weapon data, not from the fixed 0.3 to 1.1 seconds. It is the weapon's FiringTimeout (a centre and a spread in seconds), scaled by distance with FiringTimeoutDistanceFactor on bullet weapons, and multiplied by the difficulty's firing_timeout. A launcher's wait uses the difficulty's grenade_timeout instead. A new wait is drawn for every shot, so infantry rate of fire is set in the weapon files.
  • An attack order no longer adds its own random wait before shots.
  • A vehicle's pause between bursts is the weapon's FiringTimeout, where this game uses a random 0.2 to 0.7 seconds. A vehicle with several guns keeps them all busy: spare guns take enemies that another gun already has.
  • Suppression fire ordered by the player lasts 60 seconds from the first shot (8 seconds here).
  • The console variable (on by default) makes an attacker move to where a moving target will be. Set it to 0 to aim at where the target is now.

5. Vehicle behaviour

A vehicle walks its single ordered enemy list and gives each weapon at most one enemy per think cycle. A weapon is skipped if the gun cannot be aimed there, if the ammunition rule has negative priority, or if the gunner seat is empty or the gunner is about to leave.

  • Approach. If the best-ranked enemy is farther than the chosen weapon's aim range, the vehicle drives toward it.
  • Detour. If no aiming solution exists (the target is behind a ridge, blocked, or covered by a volume "body" rule that no longer applies), the vehicle retries every 2 to 4 seconds and may reposition. When a tank selector ranks tanks above infantry and the first tank cannot be aimed at, the vehicle can circle or shuffle. Exactly how it moves then is not known (unconfirmed).
  • Gunner release. When the local threat ratio is above 4, when crew are injured, or when only one seat remains filled, hatch gunners leave their bone-mounted machine guns and those guns go silent.
  • Crew leaving. A crew that leaves a damaged vehicle does so because of the vehicle's interaction scripts, not the brain. The bot script has no boarding order, so whether a bot's crew climbs back in by itself is not known (unconfirmed).
  • Guns return to an idle state after 4 seconds without orders.

In Gates of Hell

  • An idle vehicle does not turn its turret to scan the area unless its brain data switches that on. Here every tank does it by default.
  • A gun keeps aiming at the same part of the same enemy about half of the time instead of picking again.
  • A unit getting out of a vehicle keeps trying while the way out is blocked, and stays inside if it cannot. Here it gives up at once.
  • A gun crew (units tagged cannon) leaves its gun when a crewman is down to half health and the attacker is behind the gun. This also happens to the player's guns.

6. Infantry tactics

Once per second a soldier decides on a stance, from 0 (retreat or stay low) through 1 (cautious), 2 (hold), 3 (advance) to 4 (strong advance). Its inputs are the threat against it, the spread of its allies, and its morale, a number from 0 to 100. Morale is pulled down toward current health when health is lower, and nudged toward the morale of nearby allies.

In plain terms:

  • Compute a retreat limit and an advance limit by multiplying retreat_ratio by the threat and advance_ratio by the spread. Both limits grow by half when the soldier is in or near cover.
  • Advance when morale is above 70, advancing is allowed, and the threat is above the advance limit. If the threat is more than double the limit, advance strongly.
  • Unless retreating is disabled: fall back when the spread exceeds the retreat limit, turn cautious below morale 50, and retreat below morale 30. A retreating soldier stays in that state until the retreat limit catches up with the spread.

These are brain properties of the soldier's definition. Vanilla writes none of them, so the defaults apply; a mod sets them like this:

{brain "human"
  {Properties
    {advance_ratio 2.0}
    {retreat_ratio 2.0}
    {move_radius 7}
  }
}

The defaults for advance_ratio and retreat_ratio are both 2.0, and move_radius (how far a unit may stray from its anchor in zone mode) is 7 metres. Other properties are no_advance, no_retreat, fire_mode, move_mode (hold, zone or free), control and, for vehicles, look_around. Missions can override several of them per unit with the actor_state command (see chapter 12). The vanilla {brain "human"} block in properties/human.ext holds other settings: the distances at which soldiers notice and flee explosives and grenades, and fight/distance, where melee starts (1.5 metres).

Setting no_retreat 1 together with retreat_ratio 0, a large advance_ratio and a large move_radius produces infantry that never fall back, roam far from their anchor and fight to the death. Also, control user written in a definition is overwritten for multiplayer units, so it only affects units a mission places outside multiplayer; whether look_around and control user change such placed units is not known (unconfirmed).

Soldiers seek cover within about 15 metres. They go prone when approaching beyond 25 metres, crouch beyond 10 metres, and stand within 7 metres.

In Gates of Hell

  • The formula is the same, but Gates of Hell's own properties/human.ext sets advance_ratio 0.5 and retreat_ratio 4, where this game uses the defaults of 2 and 2. If you carry that file over, your infantry advance and retreat differently.
  • A retreating soldier who is still outnumbered but has morale above 50 counterattacks for 1 to 2 seconds, then retreats again, over and over. no_retreat stops this, because the soldier never enters the retreat state.
  • A soldier who is shot dives for cover, crawls or crouches only when the enemy is more than 20 metres away (here 10 metres). A console variable coverLeaveEnemyDistance with the default 20 exists; whether it changes this distance is not confirmed.
  • One key, bomb/danger_zone (default 4, 7 in Gates of Hell's data), replaces danger_zone_run, danger_zone_jump and danger_zone_hide. Soldiers simply run from a grenade; they do not jump or dive.
  • A soldier standing in a fire does not look for a way out of it unless something else moves him. This is a fault in that game.

7. Vision as an AI input

Spotting is controlled by the Sensor block in a unit's .ext file. This is the vanilla soldier's, from properties/human.ext:

{Sensor
	{Visor "eyes"
		{vision "human"}
		{bone "visor"}
	}
	{Visor "telescope"}
	{AttackZone 2.5}
	{RecognizeTime 0.25}
	{InformRange 40 40}		;first - AI ;second - USER
}

A contact is noticed once the time it has been visible exceeds distance / sightRange * RecognizeTime. A tiny RecognizeTime therefore means instant spotting. If a modder sets it near 0.01 and InformRange near 120, every unit spots everything and tells all its friends. InformRange takes two numbers, one for AI-controlled units and one for the player side; a spotter informs allies within that distance. If a key is absent the game falls back to a recognize time of 2 seconds, inform range 20, threat zone 15, attack zone 5 and remember time 120.

The folder set/vision/ sets how far a unit sees. Each vision profile, named by the vision line of a visor, has uncover (the range at which a still target is spotted), h_fov, v_fov and radius, with multipliers for cover, squatting, crawling, standing still and firing. Vanilla profiles include human, mp_soldier, mp_sniper, field_glass, cannon_main, vehicle_main and tank_main-l, tank_main-m and tank_main-h for light, medium and heavy tanks. set/vision/vision.set wraps every radius in one macro, (* 0.75 %r), so changing that one factor scales the sight of every unit. Firing multiplies the range above 1, so a shooter gives itself away. set/unmasking.set (unmasking) controls how quickly hidden units are exposed by speed, pose and what they hold.

One trap: set/detect.set does not affect AI spotting. It only controls how many seconds an enemy stays revealed to a human player when fog of war is on. A long value gives a long afterglow, not a slow detection.

Further detail on the data behind vision, effects and sound is in chapter 16.

In Gates of Hell

  • The sensor works more slowly: it looks around every 0.5 to 1 second (here 0.1 to 0.5), and the brain thinks every 0.5 to 1.5 seconds (here 0.1 to 0.3). Units can react up to five times later than in this game.
  • A new sensor key, MinRecognizeTime (default 0), sets the shortest time recognising can take. A unit that hurt you is recognised at once. This game does not know the key and reports an error for it, so remove it from any sensor block you carry over.
  • RememberTime has no random spread: every unit of a type forgets a contact at the same age. Here each unit gets up to 20 percent more or less.
  • A unit counts as firing for 1 second after its last real shot. Pulling the trigger on an empty gun does not give it away.
  • The grid that hides units behind terrain uses 5-unit cells (7 here), so the same map can see differently.

8. Multiplayer bots

Multiplayer bots are driven by Lua, the only Lua in the game. It runs on the host only, one Lua state per bot. The entry file script/multiplayer/bot.main.lua loads bot.lua with require, and bot.lua loads the data file bot.data.lua. Files with the same path in a later-loaded mod replace the originals. The Lua has no sandbox (all standard libraries are open), so a script can touch the file system, which is another reason to read other people's scripts before you run them. print writes to game.log with a [LUA] prefix, which makes it the easiest way to see what a bot script is doing. A Lua error does not stop the game: the bot goes idle and the log records the failure (Lua errors).

Getting a bot into a LAN game

The stock multiplayer game cards have no bot switch, so a LAN lobby will not let you add a bot. A mod that overrides set/multiplayer/games/combat.set and puts {enableBots 1} inside its {settings} block (not {options}) allows the lobby command mp_slot 2 normal to fill slot 2 with a normal bot. In the ARSENAL window, the Maps page has an "Allow bots" tick for a copied map. A map that allows bots also needs flag points, or bots buy units and never give an order. Because bot Lua runs on the host only, a bot script you override by path takes effect only on the machine that hosts the game.

What a bot can do

The bot functions are few:

CallEffect
BotApi.Commands:Spawn(unit, split)buy one unit at the bot's spawn point
BotApi.Commands:CaptureFlag(squad, flag)order a squad to move to a flag
BotApi.Commands:SayChat(text)send a chat message
BotApi.Commands:Income(player), BotApi.Commands:EnemyHasTanks()read the bot's income and whether the enemy has tanks
BotApi.Instance, BotApi.Scene.Flags, BotApi.Scene.Squadsread-only information: the bot's player, team, army and team size; the flags; its squads

The Commands table holds exactly Spawn, CaptureFlag, SayChat, Income and EnemyHasTanks; there is no ClearOrders, so calling it is an error. The Events table holds Subscribe, Unsubscribe, SetTimer, KillTimer, SetQuantTimer and KillQuantTimer.

A bot has no attack, retreat, boarding or fire-mission order. All fighting is done by the normal unit brains described above. New order types would need a change to the game itself. Events you can subscribe to are Init, Done, GameStart, GameEnd, Quant, GameSpawn and NonQuant, one handler per event. The first handler subscribed for an event stays. If your script subscribes before it requires the stock bot.lua, the stock handler is dropped and the bot never spawns anything. Load the stock script first, then wrap or add your handlers after it.

Spawn has a quirk. It returns true when the card does not exist, is hidden or is not for sale, so the caller cannot detect a typo in a unit name; the stock script then simply moves on to its next pick. If a bot never buys something you listed, check the exact card name. Squad cards carry the army in brackets, such as smgs(eng); vehicle cards are plain names, such as dodgewc55.

The data file

bot.data.lua holds the bot's shopping plan. The names that the stock script actually reads are:

NameEffect
MaxSquadSizethe split threshold passed to Spawn (stock 5)
OrderRotationPeriodhow often capture orders are re-issued, in milliseconds (stock 3 * 60 * 1000, three minutes; only the bot script reads it, so a replacement bot.lua that does not use it ignores it)
FlagPriorityweights for choosing which flag to go for: Captured = 1, Enemy = 2, Neutral = 3 in stock
UnitClassthe class names: Infantry, ATInfantry, Vehicle, Tank, AATank, ATTank, HeavyTank, ArtilleryTank
Purchasesstages, each with a Repeat count and, per army, a list of unit entries

Two names are not read by anything: AttackBaseTime and the per-entry period. Which units a bot may buy in a given era comes from the preset's unit set, not from period. ARSENAL fix <mod folder> plan|apply --out <patch folder> --only botkeys removes both from your mod's bot.data.lua into a patch mod, and refuses when another Lua file of the mod names the key.

Stock data has eight stages for six armies (eng, ger, ger2, usa, rus, jap). A stage in the same pattern looks like this:

Purchases = {
	{--purchase 1
		Repeat = 4,
		Units = {
			["usa"] = {
				{priority = 3.0, class = UnitClass.Infantry, unit = "riflemans(usa)"},
				{priority = 1.0, class = UnitClass.Vehicle, unit = "willysmb"}
			},
		}
	},
	{--purchase 2
		Repeat = 0, --infinite
		Units = {
			["usa"] = {
				{priority = 1.0, min_income = 3.0, min_team = 2, class = UnitClass.ATTank, unit = "m36"}
			},
		}
	},
}

Repeat is the number of purchases in that stage before moving on. A value of 0 means "forever" and belongs on the last stage; without it the bot runs off the end of the list and stops buying. An army that is missing from a stage buys nothing at that stage, so list every army in every stage. Your copy of bot.data.lua replaces the whole stock file.

The stock bot.lua picks a unit by weighted random choice on priority, among the entries whose min_income and min_team are met. It multiplies the weight of Infantry entries by 2.5 when the bot holds fewer flags than the enemy. When the enemy has no tanks, ATTank entries get weight 0; when the enemy has tanks, ATInfantry and ATTank entries get double weight. It tries to buy on every game quant.

Bot economy and difficulty come from the bots block in set/multiplayer/games/bots_generic.inc, which has entries for easy, normal, hard and heroic (Bot difficulty). In stock data each sets balancingFactorBonus for command points, manpower and payback (0.75 for easy, 1.0 for normal, 1.25, 1.5 and 1.5 for hard, 1.5, 2.0 and 2.0 for heroic) and a chargeFactors block. Always set chargeFactors in any bot entry that also sets balancing (explained in chapter 12). Bot difficulty changes only that preset entry, not the Lua logic, apart from the difficulty value passed to the GameStart event.

A replacement bot.lua can add wave spawning, phase-based unit pools, per-tier ratios and attack groups, but it cannot touch brains, selectors, vision or ammunition rules. A well-behaved replacement caps its live squads.

Bots in the ARSENAL window

  • The Bots page (Game Modes & AI > Bots) shows "What bots buy" for each army, stage by stage, and lists units of your mod that no bot buys yet. "Make bots buy a unit" adds one entry to your copy of bot.data.lua, and "Bot difficulty" changes the numbers in bots_generic.inc. The command-line tool is ARSENAL botrecipe; see Bots: what they buy and how they play for its options.
  • The Bot Doctrine page beside it applies a ready-made way of playing (a persona) to your mod and checks the result. The command line is ARSENAL doctrine list personas, ARSENAL doctrine gen --persona <id> --out <mod folder> --game <game folder> --plan and ARSENAL doctrine check <mod folder> --game <game folder>. With the stock bot.lua a persona can change only the three settings the stock script reads; the persona numbers are starting values that have not been tried in a match (unconfirmed).

More about the two pages:

  • "What bots buy" warns when your mod has its own bot.lua, because that script may ignore the list.
  • "Make bots buy a unit" asks for the "Unit name", "Army", "Stage" and "Kind of unit". "Buy it first (priority 1000, picked almost every time)" makes the bot pick it almost every time, and "Make it cheap and quick to unlock (for testing only)" lets you see it in a short test match. If your mod has no buy card for the unit, you can copy the card of another unit. "Preview" shows the change and "Write into my mod" writes it. After a write, "My change is not showing" opens the help for that case.
  • "Bot difficulty" has one row each for Easy, Normal, Hard and Heroic, with "Army size x", "Income x" and "Payback x". "Preview changes" shows the result, "Write into my mod" writes your copy of bots_generic.inc, and "Back to stock (remove my copy)" deletes your copy so the stock values return.
  • "Multiplayer start settings" changes start money and grow time in a preset file; chapter 12 explains it.
  • The Bot Doctrine page has its own tabs Rules, Personas, Scenarios, Profile, Generate and Check. "Profile" tells the generator which bot your mod uses: "vanilla (stock bot)" or a larger replacement script; "Detect from my mod" chooses for you. "Generate" takes a persona and a "Strength" from 0 (no change) through 1 (the persona as written) to 2 (twice as strong), and an optional "Base bot file", then "Preview" and "Write into my mod". "Check" ("Check my mod") reads the result back. The universal persona puts the original numbers back.

The quick way: in the Quick Guided Task row choose "I want to" "change" "what bots buy and how they play". It walks you through the same jobs one step at a time: one army's first purchase, bot difficulty, lobby money, and how the bots fight. See Use the Quick Guided Task and chapter 19.

In Gates of Hell

Bots there are still Lua, but the script, its functions and where it runs all differ. A bot script written for this game does not run there unchanged, and the other way round.

  • Where bots run. In a Steam match the bots run in the separate server process; on LAN they run on the host. The entry file is still script/multiplayer/bot.main.lua; Gates of Hell's own script is that file plus one file per mode under script/multiplayer/modes/ (for example battlezones.lua, frontlines.lua, conquest.lua), with shared helpers in modes/utility.lua. The console variable dev_enableBotAi (default 1) set to 0 starts bots without loading the script, so they neither buy nor move.
  • Events have other numbers. Init 0, Done 1, GameStart 2, PrepTimeOver 3, WinnerDecided 4, GameEnd 5, Quant 6, GameSpawn 7, NonQuant 8, Waypoint 9. Here GameEnd is 3 and Quant 4, and the three new events do not exist. Subscribe by name (BotApi.Events.Quant), never by number, and the same handler works in both games. WinnerDecided passes the winning team's name, and Waypoint the squad that reached a waypoint.
  • Commands. EnemyHasTanks is gone; a script that calls it fails. Spawn(unit, split) is the same as SpawnAt(unit, split, -1), where the index picks one of the team's map points. An unknown unit name crashes the game instead of returning true, so test names first with IsUnitAvailable(unit). Also new: CanSpawn(), TimeToSpawnUnit(unit) (in milliseconds; an unknown unit crashes here too), GameOver(winner) and SeekAndDestroy(squad), which sends a squad to a random enemy within 50 metres: the first attack order a bot has.
  • CaptureFlag sends the squad to the flag zone's centre, within a radius per kind of unit read from a Lua table FlagCaptureArea (kinds Helicopter, Artillery, Captor, Mortar, ATgun, Vehicle, Infantry). Without the table the radius is 0 and the log reads "DBG: FlagCaptureArea is not found". A vehicle with a free seat unloads at the flag. Here the squad goes to half the zone radius and does not unload.
  • Information. BotApi.Instance calls the team size ownTeamSize (here teamSize) and adds spawnPointName, gameMode, unitMode, difficulty, IsMultiplayer(), IsCooperative(), TeamSize(team), HumansInTeam(team) and Relation(side). BotApi.Scene adds QueryScene(props, seconds) (counts of units by tag per side, which is how a script counts enemy tanks there), Waypoints, the mission variables Vars, GetVar and SetVar, and IsSquadTagged(squad, tag). BotApi.Scene.Flags leaves out flags that cannot be captured. The global module_exists(name) tells whether a Lua file exists, and BotApi.Conquest gives Conquest data.
  • Brains on clients. In a Steam match each player's game looks for a brain named <name>_client first (human_client, vehicle_client and so on). Changes to AI brains therefore act only in the server process, not on players' machines.
  • In ARSENAL the bot shopping list of the Bots page, the Bot Doctrine page and the bots task of the Quick Guided Task are for this game only, because Gates of Hell has no bot.data.lua. Under the Gates of Hell button they say so in one line; the Bots page still changes the multiplayer settings there, and the Game Modes page changes bot difficulty and start money.

Each new function has a short entry under Gates of Hell only in the bot reference.

Brain, sensor and target-file mistakes often fail quietly. An unknown key in a brain or sensor block may be skipped or may log an "unexpected token" message depending on the file, so after every edit read game.log (chapter 18) and run the lint tools described in chapter 19, for example ARSENAL keylint and ARSENAL milint (the latter checks bot data, and warns when a mode with bots has a map without flag points).

Gates of Hell: summary

The Gates of Hell notes in this book have not been tested in a running game. Check them in your own game before you depend on them.

SectionGates of HellIn a few words

The job-by-job view is in Bots: In Gates of Hell.

Helicopters and air orders

Gates of Hell has helicopters, which this game lacks. They use their own brain helicopter, and the talk condition seen knows the word helicopter for call-outs. Air units can be ordered to make an airstrike (fly to the target, drop the strike's bomb, leave) or a reconnaissance flight (circle a point for a given time). This game knows neither the brain nor the talk word and has no such orders, so a helicopter cannot be carried over as data.

Pitfalls

  • A contact that matches no selector group is never attacked, with no error.
  • A missing ammunition rule means "never fire" with no error.
  • detect.set does not change AI spotting.
  • Bot Lua cannot give attack, retreat or boarding orders, and Spawn hides bad unit names.
  • Subscribing a bot event before loading the stock bot.lua drops the stock handler.
  • control user in a definition is overwritten in multiplayer.
  • Change one lever at a time and read game.log after each change.

Next

Chapter 11, Interaction scripts explains the language of the scripts that change firing and crew behaviour.

11. Interaction Scripts

Every event, condition and command named in this chapter has its own entry in Reference 10: Interaction scripts, with its exact arguments and what silently fails. Use this chapter to understand how scripts work, and the reference to look up one word.

What you will learn

  • What interaction scripts are and which behaviour they control (damage, fire, smoke, cook-off, crew reactions, wrecks).
  • How the game decides which script blocks apply to which unit, and in what order they run.
  • The event, condition and action vocabulary, with worked examples.
  • How timers, flags, tags and custom events work, and where their limits are.
  • How to write scripts in the ARSENAL Editor and check them with ARSENAL ialint.

Interaction scripts are a small event-driven language. Most of what you see a vehicle or soldier do when something happens to it, such as a hit, a fire, a crash or a death, is decided here and not in the game's program. That makes it one of the most powerful and most editable parts of the game.

Work in your own mod folder (for example mods/mymod/resource/set/interaction_entity/). Text files use CRLF line endings; the 64-bit build reads every string value as UTF-8, in data files and .lng files alike, and identifiers must be plain ASCII. Original data is ASCII outside ; comments, where some old cp1251 bytes remain; leave them as they are. See chapter 3 for how your files override vanilla ones.

1. Where scripts live

The entry file is set/interaction_entity/entity.set. In vanilla it only lists other files, in order: generic.inc, human.inc, vehicle.inc, car.inc, tank.inc, cannon.inc and many more. Those files hold top-level blocks, each named by a space-separated list of tags. This is part of the vanilla block for medium tanks in tank.inc:

{"medium tank"
	{inflammation_time 30}
	{on blast_hit
		{if min_energy 30
			{impulse up 2.5 0.1 dir 4 0.1}
			{if volume "turret"
				{if rand 0.8
					{call "tear_turret"}
				}
			}
		else min_energy 7
			{impulse up 0.3 0.1 dir 0.4 0.1}
		}
	}
	{on "_explosion"
		{blastwave c4 10 r0 2.5 r1 10}
	}
(include "tank/tank_medium.inc")
}

Inside a block you can write {inflammation_time N}, handlers {on <event> ...} and (include "name.inc") lines. Any other bare word inside a block stops the file with "unexpected token". Terrain reactions use a separate set of files, described in section 9.

A file in your mod replaces the vanilla file at the same path as a whole. To add a block of your own, either copy the vanilla .inc file that should hold it and add your block, or copy entity.set and add an include line for a new file of your own at the end.

2. Which blocks apply to which unit

A block applies to a unit if every tag in the block name is among the unit's definition tags, or if the block is named generic, which applies to everything. The unit's own name also counts as a tag, so a block named after one unit applies to just that unit. The unit's tags come from its definition and the .ext files it includes.

Two consequences matter:

  • Matching happens once, when the entity description is loaded. Adding a tag at run time with {tags add} does not make more blocks apply. Run-time tags only change what {if tagged} tests.
  • Properties that no block mentions produce a harmless "Unknown props" message in the log.

Blocks are stacked in levels, in the order they appear in the files. A typical stack for a medium tank is generic, then tank, then medium tank, then the unit's own block. By default each handler is inherit: when an event happens, the less specific levels run first and the most specific block runs last. If you write overload, only your level runs for that event, and an {inherited} action inside it runs the next lower level at that point:

{"my_heavy_tank"
	{on engine on overload
		{inherited}
		{set "my_flag"}
	}
}

You may define a given event only once per block. Writing {on spawn} twice in the same block gives an "event already defined" error. Merge the two into one.

Class names such as tank, light tank, medium tank, heavy tank, armored_car, turret, human, car, cannon and airborne are just tag sets that come with unit definitions. There is nothing special about them in the script language.

3. The command

Every event carries a command with optional fields: target, instigator, volume, part, bone, value, position, direction, normal, source, bullet and sender. Not every event fills every field. A condition that needs a missing field is false, and an action that needs one does nothing.

Timers lose some of this context. {delay} and {delay_effect} run their actions with a fresh, empty command. {delay_ex} keeps a copy of the command but drops the instigator, bone and bullet. If you need to know who shot the vehicle after a delay, save a flag first.

In Gates of Hell

On bullet_hit two command fields mean something else. The hit side is kept in a field of its own, so the command's value is empty there; a script that reads the value as the hit side gets nothing. The normal is the surface normal at the hit, where this game passes the reflected direction. Effects that use the normal point another way.

4. Events

Combat and lifecycle events:

EventWhen it happens
spawnthe entity is created
bullet_hita bullet touches it, before the game decides whether it passes; value is the hit side (0 front, 1 top, 2 left, 3 right, 4 back, 5 bottom)
piercearmour is penetrated (not sent when a shell detonates on the armour)
break_armor, break_armor_againarmour breaks for the first time, or again; value is the energy and the sender is pierce or blast
blast_hitthe first blast hit on the entity from one explosion; value is the blast energy
blastonce for every part a blast reaches
contactphysical collision
ground_hittouches the ground; the value is negative
break, repaira part breaks or is repaired
fire "place"a weapon fires; the name is the weapon's place name
blow, blow opponenta melee strike: blow on the soldier who strikes, blow opponent on the soldier who is struck

Neither blast_hit nor blast means that the entity itself explodes; vanilla scripts make that happen by calling their own events, such as "_explosion" above.

Actor events cover units that move or have crews: operatable, move, turn, movement_mode_changed, grounded, board in|out, crew in|out, overlap begin|end, terrain_pp enter|leave, terrain_fx enter|leave, animation_end and ik begin|end. Four of them need the word on or off after the name: accelerate, brake, engine and swim, as in {on engine on ...}.

An event name the game does not know produces an "unexpected token" error at load. Names are not case sensitive.

Custom events

{on "name" ...} defines your own handler. You run it with {call "name"} (immediately, with the same command), with {delay_effect}, or the game may call certain well-known names itself (for example die, burn, burn_volume, break_window, fallen, link_weapon and slice_load). If you call a name that has no handler, nothing happens and nothing is logged, so a typo in a call is invisible. ARSENAL ialint finds these for you.

In Gates of Hell

Gates of Hell adds events, and this game stops loading at each of them with "unexpected token". Remove or rewrite them in any script you carry over.

EventWhen it happens
destroya part is destroyed (this game runs break for that too)
blast_wreakeda blast pierces the entity
animation_event "name"a named event inside an animation is reached
hatch open, hatch closea hatch opens or closes; what triggers it is not confirmed

The game also calls more well-known handler names by itself: bullet_hit_effect on the first bullet hit and pierce_effect on a penetration (the place for hit effects), blast_wreaked_effect, contact_effect on a physical hit, blow_effect and blow_opponent_effect around a melee strike, reload when a unit reloads, and environment_changed when the scene's environment changes. In this game these names are ordinary custom events that nothing calls.

An entity can have up to 65535 distinct events across its scripts. Here the limit is 255.

5. Conditions

The conditional looks like this:

{if not tagged "burning"
	{call "start_fire"}
else rand 0.3
	{call "maybe_fire"}
else
	{con "no fire"}
}

There are no comparison operators, no and and no or. Thresholds are always "greater than". For AND, nest one {if} inside another. For OR, use an else chain. A bare string such as {if "damaged"} tests a per-entity flag (see section 7).

Commonly used conditions: tagged, stuff, rand p, volume, min_energy N, effector, work, broken, destroyed, explosive_amount, component, name, able, hit_side, velocity, min_mass, operatable, linked, place, crew_in_place, burned, terrain_fx, altitude, water_level, under_water and difficulty.

hit_side takes a side name: front, back, left, right, top or bottom. A number, such as {if hit_side 4}, is a load error ("Unknown side"). Without a bullet in the command only front and back work, judged by position. min_energy tests the command's value, which is an energy only for events that carry one (blast_hit, blast, break_armor); on bullet_hit the value is the hit side.

Some conditions modders expect do not exist: there is no hit_angle, no terrain "water" and no bullet "shell". An unknown condition name is a fatal error when the file loads: the game stops with "unknown condition". A branch written with no condition word at all has no test and runs every time, like a plain else.

In Gates of Hell

  • New conditions: prop (a tag of the unit's description), volume_any, no_stuff (empty inventory), active, friendly_fire, standing, squatting, in_cover, cover_type (needs at least one kind of cover), idle_low_health, hold_strap (weapon slung), gamemode (the multiplayer game type), season (the season of the multiplayer game card), weaponry_sealed (a seat is sealed) and cannon_state fire|move|trailing. gamemode and season are false outside multiplayer. cannon_state on a unit that is not a gun can probably crash the game. Since this game stops at an unknown condition, every one of these must go before a script is carried over.
  • stuff takes one or more tag lists and is true when the item has all tags of any one list, so one condition can test "this or that".
  • crew_in_place is false for a sealed seat, such as a commander with the hatch shut.

6. Actions

Flow control: set, call, delay, delay_ex, delay_effect, kill_delay, inherited and with_effector. con prints text to the debug console. Note that log does nothing, and rtfunc only prints a warning.

Timer details:

  • A range is written as a centre and a spread, so {delay 2 0.5} waits between 1.5 and 2.5 seconds.
  • A {delay} is keyed to its own action. Running the same one again restarts it instead of stacking a second copy.
  • {kill_delay "name"} cancels a named delay. An empty name is an error.
  • For yes/no values, a number other than 0 or an omitted value means yes.

Spawning and removal: spawn (with options and nested actions), delete and hide.

Sound and visuals: link_sound, play_sound, stop_sound, start_sound, view show|hide|start|stop|pause, add_view.

Animation and mesh: ani_play (it can call back with animation_end), ani_stop, ani_wind, ik_enable, bone show|hide|cut, tear, tex_mod, tex_morph, scale. use_blend_tex is not supported and only logs.

Physics and damage on an entity: tags add|remove, impulse, burn, fire, blastwave (it centres on the entity origin unless you give a position), explode_inventory, bullet_detonate, volume enable|disable, stat_notify, for_each_volume, with_linked_entity.

Actor actions: components, component, damage_report, kill_crew, crew_emit, crew_throw_off, weapon_work, chassis_work, able, stunned, die, the health_damage_* family, kill_flags, knockdown, spawn_human and others.

Notes on a few of them:

  • burn sets the entity or one volume on fire, but shows a flame only when you give fx "effect". Without fx it burns with no visible flame. time sets how long, and stop puts the fire out.
  • explode_inventory is the cook-off action: a random 40 to 90 percent of the explosives the entity carries go off. Amounts of 0.1 or less do nothing.
  • damage_report shows a message to the local player for their own units only. A misspelt text key shows the raw key.
  • weapon_work and chassis_work switch weapons or movement on and off. A pause between machine-gun bursts (chapter 10) is built with weapon_work.

A few actions and conditions are never used in the stock data (for example rtfunc, change_obstacle, movement_type, spawn_human, true, false, inactive and the crew event pair). Whether they behave as described in the installed game is not known (unconfirmed).

In Gates of Hell

  • New actions: set_idle_animation "a" "b" ... (one picked at random as the idle), holder_drop "holder" (the item in that holder falls to the ground), call_synced (a call that the host also sends to the other players), vehicle_health_damage_pierce and vehicle_health_damage_blast (damage to a vehicle part's health), linear_damping f, restore_volume_states, mark_for_persistence and wind_detail_bending.
  • unlink replaces get_off. It frees any seat of any kind; a soldier gets off.
  • crew_emit does nothing on an aircraft more than half a metre above the ground, and takes a new word force.
  • gravity is a multiple of normal gravity (1 is normal). Here it is in metres per second squared (9.8 is normal), so divide by 9.8 when you carry a value over, or a body falls almost ten times as fast.
  • spawn takes the new words texmod, random_position <radius>, random_orientation, local (this machine only) and constrain_after_dir.
  • Timers: delay_ex takes uniq, which gives every call its own timer that a later call never restarts.
  • Other new words: norestart on ani_play keeps the animation time, use_position on the sound actions, multiple on component, truncate as a bone mode, more add_view view modes and the relation my. tear copy works the other way round from this game.

This game does not know these words. A script that uses them probably fails to load here, so take them out or rewrite them when you carry a script over.

7. State: flags, tags, abilities

There are three places to keep state, each with a limit.

KindSet withTest withLimit
Flag{set "x"}{if "x"}at most 128 distinct names in the whole game
Tag{tags add "x"}{if tagged "x"}no limit
Ability{able ...}{if able ...}at most 32 names; an unknown name is a load error

Flags belong to one entity each, but the 128-name limit is global and counted over every interaction file when the scripts load. More than 128 names is an error at load. Since the vanilla scripts already use many names, a big script mod can hit this, so prefer tags where you can.

There are no global variables and no numeric counters. To count, use a tag ladder: hit_1, hit_2, hit_3, and on each event add the next rung.

{on bullet_hit
	{if tagged "hit_2"
		{tags add "hit_3"}
	else tagged "hit_1"
		{tags add "hit_2"}
	else
		{tags add "hit_1"}
	}
}

In Gates of Hell

Volumes have one more ability, blockcamera (the volume blocks the camera), and volume enable|disable can switch it from a script. This game does not know the name: able blockcamera in a definition or script stops the load with "unknown flag".

8. Worked example: a fire after a blast from behind

Goal: when a strong explosion hits a vehicle from behind, start a fire that burns for a few seconds and then ends.

{"my_tank"
	{on blast_hit
		{if hit_side back
			{if min_energy 9
				{if not tagged "rear_fire"
					{tags add "rear_fire"}
					{burn fx "smoke_dead_small" time 8 2}
					{delay 12 "rear_fire_out"
						{tags remove "rear_fire"}
					}
				}
			}
		}
	}
}

The nested {if} lines are the AND. blast_hit carries the blast energy as its value, so min_energy 9 means a blast of more than 9. A blast has no bullet, so only front and back work for hit_side here, which is what this example uses. The fx option makes the flame visible, and time 8 2 lets it burn for 6 to 10 seconds. The {delay} runs its inner action with an empty command, which is fine here because removing a tag needs no command fields. Put the block after the vanilla tank.inc blocks, as section 1 describes, and replace my_tank with the name of your unit.

9. Terrain effects

When a shell lands, the ground material decides what appears. Terrain scripts live in set/interaction_terrain/effects.set and the files in set/interaction_terrain/effects/:

{"sand"
	{on detonate {spawn "crater_norm" terrain_texmod}}
}

The effect name comes from the ground material's {effect "..."} line in the terrain settings. An unknown name logs "Unknown terrain effect" and can crash the game. The terrain events are hit (a body, soldier or torpedo hits the ground) and detonate. The event bullet is never fired, so a handler for it silently does nothing.

In Gates of Hell

  • Whether a terrain effect counts as "in the air" depends on what calls it: a bullet uses its own size, an exploding item the largest of its damage radii times ground_interaction_radius, and a falling body 0. Here the height is a fixed 20 units for all. Effects that are not in the air play on the ground or water surface below the point, so big blasts raise dust from higher up.
  • Gates of Hell's terrain scripts pick winter or summer effects with the condition season, and use the new spawn words, so they cannot be copied into this game as they are.

10. Writing and checking scripts

The Editor page of the ARSENAL window (tab IDE) is a text editor for game files. It checks a file as you type, shows what a word means when you point at it, jumps from a call to its handler or from an include to its file, finds every use of a name in your mod, other mods and the game, and offers fixes for some problems. It does not start the game.

On the command line:

ARSENAL ialint <mod folder> [--game dir] [--mods a,b] [-q] [--summary]

ARSENAL ialint reads your interaction scripts together with the vanilla ones and reports, among others:

  • an event defined twice in one block, and an unknown event name;
  • call to a name with no handler;
  • a fire handler for a place the unit does not have;
  • hit_side used where the command has no bullet;
  • timers whose actions need command fields that a delay drops;
  • {tags add} written as if it changed which blocks apply;
  • terrain handlers for bullet;
  • use of use_blend_tex;
  • flag name and ability name overflow;
  • actions that do nothing (log, rtfunc, kick);
  • an empty kill_delay;
  • a tiny explode_inventory share.

Use -q to hide informational lines and --summary for counts only. See chapter 19 for the other tools.

The 64-bit build has a console only when started with -console (Reaching the console); {con} prints there. Use it sparingly, and read game.log after every change, as described in chapter 18. Load errors such as "unknown condition", "Unknown side" and "unexpected token" appear there.

See also: interaction scripts that fire weapons or pause them are part of the AI picture in chapter 10, and the damage they react to is in chapter 9.

Gates of Hell: summary

The Gates of Hell notes in this book have not been tested in a running game. Check them in your own game before you depend on them.

SectionGates of HellIn a few words
1. Where scripts livesame as far as mappedthe same set/interaction_entity/ files and .inc blocks
2. Which blocks apply to which unitsame as far as mappedtag matching and levels as here
3. The commanddifferson bullet_hit the value is not the hit side; other normal
4. Eventsdiffersdestroy, blast_wreaked, animation_event, hatch; more engine-called names
5. Conditionsdiffersfifteen new conditions; stuff takes several lists
6. Actionsdifferscall_synced, unlink; gravity in multiples of g
7. State: flags, tags, abilitiesdiffersone more volume ability, blockcamera
8. Worked examplesame as far as mappedno word of the example is mapped as different
9. Terrain effectsdiffersair height per caller; winter and summer by season
10. Writing and checking scriptsnot mappedthe Editor page and ialint check this game's words only

Carrying a script from Gates of Hell to this game means removing every word above that this game lacks, and converting gravity values. The reverse needs bullet_hit scripts that read the hit side to be rewritten. The words only Gates of Hell has are listed under Gates of Hell only in the reference.

Pitfalls

  • Only one handler per event per block.
  • A typo in a call name is silent.
  • An unknown condition name stops the game when the file loads.
  • hit_side takes side names, not numbers.
  • accelerate, brake, engine and swim need on or off.
  • {burn} without fx shows no flame.
  • {tags add} never changes which blocks apply.
  • Delays and timers drop command fields.
  • 128 flag names for the whole game; tags are unlimited.
  • log does nothing; use con.
  • Terrain bullet never fires; use hit or detonate.
  • A script file in your mod replaces the whole vanilla file at that path.

Next

Chapter 12, Missions and multiplayer setup.

12. Missions and Multiplayer Setup

The short way: Missions and multiplayer modes gives the steps for adding a mode to a map, changing starting money and army size, and checking a mission. This chapter explains how the pieces work. Every key named here has its own entry in Reference 11, Mission files.

What you will learn

  • How a multiplayer game mode is built from a game card, presets, units, budgets and armies.
  • How to write the economy: command points, unit limits, charge times and income.
  • How .mi mission files are structured, and how triggers, conditions and commands fit together.
  • How to give a map another mode with the Maps page or ARSENAL maps mode, and how to try it with the Play page.
  • How multiplayer stays in sync, and which of your changes can break it.

Work in your own mod folder (for example mods/mymod/). Text files use CRLF line endings; the 64-bit build reads every string value as UTF-8, in data files and .lng files alike, and identifiers must be plain ASCII. Original data is ASCII outside ; comments, where some old cp1251 bytes remain; the game skips them, so leave them as they are. See chapter 3.

1. How a game mode is assembled

A multiplayer mode is a game card: a file set/multiplayer/games/<mode>.set holding one {game ...} block. The vanilla cards are combat, battle_zones, battle_zones_8x8, captureflag, cooperative and frontline. The load chain is:

  1. The game card sets the game class, player counts, lobby settings and teams.
  2. Inside {game ...} it includes presets.inc, which in vanilla includes four preset files (presets_competitive.inc, presets_all.inc, presets_user.inc and presets_test.inc). Together they fill the lobby dropdowns.
  3. When a game starts, the unit list loads from the first file that exists of units/<gameName>.set, units/<class>.set and units/common.set under set/multiplayer/. The vanilla common.set includes soldiers.set, squads.set and vehicles.set.
  4. A preset's {apply "<name>"} loads units/<name>.set on top of that list, adding to it. {apply remove "<name>"} first flags every unit that is not marked basic for removal, so you can start from a clean list.

The lobby dropdowns come from three preset keys: gameMode ("Game settings"), unitMode (the era or unit list) and specMode (the command point choice). Vanilla preset names start with c:, s: or f:, but the game does not read these prefixes; the name is only a unique key. The preset whose gameMode is test is the built-in test mode: its countdown is 0 and rank checks are skipped.

During a multiplayer mission load the text preprocessor mod mp is active, so (mod "mp") sections in data files apply (see chapter 5).

Game card keys

This card follows the shape of the vanilla combat.set:

{game
	{class combat}
	{order 5}
	{parameters "freezeTime=30"}
	{settings
		{options            scoreFinal gameDuration enableSpectators}
		{optionsAdvanced    preparationTime friendlyFire fogOfWar}
		{fogOfWar           fog_realistic}
		{difficulty         multiplayer}
		{gameDuration       "90 min"}
		{preparationTime    15}
		{useUnitLevelRestrictions 0}
		{enableBots 1}
	}
	{teamSettings
		{teamsMode normal}
		{armySelectionMode alliance}
		{teams {"a"} {"b"}}
		{alliances (include "preset_alliances.inc")}
	}
	(include "presets.inc")
}
  • class is one of the registered game classes: combat, captureflag, cooperative, frontline, battle_zones, battle_zones_8x8, armored_warfare and combined_arms. Without class the file name is used, which is why the vanilla combat.set has no class line. armored_warfare and combined_arms are registered but ship no card. See class.
  • order is the place in the lobby list. minPlayers, maxPlayers and texMod are mostly set per map in map.info (chapter 13); player counts are rounded up to an even number and clamped to the console variable mp_maxPlayers (16 by default).
  • parameters is one string of key=value pairs separated by semicolons. Which keys a class reads depends on the class: combat reads freezeTime; captureflag and battle_zones read freezeTime, flag_capture_time, flag_release_time and flag_capture_factor, and battle_zones also points_table; frontline reads its own score and phase keys. See parameters.
  • settings holds the lobby options and their starting values. The game writes words, not numbers: fogOfWar is fog_off or fog_realistic, difficulty is multiplayer, and gameDuration is one of a fixed list from "10 min" to "120 min". options, optionsAdvanced and optionsRanked list which settings the lobby shows. Other keys are friendlyFire, scoreMin, scoreMax, scoreFinal, preparationTime with its Min and Max, resourceAmount, useUnitLevelRestrictions, enableSpectators, enableBots, randomSpawnPoints and veterancyMode (all, beginners or veterans). See settings.
  • The vanilla combat card has no enableBots line, so the lobby offers no bots there. A mod that wants bots must override the card and add {enableBots 1} inside {settings}. The Maps page "Allow bots" switch does this for you (see chapter 10).
  • teamSettings holds teamsMode (teammatch, normal, default, deathmatch or none), armySelectionMode (alliance, team, player or default), equalizeTeams, teams and alliances. A team entry can hold title, armies, minTeamSlots, maxTeamSlots, aiTeamPlayers and hidden. The keys minTeamPlayers and maxTeamPlayers from the template file are not read by anything; use minTeamSlots and maxTeamSlots. In an alliance, armies may be repeated ({armies "usa"} {armies "eng"} adds up) or written as one string; every army named must exist in set/multiplayer/armies/.
  • The vanilla card's bare {teammatch} at the top is not a key and is skipped.
  • ranked {enabled} {minPlayers n} {maxPlayers n} allows ranked games, and mission_options is the lobby group that the mission_option condition term reads.

Unknown keys in game cards, presets and unit lists are skipped without a message, so a misspelt key simply does nothing.

In Gates of Hell

Game cards have the same shape, but the classes and many keys differ. Because unknown keys are skipped in both games, a card carried either way loads and quietly loses those settings.

  • Classes. New: ammunition, evacuation, guerrilla, heroes, campaign_capture_the_flag (Conquest battles, see Conquest) and koth (King of the Hill; this game has no koth class, so such a card makes no game here). The front line class is frontlines, not frontline. armored_warfare, battle_zones, battle_zones_8x8, combined_arms and heroes all play by one set of battle zone rules. combat is not registered.
  • New settings: manualControlMode (rts_mode, dc_mode, tpc_mode or any_mode: whether players may take direct control), loseOnZeroPoints (a team whose score reaches 0 loses), pauseDuringPreparation (default on; off lets the battle run during the countdown), chargeFactorMod, coldWarSpawn and customClipper (players take map points tagged a or b, and a coin decides which half each team gets), assignReinforcementsToPlayer, and waveTime and firstWaveTime (120 and 360 seconds by default, for evacuation waves). enableDuration is read but probably does nothing.
  • Removed: allowRejoin.
  • gameDuration has 14 lengths: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 and 120 minutes. 35, 45, 70 and 80 are unknown here.
  • New parameters: invertedUnitScores (a kill takes score off the victim's team instead of paying the killer; pairs with loseOnZeroPoints), scoreStart (score every team starts with), teamsize_cp_factor (scales command points by the larger team's size), kill_personal_score_multiplier, kill_unit_score_multiplier, kill_score_multiplier, and for battle zones flag_team_score and flag_team_table (a held flag pays its team a share of the score limit). In front line games freezeTime has no effect (the countdown is preparationTime), and a mode without rounds probably plays one round instead of two.

2. Presets

A preset has this shape (vanilla builds its presets with macros such as ("custom_user" start(160) finish(3000) cp(100)); this is the same thing written out):

{"c:my_custom_100"
	{gameMode "custom"}
	{unitMode "user"}
	{specMode "cp_100"}
	{common
		{unitset {value "all"}}
		{commandPoints "*=100"}
		{unitLimits "heavy=2;tank=6"}
		{balancingFactorBonus {cp 1.0} {mp 1.0}}
		{chargeFactors {value "*=1"}}
		{budgets ...}
	}
	{bots (include "bots_generic.inc")}
}

The common block, a team block inside {teams {a {...}} {b {...}}} and a bot block inside {bots {easy {...}} {normal {...}} {hard {...}} {heroic {...}}} all take the same data keys. An empty field in a team or bot entry falls back to the value in common; bots use their difficulty name as their team key. The exception is balancingFactorBonus: in a team or bot entry it falls back to common only when that entry's chargeFactors value is empty. If a team or bot entry sets balancing, always set chargeFactors in the same entry too. See Presets and team data.

In the window, Game Modes & AI > Game Modes has a "Multiplayer start settings" section: you pick one of the vanilla preset files, find a preset and change its start money, top money, command point cap and grow time; it writes your copy of the preset file into your mod after a preview. Remember that your copy replaces the whole vanilla file.

Unit sets

unitset {value "inc1|inc2^exc1|exc2"} lists tags to include, a caret, then tags to exclude. A unit passes if it has any include tag, no exclude tag, and the tag of the player's army. A set with only an exclusion, such as "^x", matches nothing, because its include list is empty. To exclude something from everything, write all^x and give your units an all tag (the vanilla units all have it). See unitset.

Command points

commandPoints "tag=table;tag=table" sets pools. The key * is the main pool. Each table is either one limit, or a list of seconds:limit steps separated by commas, so the cap rises as the game goes on: "*=0:60,300:120,900:180;infantry=0:40". A unit is checked against the main pool and against the first pool, in list order, whose tag it has. Buying a squad takes the squad's total cp; each member's death gives back that member's own cp. The limits are scaled by balancingFactorBonus cp and by team balance. See commandPoints.

Unit limits

unitLimits "tag=N;tag=N" caps purchases. The semicolon is the only separator: a comma breaks the line and silently drops the limits after it. Only the first tag in list order that a unit has applies to it. The cap counts purchases and is never lowered when a unit dies or is refunded. See unitLimits.

Charge factors and balancing

chargeFactors {value "tag=f;*=f"} scales each unit's cooldown (charge): the first matching tag in list order wins, else *, else 1. The stock bot file sets *=0, so bots have no cooldowns. The available list next to value is read only by the lobby unit browser; it does not change the game.

balancingFactorBonus {cp} {mp} {payback} (each 1 by default) multiplies the command point limits, the budget start and finish, and the payback rate. It is multiplied again by team balance (the size of the largest team divided by this team's size), so a smaller team receives proportionally more.

In Gates of Hell

  • balancingFactorBonus has seven keys: cp, mpStart, mpFinish, payback, periodicFactor, chargeDelay and charge. There is no mp. Each game reads only its own names, so a block carried over loses its money settings without a message.
  • Bot blocks are found as <difficulty>_<team>, for example normal_a. A block named only by difficulty, as here, is not matched there, and the reverse falls back to common here.
  • chargeFactors names its lobby choice list customize (here available). The lobby value is a number, chargeFactorMod on the game settings, that scales the preset's factors.
  • unitScore is a new preset key: what a bought unit's kill is worth.
  • Unit sets replace. Loading a unit set drops every unit loaded before it, so a preset's apply sets replace the mode's units instead of adding to them, and apply remove has nothing left to act on.
  • Unit set text with several & parts uses the last part; here only the first part counts.
  • A command point table given twice replaces the first one; here the two are merged.

3. Budgets and income

A budgets block inside the preset data describes the currencies players spend (shown in game as manpower). This one follows the vanilla standard_user preset:

{budgets
	{vehicle
		{mode "standard"}
		{resource
			{start 300}
			{finish 3000}
			{growTime 1500}
			{payback
				{cp      "0	50	90"}
				{restore "1.5	0.75	0.2"}
			}
		}
		{buttons "squad1 squad2 v1 v2 v3 v4 v5"}
	}
	{hero
		{resource {start 10}}
		{buttons "hero"}
		{tag "special"}
	}
}
  • The block name is free, except vehicle, which is fixed: bots, the command point and manpower display and some game modes look for the budget named vehicle.
  • buttons is a list of unit button tags (vanilla uses squad1 squad2 v1 v2 v22 v3 to v12, sf and hero). A unit's cost is charged to the first budget that lists its button. A unit whose button is in no budget is free.
  • tag "special" keeps the budget's statistics apart and shows its own price hint.
  • Modes are standard, custom, with_update, without_update and fullpayback. standard grows from start to finish over growTime seconds. custom does the same, but the end value is the lobby's resource amount, offered from the speedset list and clamped to limitmin and limitmax. with_update adds the lobby amount every period seconds, without_update sets start and finish to the lobby amount, and fullpayback starts at start and gets the rest only as payback.
  • resource holds start, finish, period, speed, limitmin, limitmax, speedset, growTable, growTime and payback. growFactors "cpSpent/factor;..." sits beside resource and speeds income up or down with the command points in use.
  • In standard mode period, speed, limitmin and limitmax must all be 0, or you get an "Invalid parameter value" error. custom and fullpayback need period and speed at 0 (custom uses limitmin and limitmax for its lobby slider). without_update needs speed at 0.
  • A growTable (a list of numbers) shapes income over growTime: the time is cut into as many steps as there are numbers, each step earns in proportion to its number, and the total still comes to finish minus start. After growTime the budget catches up, so manpower you did not spend is not lost.
  • payback gives back a share of a lost unit's cost, at the restore rate of the highest cp step at or below the command points you have in use. Only standard and custom budgets pay back. The two lists must be separated by TAB characters, must be the same length, and cp must rise. Spaces will not do: the list becomes one token and gives a size mismatch error.
  • The keys restoreBegin and restoreEnd are worked out but never used; with with_update or without_update they must be 0.

See Budgets for each key. Unit prices are set in the unit entries, next.

4. Units

Vanilla writes its unit lists with macros. Written out, a vanilla entry such as the US 57 mm gun looks like this:

{units
	{"m1_57mm"
		{charge 0} {fore 1.0}
		{group "c5"} {button "v2"} {level 1}
		{cost 225} {cp 10} {score 11.25} {cw 2}
		{tags "all cannon mediumcan usa"}
		{content "* ( mp/usa/vehicle_supporter:2 )"}
	}
}

Using the same name twice merges the two entries, and their tags add up. Keys:

  • charge: the cooldown in seconds. fore: how much of the first cooldown is already served at the start; 1 means ready at once, 0 a full cooldown, and a negative value a longer one. The first lock lasts charge x factor x (1 - fore).
  • group: when you buy a unit, every available unit of the same group restarts its cooldown.
  • icon: units of one group with the same non-zero icon form a sequence; only one is shown, and the next appears after a purchase.
  • cost: the price, charged to the budget that lists the unit's button. cp: command points. score: the score value of a kill. cw: the capture weight the unit adds when it stands in a flag zone.
  • level: the rank a player needs. It is ignored when useUnitLevelRestrictions is 0, in test mode, in ranked games and for bots.
  • content: what the purchase delivers, in the form "name[:count] ... ( crew[:n] ) *". A name that is a breed spawns soldiers, * is the entry's own name, names in brackets after a vehicle are its crew, and an empty content delivers the entry's own name.
  • tags: the army tag (it must match the player's army), era tags, and the categories that unit sets, limits, charge factors and command point pools look for. The unit's own name is added as a tag.
  • info (tooltip key), breed, basic (survives apply remove), not_for_sale (hidden from the buy panel) and remove (deletes the entry once read).

All cooldowns start when the preparation countdown ends. A unit that becomes available later starts a fresh period at that moment, without fore. See Units.

In Gates of Hell

  • New keys: cost_ap and cost_sp (prices in other currencies), round_multiple, squad_cost_factor, score_factor (default 0.05), research_stage and research_stage_max (Conquest research), enabled, not_for_player_sale, conditions, action and doctrine (the lobby doctrine the unit belongs to). This game skips all of them.
  • cost defaults to 0 (here 1.0).
  • level and fore are gone. There is no rank lock, and the first cooldown always runs in full.
  • charge is a group, {charge {delay N} {interval N}}: the first wait at game start and the cooldown after each purchase, each scaled by the charge factor and by the chargeDelay or charge balancing key. Here charge is one number. Convert it both ways.
  • enabled in data is probably overwritten by the game's own check of which downloadable content you own.
  • Hidden and not-for-sale units cannot be bought there; here they pass the price check.

5. Armies

{army
	{id 6}
	{title "mp/army/mine"}
	{icon "/interface/pages/multi/flag_mine"}
}

Each army is one file in set/multiplayer/armies/. A negative id means the army cannot be picked. Stock ids are 0 usa, 1 ger, 2 rus, 3 eng, 4 jap and 5 ger2. appid_base ties an army to a Steam DLC. The vanilla files also write flag, but the game does not read it. See Armies.

In Gates of Hell

Only icon and id are read from an army file. The army's name is always the text key mp/army/<name>, so a title in your file is ignored. An army id above 99 probably stops the game. Each army can offer doctrines in the lobby: the list is the doctrine values of that army's units for the mode.

6. Bots

Bot behaviour and their purchase tables are covered in chapter 10. In a preset, the bots group sets economy per difficulty; the vanilla presets include bots_generic.inc there. ARSENAL milint checks bot data and Lua orders together with the rest of the mode (section 8).

In Gates of Hell

Bot blocks in a preset are named <difficulty>_<team> (see the presets subsection). No bot takes a seat in a cooperative game. Bots run in the server process in a Steam match. Everything else about bot scripts is in chapter 10.

7. Mission files (.mi)

A multiplayer map folder holds one .mi file per game mode: map/multi/<map>/<mode>.mi. If the file name does not match a game card, the log says the mission is skipped because the game type is undefined. A .mi file in your mod at the same path as a vanilla one replaces it. See chapter 13 for the folder layout.

An .mi file is a set of blocks:

{mission
	{Entity ...}
	{Tags ...}
	{Environment "multi/multi_01"}
	{Helpers
		{reinforcements ...}
		{waypoints ...}
		{zones ...}
		{triggers ...}
	}
	{Players {count 18} ...}
	{Fog 1}
	{EntityManager {Enabled}}
}

Helpers may hold waypoints, zones, triggers, events, edifices, cameras, tasks, reinforcements, vars, functions, mission_options and modifiers. Any other block name directly inside Helpers is an error at map load. Unknown keys inside one of these blocks, by contrast, are skipped without a message. The marker {# only marks an item as disabled; it does not make a comment. For a real comment, use ;. Field names in these files are case sensitive, while enum values (words such as open) and unit names are not. See Mission file blocks.

A multiplayer mission places spawn points, flags and ambient sound speakers, not units: players buy their units and bots bring theirs. Entity ids must be unique across the map file and every .mi file in the folder.

Triggers

This trigger ends the mission with a win once no living entity with the tag defenders is left (the entities term is true while its selector finds something, and !1 turns that round):

{triggers
	{"win_check"
		{condition
			{expression "!1"}
			{terms
				{"1.entities" {selector {tag defenders} {state "not dead"}}}
			}
		}
		{actions
			{"delay" {time 2}}
			{"gameover" {result win}}
		}
	}
}

Each trigger is a named block inside {Helpers {triggers ...}}. Triggers are checked every 0.25 seconds. A trigger can start disabled ({disabled}) until the trigger command switches it on. Without {autoreset} it runs its actions once, the first time its condition is true; with {autoreset} it switches off again when the condition becomes false and can fire again. The game writes {on} in saves for a trigger that has already fired. An empty {condition} is always true, which is how the vanilla multiplayer missions run their weather trigger once at the start. An empty {actions} block is fatal at map load. See Triggers.

Conditions

A condition holds numbered terms, each in its own block named "<number>.<term>", for example {"2.near" {...}}. A bare "2.near" without its own braces is fatal at map load (Block terminator expected!). The terms combine in one of three ways: all must be true (the default), any may be true ({type 1}), or an {expression "1 & (2 | 3)"} that refers to the terms by number. The expression accepts only digits, brackets, !, &, | and spaces; a tab or the words "and" or "or" make it an error, and the trigger never fires. The three operators have the same precedence and are worked out right to left, so 1 & 2 | 3 means 1 & (2 | 3): put brackets around every group. Every term is evaluated, even when the result is already known. See Conditions.

Inside if, while and case the condition is written inline instead: {condition {type rand} {value 0.1}}, where type names the term and its fields follow.

Condition terms: arrival, camera, cmp_i, crew, difficulty, entities, event, inventory, linked, mined, mission_option, mod, near, rand, see_actors, see_enemy, side, signal, task, trigger and waypoint_canmove. The term mod checks installed workshop mods, which is different from the (mod ..) text preprocessor directive. The near distance is in metres. See Condition terms.

Statements and commands

There are six statements: delay, if, loop, while, select and switch, with case and default inside switch (see Statements). Running a block in parallel is the thread command.

Selector fields, which pick the entities a command or term works on: type, tag, amount, zone, player, relation, state and mids (see Selectors).

Commands used in vanilla multiplayer maps include trigger, delay, event, delete, entity_state, reinforcement, actor_state, waypoint, environment, set_i, music, sound, objective_progress, task, timer, gameover (result win or loose, spelt that way; the numbers 2 and 1 are read too) and rt_function. Many more exist, such as spawn, board, actor_to_waypoint and con (which writes a line to game.log, useful for following your own triggers). The full list with fields is Commands.

A misspelt command or statement logs Unknown thread statement "<name>", and a misspelt term logs Unknown condition term "<name>". Both are fatal at map load, so read game.log after every change (see chapter 18).

In Gates of Hell

The .mi format is the same, but Gates of Hell missions use words this game does not know. A new command or term is fatal here at map load, and the new fields are unknown here, so check a carried-over mission with ARSENAL milint before you start it.

  • New commands: interface (switch the interface kind) and benchmark.
  • New fields: disable_random_spawn_position on spawn (the unit appears on the waypoint itself), cheating on actor_fire (scripted fire spends ammunition unless cheating 1; here it is always free), veterancy on actor_state (soldier rank 0 to 8), no_restart on animate, clone_places on placement (a clone takes along what sits in its seats) and stack on inventory.
  • Changed commands: air_state gains stop_engine; third_person_control keeps only lock; autoassign lost nearest; autosave saves only when the player's autosave option is on.
  • New condition terms: altitude and reinforcements_score.
  • Expressions accept the words and and or beside & and |. This game does not, so use only digits, brackets, !, & and | for a mission meant for both.
  • Selectors and variables: the selector switch user_player (units of whoever plays at this machine), and the variables @players:composition and @game:frontlinesphase.
  • Map points are sorted by name when the mission starts, which decides spawn order, and a waypoint can carry RandomPosition (a unit lands anywhere within its radius).
  • Text modes: while a mission loads, (mod "gametype:<type>"), (mod "gameclass:<class>") and (mod "training") sections apply, beside mp and coop.

The keys and commands only Gates of Hell has are listed under Gates of Hell only in the mission file reference.

8. Giving a map another mode

In the window, the Maps page does this: pick a map under "1. Pick a map", then under "2. Make my copy" choose the "Game mode", press "Preview (writes nothing)" and then "Write the copy". The page copies the map into your mod under a new name with that mode, can set the lobby name and switch bots on, and runs the map check afterwards. Copy and change a map walks through it.

On the command line:

ARSENAL maps list [--map map/multi/<m>]
ARSENAL maps mode --map map/multi/<m> --from combat --to battle_zones --out <mod folder> [--flags N] [--dry-run]

maps list shows the modes each multiplayer map has. maps mode (the same tool as ARSENAL mission-clone) copies a map's .mi from one mode to another. Between combat and battle_zones it adds or removes the flag points; for captureflag it adds a centre flag and its ring. For frontline and custom modes it copies the file as it is and marks it as needing hand work, because the structure differs. It runs milint on its result. Use --dry-run first to see what it would write. A map tagged [mod: <name>] in the list exists only in that mod's paks, and the game offers it only while that mod is enabled; hosting it otherwise fails with "no map".

ARSENAL mission-clone ... --with-mode <new> --title "My mode" also writes a new game card with {class <base mode>}, the map's map.info entry and the lobby title, so the new mode plays by its base mode's rules and the lobby lists the map under it. A mode cloned from combat gets bots switched on unless you add --no-bots. Whether the lobby shows the new title correctly, and whether flags placed by the tool capture as expected, is unconfirmed, so check both in a match.

ARSENAL misgen --map <map folder> --spec spec.json writes a captureflag mission from numbers (one flag, its zone and the spawn points of each side), together with the two capture areas captureflaga and captureflagb that this mode needs. Without them the mode crashes at the start.

Other helpers: ARSENAL misdiff <a> <b> gives a meaningful diff of two maps or .mi files, and ARSENAL milint <mod folder> [--game <game folder>] [--mods a,b] [-q] checks your mode .set against the .mi, the map.info player count, preset keys, budgets, payback tables, unit sets and limits, mission commands and terms, and bot Lua orders and bot data units. The Maps page "Check now" runs the same check.

To see the mode in the game, use the Play page ("Play a test match"): it checks and installs the mod, starts the game on a test map and reads game.log. Put multi/<map>:<mode> in its "Map" field, or run ARSENAL play <mod folder> --map multi/<map>:<mode> --dry and then without --dry. On a map other than the default test map the tool cannot judge the start by itself, so read the log yourself.

The quick way: in the Quick Guided Task row choose "I want to" "make" "a multiplayer game mode", or "change" "the rules of a multiplayer game mode". It asks for sides, goals, rules, money, alliances and units one step at a time and writes the files this chapter describes. See Use the Quick Guided Task and chapter 19.

In Gates of Hell

The Maps page, ARSENAL maps mode and the game mode recipe work on this game's maps. To bring the mode file of a Gates of Hell map over, give ARSENAL mission-clone the option --src <Gates of Hell resource folder> so it finds the files the mode includes. Gates of Hell flags are captured inside a drawn area (zoneId) instead of a circle; the tool turns each such flag into a circle of the same area, or of --flag-zone M metres (12 by default) when it finds no area. A long, thin area becomes a round one, so check the capture in a match.

9. The console and registry

The 64-bit build opens the in-game console (the key left of 1) only when it is started with the -console option; the editor build always has it, and the original executable does not take the option. Other command-line options include -safe, -no_mods, -replay and -record. The console commands and variables are listed in Reference 12. Key bindings live in profiles/<id>/keys.set and options in profiles/<id>/options.set; these are the player's own files, and mods do not ship them.

set/registry.reg includes files from registry/: resource_syncer.reg (the masks of the multiplayer data checksum, section 10), unit.reg, camera.reg, obstacles.reg, command.reg, hitpoints.reg and others. The file set/multiplayer/preload has entity "name" lines for units to load in advance.

In Gates of Hell

Useful console names that only Gates of Hell has: mp_game_set_victory and mp_game_set_personal_score (add points by host id), mp_game_list_players, mp_session_autoready (seated players are ready at once, for test lobbies), mp_rndSeed (a fixed match seed, for repeatable tests), <text> (an alert line on screen) and dbg_benchmark. mp_game_set_score adds to the team score there, not to the personal score. mp_deviceReplay, mp_slowdown and tcp_hostPortDS do not exist there.

10. How multiplayer stays in sync

The game uses deterministic lockstep with a relay host. Only commands cross the network. Each machine runs the whole simulation itself, and entity state is never sent. The host does not simulate on behalf of others; it relays commands, which come back stamped one round trip later, also to the player who sent them. Bots run on the host as if they were extra clients. There is no host migration: if the host quits, the match ends. If any other player quits, their units pass to the host. The 64-bit build waits for a player who lost the connection (the console variable mp_reconnectWait, 120 seconds by default), and a player who left can come back into the running match, and gets the units back, when the lobby allows rejoining (it does by default).

Joining

A lobby session carries the version, name, build checksum, mod list, preset, unit set and tuning values (random seed, sync period, sync level). Joining checks the version, the build checksum, the data checksum and the mod list. Different builds cannot play together.

The data checksum

The lobby compares a checksum over your game data, not the data itself. The game data tree covers /entity, /fx, /properties, /set and /sound; a separate map checksum covers /map/single, /map/bonus and /map/multi.

  • Excluded from the checksum: *.scc, *.txt, *.backup, *.bak, *.org, *.s_*, *.msg, *.lng, *.dds, *.ebm, *.bmp, *.tga and *.wav. Textures, sounds and texts are never compared.
  • Full content checked: everything under /set, and every .set, .inc, .ext, map file, .mi, .reg, .info, .def and .mdl.
  • Only the file size counts for the other files in these trees, such as .ply, .vol, .mtl, .anm, .pat and .lua.
  • Not compared at all: /script (which holds the bot Lua), /interface and /texture.

A binary edit that keeps the same file size passes the lobby and then goes out of sync during play. If you ship such a change, also change a text file or the mod folder name (unconfirmed advice). The mod list is compared by name; a player missing a listed mod gets a "required mods" message.

Sync checks

Every mp_syncPeriod milliseconds of game time (default 1000), every machine sends two checksums. The scene checksum covers game time, the shared random generator, entities and their positions, flags and bullets; at the default sync level 1 inventories are not part of it. The game checksum covers budgets, charge factors, command points and unit limits. If the scene checksum differs, that client is "desynced". If only the game checksum differs, the client is also classed as a "cheater", meaning the rules differ. The game then pauses, the host writes a snapshot into log/oos/<date>/, and the affected clients are removed. There is no live resync. The log reads "Desync detected on quant N" (see chapter 18).

Rules for staying in sync

  1. Everyone needs byte-identical gameplay data.
  2. The mod list and load order must match.
  3. The simulation must not read local state, such as the camera or the UI selection (the selection itself is part of the checksum).
  4. Randomness belongs only in simulation code, which uses a shared generator. Cosmetics such as sounds and particles use a separate local one. A rand in a script is safe only if every machine runs that same script at the same step in the same order. A script started by local state that rolls rand will desync.
  5. Avoid anything that depends on the order of a local list or on floating point differences between machines.
  6. The rules state must be identical: the presets must give the same budgets, charge factors, command points and limits everywhere.
  7. Scripts run once per simulation step (50 ms by default; a step lasts 20 to 65 ms and follows the slowest player).
  8. Hit and damage scripts are safe, because they run from simulated events on every machine.
  9. There is no host migration and no resync: if the host leaves, the match ends for everyone, and a desynced player is removed. A player who only lost the connection is waited for, and one who left may rejoin when the lobby allows it.
  10. Replays and saves depend on the current data, so changing data breaks old ones.
  11. Interaction script flags ({set "x"}) are limited to 128 different names in the whole game; the 129th gives an application error at load. Use tags for larger sets.

Testing with two players

For testing with two copies on one computer, the 64-bit executable accepts -instance N (N from 1 to 9). Each instance gets its own user folder, My Games/Men of War - Assault Squad 2 - instance N in Documents, with its own log/game.log and profiles, and its game port moves up by 10 times N; instances do not use Steam Cloud. A new instance starts with an empty mod list: your mods may be listed but are not mounted until that instance's options.set activates them. To join a session on the same computer, use the network adapter's address, not 127.0.0.1.

To compare two players' data, use:

ARSENAL mpsync --game <game folder> [--mods a,b] --export fp.json
ARSENAL mpsync --compare a.json b.json
ARSENAL mpsync --mod <mod folder>
