  • What the model, mesh, volume and animation files are, and which mistakes crash the game.
  • How a model is wired into a unit, and how the Models page edits it (SOEdit is optional).
  • How to hear, check and convert sounds, pictures and videos with the window's helpers and viewers and with ARSENAL sound.

All of this is soft code except the binary files themselves. Edit in your mod folder; the vanilla data is read-only. Text files here use CRLF line endings, UTF-8 string values and ASCII identifiers; leave old cp1251 bytes inside vanilla comments as they are (see Chapter 4 and Chapter 14).

1. Vision and detection

How far and how well a unit sees is data. The files are set/vision/settings.set and set/vision/vision.set, a wrapper that includes vision_presets.inc, vision_generic.inc and vision_main.inc. A new .inc file must be included from vision.set or from a file it includes. A vision definition accepts only these keys:

KeyMeaning
h_fov, v_fovHorizontal and vertical field of view, in degrees; h_fov 360 sees all round
uncoverDistance in metres within which the unit sees without facing the target
radiusBase sight radius in metres
wideThe power of the curve with which sight falls off towards the edge of the field of view; greater than 1 and at most 10
rulesTree of conditions with factors
modsFlat list of multipliers

Any other key is a hard "unexpected token" error that stops the game. A wide value outside its range logs "Curve power should be in range (1..10]". Do not use the same vision name twice. See Vision files.

Rules versus mods. The sight range is radius times a factor. rules is a tree in file order: siblings are alternatives and the first one that holds gives its factor, and its children then refine it. mods is a flat list in which every entry that holds multiplies the result. The conditions use the properties still, stand, squat, crawl, stealth, firing, cover and visible, plus custom terms that you define in settings.set (based on firing, actor or breed and a tag). A custom term defined twice, or an unknown property in a rule, is a hard error. Because the first sibling wins, the order of siblings matters: a soldier who is both still and squatting gets the factor of whichever of the two comes first.

A unit is given its vision in its definition:

{sensor
  {visor "main" {bone "basis"} {vision "tank_main-h"}}
}

Soldiers get theirs through breed perks, and the special-vision ability swaps the vision while a soldier aims through binoculars or a scope. The vision-mode extender allows exactly one of night, thermal or drone. See Sensor and visors.

Night. At night, sight is multiplied by the night factor (night_vision in the environment preset's light block; 0.13 when the preset does not set it). The factor is not applied to a target standing in light, such as a lamp, a burning vehicle or a flare, nor while a lightning flash is on screen. Most vanilla presets set night_vision 1, so their nights do not shorten sight. See Night.

Hearing is configured in sound folders with {signal shot 50} (see below): units within that radius hear the sound unless their hearingBias is larger.

Detection time. set/detect.set holds tables of seconds, by distance, for how long a target stays revealed after it was spotted or after it leaves view; they are not "time to detect". They do nothing when fog of war is off. Fog of war is a player video option, and a mod can only force it from a mission with the fog_mode command (see Chapter 12). See Detection and fog of war.

In Gates of Hell

  • set/detect.set has its reveal tables per unit tag; the first tag a unit has that the file names decides. Assault Squad 2 knows only soldiers and everything else.
  • The fog of war option is read when a scene starts; changing it during a game takes effect at the next one.
  • The sight grid is finer (5 units a cell instead of 7), and a sight test aims at the centres of the target's volumes instead of random points, so the same scene gives the same answer every time.
  • The fog opens for your own units and for allies that you can select or that carry the tag no_select_visor.
  • In thermal view, decals, particles and scenery show only when their material has EmitsHeat.

2. Sound

Sound names are paths under /sound/: either a folder or a file. There are no aliases. A weapon's fireSound maps to weapon/shot/... and reloadSound to weapon/reload/.... A name that matches nothing logs "unknown sound file" and plays silence.

  • Only .wav files are played. .ogg and .mp3 files in sound folders are ignored. Use mono, 44100 Hz, 16-bit PCM or IMA ADPCM, as the vanilla files are; sounds placed in the world should be mono.
  • When a name is a folder, a random file is picked each time, and every file plays once before any repeats.
  • Each folder may contain folder.set. Its keys are Tag, Loudness, Distance, MinDistance, MaxDistance, Volume, Signal and SignalPeriod; any other key is an error. A folder inherits these from its parent folder, with one exception: a sub-folder with its own folder.set starts its distances again from the default loudness class, so repeat Loudness (or Distance) there. A folder with no folder.set anywhere above it gets tiny built-in distances (silent beyond 5 m) and the general group. The vanilla gun folder has:
{sound
	{loudness "shoot loud"}
	{signal shot 50}
	{volume 1.2}
}
  • Tag picks one of four groups, effects, emotions, speech or environment; any other tag (such as main_environment) falls into a general group. ARSENAL fxlint warns about this.
  • sound/sound.set holds the loudness classes (minimum and maximum distance and a priority) and the share of sound channels each group gets. A new class there can be used at once by any folder.set.
  • At most three copies of one file play at once, and a copy that would start within 50 ms of another at the same point is dropped.
  • The sample rate and the group list cannot be changed by data.

Music is in music/ and is played by the mission music command. See Sound.

Three more rules that cost people time: sound/sound.set must have a loudness class named default, or the game crashes when it reads the first folder.set; a folder.set that names a loudness class sound.set does not have uses default; and an .ogg, .mp3 or .flac file renamed to .wav stays silent.

In the window. The Look & Sound page (tab Models & Sim) has the sound helpers:

  • "Sound of this weapon": type a weapon name and press "Find sound". It shows the sound name the weapon's file uses, the folder and the files in the game, and plays them as the game does. Weapons built by macros may not show.
  • "Check a wav file": reads a .wav and says whether the game can play it.
  • "Make this sound playable in game": turns a sound that is already in your mod folder into IMA ADPCM (small, like most game sounds) or 16-bit PCM. Mono or stereo stays as it is. "Write the sound into my mod" writes it where you say.
  • "ffmpeg recipe (make a safe wav)": two command lines for the free ffmpeg program, one for a 16-bit mono wav and one for IMA ADPCM.

A .wav opened in the window's sound viewer (see File viewers) plays as the game would play it: at a distance and direction you choose, with your own volume settings or the game defaults, and with the muffling and fall-off of the game's sound library (close to the game, not exact). "Next as the game picks" plays the files of the folder in the shuffled order the game uses. "Burst test" fires the sound again and again like a machine gun, with the game's limits: at most 3 copies of one file at a time, a copy within 50 ms of another dropped, checked every 50 ms. "Stretch to seconds" shows how a sound fits a set time; the game does this only for reload sounds. "Names that play it" lists every sound name that reaches the file, and the notes say what the game will do with it.

The same play model is a command:

ARSENAL sound resolve weapon/shot/gun/85to100_cal/88mm_flak41
ARSENAL sound info <file or name> --distance 100
ARSENAL sound decode <file or name> --out my.wav
ARSENAL sound sweep --mod mods/mymod

resolve shows the folder, files and settings a sound name reaches (a weapon's fireSound gets weapon/shot/ in front). info gives the header, notes, folder settings and how the game plays it; --bearing, --ambient and --profile (your own volumes) change the case. play plays it, decode writes a plain 16-bit wav (never inside the game folder), and sweep reads every wav of the game or your mod and lists the files that will not play.

The quick way: the Quick Guided Task "I want to make" or "change" then "a sound" (or "a voice set") covers the wav files and their conversion, the folder settings, the loudness class and a weapon's fire or reload sound. See Use the Quick Guided Task.

In Gates of Hell

  • A sub-folder keeps the distances it inherits from its parent; only the top folder starts from the default loudness class. In Assault Squad 2 a sub-folder's own folder.set must repeat them (see above).
  • A folder's Volume also scales sounds that do not come from a place, such as interface sounds and weather loops. In Assault Squad 2 it does not.
  • A sound placed in the world from a folder with no minimum distance is stopped, and the log says "An ambient sound ... not marked as ambient, otherwise minDistance and maxDistance are required".
  • /sound/filters/filters.set defines named filter chains (bandpass, lowpass, parameq) that every sound from a place goes through. An unknown filter type crashes the game.
  • The console command snd_restart restarts the sound system and loads the sounds again, so you can hear a change without a restart.
  • Sounds are probably still .wav only (not confirmed).

3. Environment presets

An environment preset is one file in set/environment/ (sub-folders are read too); its name is the file name. A map picks it with its {Environment ...} entry, and a mission can switch it with the environment {name time apply} command. The allowed blocks are light, wind, haze, sky, weather, thunder, video_overlay, grain, dof and glow. A block you leave out keeps its defaults, and an unknown block is an error. See Environment presets.

Practical rules:

  • Only one blend between presets runs at a time. A preset name that does not exist does nothing and says nothing.
  • There is no day and night clock; the time of day is whatever preset is active.
  • weather and thunder are off unless the block has {enable}. Thunder also needs a sound, or no strike ever happens. At most 2000 rain or snow drops are drawn.
  • Weather affects gameplay only through the interaction conditions {if rain} and {if sunlight}, which are evaluated when a script runs (see Chapter 11). Haze does not reduce what units see. Wind moves only water and particles that follow the wind.

In Gates of Hell

  • The wind block takes direction, main_strength, detail_strength and height_amplification, and wind also sways vegetation. The Assault Squad 2 keys speed and amplitude are not read, so an Assault Squad 2 preset has no wind there.
  • The grain block is accepted but does nothing.
  • A map can have Haze with boundary and altitude parts, and a preset can set sky_haziness. The 64-bit game refuses a map with that Haze entry.
  • A blend between presets runs at the same pace at any frame rate.

4. Effects (FX)

An FX is an ordinary entity .def whose root block is {fx ...}. Inside it you add views: SpriteView, ParticleView, LightView and DecalView. Scripts spawn an effect with {spawn "fx_name"}. There is no {emit} action in interaction scripts; using it is an error ("unknown action"), and ARSENAL fxlint reports it. See Effects (FX).

Limits:

  • At most 40000 particles exist at once. Extra ones are silently not created.
  • set/fxmanager.set defines groups with countLimit and timeLimit; when a group is full the oldest effect is removed first. Decal-like effects and tracer effects must be listed there, or the game logs "must be defined in fxmanager.set" and drops them.
  • set/entitymanager.set limits how many corpses, wrecks, flying shells and similar objects stay on the map, and how they are removed. Higher limits cost frame time.
  • Craters are land_patch entities. Surface-specific hit effects are scripts in set/interaction_terrain/effects/, one file per ground material.

Level of detail (LOD)

LOD files are level_of_detail.set (the normal camera), level_of_detail_manual.set (direct control) and level_of_detail_zoom.set (looking through sights). Distances are in map units and must strictly increase from level to level. A flag such as off carries over into every later level. An entity picks its LOD class with {lodclass "name"}. See Level of detail and rendering keys.

Texture variants

A texture T may have variants in files named T#variant.dds, such as armor#2a.dds beside armor.dds. An action {tex_mod "name"} switches to a variant, and the model's {TexMods} block can pick one by option, such as a season.

Camera

Camera parameters live in set/registry/camera.reg. Camera shake stays off unless the console variable cam_shake is not zero. The third-person camera values are not in a file you can change.

In Gates of Hell

  • Sprite views take UseHQ and Halo {Scale {Min} {Max}}. The 64-bit game stops on both with "unexpected token", so remove them from an effect you bring over.
  • Lamps use light_bone, break_fx and break_bone, and the extender weaponlight gives a weapon a light. Assault Squad 2 lamps use its own numbered scheme.
  • There is a fourth LOD file, level_of_detail_scenario.set, and the LOD files take minzoom, grassthinnerdepth, grassthinnerpower and shadowfallofffactor, with the level flags noparallax, nobump, nospecular and parallaxstepsk. The 64-bit game stops on these, so do not copy a Gates of Hell LOD file over.
  • A texture variant also finds its frames in the common textures. A skin variant can also swap the mesh: variant camo shows tank#camo.ply when that file exists. In Assault Squad 2 a #variant.ply file is never used.
  • The third person camera is set in /set/tp_control.set (see Chapter 15, Gates of Hell: summary). The field of view key is camera/main/fov. Camera shake is a player option, and the console command cam_shake is gone.

5. Model files

A unit's look is made of several files. They are found by their path in the game's virtual file system, so a mod may ship only the files it changes and reuse the rest from the game.

ExtensionWhat it isKind
.mdlThe model: bone tree, meshes, hit volumes, animationsText
.plyA mesh, the shape that is drawnBinary, starts with EPLY (or BPLY)
.volA hit volume, the shape shells hitBinary, starts with EVLM
.anmAn animationBinary, starts with EANM
.mtlA material: how a mesh surface is drawnText
.ebm, .texTexture descriptionsText
.dds, .tgaTexturesStandard picture formats
.wavSoundStandard
.aviVideoSee below

Binary files are little-endian, and the game decides the format by the file extension. Sizes and positions are in model units, 20 to the metre.

The model file (.mdl)

The .mdl is text. It holds one {Skeleton} with the bones, and may hold {Volume}, {Obstacle} and {Area} blocks. Each bone shows its mesh with {VolumeView "x.ply"} (despite the name, this is the drawn mesh, not a hit volume). A bone in a vanilla tank looks like this:

{bone revolute "turret"
	{parameters "ID=turret;"}
	{speed 0.01}
	{Position -2.94537 1.28551 12.6135}
	{VolumeView "turret.ply"}
	{bone revolute "gun_rot"
		{parameters "ID=gun_rot;"}
		{limits -8 22}
		{speed 0.01}
		...
	}
}
  • Bone types are revolute (turns about its own axis), prizmatic (slides), socket and planarsocket (turn about two axes), and wild; a bone without a type is fixed. Any other type word is "unexpected token".
  • {speed} and {limits low high} (degrees) are valid only on a typed bone. On a plain bone they give "unexpected token", and {speed 0} logs "Zero speed in ik-bone".
  • {Position}, {Orientation} and {Matrix34} place the bone relative to its parent, applied in the order they are written.
  • {parameters "..."} holds entries such as ID= (the vehicle part the mesh belongs to, used for part highlighting and components) and WheelRadius=.
  • {LODView} lists one view per level of detail, and {OFF} hides the bone from that level on.

Keep the standard bone names (body, turret, gun_rot, gun, seat01, wheell*, trackl, fx* and so on), because the unit's .def and the macros it includes look them up. A renamed bone shows up as "Bone X not found" (the setting is ignored) or a fatal "unexpected token". See .mdl and bone (model).

Animations in the model. An {animation} block on the root bone or on any bone declares sequences by name, such as {sequence "open" {resume}} or {sequence "repair" {file "turret_r.anm"} {speed 0.8}}. A sequence without {file} loads <name>.anm from the model's folder. Options are speed, resume (keep the last pose), store, movement, pinback, smooth, autostart, duration, rotate, dynamicspeed and blend with pose; any other word is "unexpected token". The .def and scripts start sequences by these names. See sequence.

Bone changes from the .def. A .def can change bones of its model, for example {bone "gun_rot" {limits -5 15}}, but only after its {Extension} line, or the game logs "Bone modifiers must be placed after skeleton load".

Meshes (.ply)

A mesh is a list of chunks: BNDS (the bounding box, which must be the real extent), SKIN (bone names, for skinned meshes such as soldiers), one MESH header per material part, then VERT (the vertices) and INDX (the triangles). The chunks have no stored lengths, so one wrong field makes everything after it unreadable ("Invalid chunk in .PLY file"). Triangles use 16-bit indices, so one mesh holds at most 65535 vertices, and one skinned part can use at most 25 bones. Each part names its material; ship every .mtl the mesh names (or a .materials file beside it), or the game crashes while loading. This holds for a copied mesh too: copy the .mtl beside the .ply. See .ply.

Hit volumes (.vol)

A .vol holds the chunks VERT, INDX and SIDE. SIDE gives each triangle a side number, which picks the armour thickness from the unit's {thickness} list: 1 front, 2 top, 3 left, 4 right, 5 rear and 6 bottom. Every triangle needs a side number. Hit volumes defined in the .mdl and in the .def are merged by name; a volume without a shape, or one on a bone that does not exist, is dropped without a message, and its armour is lost. Reference 7, Armour, volumes and damage describes the {Volume} block and the thickness list.

Animations (.anm)

An animation starts with EANM and a file version, which must be version 3 or later (the game's own files are version 6). It lists its bones (at most 255) and then the frames (at least one). Frames between two key frames are interpolated, and a bone the animation does not key keeps its rest pose. A track for a bone that is not in the skeleton is skipped without a message, so keep bone names exactly as in the .mdl. See .anm.

Materials and textures

A material file names its type and its textures. A vanilla tank material is:

{material bump
	{diffuse "t34s"}
	{bump "$/model/t34s_bp"}
	{specular "$/model/t34s_sp"}
	{color "229 229 229 0"}
	{blend none}
}

Types are simple, bump, layered, envmap, ocean and gui.text. Texture names carry no extension; a bare name is looked up next to the model. See .mtl and textures.

For a texture name, a .tex or .ebm description wins (.tex before .ebm). Otherwise the game tries .dds, .tga, .bmp, .jpg and .png in that order and the last one found wins, so a stray .tga next to your .dds replaces it (unconfirmed for the order between them in play). DDS rules: DXT1 to DXT5 and 32-bit are fine; the DX10 header and volume textures are not supported ("DXT10 textures are not supported"), ATI2 (BC5) gives "Unknown DDS picture format", and a compressed texture needs a width and height divisible by 4. Save new DDS files with mip maps. See .ebm and .tex. The window's picture viewer shows a texture with its channels and mipmaps and says whether the game can load it; its rules are listed in Chapter 15, Icons from your own PNG.

The quick way for a new paint: the Look & Sound page's "Camo helper" writes the {TexMods} line for a new option (for example {"Autumn" "aut"}) and tells you the variant file to paint, name#variant.dds. The Quick Guided Task "a skin or camouflage" does the same and can get you a game texture to paint.

Video

Video .avi files use an Xvid or other MPEG-4 Part 2 picture (H.264 does not play) and an MP3 sound track. The exact conversion settings that work are unconfirmed. See .avi.

The window's video viewer (see File viewers) reads an .avi the way the game does and says for "Picture in the game" and "Sound in the game" whether each plays, with the reason. The rules it checks:

  • The game decodes only MPEG-4 Part 2 pictures (XVID, DIVX, FMP4); H.264 and others show garbage or nothing.
  • Stream 0 must be the picture and stream 1 the sound. A file with one stream plays without sound.
  • The sound plays only as MP3.
  • Frames inside rec lists are skipped, and the idx1 index is not used.
  • When video and sound have different lengths, they drift apart.

When the file will not play, the viewer gives an ffmpeg command line that makes one the game plays. "Play in my video player" opens the file in the computer's own player, after asking.

In Gates of Hell

The file kinds are the same, but Gates of Hell reads more in them and fails more gently. A Gates of Hell model brought to Assault Squad 2 must lose what the 64-bit game does not know; see Bring a unit from Gates of Hell.

  • Textures. BC5 (ATI2) DDS files load; Assault Squad 2 logs "Unknown DDS picture format" and shows nothing, so convert them to DXT5 or 32-bit. A texture that exists but cannot be read shows a checker pattern and the log says "Unable to create image from resource ... Using checker"; a missing one logs "Texture not found, using the checker". A picture listed twice in a common texture stops the game ("Duplicate bitmap in common texture"). Under interface/ and map/ only name02 or name_02 counts as a frame of name.
  • Materials. New .mtl keywords: lightmap, No_Outlines and Dxt1OpacityFix, and on bump materials specular_intensity, gloss_scale and full_specular. The 64-bit game stops on them. The same parallax_scale draws half as deep in Gates of Hell. EmitsHeat is a flag there with no number.
  • A missing material does not crash: the mesh loads grey and the log says "Material not found ... Using dummy texture." In Assault Squad 2 the same model crashes the game.
  • Animations. New animation types blendspace and aimset, sequence options additive and events, and a sequence file that names a folder picks one .anm of that folder at random. Two animations with the same name are an error ("Animation with duplicate name"). The 64-bit game knows none of these. Gates of Hell .anm files are version 6.1, which the 64-bit game reads with the same layout.
  • Skeleton. The bone name ##skeleton_views## is reserved, and bones may have the parameter Land, which the 64-bit game does not know.
  • Video is decoded by a newer Xvid; the format rules are the same.

6. Wiring a model into a unit

A vehicle has a chain of references. The unit's .def names its model with {Extension "x.mdl"}. The .mdl names a mesh for each bone, each mesh names its .mtl, and the .mtl names the textures. Sequences name .anm files, and {Volume} blocks name .vol files. Everything is joined by name only. Any referenced file that is missing ends the game with "Resource not found". A path in a model file is read from the folder of the file that names it, unless it starts with /.

Broken and destroyed views. When a part is broken, the game loads the entity <id>_x, and when it is destroyed, <id>_xx. Bone names in those models must match the live model.

Private copies. When you change a model that other units share, copy it under your own name first: <unit>.mdl with volumes <unit>__<vol>.vol, and point your unit's {Extension} at it. Nothing is then changed by accident for a vanilla unit.

In Gates of Hell

Some bone and animation names the game looks for differ, so a model moved between the games may load but not move right.

  • Track rollers are numbered bones roller_01, roller_02 and so on, each with its own roller_NN_joint; the single Assault Squad 2 bone roller is not found. An Assault Squad 2 tank in Gates of Hell has running gear that does not follow the ground, and the other way round no roller moves.
  • A wheel whose parent bone is named exactly suspension rides the terrain.
  • Soldiers aim with the bones ik_lng, ik_lat and ik_socket instead of ik_updown.
  • The empty-hand idle animation is stand_idle_empty; Assault Squad 2 uses stand_idle_empty_1 to _4.

7. The Models page and SOEdit

Mesh, volume and animation files are binary: change them with an editor, never by hand. The Models page (tab Models & Sim) is that editor. It opens every file of a unit's model for editing in the window; the game files are only read, and Save writes the files you changed into your mod at the same paths.

  1. Pick your mod folder ("Pick mod folder"), then find the unit by name, or give the path of a .mdl and press "Use this file" (or "Browse...").
  2. The page lists the "Files of" the model in groups (model, meshes, volumes, animations, materials, textures), each marked as in your mod, only in the game, or not found.
  3. Make your changes on the page's own tabs. Undo and Redo work for every change (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y).
  4. Press Save (Ctrl+S). It first lists the files it will write, what a save would lose and what the file checks found; "Write these files" writes them. The old copies of files already in your mod are kept in .arsenal/model-edit/backup in your mod first.

The page's own tabs:

TabWhat you do there
ModelThe 3D view of the model, the file list and the Shot tool.
AnimationPlay an animation in the 3D view frame by frame; set and delete a bone's key at a frame; insert, delete or stretch frames, reverse, make it loop, add a closing frame; add, rename, copy or remove a bone's track; a timeline to drag keys, copy ranges and fill between two keys with an ease; the model's sequences.
Skeleton"Bones of the model": add, delete, move, duplicate and rename bones (also inside the animations), joint type, place, limits and speed, the bone's mesh, levels of detail and sequences.
Volumes"Collision volumes": add a box, cylinder or sphere, or one made from the bone's mesh; shape, place, tags, component and material; "Apply thickness" sets the armour in mm per side; polyhedron .vol files; "Obstacles and areas".
Meshes and materialsPut a mesh on a bone or take it off; move, resize, mirror, flip faces, make normals and tangents, join close vertices, levels of detail, skin bones, join or split meshes; "Save as OBJ"; "Bring in a mesh" from an .obj or .ply; set textures and make materials.
FilesSave, "Check before saving", "Undo all changes", "Save as" or "Save a copy" under a new name, the file list, "The model as text" (and "Open in Editor"), Export to a folder or zip, a draft copy every few minutes, Preferences and Keys. The Start card reopens a recent model or makes a "New model" from a template.
Armor"Armour: thickness, map and shot test" and "Behind the armour".

The 3D view shows one or four panes, with the model's look, its collision volumes or both, and switches for meshes, volumes and bones. Q, W, E and R pick the select, move, turn and scale handles for the selected bone or volume.

When an animation is opened, the page says its file version: version 6 is the kind the game ships, older kinds (mostly soldier animations) still load, and a very old one is refused.

SOEdit is an outside model and animation editor. Everything on the page works without it; the fold "External SOEdit (optional)" on the Model tab is for those who still want it. "Copy into my mod" copies the model, meshes, volumes, animations and materials to the same paths in your mod (files already there are kept; textures go to a view cache, not into your mod). "Open in SOEdit" opens your mod's copy. After you save and close SOEdit, "Check what changed" compares your files with the copies taken before and lists what was lost on saving, such as a setting inside a bone or volume, a whole block of the model file, comments, or an animation saved in another file version. If SOEdit is not on the computer, the card at the foot of the page offers "Get SOEdit and open it", which asks first, downloads the package and checks it. The command way:

ARSENAL soedit locate
ARSENAL soedit stage <unit> --out <mod folder> --dry
ARSENAL soedit open <mod folder>/.arsenal/soedit/<model>.stage.json
ARSENAL soedit check <mod folder>/.arsenal/soedit/<model>.stage.json

The animation changes of the Animation tab also exist as a command: ARSENAL soedit ops anim <operation> <file.anm>, with --dry to preview. ARSENAL soedit ops alone lists every operation, including ones for meshes (ply) and volumes (vol).

The Armor tab shows the armour thickness of each part of a vehicle and tests a gun and shell against it; see Chapter 9, section 11 and Chapter 17.

The quick way: the Quick Guided Task "I want to make" or "change" then "a model" copies a game model or brings your files, then changes bones, meshes, volumes, animations and the unit's definition. See Use the Quick Guided Task and Edit a model or an animation.

See also: Chapter 19, Models & Sim.

In Gates of Hell

Under the GoH button the Models page opens, edits and saves Gates of Hell models as well, with the built-in editor or SOEdit; only its Armor part is switched off there, because Gates of Hell works out armour in another way. It reads a Gates of Hell .anm (version 6.1) like any other. A model taken from Gates of Hell must first lose the animation types and bone keys the 64-bit game does not know (section 5); Bring a unit from Gates of Hell shows how ARSENAL does that.

8. Checking headers and effects

ARSENAL binhdr <game folder> --mods mymod
ARSENAL fxlint mods/mymod --game <game folder>

binhdr reads the header of each .ply, .anm, .dds, .vol, .mdl, .ebm and .wav, and checks across files: does each volume the .def names exist in the .mdl, does each animated bone exist, does a stray .tga hide a .dds. fxlint finds sound tags the game does not know, unknown interaction actions such as emit, weather or thunder without {enable}, thunder without a sound, and tracers missing from the FX manager list. The Art check on the Look & Sound page checks pictures, meshes, animations and sounds of your mod.

See also: Chapter 18: Testing and Logs for the log lines these files cause, and Check a mod, fix it, read the log.

Gates of Hell: summary

The Gates of Hell notes in this book have not been tested in a running game. Check them in your own game before you depend on them.

SectionGates of HellIn short
1. Vision and detectiondiffersReveal tables per unit tag, finer sight grid, no_select_visor, EmitsHeat for thermal view
2. SounddiffersSub-folders keep distances, folder volume on all sounds, filters.set, snd_restart
3. Environment presetsdiffersNew wind keys, grain ignored, map haze
4. Effects (FX)differsNew sprite and lamp keys, more LOD keys, mesh variants, tp_control.set
5. Model filesdiffersBC5 textures, checker and grey dummy instead of crashes, new material and animation keys
6. Wiring a model into a unitdiffersNumbered rollers, suspension bone, new aiming bones
7. The Models page and SOEditdiffersNo model page for Gates of Hell; its .anm files read fine
8. Checking headers and effectsnot mappedbinhdr --paks <folder> also reads Gates of Hell paks

Pitfalls

  • Unknown keys in a vision definition are fatal.
  • Misspelled sound names are silent.
  • A stray .tga can hide your .dds.
  • A missing .mtl crashes the game at load.
  • Removing or renaming a standard bone breaks the .def.
  • {speed} or {limits} on a bone without a type is fatal.
  • An animation track for a bone the model does not have does nothing.
  • A volume whose bone is gone loses its armour without a message.
  • FX that are not listed in the FX manager are dropped.
  • DX10-format DDS files do not load.
  • Model files under entity/ are compared between players: everyone in a match needs the same version of your mod.

Next: Chapter 17: Balance, Pricing and Gameplay

17. Balance, Pricing and Gameplay

The short way: Change armour and see the result gives the steps for reading and changing a vehicle's armour and testing a shell against it. This chapter explains what a number change does in play, where prices and unlock times live, and which tools show a change before you play it. The armour, volume and material keys are in Reference 7, Armour, volumes and damage.

What you will learn

  • How the main mechanics feel to a player, so that you know what a number change will do.
  • A table of common data changes and their effect.
  • How multiplayer prices, unlock timers, limits and bots are set up, and where each number lives.
  • A balance workflow with the Balance page, the armour simulator and the command-line tables.
  • The rules that bite when you tune data.

Some player-side behaviour here comes from the game manual and common play rather than from the game files; those statements carry "(unconfirmed)".

1. Mechanics as the player sees them

Armour and anti-tank

Whether a shell goes through depends on four things: the shell's penetration at that range, the armour thickness, the angle of the hit (a sloped plate counts as thicker), and the distance (penetration falls with range). There is no dice roll in this test. Armour-piercing (AP) shells suit lighter armour, armour-piercing composite rigid (APCR) shells suit heavy armour, and high-explosive (HE) shells suit infantry, guns and buildings. Hits to the side, rear or engine are the most effective. Shell tip colours in the game are green for HE, grey for AP, black for APCR and white for smoke.

A shell that fails may bounce off (ricochet). For steel the chance is 1 for a shell that grazes the plate at up to 15 degrees, 0.6 at 30 degrees, 0.3 at 45, 0.15 at 60 and 0 from 75 degrees, counted from the plate's surface; values in between are interpolated. See ricochet and chance.

When the player aims in direct control, the reticle shows the distance on the left and the weapon's penetration at that range on the right. That number is the quickest way to see a data change in the game.

Other behaviours worth knowing:

  • Crew roles swap automatically when a vehicle is short of crew; a lone crewman drives, loads and fires one at a time (unconfirmed).
  • A crew-less or abandoned vehicle or gun can be captured by sending a soldier in and repairing it. One big HE round can kill a whole crew and leave the vehicle intact and capturable.
  • Damaged wheels or tracks stop a vehicle until they are repaired (unconfirmed).
  • Anti-tank guns should be set to return fire or have their HE removed, so that they shoot AP at armour.
  • Towed guns cannot fire while towed.

Infantry

Infantry are the backbone. Prone is the strongest posture (a smaller target and more accurate), cover and bushes hide soldiers until they fire, and sandbags stop small arms but not anti-tank grenades or tank shells. Squads share ammunition. Direct control (the E key) is the core skill because the AI aims poorly with guns.

Soldiers gain rank from their score, which rises with kills. A multiplayer soldier in vanilla reaches the five ranks at a score of 2, 4, 12, 24 and 40 (4, 8, 24, 48 and 80 outside multiplayer). Only the highest rank reached applies; its bonuses (health, reload, weapon skill and others) are in set/ability/veterancy.set.

Artillery and support weapons

Mortars and howitzers fire indirectly; they are best against fixed positions rather than moving infantry. Howitzers have limited traverse and need turning. Rocket artillery covers areas. Mines use contact fuses; dynamite uses a timer. Heavy ammunition crates resupply artillery; light crates resupply infantry and machine guns (unconfirmed for the exact split).

Interface signs

Floating icons show squad members as dots coloured by health, a flashing red icon means out of ammunition, and orange or yellow stripes mark anti-tank weapons. In multiplayer, friendly fire is a lobby option and is on by default, so your own losses can add to the enemy's score.

In Gates of Hell

Several rules a player feels are different, so a balance that works in one game does not carry over as it is.

  • Repair needs a repair kit in the hand, for a mechanic too, and uses one kit per part. A vehicle looks for kits in its own stock first, then with allies within 20 m. Damaged parts are repaired too, not only broken ones, and the time follows the health lost.
  • A captured vehicle no longer pays its price back to the buyer.
  • A squad the player forms can have up to 12 soldiers (Assault Squad 2: 10).
  • Under direct control a gun fires only at a target within its range and not inside its MinRange (unless the weapon has UnlimitedRangeTPC), and a soldier does not fire while crawling, swimming or running.
  • Building fortifications costs the squad's resources and its speed follows the fortification ability.

See Chapter 15, Direct control and the third person camera.

2. What a data change does

The damage after a hit is mostly decided by interaction scripts, not by the game program (see Chapter 11: Interaction Scripts).

You changeEffect in game
A gun's penetration tablePenetration at each distance is interpolated in straight lines between the table points, and the table ends five metres past the gun's range.
An armour number in the unit's armor macro or areaA non-zero number overrides the volume's own {thickness} on that side. The first area that covers a volume wins. Left and right share the area's side number, and the bottom uses the top number.
pierce_dur in the tank armour macroIt sets durability {pierce {koef ...}} for hull and turret. Vanilla passes 999, so AP shells practically never break those areas; only blast does.
A shell's {tag}Moves it to another row of the damage scripts (crew kill chances, internal damage, fire, drive and breech breaks).
HE carried in a vehicleRaises the cook-off risk; carrying more than the vehicle class allows multiplies the chance. Keep the total ammunition load the same when you edit a loadout.
A material's ricochet tableChanges the chance that a failed shell bounces. In the angle table, an out larger than in logs "Invalid ricochet angle" and is clamped to in.
A soldier's accuracy-by-motion presetRaising the penalties forces "stop to shoot".
Vision and stealth valuesLonger spotting and harder hiding (see Chapter 16).
Resupply macrosA regeneration of 0 makes ammunition boxes and trucks run out.

Three more rules:

  • HE blast does not weaken with the distance the shell flew. Blast energy falls in a straight line from the centre of the explosion to zero at the outer radius, and only volumes that keep the blast flag of able take any. HE is therefore good against distant guns.
  • Blast damage reaches each volume slightly later, at about 15 metres per second, so damage is delayed per volume.
  • A new weapon's ammunition needs the right tag, or the infantry damage scripts fall into their default branch.

An ability level written as a string such as "150%" is just a name that the ability's data file defines. An undefined level string gives the soldier the top level, a silent buff, so check the spelling. ARSENAL statsheet reports it.

3. Multiplayer economy and prices

Multiplayer games are described by presets (in set/multiplayer/games/presets*.inc). A preset sets the unit set by year tags, the command point (CP) cap, the manpower (MP) at start and at the top, unit limits, the budget growth, payback, the purchase buttons, bots and charge factors. See Chapter 12 for game modes and Budgets for the budget keys.

Prices are paid from a budget. The vehicle budget pays in MP for the infantry and vehicle buttons; the hero budget pays in special points, with a fixed start and no growth. The two are not on one scale, so never compare a hero price with an MP price.

Unlock timers and limits

A unit unlocks charge x chargeFactor x (1 - fore) seconds after the game starts, where charge is the unit's own cooldown, chargeFactor is the first tag match in the preset's list (otherwise *, otherwise 1), and fore is the share of the cooldown already done at the start (1 is ready at once, 0 is one full cooldown, a negative value is longer). After you buy a unit, every unit of its group restarts at charge x chargeFactor. The lobby test mode sets the charge factors to zero, so everything is available at once.

unitLimits counts purchases, so a lost unit is never refunded and limits fill for good. Separators matter: unitLimits entries are separated by semicolons, while payback lists are separated by tabs. A comma or other wrong separator silently drops the entries after it (the log says "Unread data"). Unknown keys in multiplayer data are skipped too, so a typo gives no error.

Bots

Vanilla bots ignore unlock timers. A preset can make them obey and can scale payback by difficulty. Bot purchases are described per nation in script/multiplayer/bot.data.lua (see Chapter 10: AI and Bots).

Where the price lives

The vanilla buy list is set/multiplayer/units/common.set, which includes soldiers.set, squads.set and vehicles.set; vehicles.set holds the macros and the nations' vehicles_<nation>.set files hold the vehicles.

  • Soldiers: soldiers.set gives each soldier type its {cp}, {score} and {cw} (capture weight), through one define per type, such as tankman, used for every side.
  • Squads: squads.set builds each squad card with a macro such as ("squad_with2types" side(rus) name(home_guards) c(30) ... level(1) cost(60) f(-1.0)), where c() is the cooldown, cost() the price, level() the rank needed and f() the fore.
  • Vehicles: each entry looks like {"m1_57mm" ("vs" c(0) t(all cannon mediumcan) s(usa) n(2) g(c5) sc(11.25) b(v2) cw(2) cp(10)) {level 1} {cost 225} {fore 1.0}}: cooldown, tags, side, crew, group, score, button, capture weight and CP, then the rank, the price and the fore.

score is the kill score: when a unit dies, the killer's team gets it. In vanilla a vehicle's score is about its cost divided by 20, and the ratio of score to cost decides how profitable a kill is. See Units.

The quick way: the Quick Guided Task "I want to change" then "prices of an army" changes every price of an army, command points, score and money rules in one go, and "what bots buy and how they play" covers bot buying, bot money and cooldowns. See Use the Quick Guided Task.

In Gates of Hell

The buy card and the preset are read differently, and most keys of one game are silently ignored by the other.

  • No rank lock and no head start. level and fore are not read. A unit's cooldown is a block {charge {delay N} {interval N}}: the first wait, once at the start of the game, is delay x chargeFactor x chargeDelay, and after each purchase the group waits interval x chargeFactor x charge, where chargeDelay and charge come from the preset's balancing. Units of group none do not share a cooldown.
  • Squad prices are summed. A squad costs its own cost plus, for each member, count x member cost x squad_cost_factor, rounded up to round_multiple. The buy button shows that sum. A card's cost is 0 when it is left out (Assault Squad 2: 1).
  • Kill score from the price. A member is worth its own score when that is above 0, otherwise its cost x score_factor (0.05 by default), then x the preset's unitScore.
  • More card keys: cost_ap, cost_sp, enabled (probably replaced by the game's own content check, so it has no effect; not confirmed), not_for_player_sale, conditions, action, doctrine and research stages. A card that is not_for_player_sale or whose group is waiting cannot be bought.
  • Preset balancing (balancingFactorBonus) has seven keys: cp, mpStart, mpFinish, payback, periodicFactor, chargeDelay and charge. There is no mp; the Assault Squad 2 key mp is ignored there, and the 64-bit game reads only cp, mp and payback.
  • The list of charge factors a player can choose is customize (Assault Squad 2: available). Bot settings are found by <difficulty>_<team> instead of the difficulty alone. A command point table read twice replaces the first one instead of merging.
  • New session defaults: a pause during preparation, a first reinforcement wave after 360 s and then one every 120 s.

When you bring a unit over, the Quick Guided Task "a unit from Gates of Hell" ends with an Assault Squad 2 buy card for it, and the fold Translate numbers on the GoH unit page shows how other numbers are translated; see Chapter 19 and Bring a unit from Gates of Hell. Set its price, cooldown and rank on the Assault Squad 2 scale afterwards.

4. A balance workflow

The Balance page

The Balance page (Balance) shows every unit of the buy panel as one row, with your mod laid over the game. Columns include the army, class, who pays ("Paid with"), "Price", "Model price" (what units of the same class with the same armour, gun and speed cost), "Rank", "Cooldown s", "Fore", "Wait at start s", "Command pts", armour on four sides, "Top speed", the gun with its calibre, "Pen 100 m" and "Reload s".

  • Filter with a name or with conditions such as army=ger cls=tank cost>500 res=mp.
  • View the list as a Sheet, in Groups (rows and columns with the middle value, average, lowest or highest), as a Graph of any two columns, or side by side under Compare, including "The mod against the game".
  • Odd ones lists units that do not fit the pattern: cheap or expensive for what they are, costing more but no better, the same stats at another price, a price that can never be paid, or a unit ready too early.
  • Change edits the price, rank, cooldown, fore, the wait at start (the page sets fore to give it), top speed, armour (every number of the armour line scaled together) or the main gun's reload, by percent, by adding, by multiplying, by setting, or "to the model price". "Preview" shows each change, then "Write into the mod" writes it into your mod only. A price change is refused when the selection mixes resources.

The command way is ARSENAL balance <game folder> --folder <mod folder>, with --where, --group, --odd and --change "cost pct 10" --plan to preview.

The Units page

The Units page (Units) is the place for one unit at a time. "Find a unit" shows its numbers with the mod's value next to the game's. "Quick change" changes one unit's price, name, armour part, unlock time, rank or head start: choose what to change, type the "New value", press Preview, then Write. Its "Balance" part has:

  • "Compare mod with the game": every unit your mod adds or changes, with the old and new price, rank, unlock time and armour.
  • "Change all prices of an army": a percent for every price of one army; 10 makes them 10% more expensive, -20 makes them 20% cheaper, and prices are rounded to 5.
  • "Price hint for this unit": what units like this one cost, lowest to highest and the middle, next to its own price.
  • "Buy panel checklist": six points to check in the game, from the right army and button group to the price, rank and unlock wait you set, and whether bots buy the unit.

See also: Change a unit's numbers and Chapter 19, Units and Balance.

The armour simulator

The Armor part of the Models page ("Armour: thickness, map and shot test") reads a vehicle's armour as the game would. Its table "Thickness of each part" gives each volume's six sides in millimetres and where each number comes from; you can click a number to change it in your mod. Under "Who shoots", pick a gun, one of its shells and a range: the page says how much flat armour that shell goes through, colours a map of the whole side by what happens, and shows a single shot plate by plate. It follows the game's rules for thickness, slope and penetration; it does not model gun spread, the flight after a ricochet, blast, or what happens behind the plate. See The armour table on the Models page. The command way:

ARSENAL armorsim table <unit>
ARSENAL armorsim shot <unit> --weapon "<gun name>" --ammo "<shell tags>" --range 500 --from 0,0
ARSENAL armorsim edit <unit> --volume turret --side front --mm 60 --out <mod folder> --dry

Step by step

  1. Get a "before" table. ARSENAL statsheet <game folder> --mods mymod --sheet weapons,ammo,armor,price -o before.md, or save the Balance sheet as CSV.
  2. Make a small change in the Balance page, the armour simulator or your mod's files. For one key in one entity, ARSENAL patch-entity writes a single-key override instead of a copy of the whole file; see Chapter 19.
  3. Get an "after" table the same way and compare, or use Compare, "The mod against the game", on the Balance page. A before and after table is the clearest way to explain a balance change to other people.
  4. See what you changed against what you cover. ARSENAL overdiff mods/mymod --game <game folder> --summary lists, for each file you replace, which keys you added, removed or changed. A full-file replacement that drops vanilla keys is flagged.
  5. See who wins. ARSENAL conflicts --game <game folder> --mods a,mymod shows each key changed by more than one mod and which one wins (the last in the load order, Chapter 3).
  6. Check multiplayer. A file edited without changing its size can pass the lobby check and then go out of sync in play. ARSENAL mpsync reports which edits the check misses (see Chapter 21).
  7. Play it with the loop in Chapter 18, and compare the MP and CP on the purchase panel with your sheet.

In Gates of Hell

The armour simulator and the price calculator work on Assault Squad 2 data only. Under the Gates of Hell button the Units and Balance pages read Gates of Hell data, but some of their columns mean something else there: "Rank" and "Fore" are not read, a squad's price is a sum (section 3), and the cooldown has two parts. For a Gates of Hell mod, also compare the buy cards and the preset's balancing by hand.

5. Things that bite

  • Interaction {set "x"} flags are limited to 128 distinct names across the whole game; more stop the game at load with an application error. Use tags instead.
  • {delay} restarts its timer when it runs again and loses the bullet and volume. {delay_ex} keeps the value, position and source but drops the bone, the bullet and the instigator.
  • Defines ((define ...)) are seen only within the top-level file being read and the files it includes; parameters are plain text substitution with no defaults. A call to a define that is not visible stops the game with "define not found" (see Chapter 5).
  • Sound names have no aliases (Chapter 16).
  • Some actions work only in direct control (the ammunition-drop grenade, the radio signal and the regular flamethrower) (unconfirmed).
  • A mod file with the same path as a vanilla file replaces it entirely, so tuning with a copy of a big file hides every vanilla change made to it later. Prefer single-key overrides.

Gates of Hell: summary

The Gates of Hell notes in this book have not been tested in a running game. Check them in your own game before you depend on them.

SectionGates of HellIn short
1. Mechanics as the player sees themdiffersRepair kits, no refund for a captured vehicle, 12-soldier squads, direct control fire rules
2. What a data change doesnot mapped hereArmour and damage in Gates of Hell: see Chapter 9
3. Multiplayer economy and pricesdiffersNo rank or head start, two-part cooldown, summed squad prices, seven balancing keys
4. A balance workflowdiffersThe balance pages read 64-bit game data only
5. Things that bitenot mapped

Game modes only Gates of Hell has

  • Ammunition: a flag opens every enable_time seconds (120 by default); capturing it pays each player into the vehicle budget, at most maximum_ammo_payback (250), and the flag is then gone.
  • Evacuation: team A holds until the time limit while team B comes in waves (firstWaveTime, then every waveTime); supply_waves open supply flags that pay the next amount of ammo_table. Team B wins when team A has nothing it can operate for 20 seconds.
  • Guerrilla: team A against waves, with preparation_time (15) and waves_to_win (10).

Their texts are new keys in the text group under mp and game (Chapter 14, section 4). A .set for one of these modes makes no game in the 64-bit game.

Supply, fuel and unit resources

  • A supply zone is switched with enabled (default on); the Assault Squad 2 key disabled is not read, so write {enabled 0} instead.
  • A supply zone can also hand out fuel and mechanicResources, each as {amount}{max}{value}.
  • A unit can carry a stock in {Resources {max}{current}{income}} (100, 100, 0 by default), which fortifications are paid from. An unknown field there is an error ("Unknown resources field").
  • A moving supply truck never supplies; the zone works only while it stands.

Pitfalls

Check these before you publish a balance change:

  • a wrong unitLimits or payback separator;
  • an undefined ability level;
  • an armour macro number that overrides your per-volume thickness;
  • a volume without the blast flag that HE can no longer hurt;
  • a .set whose string values were saved as cp1251 rather than UTF-8 (they show as boxes);
  • a hero price compared with an MP price;
  • a same-size edit that passes the lobby check and goes out of sync.

Next: Chapter 18: Testing and Logs

18. Testing and Logs

The short way: Check a mod, fix what the check finds, read the game log walks through the same job in seven steps. This chapter explains what happens at each step and how to read what the game tells you.

What you will learn

  • A repeatable test loop for every change.
  • How to start the game, activate your mod and confirm that it is the one running.
  • How to use a LAN match with the "Test mode" preset as your test bed.
  • How to read game.log, tell fatal errors from warnings, and ignore harmless noise.
  • How to read crash dumps and out-of-sync dumps, and how to find the cause of a crash by bisecting.
  • Which ARSENAL pages and commands read the log for you.
  • What is different when you test a Gates of Hell mod.

The rule for this whole guide: a data change is not done until you have seen it work in the game and read the log afterwards.

1. The per-change test loop

  1. Save your work. Commit the change in version control, and copy your pak file somewhere safe before you overwrite it, because version control does not hold paks. If your mod is a loose folder, no repack is needed; if you pack paks, repack and check that the pak's timestamp is newer than your edits (see section 2).
  2. Check without the game first. On the Check page of the ARSENAL window, press "Check the mod" (the "quick check" tick starts ticked for a mod of 300 files or more and unticked for a smaller one; tick it for a fast run). The command way is ARSENAL check <mod folder> --fast -q. It takes seconds and tells you whether the mod loads statically, that is, whether the files contain a mistake the tools know will stop or crash the game (chapter 19). The answer LOADS_STATIC means "no known crash pattern found", not "works".
  3. Start the game with only the mod under test active (section 2). The Play page can do this for you: it checks the mod, installs it, starts the game on a test map in a separate copy of your settings and reads the log for a load verdict (section 9).
  4. Start a LAN test match (section 4), buy the changed units and use them: fire, take hits, reload, burn.
  5. Read the log after the test or after a crash. On the Read Game.log page (Mods > Check & Fix > Read Game.log), press "Explain my last game log", or search the log yourself for the names of the files you changed, "may lead to crash" and "define not found".
  6. Write it down. Record the date, which commit, which unit and the result. Keep screenshots and the full log in a folder per test. Record any new but harmless warning in a "known warnings" list for your mod.

Test the real thing by playing it. Decisive shots (flank shots, engine hits, high explosive against gun crews) are best done in direct control, where you aim yourself.

The quick way: the Quick Guided Task ends every make or change task with "Check now", "Go to the Play page" and a tick list "What to look at in the game", which is steps 2 to 4 of this loop. The explore task "what went wrong in the last run" is step 5. See Use the Quick Guided Task.

Packaging reminders

  • The game loads .pak files, which are plain zip files, from a mod's resource/ folder. Loose folders such as entity/, set/, properties/, script/, interface/ and map/ beside them are extractions, and the paks often hold more than the loose copies.
  • Loose files win by scan order, not by timestamp. A leftover extracted copy of set/... in resource/ can override the same file in a pak inside resource/, so delete stale extracted copies. See chapter 4.
  • Pak roles: gamelogic.pak holds set/, properties/ and script/; entity.pak holds entity/; map.pak holds map/; interface.pak holds interface/; texture.pak holds textures, model definitions and effect definitions; sound.pak holds sound/; music.pak holds music.
  • Encoding: text data files use CRLF line endings, and the 64-bit build reads every string value as UTF-8, in data and .lng files alike; identifiers must be ASCII. Vanilla files are ASCII except inside ; comments, where old cp1251 bytes remain. Some editors guess those comments wrongly and rewrite the file. Use an editor that lets you choose the encoding (the ARSENAL Editor page keeps bytes you did not touch), or a script that copies the bytes it does not change and keeps CRLF. See chapter 14.
  • If you use git for a mod, keep the repository at the mod root, track text sources, ignore *.pak and large binaries, and set it not to convert line endings, so files with old comment bytes stay byte for byte identical. A Workshop upload copies the whole mod folder, including a .git folder, so exclude it. See chapter 20.

2. Launching and activating a mod

Start the game from Steam. A dialog titled "Select launch option" offers Play, Editor, Safe mode and Safe mode (no mods); choose Play. About 20 seconds later the main menu appears.

Mods are applied in the Options screen, on the MODS tab (the last tab). Disabled mods are on the left, active ones on the right; select one and use the arrows to move it. Then press Apply. The game shows "Applying mods..." for around 30 seconds (a large mod can take a few minutes) and does not need a restart. Menu buttons often ignore single clicks, so double-click them. Activate only the mod under test, because other global mods can conflict. A mod made for the 64-bit build needs the built-in extras mod as64+ active and listed before it (chapter 3).

How to verify that your mod is active: open your profile's options.set and find the {mods block. It has one line per active mod, such as "mymod:1". The Read Game.log page reads the same list for you: "Show what is switched on" lists your mods in the order the game uses and warns about folders the game does not know and about as64+ in the wrong place. In the original game this file is the only reliable check, because its log does not name local mods and the main-menu footer only shows a version text. The 64-bit build's log does list them (section 5). If you rename a mod folder, its line is dropped and the Activated list is empty, so re-activate it. The keys of mod.info and the active list are described one by one in Reference 1.

Where files live: the game keeps its data under your Documents folder in My Games/Men of War - Assault Squad 2/ (Documents can be redirected by OneDrive, so the plain path may not exist). Inside are profiles/<id>/options.set (profile and options), profiles/<id>/keys.set (your hotkeys), and log/ containing game.log, minidumps/ and oos/.

Two game programs. The original game is mowas_2.exe (data version 3.262). The 64-bit build is as64.exe; mods for it declare a minimum version of 3.301. Both share one profile, so the active mod list stays the same when you switch between them. Only the 64-bit build keeps the previous log, lists the mounted mods in its log, takes start options such as -instance, -console and -control, and has a control pipe for automation (section 9).

Console. The retail 3.262 build has no console (the ~ key does nothing). The 64-bit build opens one when it is started with -console, with the key left of 1. How to reach it and what each command does is in Reference 12, Reaching the console.

Console exec. The console command exec runs a script file, and the path rules are easy to get wrong. A bare exec "x.cfg" finds x.cfg only inside resource/at/. Both exec "at/x.cfg" and exec "x.cfg" for a file sitting in resource/ answer "file not found". For any other place, start the path with a slash from the mount root: exec "/x.cfg", exec "/set/d/x.cfg", or write it as exec "resource/x.cfg". Script files must be .cfg; a loose .txt is invisible to the game. See Reference 12, exec.

Several copies at once. On the 64-bit build, -instance N (1 to 9) starts a separate copy with its own user folder (My Games/Men of War - Assault Squad 2 - instance N/), log and profiles; see chapter 12. Its mod list starts empty, so activate your mods in that instance's options.set first. The Play page and ARSENAL play use instance 1, so your own settings (instance 0) stay as they are.

Do not assume a console variable exists. Some console variable names you may meet are not present in the 64-bit build 3.301 (thirteen are known); some exist only in the editor build. Read the variable first and see what it answers before you build a test on it.

In Gates of Hell

  • User folder. Gates of Hell keeps its data in Documents/My Games/Gates of Hell/. Started with -useLocalDataFolder, or when Documents lies in OneDrive, it uses %LOCALAPPDATA%/Digitalmindsoft/Gates of Hell/ instead. Its log folder is inside.
  • Is my mod active? Unlike the original Assault Squad 2, the Gates of Hell log names its mods: Scanning mods in, Found N available mods, Mod: activate mod <name>, and one Mount package <file> with <n> entries line for each pak it mounts. Search the log for your mod's folder name.
  • Console helpers that Gates of Hell adds for testing: tut_clear_all forgets the one-time tutorial hints so they show again, snd_restart restarts the sound system and reloads the sounds, dev_l10n_reload reads the texts again, logs_flush writes the debug logs out at once. ui_armorDisplay is a command there (ui_armorDisplay true), not a variable, so the form ui_armorDisplay = 1 fails.
  • ARSENAL does not start Gates of Hell: the Play page is there under GoH, but play refuses this game. Start the game yourself.

3. Controls cheat sheet for testing

Click the game window before pressing keys; otherwise the keys go to whatever had focus. After the game loses focus, the first click only refocuses.

ActionHow
Direct controlTap E (toggle). W/S drive, A/D turn, mouse aims, left click fires, right click next weapon, Space next ammo
Jump cameraRight-click the minimap
Pause menuEsc, then Back, Options or Close

(Hotkeys are the ones in a typical custom profile; the defaults differ a little, and the player's profile wins. See Chapter 15.)

Aiming in direct control: put the cursor on the white dot in the reticle and wait for the orange ring to form. Clicking before the ring forms does nothing. A solid red dot means reloading.

Other points: the keyboard has no pan or zoom keys bound; edge scrolling is extremely fast, so avoid it. Screenshots can come out entirely grey, so wait a moment and take another. Check the ground before you trust a speed or route test, because a painted river can be only a water material that vehicles drive across. In direct control the camera seems to turn with the hull, so landmark distances are unreliable (unconfirmed).

4. The LAN test bed

A LAN match with the Test mode setting is the standard unit test.

  1. Main menu: Multiplayer, then LAN, then New game. In the lobby, use single clicks on menu entries (a double click can land on a neighbouring entry), but double-click "New game".
  2. Choose the game type Combat. The test preset is included only by Combat and Assault Zones, and Combat is the simplest.
  3. Pick a two-player map, set Players to 2, and create the game.
  4. In "Game settings", choose Test mode and confirm the warning. This gives 50000 MP, 1000 command points, no unit limits, zero unlock times, and no countdown before the start.
  5. Units are limited to the preset's year tags, so a unit from another era will not appear in the purchase panel.
  6. There are no bots in this lobby unless a mod enables them (see chapter 10). You play alone, and you place enemies yourself or build a scenario in the editor (see Chapter 12).
  7. Double-click Ready, then Start. Loading takes about 22 seconds.
  8. In game, the right-hand panel shows "N / 1000 CP", "50000 / 50000 MP" and the category buttons. Buying spawns the unit in about five seconds.

The purchase panel's categories, top to bottom, are infantry squads, specialists, supplies, support weapons, artillery, light vehicles, two tank categories and heroes. If a category opens an empty tooltip instead of a list, click another category and come back.

Friendly fire is on. Your own losses add to the enemy score, so keep your test units out of the impact zone unless they are the target.

Screenshots and records

Centre on the unit (double-click its card) or jump with the minimap, take a screenshot, and save it in a folder per test next to a copy of the log. Photos of damage reports on screen are the best record.

In Gates of Hell

Whether Gates of Hell has the same "Test mode" preset is not mapped. It has console settings that make a test lobby quicker and repeatable:

Console nameWhat it does
mp_session_autoreadyoff by default; when on, a seated player is ready at once, so you skip the ready clicks
mp_rndSeed0 by default; any other value gives every match the same random seed, for repeatable tests
dev_enableBotAion by default; off starts the next match without the bot script, so computer players neither buy nor move
mp_game_set_victory, mp_game_set_personal_score[hostId value] add victory points or personal score to a player
mp_game_list_playerslists the players with their host id
mp_checkCombatchecks the spawn points of a "combat" mission
g_component listlists the resource id and part names of the selected units
dbg_damageoff by default; when on, prints the hit points of vehicle parts to the console when a part takes damage

5. The structure of game.log

game.log lives in the log folder of the game's user folder (section 2). It is overwritten every time the game starts, so copy it before you relaunch. The 64-bit build first renames the old log to game.prev.log, which keeps exactly one earlier run; the original mowas_2.exe simply truncates it, so after a crash and restart the crash log is gone.

The first thing to do when reading it is to skip the profile-sync noise: about a hundred lines beginning SyncFile or Result is. The Read Game.log page and logtriage (section 9) filter them for you.

The log runs in this order:

  1. A header with the executable, the Steam application id, the working directory and the command line. The 64-bit build adds a Mod 'name' from path line for every mounted mod.
  2. A first localization pass, with harmless key-redefinition warnings from the editor texts file.
  3. Profile synchronisation lines.
  4. Build and Product lines, then Repository: N resources. N changes when files are added or removed, so it is a quick "did my pak load?" check. Compare it between players when looking for a desync.
  5. Resource-load warnings. The game parses all soft code here, so syntax errors, duplicate definitions and missing-item warnings appear in this part.
  6. Phase ... lines such as "Phase Loading...", "Phase Mounting mod resources from Steam Workshop..." and "Opening main page". They print after the data warnings, so a warning's position relative to them says nothing about whether it came from vanilla or your mod. The Mounting phase never names your mod.
  7. Menu and lobby messages: "Mission '...' is skipped" and "Unread data detected". The lobby builds the map list twice, so lines repeat.
  8. Starting "multi/<map>:<gametype>": the map load; warnings about map entities and roster preloads follow.
  9. GameThreadStart: the match is running. Messages marked @ [quant] are runtime events tied to something that happened in the simulation (a quant is one tick of game time); match the timestamp to what you did.
  10. GameThreadStop is a normal end. A crash instead leaves an ***** Exception ***** block.

How to read one line:

  • [hh:mm:ss] message (/path/file.def, 188) is a warning raised while a data file was being parsed. The path and line point into your soft code, and the path is how you decide whether a warning is yours.
  • [..] message (a program file name, a number) @ [quant] was raised by the game program at runtime. It does not name the unit; work out which unit it was from what you did at that second.
  • Those program line numbers belong to the build that wrote them. Treat them as a hint about which part of the game spoke, not as a place to look.

Warnings print and the game continues with a fallback. Errors print an Exception block and the game ends; they cannot be skipped.

In Gates of Hell

The Gates of Hell game.log has the same kind of content with a different line form, so a search or a script made for one game needs care on the other:

  • Every line starts with [hh:mm:ss] , the time since the game started. In Assault Squad 2 only warnings carry a stamp. On the Gates of Hell console the warnings carry none.
  • A program place in brackets is written (name:number), the name in lower case and without its extension, instead of (name, number). The crash report names the kind of error and the version of the game.
  • Game events (kills, flags, zones) are written to game.log as [EVT] <text> lines, whatever the console's message setting is.
  • Start-up lines name the mods and paks (section 2) and the launch: Launcher: Loading phase ..., Start mission <map path> on difficulty ... with options [...]. A dialog that cannot be found writes GUI: Failed to find dialog of type <x>, an entity that cannot be spawned writes Failed to spawn entity <name>.
  • Multiplayer lines include Workshop item <id> installed successfuly (spelled so), Steam is in OFFLINE mode. Some features are disabled, and a game preset reset to <name> when it did not change with the new game mode. With logs_on and log_mp set, the mp debug log adds the winner, each SPAWN <unit> and the match seed.
  • Numbers in some log lines print as 0x hex where Assault Squad 2 prints them in decimal.
  • Debug logs (logs_on 1 plus one log_<name> variable each) are written as whole lines, so lines of different threads no longer mix, but the file can lag up to 5 seconds behind the game. Most of them, mp and mp_tcp included, start over at each new mission, so copy them before the next mission starts. A log past log_maxLogFileSize (250 MB by default; the 64-bit build uses 512 MB) goes on in <name>.<n>.log. Gates of Hell has two more debug logs, log_interaction and log_aiming.

6. Fatal errors and warnings

Fatal (the game ends)

MessageWhat it usually means
define not foundA ("name" ...) call has no visible (define "name" ...). Defines are scoped to the top-level file being read. Add the define, include its file, or rename the call.
unexpected tokenThe parser wanted something else. A bone or volume name vanished after a model swap, a brace or bracket is missing or extra, a number sits where a string should, or a keyword is wrong. Compare with a working sibling file.
String expected, Number expected, Block terminator expected, ')' required, End of SDL file expectedMalformed SDL.
Nested mods not supportedA (mod ...) inside another (mod ...).
pattern not foundA {from "pattern X"} base is not defined.
Unknown materialThe material is not in the material list.
Bone modifiers must be placed after skeleton loadA {bone "x"} block came before the skeleton line.
Resource not found - <path>, File is not found - <path>A mesh, volume, animation or material named in a .def or .mdl does not exist. Check name and case.
Invalid block in .VOL file, Unsupported animation version, Zero speed in ik-boneCorrupt or wrong-format model data.

The debug stack inside the Exception block gives the data file and line. More than 128 different {set} flag names in interaction scripts also stop the game at load; use tags instead (chapter 11).

Warnings that matter, by impact

  1. No Stuff found for tags 'X' (may lead to crash). No weapon or ammo item carries those tags, so a dummy is substituted. Loading is fine; the crash comes when the item is used. Ammo tags have the form <caliber> <type>. This is the one warning that turns into a crash.
  2. Can't preload, Unread data, or missing breeds in a roster: a faction imported incompletely.
  3. invalid level param (an ability level that is not defined; the soldier silently gets the top level), Unknown props typos, Bone X not found, Can't find bone X.
  4. Invalid ricochet angle: clamped, no gameplay effect. Fix out <= in.
  5. Per-unit runtime warnings: bone 'X' has no broken view, a wheeled vehicle without its pivot bones, unknown sound file, Undefined material.

Benign background noise

These appear in a normal install; do not chase them: hundreds of Localization key redefinition lines, Mission ... is skipped for leftover mission titles, Entity redefinition for helmets, bushes, wire, wrecks and shells, Automatic MIP generation not supported and No MIP levels, No obstacle ID, unknown terrain_pp type - snow, 'use_blend_tex' is not supported, Media file ... story not found, trench-related Unknown control panel item, and Unknown props "crater big".

How to tell new from old: counts differ between runs, so keep a baseline log of a clean run. New message types, or higher counts of No Stuff found, Unknown props, Unread data, Can't preload or invalid level param, point at your latest change.

See also: chapter 5 for the syntax behind the parse errors, chapter 9 and Reference 6 for ammo tags, and chapter 21 for symptoms without a log line.

In Gates of Hell

Some messages are new, some are gone, and two faults change from a crash to a warning or the other way:

Gates of HellWhat it means
ammunition in a magazine with an empty idfatal in Gates of Hell; give every ammo item its id
Can't find fxBone in weapon <x> held by <y>, No launch bone in <x>a missing effect or launch bone is a warning in Gates of Hell; in Assault Squad 2 the same fault crashes
a warning that a weapon carried by an entity has no shooter bonenew: names a weapon without a foresight bone, which Assault Squad 2 accepts silently
Unable to board <x> into <y>new: a unit could not board (no seats, or no vehicle to own it)
Invalid placement matrix for entity <x>new: a script put an entity at a broken position
[EFX] Wrong signaturenew: an effect file of an unexpected form; it is still read
Can't apply preset <name>new: an environment preset the editor could not apply
Warning: Invalid land materials found. Fix them in textoolnew, in the editor: an old land is given new materials and asks to be saved
double Create() call detected, Multiple notify mappings, Unknown bitmapnew interface warnings that point at a layout fault
Unknown propsgone: a misspelled props name is silent in Gates of Hell, so a typo there no longer shows in the log
unit ... can't look for coversgone: a vehicle asking for cover is refused without a warning
a wrong component id in an interaction conditionwritten as unexpected token, not "invalid parameter"

7. Crash dumps

Minidumps

A crash writes two files into log/minidumps/: a Windows minidump (about 45 MB, no heap) and a sidecar of the same name ending .mdmp.log that holds the game log at the moment of the crash plus the Exception block. Read the sidecar first. You rarely need a debugger. On the Read Game.log page, "Read every game window" lists the crash reports of each game copy, and "Read this crash" explains one.

The block shows the exception type, the name of the program function that failed, and a call stack. Read it this way:

  • A tiny address in the exception (such as 0x28 or 0x54) is a null pointer: something the code referenced does not exist.
  • Words in the function name point at the area: cannon means a towed gun's weapon or ammo; actor with sensor means a soldier with incomplete breed or vision data; chassis means wheels or tracks; ammo with reload means a reload on missing ammo; armor means damage; an SDL reader means a parse error.
  • Look at the lines just above the block. The last warnings before the crash (No Stuff found, Bone ... not found, Undefined material, unknown sound file) are your suspects.
  • Typical cases: a soldier sensor crash means one of the squad's breeds is incomplete (buy squads one at a time to find it); a cannon reload crash means a towed gun or howitzer with a missing ammo item.

The dump holds no data file names, so scanning its strings finds almost nothing useful. Dump size is set by a console variable (0 none, 1 small, 2 full). The 64-bit build writes small dumps by default; what the original build does by default is unconfirmed, so a crash there may produce a very large file.

If the game vanishes with no Exception block and no dump, suspect a stack overflow: the game had no room left to write its report. Undo your last change and bisect (section 8).

Out-of-sync dumps

Multiplayer is lockstep: every machine simulates the same game, and at regular intervals each client sends checksums of the scene (units, positions, random numbers) and of the rules (scores, budgets). If the host sees a difference, the client shows a dialog and writes a dump into log/oos/, in a folder named after the local date and time with one file per player. Only the host, a desynced client or a flagged master writes, so you may find two or three files.

Tiny files (a few hundred bytes) hold checksums only. Large ones hold a full snapshot you can compare as text: take the host's file and a client's file from the same folder; if the rules checksum matches but the scene checksum differs, the scene diverged; the first differing line in the snapshots names the entity or field. A different random-draw count means the draws differed; a different entity count means a spawn happened on one side only.

The causes, most likely first:

  1. Different mod or pak content between players. Everything must be identical, including load order. Compare Repository: N resources in each player's log.
  2. A different game version, or a mix of 32-bit and 64-bit builds.
  3. Interaction scripts reading something particular to one machine (profile, keys, options, graphics settings).
  4. A model or file edited in a way the lobby does not check. The lobby compares some binary files only by size, and some types not at all, so a same-size edit passes the lobby and desyncs in play. Run ARSENAL mpsync (chapter 20).
  5. A crash on one machine often shows as a desync on the others.

There is no live resync: desynced clients are removed.

In Gates of Hell

  • Which errors leave a dump. An ordinary error, a data file (SDL) error and an out-of-sync error write a minidump and a crash report, as in Assault Squad 2. Out of memory and a failed signature check show an Error box and end the game with exit code 2, with no dump. A DirectX error ends the game at once with no box and no dump: a Gates of Hell game that vanishes without a trace points at the graphics side first.
  • How many dumps are kept. dbg_minidumpFileLimit (5 by default) is the number of minidumps kept in log/minidumps/; 0 deletes none.
