  • Reports sent away. Crash, out-of-sync and feedback reports are uploaded to the BugSplat service. A BugSplat.ini in the game's working folder with Enabled=0 under [BugSplat] stops the uploads; none is shipped. No report is sent while any mod is applied or being switched, and the local minidump is written either way. Before the upload, copies of log/game.log and the dedicated server's log have the Steam id, the Steam name and the Windows account name replaced, but only names longer than 4 characters; your local game.log is not changed.
  • Out-of-sync dumps compare to the bit: each number is followed by its bytes in hex, and binary records print as bytes. The report players send in probably starts with a fixed head (single or multiplayer, map, preset, seed, mod names, time played, the players); this is not confirmed.

8. Triage checklist and bisecting

  1. Was there a crash? Look for ***** Exception ***** in game.log or a new file in minidumps/. If not, the problem is gameplay-side; look at warnings tied to your unit.
  2. Read the sidecar: exception type, function, call path.
  3. Read the 10 to 30 lines above the exception. The one with a file path in brackets is the culprit; open that file at that line.
  4. For load-time define not found or unexpected token, take the file and line from the debug stack. For a define, search for (define "<name>" across the data and check the top-level include chain (the Editor page's "Find in files" can search the game's own files too). For a token, compare against a working sibling file and check bone names against the model.
  5. Check mod state: options.set lists only the intended mod; the pak is newer than your edits; the pak was repacked after your last change; Repository: N resources is as expected. On the Read Game.log page, "Why is it missing?" checks the mod's mod.info, version lines, folder name and whether it is switched on (tick "Also check against the game's own load rules (slow, about a minute)" to ask the game's own rules as well), and "Check this unit" follows one unit from its file to its model, materials, buy card, army and picture and names the first broken link (tick "Also scan for broken links (slow)" for a deeper scan).
  6. Compare with your baseline of known warnings.
  7. Bisect. Revert your last edit (version control for text, your backup for paks), relaunch and test one unit in the LAN test bed. Or restore all paks from backup and reapply one at a time.
  8. For a multiplayer desync, verify identical paks and versions on all machines first, then compare the snapshots.
  9. Record the result. Do not delete logs until the finding is documented, and copy game.log before every relaunch.

Past crash causes worth remembering: a preset that was called but never defined, a weapon name that does not exist, a bone renamed in a model, and a mesh without a material.

9. Letting ARSENAL read the log

Three pages and three commands save time here. The commands are run as ARSENAL <tool> (see Chapter 19: The Toolchain).

The Read Game.log page (Mods > Check & Fix > Read Game.log) reads the newest game.log without starting the game, and changes or deletes nothing. "Explain my last game log" turns it into cards in plain words, each marked STOPS, CRASH, CHECK, NOTE or OK and each with "What to do"; "Show the game's own text" shows the original lines. "Log files the game left" lists game.log and game.prev.log of each game copy ("Main game window", "Extra game window N"), with its crash reports and out-of-sync folders, newest first: "Read every game window" reads them all, "Read this crash" explains one crash report, "Look again" reloads the list, and "Pick another log folder..." reads a folder you copied aside. "Try these in the game" is a tick list of what to test after you play, made from the notes written when your mod was upgraded plus the basics; your ticks are kept in this browser, and "Clear the ticks" starts over. The other boxes of the page are in sections 2 and 8.

The Editor page (tab IDE) has a Game log panel: press "Read last log" (Ctrl+L) or "Read the newest log" after you played. A click on a finding opens your file at that line, and "Next log error" goes to the next one (chapter 19, Editor).

The Quick Guided Task has the explore task "what went wrong in the last run": it reads the last run, lists its errors in plain words with the file and line each points at, and says what to do about each. It writes nothing, and its last step offers the change task "a mod with problems (fix them)". See Quick Guided Task.

On a phone or tablet, with LAN Remote on, you can read these results on another device while the game runs on the PC; it views only (LAN Remote and the phone view).

ARSENAL logtriage is the command behind those pages. It reads a log folder (or a single game.log), collapses duplicates, sorts messages into findings and known noise, and names the likely cause for each one. Given a folder, it also reads game.prev.log, the minidump sidecars and the out-of-sync folders:

ARSENAL logtriage <log folder> --summary
ARSENAL logtriage <log folder or game.log> --mod <mod folder> --game <game folder>

--mod marks which of the logged data paths your mod supplies, so you can tell your warnings from vanilla ones at a glance.

The Play page and ARSENAL play do a whole boot test: check the mod, install it into the game's mods folder, start the game on a test map in instance 1 with the mod active, and read game.log for the load verdict (BOOT). In the window, switch on "Let ARSENAL start the game" first; "play: dry run" shows every step and changes nothing.

ARSENAL play <mod folder> --dry
ARSENAL play <mod folder>

A clean BOOT means the game loaded your mod without an error. It does not mean the mod does what you meant, so still play it.

ARSENAL testrun drives a whole test through the 64-bit build's control pipe: it copies the old logs aside (never deletes), starts the game without sound, activates your mods, opens a LAN lobby, hosts a map, starts, waits for the map to load, quits, then runs logtriage and prints one summary. --dry prints the steps and launches nothing:

ARSENAL testrun --map multi/<map>:combat --exe <game folder>/as64.exe --dry

A map id looks like multi/<map>:<mode>, for example multi/1v1_road:combat; a bare map name gets the combat mode. The retail mowas_2.exe has no pipe, so testrun only works with the 64-bit build.

A scripted test can pass or fail with nobody watching. Be careful what you test for: a check that only says "no error appeared" proves little, because a broken mod can be just as quiet. Prefer a positive signal, such as a log line that only appears when your change worked.

Game length matters when you wait for the end of a match: a side that has no units at about 60 seconds of game time loses, and the match ends. A test that spawns nothing for one side finishes almost at once. A mod folder with a broken mod.info stops every launch, so check it first (ARSENAL modinfo <mod folder>).

In Gates of Hell

Under the GoH button the Read Game.log page reads the game.log in the Gates of Hell user folder (logtriage --exe goh), and so does the Quick Guided Task "what went wrong in the last run". The Play and Test Run pages are there too, but play and the test runs start only Assault Squad 2: the GoH editor does not start a mission by itself, and Gates of Hell has no control pipe. Start Gates of Hell yourself and read its game.log with the line forms of section 5 in mind. logtriage reads the Gates of Hell log form, but many Gates of Hell lines still come out as unknown kinds, so read its cards with care.

Gates of Hell: summary

The Gates of Hell notes in this book have not been tested in a running game. Check them in your own game before you depend on them.

SectionGates of HellIn a few words
1. The per-change test loopsame as far as mappedthe same loop; ARSENAL can check a Gates of Hell mod but not start the game
2. Launching and activating a moddiffersown user folder; the log names mods and paks; extra console helpers
3. Controls cheat sheet for testingnot mapped
4. The LAN test beddiffersconsole settings for quick, repeatable test lobbies and bot-free matches
5. The structure of game.logdiffersevery line stamped; [EVT] event lines; other place form; debug logs restart per mission
6. Fatal errors and warningsdiffersempty ammo id is fatal; missing fx bone is only a warning; Unknown props is gone
7. Crash dumpsdiffersno dump on DirectX or memory errors; dump limit; reports uploaded to BugSplat
8. Triage checklist and bisectingsame as far as mappedthe same method
9. Letting ARSENAL read the logdiffersRead Game.log reads the GoH log; Play and Test Run start no GoH game

Benchmark runs

Gates of Hell has a benchmark that Assault Squad 2 lacks. dbg_benchmark start|stop [profile "<name>"] [camera "<name>"] [start_camera] runs it from the console; the profiles are in /set/benchmark.set, and each run writes its results into a new folder under benchmark/ named after the date and time. It measures FPS, the quant time in ms, the render time and the memory load in MB (the video memory value is always 0). A mission can start one with the benchmark command; a bad profile name answers Invalid or unknown benchmark profile selected. Request rejected.

Pitfalls

  • Trusting the main-menu footer to prove a mod is active. Read options.set, or "Show what is switched on" on the Read Game.log page.
  • Forgetting that game.log is replaced at the next launch, and that only the 64-bit build keeps one earlier run.
  • A leftover loose file overriding the pak you just rebuilt.
  • Saving a string value as cp1251 in a .set or .lng file (it shows as boxes), or letting an editor rewrite the old cp1251 comment bytes of a copied vanilla file.
  • Mistaking harmless noise for your bug, and mistaking a No Stuff found for noise.
  • Testing a vehicle on a river that is really ground.
  • Forgetting that friendly fire is on in the test setup.
  • Taking LOADS_STATIC or a clean BOOT as proof that the change works.

Engine reference

Warnings and errors are written by the engine's exception handler; the crash dump writer and the multiplayer sync checker are separate modules.

Next: Chapter 19: The Toolchain

19. The toolchain

Modding by hand works, but many mistakes in this game are silent: a typo in a key name, a missing file, or a wrong encoding often gives no error, only a mod that quietly does nothing. ARSENAL is the toolchain that comes with this guide. It reads your mod and the game's data, tells you about problems before you start the game, and writes new content only into the mod folder you name. You can use it as a window with pages or as commands in a terminal; both do the same work.

The short way for the common jobs is in Part I: Use the Quick Guided Task, Check a mod, fix what the check finds, read the game log, Pack and share, Find guides and tools others made and Bring an old mod up to the 64-bit build.

What you will learn

  • How to get ARSENAL and run it, as a window or as commands.
  • The front-door commands check, fix and gen.
  • What each page of the window does, and which game it serves, with the Quick Guided Task, the whole documents, the file viewers, LAN Remote, Settings, Arrange mode and the confirm box.
  • The commands behind the pages: soedit, armorsim, balance, gemindex, gen --describe and the others.
  • The flags many tools share, a sensible order to run them in, and workflows for common jobs.
  • What the tools cannot catch.

1. Getting ARSENAL and running it

The release is a zip file in four forms, listed in chapter 1: the full download, a small download, and each of those with the historical sources database (-ww2). Unzip it into a folder of its own, outside the game folder. The full download holds:

  • ARSENAL.exe, the one program. Double-click it to open the window (section 3), or open a command prompt in that folder and type ARSENAL.exe followed by a command.
  • ARSENAL-gui.cmd, which opens the window too (it runs ARSENAL.exe gui).
  • Install-ARSENAL.cmd, the installer (chapter 1 describes it). You can also run everything straight from the unzipped folder.
  • START-HERE.md, a one-page path through the first commands, and the guide folder with this book.
  • A gemindex folder with the index of other modders' guides and tools, when the release carries it (section 3, Help & Docs > Guides & External Tools).

SOEdit, the model, animation and volume editor, is not in the download. When you want it, the Models page (Get SOEdit and open it) or ARSENAL soedit install downloads its latest release from GitHub (ThatFrostyy/SOEdit-PatchByFrostyy).

ARSENAL.exe contains Node.js and every tool, so the machine that runs it needs nothing else installed. It is unsigned, so Windows may warn the first time. The tools keep their caches in your user folder (%LOCALAPPDATA%\ARSENAL\cache on Windows), so the folder you unzip into may be read-only; you can delete the cache folder at any time.

The small download has the same tools as plain files, with start files instead of the program: ARSENAL.cmd and ARSENAL-gui.cmd on Windows, arsenal and arsenal-gui on Linux and macOS. Type ARSENAL.cmd (or ./arsenal) wherever this guide writes ARSENAL. The first time, the start file looks for Node.js: the program named in the environment variable ARSENAL_NODE, a copy it fetched before, or a Node.js 26 or newer that is already installed. When it finds none, it downloads Node.js 26.13.0 from nodejs.org, checks it against the checksum written in the start file, and keeps only the node program, in a node folder next to the start files or in your user folder when that folder is read-only. After that it needs no internet.

What the release needs:

  • For the full download: Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit. ARSENAL.exe does not start on Windows 7, 8 or 8.1, or on 32-bit Windows, and running it under Wine or Proton has not been tried. The small download is written to run on Linux and macOS too, but has not been tried on a real machine there; starting the game and test runs work on Windows only.
  • About 300 MB of disk space. No administrator rights.
  • A web browser for the window. The 3D model view needs WebGL; without it the page shows the model as text.
  • The game for the commands that read the game's files, install a mod or start a match. play needs the 64-bit build (as64.exe). Tools that only read a mod folder work with no game installed.
  • A graphics driver with OpenGL for SOEdit.
  • An internet connection only for updating the guide index from the web, the optional AI in gen, and the game version check in release-check.

The tools find the game's profile and game.log also when your Documents folder was moved to another drive or to a OneDrive folder: they ask Windows where Documents is, then try the usual OneDrive places. install --link needs the mod and the game on a local NTFS drive.

From a source checkout you run the same tools with Node.js: open a terminal in the folder that contains tools/ and type node tools/as2/as2.js <command>. This guide writes ARSENAL <command> for both: read it as ARSENAL.exe <command> in the release, or node tools/as2/as2.js <command> from source. The old name as2 is the same command.

A few tools exist only for people who maintain the knowledge base. They run as ARSENAL dev <tool> from source and are not covered here.

Finding the game

The tools find your Assault Squad 2 folder through Steam. ARSENAL game prints the folder they found. If it is wrong or missing, add --game "<game folder>" to any command, set the environment variable AS2_GAME to that folder, or put a file as2.json holding {"game": "<game folder>"} in the folder you run the command from (or any folder above it). The game folder is the one that holds as64.exe and the mods folder.

Gates of Hell is found the same way: through Steam, or --goh "<GoH folder>" on a command, or the environment variable GOH_GAME, or a "goh" entry in as2.json. The Gates of Hell folder is the one that holds call_to_arms.exe.

Placeholders in this chapter

<game folder> is your Men of War: Assault Squad 2 install with the 64-bit build. <mod folder> is your own mod folder. Some tools need it to sit in <game folder>/mods/ so the game can mount it (see section 6). The tools never write into the game's own data. They read it, and they write only into the mod folder you name, or into the game's mods folder when you install. Keep that habit yourself: never edit vanilla files in place. See chapter 3 for the mod folder layout.

In Gates of Hell

ARSENAL reads a Gates of Hell install but never writes into it, the same rule as for Assault Squad 2. Some commands take a Gates of Hell folder as a second game: check --goh <GoH folder> reads a mod with the Gates of Hell rules too, upgrade --to goh copies an Assault Squad 2 mod into a new Gates of Hell mod folder, and the porting tools (section 9) read a Gates of Hell mod to bring a unit into Assault Squad 2. In the window, pick GoH at the top: it shows the same tabs as the other games, and section 3 says what each page can and cannot do there. The summary lists what each section of this chapter offers for Gates of Hell.

The front-door commands

ARSENAL help lists nine commands (the one-page path through them is START-HERE.md). One line each, with the example ARSENAL help prints. Options of one command: ARSENAL <command> --help.

CommandWhat it doesExample
newmake an empty AS64 mod folder (MinGameVersion 3.301, lowercase folder name)ARSENAL new mymod --name "My Mod"
genmake mod content (units, text, settings) from a spec fileARSENAL gen spec.yaml --target as64 --out mymod
checkread a mod and say whether it would load, crash or be refused (does not start the game)ARSENAL check mymod
fixplan or write a patch mod that fixes text and reference errors check foundARSENAL fix mymod plan
upgradebring an older mod up to AS64 (or copy it to Gates of Hell); the old mod folder is never writtenARSENAL upgrade oldmod --to as64 --plan
installcopy (or link) a mod folder into the game's mods folderARSENAL install mymod
uninstallremove a mod that ARSENAL install put thereARSENAL uninstall mymod --yes
playinstall a mod and start a test match, then say if it loaded cleanlyARSENAL play mymod --dry
mapsmultiplayer maps: list, view, clone, add a game modeARSENAL maps list

ARSENAL advanced lists the tools kept off the front door, and ARSENAL --all lists every tool with its argument line. Section 2 describes check, fix and gen in detail; upgrade is explained in Bring an old mod up to the 64-bit build and play in chapter 18.

2. The front door: check, fix and gen

check: one command for "will this mod load?"

ARSENAL check <mod folder> --fast -q

The mod folder can be anywhere. If it is not under <game folder>/mods, check builds a temporary view of the game folder around it and reads both; nothing of yours or the game's is changed. It prints findings by severity, then one verdict for each game build:

  • LOADS_STATIC: no crash pattern the tools know was found, and the version is accepted. This means "static check passed". It does not mean the mod works.
  • REFUSED: the mod's mod.info is not valid for that build. A mod with only a Min of 3.301 is refused by the old game and by Gates of Hell, and accepted by AS64. That is right for an AS64 mod.
  • LIKELY_CRASH: a known crash pattern was found; the findings above it say where.

The exit code follows the verdict for the mod's own target build, which is AS64 unless you pass --target mowas2 or --target goh: 0 for LOADS_STATIC, 1 for LIKELY_CRASH or REFUSED, 2 for a usage error, a failed tool or no verdict (UNKNOWN). The other builds' verdicts are printed as information.

--fast skips the slow checks and says so in the output. A small mod takes seconds; drop --fast for the full check, which takes minutes on a big mod. --with <patch folder> checks a mod together with a patch folder made by ARSENAL fix. Do not use it for an ARSENAL upgrade --out folder: that is a whole mod with its own mod.info, so run check on it directly.

fix: a patch mod for common problems

ARSENAL fix <mod folder> plan --out <patch folder>
ARSENAL fix <mod folder> apply --out <patch folder>
ARSENAL check <mod folder> --with <patch folder> --fast -q

fix never writes your mod. It writes a separate patch mod (with its own mod.info that requires yours) into --out; to undo, delete that folder. plan writes nothing. The passes: lng (a .lng at an original path that would hide the original keys gets them appended), repoint (a missing model, texture, sound or environment preset reference with exactly one same-name file in the game is pointed at it), include and macro (a missing include or define with exactly one candidate), stubmtl (a missing material that crashes at load gets the nearest same-folder one, which may look wrong) and set (--set file:path=value). Four more passes work on single lines: enc (text values saved as cp1251 are resaved as UTF-8 for AS64; --target classic leaves them, and text that does not read as Cyrillic is refused), asread (a value the game clamps or rounds on read is written as the game uses it), syntax (a bare texture name gets quotes, split tag strings are joined) and spell (a name the game skips because of its case is respelled, so the line starts to work: look at the result in game). A line the original game file also has is never changed. --only lng,repoint picks passes; quarantine runs only when named in --only. Each changed file must pass the linters again, else it is reverted. To use a patch, put it in <game folder>/mods and activate it after your mod.

gen: make a small mod from a spec file

A spec is a short text file listing what you want. The smallest useful one:

name: demo
title: Demo
ops:
  - op: mod
    title: Demo
  - op: text
    key: desc/entity/demo
    text: Demo text
ARSENAL gen demo.yaml --target as64 --plan --out <new mod folder>
ARSENAL gen demo.yaml --target as64 --out <new mod folder>

The first line only prints what it would do. The second writes the mod into the folder you name (mod.info, a localization/#demo.lng, and folders), runs the checks, and writes a notes file next to it. It ends with the verdict partial, untested: gen does not play the game, so you still test in game (chapter 18).

ARSENAL gen --sample prints a small sample spec that gives one vanilla unit a new name (ARSENAL gen --sample > sample.yaml saves it). ARSENAL gen --sample list names the other samples with one line each: rename-unit, change-price, clone-unit, armor, squad, iblock, macro, preset, army, kit, gun-class, shell, item, sound, soundclass, voice, skin, stuffmodel, mapinfo and all. ARSENAL gen --sample all has one example of every op. The ops are:

OpWhat it makes or changes
modthe mod folder and its mod.info
clone, set, armor, texta copy of a unit, one key, armour numbers, a text key
roster, card, breed, squadbuy cards in an army list, soldier breeds, squads
map-clone, mission-clone, place, mapinfoa copy of a map, a game mode on a map, an object on a map, the map.info settings (players, texture variant)
gun, weapon, kitbasha new gun file from an existing one, the gun a unit carries, the turret of one vehicle model on the hull of another
shell, item, kita new shell, a new grenade, mine or other item, what a soldier carries
iblock, macro, preseta unit's own block in an interaction file (for example its engine and track sounds), one argument of a macro call, buy limits in a multiplayer preset
armya new army with its own id, lobby name, flag and side
sound, soundclass, voicea sound folder, a loudness row in sound.set, a talk language for soldiers
skin, stuffmodela soldier skin, an inventory model

Many recipes of the Quick Guided Task run these same ops from your answers, so you get the result without writing a spec. Every sample uses real vanilla names, so --plan on a real game folder resolves them as written. Change the names to your own. An op that names a unit the game does not have is reported, not written. --check-spec checks a spec and writes nothing; --schema prints the full spec format.

gen --describe builds a spec from a plain-English description instead of a file; it is explained with the Units page in section 3.

Add a unit with gen

Three ops make a new unit: clone copies a vanilla unit under a new name, text gives it a display name, and roster copies the card of an existing unit into an army list so the new unit can be bought:

name: newtank
title: New Tank
ops:
  - op: mod
    title: New Tank
  - op: clone
    entity: pz3
    as: my_pz3
  - op: text
    key: desc/entity/my_pz3
    text: My Pz III
  - op: roster
    unit: my_pz3
    like: pz3
    army: ger
    fields: {cost: 150}
ARSENAL gen newtank.yaml --target as64 --plan --out <game folder>/mods/newtank
ARSENAL gen newtank.yaml --target as64 --out <game folder>/mods/newtank
  • entity and like are vanilla names: the unit's file name without .def, and its card name in the army list. army is the army list name (ger, rus, ...). bots: true in the roster op lets computer players buy it too.
  • fields changes keys of the copied card; a key the card does not have stops that op with GEN_FIELD_UNKNOWN.
  • The notes go to <out>.gen/ beside the mod (TESTNOTES.md lists what to look at in game). With --out under <game folder>/mods, they go to gen-out/<name>.gen/ in the folder you run from instead, so mods gets no extra folder. --report <dir> picks the folder yourself.
  • A clone has no destroyed variant of its own (_x, _xx) unless you clone those too. Check the new card in the purchase panel in a test match; the Units page has a "Buy panel checklist" for this.

ARSENAL-gui: the same tools in a window

A double-click on ARSENAL.exe, or on ARSENAL-gui.cmd (with the small download, ARSENAL-gui.cmd or ./arsenal-gui), opens the ARSENAL window: it finds the game folder, starts a small server on your own machine (nothing is reachable from outside it) and opens your default browser on it. As a command, the same is ARSENAL gui --open. Options of that command: --no-open starts the server without opening the browser, --port N picks the port, --allow-launch lets buttons that start the game work from the first moment, and --remote starts with LAN Remote on (LAN Remote and the phone view). Without --allow-launch, those buttons stay grey until you switch on "Let ARSENAL start the game" on the Play page; the switch lasts until the window closes. ARSENAL.exe started with no command opens the window too.

The window runs the same tools as the commands, from the same exe. The commands probe, e2e and dev-loop start Node and the game themselves and run only from source; soedit build is not in the release: SOEdit is not part of ARSENAL, and ARSENAL soedit install (or Get SOEdit and open it on the Models page) downloads it.

In Gates of Hell

  • check --target goh makes the Gates of Hell verdict the one the exit code follows; --goh <GoH folder> lets it read the Gates of Hell game too. A mod with only a Min of 3.301 is refused by Gates of Hell, which is right for an AS64 mod.
  • fix --target goh writes a patch mod in the Gates of Hell form: the mod.info range follows the Gates of Hell version, and texts go under localizations/default/. Seven fixes that follow Assault Squad 2 rules do not run there, and each says why in one line: enc, syntax, asread, botkeys, lngdup, stubmtl and quarantine. The Check page under GoH uses it for its fix steps. The Quick Guided Task "a mod with problems (fix them)" still only looks under GoH: it shows the findings, says what to change by hand, and writes nothing.
  • gen --target goh writes the Gates of Hell forms where they differ: texts go into a .pot file under localizations/default/interface/text/ instead of a .lng, and a squad goes into units/<period>/units_<army>.set. Gates of Hell probably does not read a .lng file at all; this is not confirmed in the game.
  • upgrade --to goh copies an Assault Squad 2 mod into a new folder in the Gates of Hell layout. The result is a start, not a tested mod.

3. The pages of the window

At the top of the window you pick the game you are modding: MoW:AS2 (the original 3.262 game, mowas_2.exe), AS64 (the 64-bit build with 3.301 data, as64.exe) or GoH (Gates of Hell, call_to_arms.exe). Each game keeps its own mod, game folder and last tab. Every game shows the same nine tabs and the same pages; GoH adds the GoH unit page. Where one part of a page cannot work for a game, that part stays in its place and says so in one line: "Not available in" the game, and the reason. The window has three levels: a row of tabs, a row of sub-tabs under the tab, and a third row of items above the page. A tab with only one sub-tab shows no sub-tab row, and a sub-tab with only one item shows no third row. A tab opens the item you last used in it. A link to a page of another game switches the game and says so.

In the table, sub-tabs are separated by semicolons and the items of a sub-tab are in brackets. "(Advanced)" marks an item that shows only with Advanced on (Settings).

Tab (key)Sub-tabs and itemsMoW:AS2AS64GoH
Help & Docs (Alt+1)Start Here; Prepare; Docs (ARSENAL, Modding, Engine, Project Notes (Advanced)); Guides & External Tools; Claude; Historical Sourcesyesyesyes
Mods (Alt+2)Mods (Mods, Upgrade or Port, Mod Files (Advanced)); Check & Fix (Check, Read Game.log)yesyesyes; the easy upgrade card is not shown
IDE (Alt+3)one page, the Editoryesyesyes
Models & Sim (Alt+4)Models, Look & Soundyesyesyes; no Armor part on Models
Maps & Missions (Alt+5)Maps; Map Viewer; Missionsyesyesyes; no "Add a game mode to this map"
Game Modes & AI (Alt+6)Game Modes; Bots (Bots, Bot Doctrine); Unit AI; Map Scripts for AIyesyesyes; several parts not available, see In Gates of Hell
Units & Balance (Alt+7)Units (Units, and under GoH the GoH unit page); Balanceyesyesyes; no price calculator, no "Describe a new unit"
Test, Share & Play (Alt+8)Test Run (Test Plan, Test Run); Share; Playyes; real test runs only as a dry run or a planyesyes; no test game runs and no Gates of Hell start, see below
Tools & Settings (Alt+9)Other Tools (Generator, Expert Tools (Advanced)); Settingsyesyesyes

The header holds:

  • The game picker: MoW:AS2, AS64 and GoH.
  • The mod and the game folder. "Change" picks another mod folder (it must hold a mod.info); "Game folder..." points at another install and "Reset" goes back to the one found. Under GoH the header shows the Gates of Hell folder and the Assault Squad 2 folder that the GoH unit page writes its ported units to.
  • LAN Remote, Colours (As the system, Light, Dark) and Language (English, Russian, Ukrainian, Chinese; the first start follows the browser).
  • "Advanced on", a small chip that shows only while Advanced is on. Pressing it opens Settings.
  • A link to the community Discord, "Join The AS64 Community!".

Advanced and Arrange have their place on Tools & Settings > Settings (Settings, Arrange mode), and Ctrl+K has both too. Window settings are kept in one file, %LOCALAPPDATA%\ARSENAL\settings.json, shared by every browser on this PC; they never keep a password, token or key.

Keys on every page: Alt+1 to Alt+9 open a tab. The same tab has the same key in every game, and a key whose tab the game does not have does nothing. Pressing the key of the tab you are on steps through its sub-tabs (in a tab with one sub-tab, through its items). Ctrl+Enter runs the page's main button, j and k move in a list and / jumps to the mod filter, Esc cancels the run in progress (or ends Arrange). Ctrl+K opens the palette, "Go to a page or run a command": type to find a page (listed by its path, such as "Mods > Check & Fix > Read Game.log") or a game, or pick a quick action ("Check this mod", "Install: preview (writes nothing)", "Play: dry run (no game)", "Settings (Advanced, Arrange)", switch Advanced on or off, "Arrange This Page"). The "Keyboard keys" fold at the foot of the page lists the keys.

A command that runs shows its output as it streams, with a progress row and "Stop this run". Only one game run can go at a time, and a run stops after 30 minutes unless the command asks for another limit. "Copy as command" on a run card gives the same run as a line for the terminal.

Every page that writes shows first what it will write, and writes only after you confirm in the confirm box. Nothing is ever written into the game's own data. The one exception is on the Share page: "Put the uploader into the game folder" copies the Workshop uploader's files into the game folder after its own confirm (chapter 20).

Quick Guided Task

The row "Quick Guided Task" sits above the tabs on every game. It reads as a sentence: I want to [make / change / explore] [a task] Start. The first box picks the verb; the second lists the tasks for that verb, with "Type to filter" to narrow it. A task that cannot run here shows grey with the reason: "not for" and the game, "needs a mod picked", "needs the game folder", or "only on the PC, not from another device". There is no separate "fix" verb: fixing a mod is the change task "a mod with problems (fix them)", and looking at what went wrong is the explore task "what went wrong in the last run".

Start opens the task window. It asks one question at a time, plans the files, writes them into the mod you picked with a restore point first, checks the mod and sends you to test. The step by step is in Use the Quick Guided Task. The tasks, by the name the window shows (verb, then title):

TaskVerbsGames

an army (change: "an army: its name, flag, cards and side")make, changeMoW:AS2, AS64
prices of an armychangeMoW:AS2, AS64
what bots buy and how they playchangeMoW:AS2, AS64
a skin or camouflagemake, changeMoW:AS2, AS64
an iconmake, changeMoW:AS2, AS64

a voice setmake, changeMoW:AS2, AS64
a map, starting from a game map (change: "the settings of a map")make, changeMoW:AS2, AS64
