  • Vitality: the extender that holds health. Chapter 6.
  • vol (.vol): a volume file describing hit shapes and armor areas. Chapters 6 and 9.

W

  • Whole document: a document read in one piece on the Docs page: the Doctrine atlas, the Modding guide or the Engine document. Chapter 19.
  • Workshop: Steam's mod sharing service. Chapter 20 and Pack and share.
  • Workshop copy: the copy of a subscribed Workshop item. The original game copies it into mods/<Name>/; the 64-bit build loads it in place from Steam's download folder and ignores a copy in mods/. Gates of Hell also loads it in place, as mod_<item number>. Chapter 20 and Reference 1.
  • Workshop uploader: the program that uploads a mod folder to the Steam Workshop. ARSENAL's own is workshop_gui.exe, which the Share page puts beside the game program and opens; it works for Assault Squad 2, the 64-bit build and Gates of Hell. Chapter 20.

Z

  • Zip root: the folder a pak's entry paths start from. A pak placed in resource/ needs the top folder name inside it. Chapter 20.
  • Zip64: the zip extension that allows very large paks. Chapter 20.

Gates of Hell: summary

The Gates of Hell notes in this book have not been tested in a running game. Check them in your own game before you depend on them.

These glossary terms belong to Gates of Hell, or say how ARSENAL handles it:

TermWhat it is
binaries/x64Folder of the game program; the Workshop uploader goes there
call_to_arms.exeThe Gates of Hell game program
ConquestCampaign mode only Gates of Hell has
Dedicated servercall_to_arms_server.exe, a match with no player at it
develop (tag)Lifts the version check of one mod
Direct controlGates of Hell adds a third-person view
Doctrine (Gates of Hell)A lobby choice per player that filters units
GOH-ORIGIN.tsvList of ported files; such a mod is never shared
GoH unit page, Translate numbersARSENAL page and its fold that bring a vehicle into Assault Squad 2
localizations (folder)Texts per language in a Gates of Hell mod
mod_<item number>Name of a Workshop mod in Gates of Hell
pot (.pot)Gates of Hell text files
Prioritymod.info key that orders independent mods
rep (.rep)Gates of Hell replay
sav (.sav)Gates of Hell saved game
Tags (mod.info)develop and no_delete

Every chapter of Part II ends with its own Gates of Hell summary; for packaging and the Workshop see chapter 20, for problems chapter 21.

Part III

Reference

Every key and every function, one entry each, always in the same shape: where it is written, its type, the values the game accepts, what it does, its limits, an example and where to read more. Look a name up here when you need its exact facts. Names that no source describes yet are listed at the end of each page.

12 reference pages

Reference 1: mod.info and the Mod Folder

This page lists, one entry each, every key of mod.info, every item the game reads from a mod folder, the keys of a patch document, and the rules that decide which file wins when several sources hold the same path. Chapter 3 explains mod folders and load order as a story, and chapter 4 explains paks and patches. Come here when you need the exact facts about one key or one rule.

Every entry has the same parts:

  • Where: the file kind and the block the key is written in.
  • Type: what kind of value it takes.
  • Values: what the game accepts, and what happens when the key is absent.
  • Does: what the key does.
  • Limits: what silently fails, stops the game or is ignored.
  • Example: a few lines in the pattern of real data.
  • Gates of Hell: only where Gates of Hell treats the key differently. Keys only Gates of Hell has are at the end, under Gates of Hell only.
  • See: where to read more: the Part II section that explains the key, the Part I page that uses it, and related entries.

A few words used below. A virtual path is the path of a file inside the game's resource tree, such as set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle, whether the file is loose on disk or packed in a zip. The file index is the single list of virtual paths the game builds when it starts or applies mods; a file is only found if its path is in that list. A pak is an ordinary zip file with the extension .pak. Classic mode and Enhanced mode are the two ways the 64-bit as64.exe program runs: Enhanced mode is the one where the built-in package as64+ is active (entry as64+ below).

mod.info

mod.info is a small text file in the data language of chapter 5. It sits in the root of the mod folder and holds one outer block, {Mod ...}. It describes the mod; it does not list the mod's files.

Mod

Where: mod.info, the outer block. Type: block.

Values: the block name may be written Mod or mod; key names inside are not case sensitive. A ; starts a comment.

Does: holds all other keys of the file.

Limits: A folder without a file named exactly mod.info at its root is not a mod: the game skips it without a log line, which is what happens when a zip tool adds an extra folder level. Unknown keys inside the block are skipped silently, so a misspelt key does nothing and produces no message. A broken value, such as an unescaped quote inside Desc, has stopped the game from starting, even when that mod was not in the active list, because every mod.info in the mods folder is read at start. Saving the file as UTF-16 breaks it; save it as UTF-8 without a byte-order mark (or plain ASCII) with CRLF line endings.

Example:

{Mod
	{Name "My Mod"}
	{MinGameVersion "3.262"}
	{MaxGameVersion "3.262"}
}

Gates of Hell: an empty mod.info is skipped with Warning: empty mod.info file found at <path>, and one that does not parse skips only that mod with Warning: failed to load mod <path>: <error>; it does not stop the game. The block also takes Tags and Priority.

See: chapter 3, section 2; mod folder; Part I Make a mod and see it in the game; ARSENAL modinfo in chapter 19.

Name

Where: mod.info, inside {Mod}. Type: text, one quoted string.

Values: any text. Vanilla-era mods use plain titles; the built-in package uses "AS64+".

Does: the title shown in the in-game mod list. It is also the name of the folder the Workshop installer of the original game creates for subscribers.

Limits: The game never compares Name with the folder name, and the active list never uses it: a mod is identified by its folder name. If you publish a mod and later change its Name, the folder name on every subscriber's machine of the original game changes and their active lists stop matching. Each known key takes exactly one quoted string and then the closing brace; a quote inside the value must be written \".

Example:

	{Name "My Mod"}

Gates of Hell: the same key. A subscribed Workshop mod is known there as mod_<item number>, and the mod list asks Steam for the title of an item that is not loaded, so changing Name does not break subscribers' lists.

See: mod folder, Workshop copy; chapter 3, section 2; Part I Make a mod and see it in the game, Pack and share.

Desc

Where: mod.info, inside {Mod}. Type: text, one quoted string.

Values: any text. \n inside the string becomes a new line. Colour markup of the form <c(rrggbb)>...</c> is handled by the interface when the text is shown. Absent: no description.

Does: the description shown for the mod.

Limits: An unescaped quote inside the description has stopped the game from starting. Write a quote as \".

Example:

	{Desc "Changes rifle damage.\nVersion 2."}

Gates of Hell: $n as well as \n starts a new line of the description.

See: chapter 3, section 2; Part I Pack and share; Workshop upload.

MinGameVersion

Where: mod.info, inside {Mod}. Type: text, a dotted version string such as "3.262".

Values: digits and dots; other characters are ignored. A value of 3.301 or higher makes the mod a modern mod; anything lower makes it a legacy mod.

Does: the lowest game version the mod supports, and at the same time the mode label of the mod. A legacy mod loads only in Classic mode (and in the original game); a modern mod loads only in Enhanced mode.

Limits: For a legacy mod, an empty or missing MinGameVersion makes the mod unsupported, and it is skipped with a warning. Versions are compared only over the parts both versions have, so 3.262.1 counts as equal to 3.262. The legacy check uses the game's data version, which has the form 3.262.<patch>, so a slightly newer program build still accepts mods made for 3.262. A mod of the wrong mode is skipped; in as64.exe a mismatched mod in the active list at start has crashed the game with "Unable to determine fallback font" before the menu appeared, because the refusal message is written before the fonts are loaded. Take the mod out of the list, or fix this key, to recover.

Example:

	{MinGameVersion "3.262"}   ; legacy mod
	{MinGameVersion "3.301"}   ; modern mod for Enhanced mode

Gates of Hell: the value is compared with the Gates of Hell program version, which is a 1.x number (such as 1.067), so a mod.info written for 3.262 or 3.301 is refused there. The key is optional: a missing MinGameVersion means no lower limit. There is no legacy or modern label and no Classic or Enhanced mode. A mod whose Tags hold develop loads at any version.

See: MaxGameVersion, as64+, chapter 3, section 3 and section 4; Part I Bring an old mod up to the 64-bit build, Make a mod and see it in the game.

MaxGameVersion

Where: mod.info, inside {Mod}. Type: text, a dotted version string.

Values: digits and dots. Legacy mods: required. Modern mods: may be left out.

Does: the highest game version a legacy mod supports. The mod is supported when the game version is not below MinGameVersion and not above MaxGameVersion.

Limits: For a legacy mod, an empty or missing value makes the mod unsupported. For a modern mod the value is ignored completely: the only test is that the plain program version is at least MinGameVersion. A MaxGameVersion lower than MinGameVersion is not reported. The console variable dev_disableModVersionControl, when true, lets a legacy mod with an empty range load.

Example:

	{MinGameVersion "3.262"}
	{MaxGameVersion "3.262"}   ; accepts every 3.262 patch

Gates of Hell: optional for every mod; a missing bound is open, so a mod with only MinGameVersion stays active in every later version. Write both bounds to pin a range. dev_disableModVersionControl lifts the check there too.

See: MinGameVersion, lastGameVersion; chapter 3, section 3; Part I Bring an old mod up to the 64-bit build.

Require

Where: mod.info, inside {Mod}. Repeatable. Type: text, one quoted string per key.

Values: "folder" or "folder:number". Only the folder part is compared. The built-in package can be named as "as64+".

Does: names another mod that must be installed and active. When the list is applied, mods are sorted so that a required mod is mounted before the mod that requires it.

Limits: If the required folder is not in mods, or not in the active list, the requiring mod is dropped with a dependency warning. Mode words such as "as64" or "legacy" are not folders, so the game treats them as missing mods. A circular requirement (A requires B and B requires A) empties the whole active list, with a log line beginning Dependency test error!. The order of mods that do not require each other is not guaranteed.

Example:

	{Require "basemod"}
	{Require "as64+"}

See: Load order between mods, options.set mods; chapter 3, section 6; Part I Bring an old mod up to the 64-bit build.

Delete

Where: mod.info, inside {Mod}. Repeatable. Type: text, one quoted path per key.

Values: a path that starts with resource/. A path ending in / is a prefix and removes every file under it.

Does: removes a file, or every file under a folder, from the file index before this mod's own files are mounted.

Limits: The path must start with resource/. A path such as "set/x" is turned into a path outside the resource tree and matches nothing, without any message. Because it runs before the mod's own files mount, it cannot remove the mod's own files; use a patch delete for that. A deleted file leaves no marker, and anything that later asks for it stops the game with File not found - resource/<path>.

Example:

	{Delete "resource/set/stuff/junk/old_rifle"}
	{Delete "resource/set/stuff/junk/"}

See: delete (patch), chapter 4, section 5 and its part mod.info Delete instead of a patch.

FileId

Where: mod.info, inside {Mod}. Type: text, a decimal number in quotes.

Values: the Workshop item number. Written by the Workshop uploader; absent in a mod that was never uploaded.

Does: ties the folder to its Workshop item. The uploader finds the folder of an item by this key, and when it updates an item it writes only this key, keeping every other byte of the file.

Limits: Loading ignores the key. A value that is not a number gives no error; the id read is then zero or garbage. For a subscribed item the Workshop's own id wins over this key.

Example:

	{FileId "1234567890"}

Gates of Hell: read only for local mods. A subscribed item takes its id from the Workshop and is known as mod_<item number>.

See: Workshop upload; chapter 20, section 8; Part I Pack and share.

The mod folder

mod folder

Where: <game folder>/mods/<folder>/. Type: folder.

Values: a folder name made of the characters listed under file names; the game lower-cases it.

Does: one mod. The mod's identity is its folder name in lower case, not its Name. The game scans only the direct subfolders of mods (plus the built-in package and subscribed Workshop items).

Limits: A mod folder outside <game folder>/mods/ is never seen. Two folders whose names differ only by case count as one name: the second fails to register and never loads, with no log line. Renaming a folder makes it a different mod, so an active-list entry naming the old folder loads nothing. A folder named as64+ inside mods is dropped, because that name belongs to the built-in package.

Example:

<game folder>/mods/mymod/mod.info
<game folder>/mods/mymod/resource/set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle

Gates of Hell: a folder whose name holds a space, a byte above 127 or any of < > + ( ) [ ] { } ! @ # $ % ^ & * - = ; : | ' " is skipped, with the warning invalid mod folder name in game.log only, so my-mod and my mod never load there; use letters, digits, _ and .. When two mods have the same id, the first scan at start keeps the second one found and logs Warning! Duplicate mod found [...] using second.; local folders are scanned before Workshop items, so a local mods/mod_<item number> loses to that Workshop item.

See: options.set mods, file names, chapter 3, section 1; Part I Make a mod and see it in the game.

resource.pak

Where: the mod root. Type: zip file.

Values: one optional file named resource.pak.

Does: the first item mounted for the mod. Its entries are placed under resource/, so an entry set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle becomes the virtual path set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle.

Limits: Because resource/ is mounted after resource.pak, a loose file in resource/ should replace the same path in resource.pak; that follows from the order but has not been seen in play (unconfirmed), so ship each file in one place only. A pak the zip reader cannot open stops the game at mount with Can't open pak. See pak for the zip rules.

Example:

mods/mymod/resource.pak      entry: set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle

Gates of Hell: not mounted, neither in a mod nor in the game folder, and nothing is logged. Put paks inside resource/ instead, where every .pak is mounted in place.

See: Mount order inside a mod; chapter 4, section 2, chapter 20, section 3; Part I Pack and share.

resource/

Where: the mod root. Type: folder.

Values: the same layout as the game's resource tree: set/, entity/, interface/, properties/ and so on.

Does: every file under it is added to the index at its path relative to resource/. Paks found inside it are mounted as paks at their own place (see pak).

Limits: Loose files with the extensions .temp, .scc, ., ., .org, ., .msg and .txt are never indexed (.ply and .mtl are explicitly allowed), so a loose .txt file is invisible while the same file inside a pak is found. A file named .gitignore and folders named .git or .svn are skipped. Files added while the game runs appear only after the next Apply. When a loose folder and a pak in the same folder hold the same path, see Loose file against pak.

Example:

mods/mymod/resource/set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle
mods/mymod/resource/gamelogic.pak

See: chapter 4, section 3; Part I Make a mod and see it in the game.

N.pat

Where: the mod root, as 1.pat, 2.pat, 3.pat and so on. Type: zip file.

Values: numbered from 1 without gaps.

Does: a patch. Each .pat is mounted like a pak under resource/, so it may carry ordinary files, and it must also hold one patch document whose name ends in .patch (see Patch). Patches run after the mod's own resource.pak and resource/ folder.

Limits: The game counts 1.pat, 2.pat, ... and stops at the first missing number, so a .pat after a gap is never mounted, silently. A .pat without a .patch document stops the game with Wrong patch N. The number of .pat files is the mod's patch count, which the active list checks (see options.set mods). The same .patch document placed loose in the mod root is never read.

Example:

mods/mymod/1.pat     zip holding: 1.patch

See: Patch, chapter 4, section 5; Part I Pack and share.

localization.pak

Where: the mod root. Type: zip file.

Values: one optional file named localization.pak holding .lng text files.

Does: mounted after the patches, with its entries placed under resource/interface/text/.

Limits: A .lng file replaces the original file of the same name completely. Keys the mod's copy leaves out are not filled in from the original; they show blank or as the key.

Example:

mods/mymod/localization.pak   entry: desc.lng

Gates of Hell: not mounted. Texts go in localizations/ instead.

See: chapter 14, section 3; Part I Add or change text and translate it.

localization/

Where: the mod root. Type: folder.

Values: .lng text files, UTF-8.

Does: the last item mounted for the mod, scanned into resource/interface/text/.

Limits: Same replacement rule as localization.pak: a file replaces the original wholesale. Loose .txt files here are skipped like everywhere else.

Example:

mods/mymod/localization/desc.lng

Gates of Hell: not mounted, so .lng files here are probably ignored and the game shows the raw keys (not confirmed in a running game). Texts go in localizations/ instead.

See: chapter 14, section 1; Part I Add or change text and translate it.

other files in the mod root

Where: the mod root. Type: any file or folder.

Values: notes, working files of your own tools, screenshots, a .git folder, a loose .patch.

Does: nothing. The game reads only mod.info, resource.pak, resource/, the numbered .pat files, localization.pak and localization/.

Limits: The Workshop uploader sends the whole folder, so private files and development folders reach every subscriber. Keep them out of a folder you upload.

Example:

mods/mymod/notes.md        ignored by the game, uploaded by the Workshop tool
mods/mymod/1.patch         never read; pack it into 1.pat

See: Workshop upload; chapter 20, section 5; Part I Pack and share.

Patch documents

A patch document is a text file whose name ends in .patch, packed inside a numbered .pat zip. The game finds it by that ending, whatever the rest of the name is.

Patch

Where: a .patch document inside N.pat, the outer block. Type: block.

Values: children id, delete and remap; other keys are read and ignored.

Does: lists the deletions and renames this patch applies. After the patch is applied, the document itself is removed from the index, so the next .pat finds its own.

Limits: A loose .patch file in the mod root is never read. Files packed in the same .pat are mounted before its lines run, so they survive unless a delete names them.

Example:

{Patch
	{id 1}
	{delete "set/stuff/junk/old_rifle"}
}

See: N.pat, chapter 4, section 5 and its small worked example.

id

Where: .patch, inside {Patch}. Type: whole number.

Values: must equal the number of the .pat it is packed in.

Does: identifies the patch.

Limits: A different number stops the game with Wrong patch N version.

Example:

	{id 2}      ; inside 2.pat

See: Patch.

delete (patch)

Where: .patch, inside {Patch}. Repeatable. Type: text, a quoted path.

Values: a path relative to resource/, without a leading resource/. Backslashes are accepted. A path ending in / removes every file under it.

Does: removes the file from the index.

Limits: It runs after the mod's own pak and folder, so it removes the mod's own copy of that path as well as earlier mods' and the original game's copies. A later mod can add the path again. A path that does not exist is not an error. Nothing marks the deletion: anything that later asks for the file stops the game with File not found - resource/<path>.

Example:

	{delete "set/stuff/junk/old_rifle"}
	{delete "set/stuff/junk/"}

See: Delete (the mod.info form), chapter 4, section 5.

remap

Where: .patch, inside {Patch}. Repeatable. Type: two quoted paths.

Values: "from" "to", both relative to resource/.

Does: moves a file to a new virtual path: the file is registered under to and removed from from.

Limits: If from does not exist, the game stops with File is not found - <from>.

Example:

	{remap "set/stuff/gun/a_gun" "set/stuff/gun/b_gun"}

See: Patch.

The active list

options.set mods

Where: the profile file options.set, inside {options}. Type: list of quoted strings.

Values: each entry is "folder:number", split at the first colon. The folder part is the lower-case folder name. The number is the patch count the mod had when it was activated.

Does: the list of active mods, in load order. Every Apply goes through it in order: an entry whose folder does not exist is dropped with the log line Mod '<entry>' was disabled: Not installed.; an entry whose version range fails is dropped with a warning; an entry whose required mod is missing is dropped with a warning; an entry whose number is larger than the folder's patch count is dropped silently. The rest are sorted by requirements and mounted in order. The game writes the cleaned list back.

Limits: The folder comparison is exact, so an entry with a capital letter never matches. The number is only a gate: the game always mounts all of the mod's patches, even when the entry asks for fewer. After you add a .pat to an active mod, activate it again so the number is updated. A subscribed Workshop mod is listed by its normalised title, not by its item number (unconfirmed in play). A legacy mod and a modern mod cannot both load from one list: whichever mode the list is in, the other mod drops out. Let the game or ARSENAL modswitch write the list rather than editing it by hand.

Example:

{options
	{mods "basemod:0" "mymod:2"}
}

Gates of Hell: a subscribed Workshop mod is listed as mod_<item number>. Entries named twice are dropped, and when the game drops any entry it writes the list back without the :number parts. The profile folder is under Documents/My Games/Gates of Hell/, or under %LOCALAPPDATA%/Digitalmindsoft/Gates of Hell/ when the game is started with -useLocalDataFolder or the Documents folder lies in OneDrive; the log line IO: Game config directory: names the one in use.

See: chapter 3, section 5, chapter 18, section 2; Part I Make a mod and see it in the game, step 7.

lastGameVersion

Where: the profile file settings.set. Type: text.

Values: written by the game.

Does: the game version that last used this profile.

Limits: When it differs from the running version, the game empties the active mod list (the log says "Game version update detected"), and you must activate your mods again. The comparison uses the data version 3.262, so as64.exe and mowas_2.exe share one profile and switching between them keeps the list.

Example: the key is written by the game into settings.set; you never edit it. Its counterpart, the mod list, lives in profiles/<id>/options.set.

See: options.set mods.

Load order and mount rules

Override rule

Where: every mounted source. Type: rule.

Values: none.

Does: the file index holds one entry per virtual path. When a later source adds a path that is already there, the earlier entry is thrown away. The later source wins the whole file. There is no merging of file contents and no priority setting.

Limits: A mod that replaces a data file must carry the whole file; every entry the replacement leaves out is gone, including entries another mod added. File dates never decide anything. No log line marks an override.

Example:

base game   set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle   (replaced)
mymod       set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle   (used)

See: Load order between mods, chapter 4, section 1, chapter 4, section 7 for seeing which file won; Part I Change a unit's numbers.

Mount order inside a mod

Where: every mod folder, and the game folder itself. Type: rule.

Values: fixed order: resource.pak, then resource/, then 1.pat, 2.pat, ..., then localization.pak, then localization/.

Does: decides the order in which one mod's own items enter the index. The original game is mounted the same way from the game folder, with all its patches.

Limits: Patches come after the mod's own files, so a patch delete removes the mod's own copies too. The mod.info Delete lines run before all of these. On the 64-bit build as64.exe, the folder as64/core/ is mounted after the original game and before any mod (see as64/core).

Example:

1 resource.pak   2 resource/   3 1.pat, 2.pat   4 localization.pak   5 localization/

Gates of Hell: the order is resource/, then 1.pat, 2.pat, ..., then localizations/; there is no resource.pak, localization.pak or localization/ step. A game folder without localizations/ stops with Failed to mount localization. After the mods, the default language's localizations/<code>/ and then the chosen language's are laid over resource/, so a file there probably beats the same path in resource/ of every mod (not confirmed).

See: chapter 4, section 4, chapter 20, section 2.

Load order between mods

Where: the active list in options.set. Type: rule.

Values: list order, after the requirement sort.

Does: the original game is mounted first, then each active mod in list order. A mod lower in the list (mounted later) wins every path it shares with a mod above it.

Limits: The requirement sort places mods with fewer requirements first and each mod after its requirements; among mods that do not depend on each other, the order is not guaranteed. A circular requirement drops the whole list. The built-in as64+ package always comes before every player mod.

Example:

{mods "damagemod:0" "accuracymod:0"}   ; accuracymod wins shared files

Gates of Hell: the sort is stable. Mods are ordered by the number of their requirements and then by Priority, lower first, so among mods that do not require each other the higher Priority wins shared files. A circular requirement empties the list there too.

See: Require, chapter 3, section 6; Part I Make a mod and see it in the game.

Loose file against pak

Where: inside one folder of a mod's or the game's resource tree. Type: rule.

Values: none.

Does: inside a folder, the game takes files, subfolders and paks in the order the operating system lists them and does not sort them. On a normal Windows disk that is case-insensitive name order, and the later name wins.

Limits: As a result a loose set/ folder wins over gamelogic.pak (it sorts later), while a loose entity/ folder loses to entity.pak (it sorts earlier). This order is not confirmed in play for every folder (unconfirmed). Other file systems may list in a different order. Do not ship the same path both loose and in a pak.

Example:

resource/entity/       loses to   resource/entity.pak
resource/gamelogic.pak loses to   resource/set/

See: chapter 4, section 3; pak.

pak

Where: any .pak file under a mounted folder, resource.pak, localization.pak, and the .pat files. Type: zip file.

Values: plain zip, entries stored or deflate-compressed. No encryption, no special header. Zip64 archives are read.

Does: each entry becomes a virtual path made of the folder the pak sits in plus the entry name. A mod's resource/entity.pak with entry entity/-vehicle/x/x.def gives entity/-vehicle/x/x.def. The game's own entity paks sit one folder lower, in resource/entity/, so their entries start one level lower (-vehicle/...).

Limits: An extra top-level folder inside the zip (mymod/set/...) adds new paths and replaces nothing. A single entry must stay below 4 GB. Write real CRC values; a wrong CRC can still load as a resource but breaks other readers. If one zip holds a name twice, the later entry wins. Entries ending in / are ignored. Entry names longer than 1023 bytes are cut. Small text entries (.mdl, .def, .inc, .set, .reg, .info, .txt, .mi, .ext, .tpl) are read into memory when the pak is mounted, so many small text files make Apply slower.

Example:

mods/mymod/resource/gamelogic.pak   entry: set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle
mods/mymod/resource/entity.pak      entry: entity/-vehicle/tank_medium/mytank/mytank.def

Gates of Hell: every entry without a CRC-32 value logs no crc for file in package ... performance may be slowed, so write real CRCs. An entry that cannot be read stops the game with Failed to read file from pak <name>; a pak that cannot be opened still stops it. The kinds kept in memory differ (.reg .def .inc .set .ext .tpl .info .presets .pattern .ammo .fsm .xml, not .mdl, .mi or .txt), and they are read on first use, not when the pak is mounted.

See: chapter 4, section 2 and section 8, chapter 20, section 3; Part I Pack and share.

file names

Where: every virtual path and every path written in data. Type: rule.

Values: letters and digits and the characters [ ] ( ) { } @ $ % ^ - + . _ ! # & and space. A name must not start or end with a space.

Does: every name is turned to lower case and every \ to / when it enters the index, so names that differ only by case or slash direction are one name.

Limits: A path longer than 4096 bytes stops the game with path is too long. The extension of a name is the text after its last dot; files without an extension are legal and common (most weapon files).

Example:

Set\Stuff\Rifle\Example_Rifle   is the same name as   set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle

Gates of Hell: a name is also lower-cased and its \ turned to / as soon as it is read from a data file. A name with non-ASCII letters may be at most 1023 bytes after lower-casing, else path is too long. Mod folder names follow a stricter rule (see mod folder).

See: path forms; chapter 5, section 3.

path forms

Where: any path written inside a data file. Type: rule.

Values: /a/b relative to the resource tree; //a/b relative to the game folder, outside the resource tree; @a/b relative to the user data folder (<Documents>/My Games/Men of War - Assault Squad 2/); a/b with no leading slash, relative to the folder of the file being read; each leading ../ goes up one folder.

Does: decides where a written path points.

Limits: An (include "x.inc") without a leading / is looked for next to the file that holds the include line, so a copied file that keeps a relative include must stay in a folder that mirrors the original.

Example:

(include "/properties/tank.ext")    ; from the resource root
(include "grenade_smoke.inc")       ; next to this file

Gates of Hell: adds !a/b, relative to the game folder like //a/b; it works only there. @a/b points into Documents/My Games/Gates of Hell/ (or the LocalAppData folder named under options.set mods).

See: chapter 5, section 5; include of a template and Extension on reference page 2; Part I Add a new unit from an existing one.

Apply

Where: Options, MODS tab, the Apply button; also every game start. Type: rule.

Values: none.

Does: a full rebuild of the index: all resource paths are removed, the original game is mounted, then every active mod in order. The log line Repository: N resources at the end gives the size of the index.

Limits: Large mods make Apply slow. Files added to a mod folder while the game runs appear only after the next Apply. If the number in Repository: N resources does not change after you change a mod, no file was added or removed (one may still have been replaced).

Example:

Repository: N resources      ; game.log, end of every Apply

Gates of Hell: the log shows Mod: applying mods, then Mod: activate mod x or Mod: disable mod x for each change; a mod that is already applied is not applied again. At start the scan logs Scanning mods in and Found N available mods.

See: options.set mods; chapter 18, section 2 and section 5; Part I Check a mod, fix what the check finds, read the game log.

multiplayer sync folders

Where: every mounted or deleted path. Type: rule.

Values: paths starting with entity/, fx/, properties/, set/, sound/, map/single/, map/bonus/, map/multi/ or script/multiplayer/.

Does: a mod that adds, replaces or deletes any path under these folders is flagged as affecting multiplayer, and every player in a match must have the same version of it.

Limits: A mod that touches only interface/ is not compared. The content check between players covers files of the kinds .set, .inc, .ext, .mi, .reg, .info, .def and .mdl; .lng, .dds, .ebm, .wav and Lua files are not compared and may differ between players.

Example:

mods/mymod/resource/set/...         synchronized
mods/mymod/resource/interface/...   not synchronized

See: chapter 12, section 10 and its part The data checksum, chapter 20, section 6, ARSENAL mpsync in chapter 19.

Built-in layers of the 64-bit build

as64/core

Where: <game folder>/as64/core/. Type: folder with paks and loose files.

Values: shipped with as64.exe.

Does: mounted by as64.exe after the original game and before every mod, in both modes, with no patches. It carries the 64-bit build's shader and text changes.

Limits: It does not exist for the original mowas_2.exe. Any mod can override its files, because mods mount later.

Example:

<game folder>/as64/core/resource/...
<game folder>/as64/core/localization/...

Gates of Hell: has no such layer.

See: as64+; chapter 4, section 4.

as64+

Where: <game folder>/as64/plus/, with its own mod.info. Type: built-in mod.

Values: always loaded under the name as64+. Its MinGameVersion is 3.301.

Does: the Enhanced mode package. When as64+ is in the active list the game runs in Enhanced mode, where modern mods load and legacy mods do not. It is always placed before every player mod.

Limits: Every player mod overrides its files, and it cannot be moved above them. A folder named as64+ inside mods is dropped. A mod may name it in Require. How the in-game menu switches Enhanced mode on is not described (unconfirmed); the mode follows whether as64+ is in the active list.

Example:

{Mod
	{Name "My Enhanced Mod"}
	{MinGameVersion "3.301"}
	{Require "as64+"}
}

Gates of Hell: has no built-in package and no Classic or Enhanced mode. A folder named as64+ would not load there anyway, because + is not allowed in a mod folder name.

See: MinGameVersion, chapter 3, section 4; Part I Bring an old mod up to the 64-bit build.

Workshop and other layers

Workshop copy

Where: Steam's download folder for the game, and <game folder>/mods/. Type: rule.

Values: none.

Does: the original mowas_2.exe copies a subscribed item into mods/<Name>/ (the folder name comes from the item's Name), deletes any old copy there first, adds {FileId} to the copy's mod.info, and writes a stamp file named after the item number in mods/. as64.exe instead loads a subscribed item in place from the Steam folder.

Limits: On the original game, a local mod with the same Name as a subscribed one is overwritten at the next sync, and local edits to the copy are lost when the stamp is out of date. On as64.exe, a mods/ folder that is an old copy of a subscribed item is ignored, with the log line mods/<name>/ is an old copy of a Workshop item, which is loaded instead, so a fix made in that copy never loads: rename the folder or unsubscribe. Give your development copy a different folder name from the published item.

Example:

mods/<Name>/mod.info     copy made by the original game, with {FileId "..."}

Gates of Hell: loads a subscribed item in place, as as64.exe does, under the id mod_<item number>. An item whose path does not contain workshop/content/ is skipped with A workshop mod outside of standard location! (an item in another Steam library probably still loads, because its path keeps that part). A local mods/mod_<item number> loses to the Workshop item of that number. Deleting a mod in the options removes a local folder at once; a Workshop item's files stay until Steam removes them. Mods for a multiplayer session come from the Workshop; the game does not download them itself.

See: chapter 3, section 8, chapter 20, section 8.

Workshop upload

Where: the Workshop uploader shipped with the game. Type: tool rule.

Values: a mod folder, a title, a description of at most 8000 bytes, a preview image (JPG, PNG or GIF) under 1 MB, tags, visibility and a change note.

Does: uploads the whole mod folder as a Workshop item and writes the item number into mod.info as {FileId}. The preview is preview.jpg, preview.png, preview.gif or preview.jpeg in the mod folder, or else mods/previews/<folder>.jpg.

Limits: Everything in the folder is uploaded, including notes and .git folders, even though the game itself ignores them. The uploader reads mod.info loosely (first {mod} block, keys name, desc, FileId) and changes nothing but FileId.

Example:

mods/mymod/preview.jpg

See: chapter 20, section 8; Part I Pack and share, step 4.

map folder

Where: <game folder>/maps/<name>/. Type: folder.

Values: the same items as a mod folder: pak, resource/, patches.

Does: mounted at resource/map/multi/<name>/, after any files already at that path are removed.

Limits: Files outside that path are not reached this way. Chapter 13 covers maps.

Example:

maps/mymap/   is seen as   map/multi/mymap/

Gates of Hell: a resource.pak inside the map folder is not mounted; only resource/, the patches and the folder itself are.

See: chapter 13, section 2; Part I Copy and change a map.

map mod overlay

Where: a folder named mod/ inside a map folder. Type: folder.

Values: files laid out as under resource/.

Does: when that map's mission loads, its files are moved onto the matching paths under resource/ for the match, and the game data is reset. When the scene closes, the index is rebuilt and the active mods are applied again.

Limits: The overlay beats every active mod for that match.

Example:

map/multi/mymap/mod/set/stuff/rifle/example_rifle

See: chapter 4, section 6; map folder.

Switches

-no_mods

Where: the game's command line. Type: switch.

Values: none.

Does: starts the game with an empty mod list: no mod is applied and Workshop items are not installed.

Limits: Every mod.info in mods is still read at start, so a broken one can still stop the game.

Example:

as64.exe -no_mods

See: chapter 3, section 5; Part I Check a mod, fix what the check finds, read the game log.

Not described yet

Nothing in this area. Every key of mod.info and of a patch document read by the game is described above.

Gates of Hell only

The Gates of Hell notes in this book have not been tested in a running game. Check them in your own game before you depend on them.

These keys, folders and switches belong to the area of this page and exist only in Gates of Hell. as64.exe and the original game skip the two mod.info keys silently and do not mount the folder. Chapter 3 and chapter 4 compare the two games, and Part I Bring a unit from Gates of Hell covers moving work between them.

Tags

Where: mod.info, inside {Mod}. Type: text, one quoted string of words separated by spaces.

Values: any words. Two have a meaning: develop lets the mod load at any game version and leaves the version range out of its title in the mod list; no_delete hides the delete button for the mod. Absent: no tags.

Does: labels the mod. The game writes the key back when it saves the file.

Limits: an unquoted word is a read error (String expected!); a mod.info that fails to read is skipped with a warning. ARSENAL modinfo <mod folder> --goh warns about a value that is not one quoted string.

Example:

	{Tags "develop no_delete"}

See: MinGameVersion, MaxGameVersion.

Priority

Where: mod.info, inside {Mod}. Type: whole number.

Values: any whole number. Absent: 1.

Does: orders mods that do not require each other. Mods are sorted by the number of their requirements first and then by Priority, lower first; a mod applied later wins shared files, so the higher Priority wins.

Limits: it does not override a requirement: a required mod still comes first.

Example:

	{Priority 5}

See: Load order between mods, Require.

localizations/

Where: the root of the game folder and of a mod folder. Type: folder with one subfolder per language code.

Values: localizations/<code>/, texts under localizations/<code>/interface/text/. The languages offered are the folders that hold a localization.info. The codes default and en take .pot and .lng files; other languages take .po, .mo and .lng. The game's own default texts ship as localizations/default.pak.

Does: mounted after resource/ and the patches of each layer. When the game loads a language, the default language's folder and then the chosen language's folder are laid over resource/, so the chosen language's texts come first and the default ones fill the gaps. A .lng file is read here with the same key rule as in as64.exe.

Limits: a game folder without localizations/ stops with Failed to mount localization. A mod whose language layout differs from the game's logs Localization mode used in ... does not match with default mode and still loads. A .po or .pot entry without msgctxt gives no text.

Example:

mods/mymod/localizations/default/interface/text/units.pot
mods/mymod/localizations/<code>/interface/text/units.po

See: localization/, Mount order inside a mod, chapter 14.

! path prefix

Where: any path written inside a data file. Type: rule.

Values: !a/b.

Does: points at a/b relative to the game folder, like //a/b.

Limits: as64.exe and the original game do not know the prefix and read the path another way; do not use it in a mod for them.

Example:

!a/b     is the same place as   //a/b   (Gates of Hell only)

See: path forms.

-useLocalDataFolder

Where: the game's command line. Type: switch.

Values: none; any letter case.

Does: keeps profiles, saves and game.log in %LOCALAPPDATA%/Digitalmindsoft/Gates of Hell/ instead of Documents/My Games/Gates of Hell/. The game does the same without the switch when the Documents folder lies in OneDrive.

Limits: the folder is chosen once at start; game.log names it in the line IO: Game config directory:.

Example:

call_to_arms.exe -useLocalDataFolder

See: options.set mods, chapter 18.

-showmodinfo

Where: the game's command line. Type: switch.

Values: none.

Does: the mod list adds [STEAM:<item>] or [LOCAL] to each mod, a * for mods whose files take part in the multiplayer check, and a row with the mod's path.

Limits: display only.

Example:

call_to_arms.exe -showmodinfo

See: Workshop copy.

protected registry files

Where: set/registry.reg and set/registry/dlc.reg in the resource tree. Type: rule.

Values: none.

Does: at start the game checks both files against fixed checksums.

Limits: a mod that replaces either file stops the game with Resource Error. Other files under set/registry/ are probably not checked. Leave both files alone in a Gates of Hell mod.

Example:

mods/mymod/resource/set/registry.reg     stops Gates of Hell at start

See: Override rule.

Reference 2: Entity Definitions and Shared Data Sets

This page lists, one entry each, the top-level keys and blocks of an entity definition (a .def file and the .ext templates it includes), the common keys of stuff files, and the shared data sets that definitions point to by name. Chapter 6 explains entities as a story and chapter 5 explains the data language. Big blocks that have their own reference page get a short entry here and a pointer: extenders (r03), chassis and movement (r04), humans (r05), weapons (r06), armour and volumes (r07), vision and effects (r08).

Every entry has the same parts: Where (file kind and block), Type (with unit), Values (what the game accepts, and the value when the key is absent), Does, Limits (what silently fails, stops the game or is ignored), Example (a few lines in the pattern of real data) and See.

Rules that apply to every key on this page

  • Units. Lengths are written in metres and converted when read; masses are kilograms; angles are degrees; times are seconds; vehicle speeds are km/h; armour thickness and penetration are millimetres of steel.
  • Key names are not case sensitive in definitions, templates and stuff files: {Props} and {props} are the same key.
  • Unknown keys at the top level stop loading. A word at the top level of a definition that is not one of the keys below ends in the error "unexpected token". Some inner blocks are as strict; others skip what they do not know. A lint run (ARSENAL keylint) finds both kinds.
  • Tag lists are one quoted string of words split on spaces, or several quoted strings (each one tag, not split). A leading clear empties the inherited list first; a word starting with - removes that tag; reading a tag list again adds to it.
  • Definitions are read on first use. The game indexes every .def file under entity/ at start but reads one only when a map, a spawn or a purchase first needs it. A broken definition therefore shows up when a match loads, not at the main menu.
  • The shipped 3.262 build of the original game may differ in a key or an edge case from what this page says about the 64-bit build (unconfirmed for each case).
  • Gates of Hell. An entry whose key Gates of Hell treats differently has a line starting Gates of Hell:. Keys only Gates of Hell has are at the end, under Gates of Hell only.
  • Where each key is used. The See line names the Part II section that explains the key, and the Part I page that uses it where there is one: Add a new unit from an existing one, Change a unit's numbers, Change a gun or its ammunition, Change armour, Edit a model or an animation, Copy and change a map, Bring a unit from Gates of Hell.

Definition files

.def file

Where: under entity/ in the resource tree, for example entity/-vehicle/tank_medium/mytank/mytank.def. Type: file.

Values: one outer block whose name is a root type word (next entries).

Does: describes one entity. The entity's name is the file name without .def; that name is what maps, scripts, rosters and spawns use.

Limits: A .def outside entity/ is never loaded as an entity. Two .def files with the same file name anywhere under entity/ collide: the second logs Entity redefinition: <name> and is ignored. Keeping one name under two root classes has also been seen to crash the game when a grenade from it was thrown. In a running multiplayer match, a definition that was not loaded before the match started can stop the game when it is first read at the wrong moment (unconfirmed for buying a unit that was never preloaded; set/multiplayer/preload lists entities loaded before a match).

Example:

entity/-vehicle/tank_medium/mytank/mytank.def
entity/-vehicle/tank_medium/mytank/mytank.mdl

See: chapter 6, section 1 and section 9; Part I Add a new unit from an existing one.

game_entity

Where: .def, the outer block name. Type: root type word.

Values: game_entity, entity, actor, human or fx, compared without regard to case. If a second word follows the first (for example the bare word at the top of an included template), the second word is the type.

Does: an object on the map with volumes, tags, seats, extenders and scripts, such as a building, a crate or a fence. Most vanilla definitions start with game_entity; most vehicles also start with it and become actors through their template (see actor).

Limits: Any other word stops the game with "unknown entity type" when the definition is first read. A misspelt root word in a file nobody loads goes unnoticed until something loads it.

Example:

{game_entity
	{Extension "alg_tent_1m.mdl"}
	{mass 1000}
}

See: actor, chapter 6, section 2.

entity

Where: .def, the outer block name. Type: root type word.

Values: as for game_entity.

Does: the simplest kind: a model with placement and display keys only (the "Model and display keys" section below). Vanilla files that start with entity usually include a template whose first word is game_entity or actor, which then decides the type.

Limits: Game-entity and actor keys in a definition that stays a plain entity are unknown keys there.

Example:

{entity
	(include "/properties/stuff.ext")
	{Extension "type2at_ammo.mdl"}
}

See: include of a template.

actor

Where: .def outer block name, or the bare word at the top of a template. Type: root type word.

Values: actor.

Does: a game entity that can act: it has a brain, orders, a chassis, weapons and sight. Vehicles are actors: their definition starts {game_entity, includes a template such as /properties/tank.ext, and that chain reaches a file whose first word is the bare actor (vanilla tank_unarmed.ext, armoredcar.ext, car.ext, cannon.ext and others). Crews are separate human actors sitting in seats.

Limits: The actor keys (PatherID, chassis, weaponry, sensor, brain and the others in the "Actor keys" section) are only known in an actor.

Example:

;SDL
actor
(include "vehicle.ext")
("brain_vehicle")

See: Actor keys.

human

Where: .def outer block name, or the bare word at the top of properties/human.ext. Type: root type word.

Values: human.

Does: a soldier: an actor with a breed, a state machine, an inventory and fighting. Soldier skins under entity/humanskin/ get it through human.ext.

Limits: The keys only a human reads are listed on reference page r05.

Example:

{human
	(include "/properties/human.ext")
	{Extension "human.mdl"}
}

Gates of Hell: a soldier is told apart by this root type, not by a human tag; see props.

See: r05 Humans; chapter 8, section 1.

fx

Where: .def outer block name, usually under entity/fx/. Type: root type word.

Values: fx.

Does: a visual effect: an entity with views (sprites, particles, lights, decals) and an optional sound, needing no model. Texture names inside it are looked up under /texture/fx/. Scripts spawn it by its entity name.

Limits: An effect ends when all its views have finished, unless it has FromFxEditor.

Example:

{fx
	{sound "hit/small/water/01"}
	{particleview drops1 ...}
}

Gates of Hell: an effect file may also hold Local; every sound line plays (see sound).

See: FX keys, r08 Vision, effects and sound; chapter 16.

include of a template

Where: anywhere in a .def or .ext, written (include "path"). Type: directive.

Values: a path. With a leading / it starts at the resource root; without it, it starts in the folder of the file that holds the include line.

Does: reads the named file in place, as if its text were written there. Vanilla units get most of their behaviour this way, from .ext templates in properties/ (tank.ext, vehicle.ext, human.ext, stuff.ext and others) and .inc helpers.

Limits: A copied definition that keeps a relative include looks next to its new location and fails if the file is not there; keep copies in a folder that mirrors the original or write includes with a leading /. An include of itself, directly or through other files, has no guard and kills the process. Keys from an include and keys written after it simply add up; a later key of the same name acts again (for example a second props adds tags, a second volume with the same name changes that volume).

Example:

{game_entity
	(include "/properties/tank.ext")
	(include "/properties/selection/vehicle.inc" scale(1.2))
	{props "medium" "-turret"}

See: chapter 5, sections 5 to 7; path forms on reference page 1; Part I Add a new unit from an existing one.

Model and display keys

These keys are known in every root type.

Extension

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: text, a quoted path.

Values: usually the model file of the unit, "<name>.mdl". A leading / starts at the resource root; otherwise the path is relative to the folder of the file holding the key (the definition, or the include it sits in); ../ goes up. Absent: many vanilla vehicle definitions have no Extension line and sit in a folder beside a model file of the same name.

Does: reads the blocks of the named file as part of this entity. For a .mdl file that brings in the skeleton, views and volume shapes.

Limits: A missing file stops the game when the definition is read ("File not found" or "Resource not found" with the path in game.log). There is no fallback search in entity/ or the resource root: a relative name resolves only next to the file that holds it, which is why a cloned definition in a new folder should use a path with a leading /. A model mesh copied without its .mtl material file beside it crashes the game when the mesh loads.

Example:

	{Extension "afric_bench.mdl"}
	{Extension "/entity/-vehicle/tank_medium/archer/archer.mdl"}

Gates of Hell: a mesh whose .mtl is missing loads with a grey placeholder texture and the warning Material not found ... Using dummy texture. instead of crashing. A model that loads there can still crash as64.exe, so ship every .mtl.

See: chapter 16; path forms on reference page 1; ARSENAL refcheck in chapter 19; Part I Add a new unit from an existing one, Edit a model or an animation.

Skeleton

Where: .def top level. Type: block, or a quoted file name.

Values: a block with skeleton content (for example {ViewVolume {center x y z} {extent x y z}}, {TexMods ...}), or a string naming a file to read the skeleton from.

Does: adds to or reads the entity's skeleton (the bone tree of its model).

Limits: Bone changes with Bone must come after the skeleton is loaded.

Example:

	{Skeleton
		{ViewVolume {center 0 0 18} {extent 30 30 18}}
	}

Gates of Hell: the skeleton's own views are hung on an extra child bone named ##skeleton_views##. The name is taken, and a script that lists bones sees one more there.

See: Bone, chapter 16; Part I Edit a model or an animation.

SkeletonSrc

Where: .def top level. Type: text, a quoted name.

Values: a model name.

Does: sets the entity's skeleton to the model with that name.

Limits: Not used in vanilla definitions.

Example:

	{SkeletonSrc "mytank"}

See: Extension.

Bone

Where: .def top level. Type: block with a quoted bone name.

Values: {bone "name" ...} with bone settings inside, for example {parameters "Align;"}.

Does: changes one bone of the already loaded model.

Limits: A bone name the model does not have logs Bone <name> not found in <entity> and is skipped. A Bone line before the model is loaded stops the game with "Bone modifiers must be placed after skeleton load". speed or limits on a plain bone, instead of a proper joint bone, has been seen to crash the game, and a joint speed below 0.0002 gives the error "Zero speed in ik-bone".

Example:

	{bone "fence_vine" {parameters "Align;"}}

See: chapter 16; Skeleton; Part I Edit a model or an animation.

LODClass

Where: .def top level. Type: text, a quoted class name.

Values: a class defined in the level-of-detail sets. Vanilla uses human, vehicle_small, vehicle_big, vehicle_large, stuff_small, part_small, part_big, decor_small, decor_medium, decor_big, decor_tree.

Does: picks the level-of-detail table that decides at which camera distances the model switches to simpler meshes and drops shadows.

Limits: Distances in a class must grow strictly, or the set reports Distance should be farther than previous one. A level marked off stays off for every farther level.

Example:

	{lodclass "decor_medium"}

See: level_of_detail sets, r08; chapter 16.

TexMod

Where: .def top level, and placed entities in map files. Type: text, a quoted option name.

Values: an option name of the model's texture variants; vanilla uses names such as "camo", "jager", and numbers as strings ("1", "2").

Does: selects a texture variant for this entity. Texture variants are files named T#variant.dds beside a texture T.

Limits: A variant is applied only if the texture has it.

Example:

	{texmod "stosstrupp"}

Gates of Hell: a variant can also swap the mesh: with variant camo the model probably shows tank#camo.ply when that file exists beside tank.ply, and goes back to tank.ply for a variant without one (not confirmed). as64.exe swaps textures only, so such #variant.ply files do nothing there.

See: TexMods, r08; chapter 16; Part I Edit a model or an animation.

TexMods

Where: .def top level. Type: block of pairs.

Values: pairs {"Option" "variant"}. Several pairs for one option give a random choice among them.

Does: maps option names to texture variant names for this entity.

Limits: none known beyond those of TexMod.

Example:

	{TexMods
		{"Autumn" "aut"}
		{"Winter" "win"}
	}

See: r08.

NoCastShadows

Where: .def top level. Type: flag (no value).

Values: present or absent.

Does: the entity casts no shadow.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{NoCastShadows}

See: r08.

NoGetShadows

Where: .def top level. Type: flag.

Values: present or absent.

Does: no shadows are drawn on the entity.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{NoGetShadows}

See: r08.

UseShadow

Where: .def top level. Type: true or false.

Values: 0 or 1.

Does: switches the model's shadow on or off.

Limits: Write 0 or 1; words such as no or off can read as true.

Example:

	{UseShadow 0}

See: r08.

RimLight

Where: .def top level. Type: flag.

Values: present or absent. Vanilla soldier skins use it.

Does: turns on rim lighting for the model.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{RimLight}

See: r08.

UseDecal

Where: .def top level. Type: true or false.

Values: 0 or 1.

Does: switches decal projection for this model on or off.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{UseDecal 1}

See: DecalView.

DecalOrder

Where: .def top level. Type: whole number.

Values: vanilla uses 20 and 25.

Does: the drawing priority of the entity's decal against other decals.

Limits: A decimal value is rejected.

Example:

	{decalorder 20}

See: DecalView.

SpriteView

Where: .def top level, mostly in effects. Type: block.

Values: a sprite view with its own keys (Sprite, Offset, channels and timers).

Does: adds a sprite (a flat picture) to the model.

Limits: Written {#+ spriteview ...} it stays active (the + only folds it in the editor); written {## spriteview ...} it is skipped.

Example:

	{SpriteView "start" ...}

See: r08.

ParticleView

Where: .def top level, mostly in effects. Type: block.

Values: a particle view with Generator, Mover and Visualizer blocks.

Does: adds a particle emitter to the model.

Limits: The game has one pool of 40000 particles; beyond it new particles are silently not created.

Example:

	{particleview drops1 ...}

See: r08.

LightView

Where: .def top level, mostly in effects. Type: block.

Values: {type point}, {radius r}, an animator and attenuation keys.

Does: adds a light to the model.

Limits: none known here.

Example:

	{lightview ...}

See: r08.

DecalView

Where: .def top level. Type: block.

Values: a decal view projecting a sprite onto nearby meshes.

Does: adds a decal (a picture projected onto surfaces near a bone), such as a crater mark.

Limits: Target meshes need decal-target flags unless decals are allowed on all meshes.

Example:

	{DecalView ...}

See: r08.

Fogable

Where: .def top level. Type: word.

Values: auto, always or never.

Does: decides whether the fog of war hides the entity.

Limits: Any other word stops the game with "Unknown fogable mode".

Example:

	{fogable never}

See: r08.

SpawnedInFog

Where: placed entities in map files; legal in a .def. Type: flag.

Values: present or absent.

Does: marks the entity as spawned inside the fog of war.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{SpawnedInFog}

See: r08.

StoreAble

Where: .def top level, vanilla effects. Type: true or false.

Values: vanilla writes {storeable 1}.

Does: marks the entity as storeable; a saved mission holds the state of every storeable entity.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{storeable 1}

See: chapter 18.

Placement keys

The map editor writes these for every placed entity; they are also legal at the top of a definition.

Position

Where: placed entities in map and mission files. Type: two or three numbers.

Values: x y, and an optional height z.

Does: places the entity. A given height is kept instead of the ground height.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{Position -823.45 1528.34}

Gates of Hell: when its editor saves a map, positions, angles and scales are cut toward zero in the last digit instead of rounded (1.2346 is written 1.234), so the same map saved by both games differs in the last digit.

See: chapter 13, section 6, chapter 13, section 10; Part I Copy and change a map.

Turn

Where: placed entities. Type: number, degrees.

Values: any angle.

Does: turns the entity about the vertical axis.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{turn 0}

See: xform.

xform

Where: placed entities. Type: block of keyword and number pairs.

Values: zl (turn about the local vertical axis, degrees), zw (turn about the world vertical axis, degrees), y (degrees), scale (factor).

Does: sets the entity's rotation and scale.

Limits: Any other word inside stops the game with "unexpected token".

Example:

	{xform scale 0.75}

See: scale.

scale

Where: .def top level, or inside xform. Type: number, factor.

Values: a positive factor. Absent: 1.

Does: scales the entity.

Limits: Vanilla definitions never use it at the top level; vanilla maps scale placed objects with {xform scale ...}. Whether the model's obstacle and volumes scale correctly with a definition-level scale is not confirmed (unconfirmed).

Example:

	{scale 0.75}

See: xform.

Constrain

Where: .def top level, and placed entities. Type: word.

Values: none, ground, surface, zero, water. Vanilla definitions use water, zero, none and ground; maps also use surface.

Does: decides how the entity is held in height when placed: free, on the ground, on the terrain surface, at zero height, or on the water (the exact behaviour of each word is unconfirmed).

Limits: Any other word stops the game with "unknown constrain mode".

Example:

	{constrain zero}

See: chapter 13.

Player

Where: placed entities in map files. Type: whole number.

Values: a player number; vanilla maps write 0 and 1 among others.

Does: gives the actor to that player.

Limits: Placed vehicles start empty; a crew is not part of the placement.

Example:

	{Player 1}

See: chapter 12.

Game entity keys

These keys are known in game_entity, actor and human.

props

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: tag list.

Values: any tag words. Vanilla uses class words ("tank", "medium", "turret"), behaviour words ("opened", "emit_on_sink") and vision words ("vision_vehicle_medium").

Does: the entity's descriptor tags. They select the interaction scripts that apply to the entity, target selectors, vision and camouflage settings. Tags from every included template add up.

Limits: Many scripts decide their behaviour from these tags, so clear or -tag can quietly switch behaviour off.

Example:

	{props "medium" "-turret" "opened" "vision_vehicle_medium" "muzzle_large"}

Gates of Hell: many checks ask what the entity is rather than how it is tagged. A soldier is an entity of root type human, and a vehicle is one whose props held vehicle when it was loaded; squad icons, item search, shot choice, crushing, orders, bars and the unit card use these marks. An entity tagged human that is not a human (or the reverse) takes the other branch there. Gates of Hell also gives a meaning to more tags, among them helicopter, artillery, mortar, self_propelled, shield, hatch, no_scavenge, no_mouse_hint and remove_on_land_patch.

See: chapter 6, section 3; chapter 11; tag; Part I Add a new unit from an existing one.

tag

Where: .def top level, and placed entities. Type: text, one string split on spaces.

Values: any words. Vanilla uses "keep_places_without_door", "ger soldier", "destroyed".

Does: adds instance tags to the entity (tags of this one object, as opposed to the descriptor tags of props).

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{tag "ger2 soldier"}

See: props; chapter 6, section 3.

mass

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: number, kilograms.

Values: any positive number; vanilla heavy tanks use values such as 40500, small objects 1000 or less.

Does: the mass of the entity's rigid body, used when it is physically simulated.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{mass 40500}

See: r04; chapter 7, section 2.

collider

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: text, a profile name.

Values: a profile from set/colliders.set. Vanilla profiles include nothing, tree, bush, construction, human, particle, particle.small, particle.big, stuff, ammo, car, truck, armored, moto, tank.light, tank.medium, tank.heavy, cannon, cannon_small, train, marine, airborne. Absent: the template's value (vehicle.ext sets "vehicle").

Does: picks how the entity collides and makes contact with other entities.

Limits: An unknown name logs collider profile '<name>' not found and the first profile in colliders.set is used instead.

Example:

	{collider "tank.medium"}

Gates of Hell: a soldier under direct control is switched to the profile human_tpc and back to human when he leaves it, so a Gates of Hell colliders.set needs that profile.

See: colliders.set; chapter 7, section 6.

ObstacleID

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: text, a quoted name, and an optional second quoted name.

Values: a name from set/registry/obstacles.reg. Vanilla uses unbreakable, small_building, construction, building, stuff, nothing, tank, tree, human, marine, trench_wall. The optional second string names one of the entity's obstacle zones.

Does: picks the pathfinding cost class of the entity: how expensive it is for each kind of mover to path through it.

Limits: A name that is not in obstacles.reg logs only No obstacle ID in <entity>, but later crashes the game when a crushing vehicle meets the object, often minutes into a match. Add every name you use to your mod's obstacles.reg.

Example:

	{ObstacleID "unbreakable"}

Gates of Hell: also reads ObstacleId inside an obstacle block; as64.exe stops on it there.

See: obstacles.reg; chapter 7, section 5.

volume

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: block with a quoted volume name.

Values: {volume "name" ...} with keys such as tags, thickness, able, component; or {volume DefaultMaterial "name"} (the word right after volume, no inner block).

Does: sets up a hit volume, an invisible shape that bullets and blasts test against. The shape comes from the model; the definition adds tags, thickness and abilities. A second volume block with the same name changes the existing volume. The DefaultMaterial form sets the material every volume uses unless it names its own.

Limits: A name the model has no shape for creates an empty volume without any error. An unknown DefaultMaterial name stops the game with "Unknown material : <name>". A volume whose matrix cannot be inverted stops the game with "Not invertable volume matrix".

Example:

	{volume "turret"
		{component "turret"}
		{tags "turret"}
	}

Gates of Hell: a volume also takes HighHardness, CastSteel and Quality (factors of its armour), the able blockcamera (on by default; a volume with it stops the third-person camera) and the flag depend_on_wind (the volume sways with the wind). as64.exe stops loading on every one of them. A box side under 0.01 is widened to 0.01 with the warning Invalid box dimensions for volume <name>. A copied volume keeps disabled and its able entries.

See: r07 Armour, volumes and damage; chapter 6, section 5; Part I Change armour and see the result.

armor

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: block.

Values: {setting "name" ...} areas with thickness, volumes, durability and threshold.

Does: groups volumes into armour areas and gives them thickness, durability and penetration thresholds together.

Limits: A nonzero area thickness for a side overrides the volume's own thickness for that side; the first matching area wins.

Example:

	("armor_spa_light" armor(30 15 15 15))

See: volume, r07; chapter 6, section 6, chapter 9, section 6; Part I Change armour and see the result.

placer

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: block.

Values: {place "role" ...} entries.

Does: the seats of the entity and their roles (driver, gunner and others).

Limits: See r04.

Example:

	{placer
		{place "driver" {group "crew"} {visor "driver"}}
	}

Gates of Hell: a seat also takes Sealable (the vehicle then gets the tag hatch) and the flag StoredTouch; see place.

See: boarder, r04, place; chapter 6, section 7, chapter 8, section 8.

boarder

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: block.

Values: {door "bone"}, {link "door" "place" ...} and {anm "place" ...} entries.

Does: the doors through which crew get in and out, and the animations used.

Limits: See r04.

Example:

	{boarder
		{door "emit0"}
		{link "emit0" "driver" {anm "driver"} {forward putoff} {reverse puton}}
	}

See: placer, r04; chapter 8, section 8.

extender

Where: .def or template, top level. Repeatable. Type: block with a quoted type name.

Values: one of the registered extender types (inventory, vitality, shield, supply_zone, light, cannon, enumerator, talk, structure and others).

Does: attaches an add-on feature to the entity.

Limits: An unknown type name in a definition file is a fatal error: the game stops with "Extender not found". On an entity placed in a mission the same mistake only logs Extender "<name>" not found and the block is skipped, so the feature is silently missing.

Example:

	{extender "talk"
		{talker "tank"}
	}

Gates of Hell: has more extender types, among them flare, resources, heritage, waypoint, medic_tent, vehicle_vitality and weaponlight. as64.exe stops with "Extender not found" on each of them in a definition file; see Gates of Hell only on the extenders page.

See: r03 Extenders and components; chapter 6, section 7; Part I Add a new unit from an existing one.

interaction

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: block.

Values: interaction script content.

Does: adds interaction script content to this entity.

Limits: See r10.

Example:

	{interaction ...}

See: r10; chapter 11.

simulation

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: block.

Values: children able, state, disableLinked and velocity.

Does: controls rigid-body physics for the entity (used for falling parts, thrown objects, pillars, trees and the like).

Limits: Any other child stops the game with "unexpected token". An entity simulated without volumes logs Simulating entity without volumes : <name>.

Example:

	{simulation {able 1} {state 0}}

See: r04.

simulation able

Where: inside simulation. Type: true or false.

Values: 0 or 1.

Does: whether the entity may be physically simulated.

Limits: Write 0 or 1.

Example:

	{simulation {able 1}}

See: simulation.

simulation state

Where: inside simulation. Type: true or false.

Values: 0 or 1.

Does: whether the simulation is running at the start.

Limits: Write 0 or 1.

Example:

	{simulation {able 1} {state 1}}

See: simulation.

simulation disableLinked

Where: inside simulation. Type: true or false.

Values: 0 or 1; vanilla bridge parts write 1.

Does: a simulation setting for linked entities (meaning unconfirmed).

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{simulation {able 1} {disableLinked 1}}

See: simulation.

simulation velocity

Where: inside simulation, in saved missions. Type: two vectors.

Values: a velocity and a spin.

Does: restores the motion of a simulated entity when a saved mission is loaded.

Limits: Not for hand-written definitions.

Example: written by the game in saved missions only.

See: simulation.

simulatorID

Where: .def top level. Type: text, a simulator name.

Values: vanilla uses "water", "pillar", "airborne", "human" and "grenade".

Does: picks the kind of physics simulation used for the entity.

Limits: An unknown name logs unknown simulator '<name>'.

Example:

	{simulatorID "water"}

See: r04.

body

Where: .def top level. Type: block.

Values: optional quoted name, then {proper ...} and {permit ...} layer lists. Vanilla writes {proper body sensible} and {permit body}.

Does: sets which layers the entity's own body zone belongs to and which layers it reacts to.

Limits: Layer words not allowed for a body are ignored.

Example:

	{body {proper body sensible} {permit body}}

See: area, obstacle.

area

Where: .def top level. Repeatable. Type: block.

Values: optional quoted name, a shape block, and optional {permit ...}. A name starting with interior marks an interior zone.

Does: adds a zone (a region attached to the entity) used for selection and detection layers.

Limits: Not used in vanilla definitions.

Example:

	{area "zone1" {permit body} ...}

See: AreaDisable.

obstacle

Where: .def top level. Repeatable. Type: block.

Values: optional quoted name and a shape block such as {Circle2 {radius r}}.

Does: adds an obstacle zone that blocks movement.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{Obstacle
		{Circle2 {radius 6}}
	}

See: ObstacleID.

AreaDisable

Where: placed entities in map files; legal in a .def. Type: text, tags split on spaces.

Values: zone names or tags; vanilla maps write "close".

Does: hides the zones that carry these tags.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{AreaDisable "close"}

Gates of Hell: keeps this switch apart from the editor switch AreaDisableEditor. A zone switched off is taken out completely and gets no obstacle.

See: area; chapter 13.

DisableObstacles

Where: placed entities in map files. Type: true or false, or a bare flag.

Values: vanilla maps write it bare.

Does: switches the entity's obstacles off.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{DisableObstacles}

Gates of Hell: has a second key DisableObstaclesEditor for the editor switch; obstacles switched off in the editor stay off in the game.

See: obstacle; chapter 7, section 5.

impregnability

Where: .def top level, and placed entities in map files. Type: word.

Values: full, harmless (both used in vanilla maps) and disabled (unconfirmed).

Does: with full, the entity ignores every bullet and every blast.

Limits: The effect of harmless is not described (unconfirmed).

Example:

	{Impregnability full}

See: r07.

hearingBias

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: number, metres.

Values: any number; the absolute value is used. Vanilla vehicle templates use 4.5.

Does: an offset to the entity's hearing range.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{hearingBias 4.5} ; in meters

See: r08.

Actor keys

These keys are known in actor and human.

able

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: tag list of abilities.

Values: ability words; vanilla uses select, talk, fight, crew, minimap, repaired, ally_crew, emit_on_attack, emit_crew_on_injure, emit_passangers_on_enemy, with - to remove one.

Does: switches actor abilities on or off.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{able "-select"}
	{able "talk"}

Gates of Hell: adds the ability entity_manager_notouch: the game's clean-up of old corpses and props never removes an actor that has it.

See: r05; chapter 8, section 5.

PatherID

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: text, a profile name.

Values: a Profile name from the winning set/pather.set. Vanilla: human, animal, tank, tank.light, amphibia, armored, vehicle.large, vehicle.small, moto, cannon.large, cannon.small, cannon.carried, cannon.micro, airborne, railway, shallow_water, shallow_water_0, water, deep_water, deep_water_0. A mod may add profiles.

Does: picks the pathfinding profile: how the actor plans routes over terrain and slopes.

Limits: An unknown name stops the game with "Unit: Wrong pather name" when the entity is used.

Example:

	{PatherID  "tank"}

See: pather.set, r04; chapter 7, section 5.

TargetClass

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: one quoted class name and an optional quoted tag string.

Values: a class such as "tank", "light_tank", "armoredcar", "cannon", "car", "human", "airborne"; tags such as "ap fg bullet".

Does: the class other units' target selectors use for this actor ({class X} terms), and the tags used by {weapon ...} terms.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{targetClass "tank" "ap fg bullet"}

See: selector; chapter 10, section 2.

TargetSelector

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: text, a selector type.

Values: a {type ...} from set/target/. Vanilla: tank, tank_bullet, cannon_rocket, cannon_bullet, cannon_shell, human, searchlight.

Does: picks how this actor chooses its own targets.

Limits: none known.

Example:

	{targetSelector "tank"}

See: select.set; chapter 10, section 2; Part I Bots: what they buy and how they play.

brain

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: block with an optional quoted brain type.

Values: types used in vanilla: "actor", "vehicle", "airborne", "human". Inside: {state "name"}, {properties ...} and {const "a/b" N} entries.

Does: the actor's decision maker. const entries set named numbers read by the brain; the engine reads crush/min_danger_zone_time, crush/min_danger_zone_length, bomb/danger_zone_hide, bomb/danger_zone_jump, bomb/danger_zone_run, bomb/detect_explosives, bomb/detect_grenades and fight/distance.

Limits: An unknown brain type stops the game with "Unknown brain".

Example:

	{brain "vehicle"
		{state "vehicle"}
	}

Gates of Hell: adds the brain type "helicopter", built on the same base as "airborne". as64.exe stops with "Unknown brain" on it.

See: r05; chapter 10, section 1, chapter 10, section 5.

chassis

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: block with an optional quoted chassis type.

Values: a type such as "track", then chassis keys.

Does: how the actor moves.

Limits: See r04.

Example:

{Chassis "track"
	{speed {Slow 15} {Normal 25} {Fast 25}}
}

See: r04 Chassis, movement, wheels and tracks; chapter 7, section 3; Part I Change a unit's numbers.

component

Where: .def or template, top level. Repeatable. Type: block with a quoted part name.

Values: a part name ("body", "engine", "turret", "gun", "door" and others), with keys such as {RepairTime s} and {tags ...}.

Does: a repairable part of a vehicle. Volumes name it with {component "name"}.

Limits: On a placed entity, a component the definition does not have logs component '<name>' not found in <entity> and is skipped.

Example:

	{component "engine"
		{RepairTime 25}
	}

Gates of Hell: a component also takes RepairOrder (whole number), Health and HealthBroken (numbers). as64.exe stops on these keys, also when a Gates of Hell save or map carries them.

See: component, volume; r07; chapter 9, Gates of Hell summary.

fsm

Where: template, top level (vanilla human_fsm.ext, animal.ext). Type: block with a quoted name.

Values: "human" or "animal" in vanilla, with state, request, start and subset blocks.

Does: the actor's animation state machine.

Limits: See r05.

Example:

{FSM "animal"
	...
}

See: r05.

sensor

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: block.

Values: {visor "name" {vision "profile"} {bone "bone"}} entries.

Does: the actor's eyes: view points on bones with a vision profile each.

Limits: See r08.

Example:

{sensor
	{visor "main" {vision "tank_main-l"} {bone "visor1"}}
}

See: r08, sensor; chapter 16, section 1.

weaponry

Where: .def or template, top level. Type: block.

Values: {place "name" ...} weapon places and weapon settings.

Does: the actor's weapon mounts.

Limits: See r06.

Example:

{Weaponry
	{place "gun" {Rotate}}
	{place "mgun"}
}
