Values: four rising weights; 0 20 40 60 when absent, vanilla 0 20 40 100.

Does: splits carried weight into four bands. The stamina change rates in {inc} have one column per band, and the game blends between columns by the weight of the inventory.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{load 0 20 40 100}

See: inc (Stamina); weight (box); chapter 8, section 2.

inc (Stamina)

Where: {Stamina}. Type: block of rows, four numbers each, stamina per second.

Values: rows named walk, slow, normal, fast; any other row name sets the standing row. Vanilla: standing +15, +10, +9, +5; walk and slow +10, +5, 0, -10; normal +2.5, +1, 0, -20; fast -5, -10, -20, -40.

Does: how fast stamina rises (positive) or falls (negative) for each way of moving, across the four weight bands of load.

Limits: a misspelt row name silently overwrites the standing row instead of making a new row. Perk and veterancy bonuses scale only rates of zero or more.

Example:

{inc
  {stay 15 10 9 5}
  {fast -5 -10 -20 -40}
}

See: load; chapter 8, section 2.

movement_limits

Where: {Stamina}. Type: block of {Speed hi lo} rows.

Values: rows Fast, Normal, Slow, each with two stamina values. Vanilla: {Fast 1 25}, {Normal 0 0}, {Slow -1 -1}.

Does: says which speed the soldier may use at his current stamina. A speed is allowed once stamina reaches the higher of its two numbers and stays allowed until stamina falls below the lower one, so in vanilla running starts at 25 and stops below 1. When no row matches, the soldier walks slowly; with no rows at all he may always run.

Limits: while the item in his right hand is locked (a heavy weapon being carried in firing position), he can only walk, whatever this block says.

Example:

{movement_limits {Fast 1 25} {Normal 0 0} {Slow -1 -1}}

See: Stamina; chapter 8, section 2.

Inventory holders

The inventory extender in properties/human.ext defines the places a soldier keeps items: a box, two hands and armour places. Holder types are box, hand_left, hand_right, armor and weapon; an unknown type is an error.

box

Where: inventory extender of properties/human.ext or a unit .def. Type: block.

Values: {Size}, {Weight}, and starting contents with {item}, {cell}, {user}, {clear}.

Does: the grid the soldier carries his kit in. Vanilla soldiers have a 6 by 10 grid.

Limits: items that do not fit are dropped silently.

Gates of Hell: when the game looks for an item by its tags (a weapon to take, a grenade to throw, a mine to lay, a repair kit) it walks the box in the order the items were put in; here it walks the cells row by row. With two matching items the two games may pick different ones. The weapon list for direct control holds what is in the hands and in the box, and throwable items are those tagged throwable. A spent one-shot launcher is dropped to the ground, not packed.

Example:

{box {Size 6 10} {Weight 100}}

See: inventory (breed); chapter 8, section 7.

Size (box)

Where: {box}. Type: two whole numbers, cells.

Values: width and height in cells, each up to 127.

Does: the size of the inventory grid.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{Size 6 10}

See: size (item); chapter 8, section 7.

Weight (box)

Where: {box}. Type: number.

Values: positive; vanilla 100.

Does: the weight one cell can hold. Stackable items such as ammunition stack in one cell up to this weight divided by the weight of one item (unconfirmed).

Limits: it is a per-cell weight, not a limit on the total weight the soldier carries.

Example:

{Weight 100}

See: weight (item); chapter 8, section 7.

item (box)

Where: {box}. Type: tags and an optional count.

Values: {item "tags" [n]}.

Does: puts items with these tags into the box when the entity is created.

Limits: only items with the stackable tag can take a count above one in a single cell.

Example:

{item "bandage" 2}

See: item (breed); chapter 8, section 7.

cell

Where: {box}. Type: two whole numbers.

Values: two whole numbers, column and row in the grid.

Does: places the item at this cell instead of the first free one (unconfirmed).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{box {item "bandage" 2} {cell 0 0}}

See: box; chapter 8, section 7.

user

Where: holder block. Type: block with a word.

Values: {user "mount"} and similar.

Does: places an item for a named user of the holder, such as the weapon mounted on a gun.

Limits: an item without the stackable tag must have a count of 1 here, else the warning Invalid amount for non-stack item in holder box is logged.

Example:

{user "mount"}

See: weapon (holder); chapter 8, section 7.

clear

Where: holder block. Type: flag.

Values: present or absent.

Does: empties the holder of what the parent class put in it, so a .def can start from nothing.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{box {clear}}

See: box; chapter 8, section 7.

hand_left

Where: inventory extender. Type: block.

Values: none needed.

Does: the soldier's left hand.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{hand_left}

See: hand_right; chapter 8, section 7.

hand_right

Where: inventory extender. Type: block.

Values: none needed.

Does: the soldier's right hand. Weapon skills, special vision and the stance machine all look at the item held here.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{hand_right}

See: item (ability); in_hands; chapter 8, section 7.

armor (holder)

Where: inventory extender. Type: block with a name.

Values: {armor "name" {mask} {bone} {volumes} {pierceAbsorb} {HeatDamping}}. Vanilla has "head" and "body".

Does: a place for an armour item, such as a helmet or a vest, that protects certain hit volumes.

Limits: the protection belongs to the holder, not to the item: any item with the armor tag switches the holder's pierceAbsorb on.

Example:

{armor "head" {mask "head"} {bone "head"} {volumes "head"} {pierceAbsorb 30}}

See: armors; Reference 7 (armour, volumes and damage); chapter 8, section 7.

mask

Where: {armor} holder. Type: text.

Values: a mask name; vanilla uses "head" and "body".

Does: picks which armour items fit this holder.

Limits: an item that does not fit logs Can't put armor %s to %s.

Example:

{mask "body"}

See: armor (holder); chapter 8, section 7.

bone

Where: {armor} holder. Type: text, a bone name.

Values: a bone of the soldier's skeleton; vanilla uses "head" and "IK_UpDown".

Does: the bone the armour model is attached to.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{bone "IK_UpDown"}

See: armor (holder); chapter 8, section 7.

volumes

Where: {armor} holder. Type: text list, volume names.

Values: names of hit volumes in the soldier's model.

Does: the hit volumes this armour protects. Vanilla body armour covers "body" and the four foot volumes.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{volumes "body" "foot1l" "foot1r" "foot2l" "foot2r"}

See: Reference 7 (armour, volumes and damage); chapter 8, section 7.

pierceAbsorb

Where: {armor} holder. Type: number, millimetres.

Values: vanilla 30 for the head and 32 for the body.

Does: how much a bullet must penetrate before it hurts a soldier wearing armour in this holder.

Limits: it works only while an armour item is in the holder.

Example:

{pierceAbsorb 32}

See: How penetration is worked out; chapter 8, section 7.

HeatDamping

Where: {armor} holder. Type: number, a factor.

Values: 1.0 when absent; vanilla body armour uses 0.6.

Does: multiplies the fire heat that reaches the soldier while armour is worn.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{HeatDamping 0.6}

See: fire (avoidance); chapter 8, section 7.

weapon (holder)

Where: inventory extender of guns and vehicles. Type: block.

Values: one item per weapon place.

Does: holds the weapon of a weapon place.

Limits: a second item on the same place logs HolderWeapon: set user ... ignored and is not used.

Example:

{weapon {user "mount"}}

See: Weaponry; chapter 8, section 7.

spread_items and dropped items

Where: tag on the soldier entity. Type: tag.

Values: present or absent.

Does: a dead soldier drops up to 7 of his items on the ground. With the tag spread_items he does not.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{tags "spread_items"}

See: box; chapter 8, section 7.

Item inventory block

These keys sit in the {inventory} block of a piece of stuff (a weapon, ammunition, a grenade, a bandage) and say how it sits in a soldier's box and hands.

size (item)

Where: stuff file, {inventory}. Type: two whole numbers, cells.

Values: width and height; 0 0 when absent.

Does: how many cells the item takes in the box.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{inventory {size 2 1} {weight 1}}

See: Size (box); chapter 8, section 7.

weight (item)

Where: stuff file, {inventory}. Type: number, per item.

Values: positive.

Does: the weight of one item. It counts toward the stamina weight bands and decides how many fit in a stack.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{weight 0.5}

See: load; Weight (box); chapter 8, section 7.

block

Where: stuff file, {inventory}. Type: number, whole.

Values: a count.

Does: the size of one lot of this item when it is handed over or split (unconfirmed). Vanilla machine-gun belts use 100.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{block 100}

See: Weight (box); chapter 8, section 7.

fsm

Where: stuff file, {inventory}. Type: text, a state machine file name.

Values: a file in set/stuff/_settings.

Does: picks which animation states the soldier uses while holding this item.

Limits: an unknown name logs Unknown fsm state.

Example:

{fsm "belt"}

See: Stance machine; chapter 8, section 7.

link_bone

Where: stuff file, {inventory}. Type: text, a bone name.

Values: a bone of the soldier's skeleton.

Does: the soldier's bone the item is attached to when held.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{link_bone "gun_back"}

See: handle_bone; chapter 8, section 7.

handle_bone

Where: stuff file, {inventory}. Type: text, a bone name.

Values: a bone of the item's model.

Does: the point of the item that sits in the soldier's hand.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{handle_bone "handle_box"}

See: link_bone; chapter 8, section 7.

noview

Where: stuff file, {inventory}. Type: flag.

Values: present or absent.

Does: the item is not drawn on the soldier.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{noview}

See: size (item); chapter 8, section 7.

Melee blows

Each file in set/blow/ defines one blow. A key the blow reader does not know is an error and the whole file fails to load.

blow

Where: set/blow/*.set. Type: block.

Values: {tags}, {distance}, {self}, and one or more {opponent} blocks.

Does: one hand-to-hand move. The striker must face the target within 45 degrees.

Limits: any key not listed in this section stops the file loading with an unexpected token error.

Example:

{blow
  {tags "butt" "basic" "head"}
  {distance far}
  {self {animation "fight_front_club_begin"}}
}

See: chapter 8; chapter 11, section 4.

tags (blow)

Where: {blow}. Type: text list.

Values: words matched against the strokes of a soldier's melee level, such as "butt", "knife", "basic".

Does: decides which soldiers may use the blow.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{tags "butt" "basic" "head"}

See: strokes; chapter 11, section 4.

distance (blow)

Where: {blow}. Type: word.

Values: near, medium, far; near when absent.

Does: how far from the target the blow is made.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{distance far}

See: blow; chapter 11, section 4.

self

Where: {blow}. Type: block.

Values: {animation}, {enable_items}, {disable_items}, {fatigue}.

Does: describes the striker's side of the blow.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{self {animation "fight_front_club_begin"} {enable_items "smg" "rifle"}}

See: animation (blow); chapter 11, section 4.

animation (blow)

Where: {blow} › {self}. Type: text, an animation name.

Values: an animation of the soldier's skeleton.

Does: the animation the striker plays.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{animation "fight_front_club_begin"}

See: self; chapter 11, section 4.

enable_items

Where: {blow} › {self}. Type: text list of tags.

Values: item tags; an empty hand counts as the tag hands_empty.

Does: the blow is offered only while the item in the right hand has one of these tags.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{enable_items "smg" "mgun" "rifle" "flame_thrower"}

See: disable_items; chapter 11, section 4.

disable_items

Where: {blow} › {self}. Type: text list of tags.

Values: item tags.

Does: the blow is not offered while the item in the right hand has any of these tags.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{disable_items "pistol"}

See: enable_items; chapter 11, section 4.

fatigue

Where: {blow} › {self}. Type: number.

Values: any.

Does: nothing; the value is read but used nowhere.

Limits: ignored.

Example:

{fatigue 10}

See: self; chapter 11, section 4.

opponent

Where: {blow}. Type: block.

Values: {orientation}, {movement}, {damage}, {knock_down_chance}, {knock_down_time}.

Does: describes what happens to the target. The game picks the opponent block that matches the side the striker is on and the target's pose.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{opponent {orientation back} {damage 60 0.75}
  {knock_down_chance 0.8} {knock_down_time 6 8}}

See: orientation; chapter 11, section 4.

orientation

Where: {blow} › {opponent}. Type: word.

Values: front or back.

Does: the side of the target the striker is on for this opponent block.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{orientation front}

See: opponent; chapter 11, section 4.

movement

Where: {blow} › {opponent}. Type: word list.

Values: stand, squat, lie.

Does: the target poses this opponent block applies to.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{movement stand squat}

See: opponent; chapter 11, section 4.

damage (blow)

Where: {blow} › {opponent}. Type: one or two numbers.

Values: A and an optional B.

Does: A times the striker's melee strength is sent to the target's damage scripts as the value of the blow event. B is used by the fight order for its timing. Vanilla rifle-butt blows use 60 from behind and 40 from the front; knife blows use 150 and 200.

Limits: the result only does harm through the target's blow event script.

Example:

{damage 40 0.75}

See: strength; chapter 11, section 4.

knock_down_chance

Where: {blow} › {opponent}. Type: number, 0 to 1.

Values: 0 to 1.

Does: the base chance of knocking the target down. With a blow chance c below 0.99, the final chance is ((1 - c) x knockdown_blow + c) x (1 - knockdown_melee), using the striker's melee level and the target's avoidance.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{knock_down_chance 0.3}

See: chance (melee); knockdown_melee; chapter 11, section 4.

knock_down_time

Where: {blow} › {opponent}. Type: two numbers, seconds.

Values: shortest and longest time.

Does: how long a knocked-down target stays down.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{knock_down_time 3 4}

See: knock_down_chance; chapter 11, section 4.

Stance machine

The stance machine (a finite state machine, FSM) is the set of states a soldier's body can be in (standing, walking, lying, aiming) and the requests that move him between them. Vanilla writes it in properties/human_fsm.ext as {FSM "human" (include ...)}.

FSM

Where: properties/human_fsm.ext. Type: block with a handler name.

Values: the handler name must be "human".

Does: holds the soldier's state machine.

Limits: any other handler name logs Unknown Fsm handler. At load the game warns about states that are referenced but missing (fsm: state "x" not exist, but referenced), states with no exit, and states that cannot be reached from start.

Example:

{FSM "human"
  (include "human_fsm.inc")
}

See: State; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

Split

Where: {FSM}. Type: number, whole.

Values: the number of parallel tracks; vanilla uses 2.

Does: splits the machine into tracks that run side by side, such as legs and arms.

Limits: it must come before any split inside a state or switch.

Example:

{Split 2}

See: split; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

Request

Where: {FSM}. Type: block with a name.

Values: {priority n}, {duration s}, {exit "state"}, {interrupt}, {switch "map" 0|1}.

Does: an order the body can be given, such as move or fire. A higher priority request wins over a lower one. Vanilla priorities: dead 50, throwoff 48, knock-down 47, kick 46, hold 45, pick and drop 43, up and down 40, reload 35, unload 34, stop-move 32, move 30, snipe 29, hold-back 27, fire 25, aim 20, repair 5, idle 0.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{Request "move" {priority 30} {duration 2} {exit "stop-move"} {switch "walk" 1}}

See: priority; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

priority

Where: {Request}. Type: number, whole.

Values: higher wins.

Does: decides which request runs when two arrive together.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{Request "dead" {priority 50} {interrupt}}

See: Request; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

duration

Where: {Request}. Type: number, seconds.

Values: positive.

Does: how long the request lasts before it ends.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{duration 2}

See: exit; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

exit

Where: {Request}. Type: text, a request name.

Values: another request name.

Does: the request that runs when this one ends.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{exit "stop-move"}

See: Request; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

interrupt

Where: {Request}. Type: flag.

Values: present or absent.

Does: lets the request cut into a running one instead of waiting.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{Request "dead" {priority 50} {interrupt}}

See: Request; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

switch

Where: {Request}, or {FSM} as a map. Type: block.

Values: inside a request, {switch "map" 0|1} turns a map off or on. As a map, {switch "map" {link A B} {split idx from to}} swaps state A for state B while the map is on.

Does: lets one request change the meaning of states, such as walking instead of standing while move is active.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{switch "walk" {split 0 "stand" "walk"} {link "stand" "walk"}}

See: link; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

link

Where: a {switch} map. Type: two state names.

Values: {link A B}.

Does: while the map is on, state A is replaced by state B.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{link "stand" "walk"}

See: switch; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

Start

Where: {FSM}. Type: text, a state name.

Values: an existing state.

Does: the state the soldier starts in.

Limits: a state that cannot be reached from it gets a load warning.

Example:

{Start "stand"}

See: State; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

State

Where: {FSM}. Type: block with a name.

Values: {tag}, {to}, {from}, {transit}, {fromTagged}, {condition}, {split}.

Does: one pose or action of the body and the ways into and out of it.

Limits: transitions into dead and states without an exit get load warnings.

Gates of Hell: the game knows more states, among them squat_idle, revive, stand_noaim, walk_start, walk_stop, lie_idle, lie_bolt, lie_revive and prone self-treatment states (head, hand, leg). They run only when the stance data names them and the animations exist. The smoking idle is gone, and a soldier who dies standing in a swamp no longer plays the drowning animation.

Example:

{State "board"
  {condition "board"} {from "stand"} {tag "board"}
}

See: Start; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

tag (state)

Where: {State}. Type: text.

Values: any word.

Does: groups states so that fromTagged can name them all at once.

Limits: none recorded.

Gates of Hell: the state tag no-fire stops the soldier from firing, firing in a move state needs the weapon tag shoot_walking or direct control, and a rocket launcher fires only from an aim state.

Example:

{tag "board"}

See: fromTagged; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

to, from

Where: {State}. Type: text, a state name.

Values: an existing state.

Does: the states this one can go to and come from.

Limits: a name that does not exist logs fsm: state "x" not exist, but referenced.

Example:

{to "stand"} {from "squat"}

See: transit; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

transit

Where: {State}. Type: text, a state name.

Values: an existing state.

Does: a state passed through on the way, such as the animation between lying and standing.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{transit "stand"}

See: to, from; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

fromTagged

Where: {State}. Type: text, a tag.

Values: a state tag.

Does: the state can be entered from every state with this tag.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{fromTagged "up"}

See: tag (state); chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

condition

Where: {State}. Type: text.

Values: a condition word known to the soldier's handler.

Does: the state is only used while the condition holds.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{State "board" {condition "board"} {from "stand"}}

See: subset; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

split

Where: {State} or a {switch} map. Type: number and state names.

Values: a track index below Split.

Does: says which track of the machine the state or swap belongs to.

Limits: Split must be set first.

Example:

{split 0 "stand" "walk"}

See: Split; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

subset

Where: {FSM}. Type: block with a name and an optional from.

Values: {enable ...}, {disable ...} with request names.

Does: switches a group of requests on or off while the subset is active. Vanilla's with_item subset disables down, squat, looking, repair and step-aside while the soldier carries a heavy item.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{subset "with_item" {disable "down" "squat"}}

See: enable, disable; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

enable, disable

Where: {subset}. Type: text list of request names.

Values: request names.

Does: requests allowed or blocked inside the subset.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{disable "repair" "step-aside"}

See: subset; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

weapon mode tags

Where: tags on the held item. Type: tags.

Values: one of rocketlauncher, mgun, smg, rifle, pistol, flamethrower, together with the tag weapon.

Does: picks the weapon pose set of the soldier. When an item has several of these tags, the first in this order wins.

Limits: an item without the weapon tag never gets a weapon pose, even if it has a type tag. A pistol plays its walking fire animations only when it also carries the tag shoot_walking; without it the soldier runs with the empty-handed run animations.

Gates of Hell: adds the weapon class shortsmg between mgun and smg (it wins over smg), the tag bolt_action for bolt cycling after a shot, and the tags shoot_walking_manual and shoot_walking_ai beside shoot_walking (see Gates of Hell only). Prone riflemen and rifle walking fire use their own rifle animations, and long guns lose the look-around and assault standing poses. Each of these needs its animations in the soldier's animation set.

Example:

{tags "weapon" "rifle"}

See: fsm; chapter 8, section 4; chapter 16, animations; Part I: Edit a model or an animation.

Morale and self-healing

Morale has no keys you can set in data; it is described here because breeds and scripts work around it. Morale runs from 0 to 100. It rises by about 0.83 a second on its own, but not for 10 seconds after a loss. A wounded soldier loses 20 times the fraction of health he lost, and his attacker gains the same. A kill gives +10. Friends within 20 metres share +10 when an enemy is killed and share -60 when a friend dies. The bots change tactics at 70, 50 and 30. A computer soldier may flee: always below 10 percent health, with a 70 percent chance below 20 percent and a 30 percent chance below 30 percent. There is no suppression in this game. The brain properties no_retreat and retreat_ratio control retreat (see Reference 12, bot Lua functions and console commands).

A soldier heals himself when his health is below 70 percent, he has a bandage, he has not seen an enemy for 5 seconds, and the player is not holding him in place. Healing gives 9.6 percent a second, 30 percent per bandage, and repeats while his health is at most 85 percent.

Gates of Hell: self-healing uses the same bandage and 85 percent rules, but health comes back while the bandaging animation plays, and when he stops he takes his last item back into his hand. A soldier with a medic ability goes to wounded friends on his own, in cover and in battle, before he attacks; whether he also does so when standing idle in the open is not confirmed.

Save fields

These names appear in save files and in some vanilla .def files. They hold the state of a soldier and are written by the game; you rarely set them by hand.

Veterancy, Dying, Dead

Where: soldier entity in a save or .def. Type: number or flag.

Values: as saved by the game.

Does: the soldier's rank, whether he is dying, and whether he is dead.

Limits: none recorded.

Gates of Hell: Veterancy runs from 0 to 8; a GoH save or .def with rank 6 to 8 loads here as rank 5. A knocked-out hero saved while dying keeps his remaining time to death; here each load starts a fresh delay.

Example:

{Veterancy 2}

See: veterancy (breed); chapter 8, section 1.

Human state fields

Where: soldier entity in a save. Type: varied.

Values: Cover, FsmState, RunningSpeed, LastItem, LastThrowItem, Armor, Attack, Physics, NameId, Skin, Knockdown, LastDyingAnimation, StandFromLieBack.

Does: hold the soldier's cover, stance, speed, held item, name, skin and knockdown state between save and load.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{Skin "ger_t2"}

See: Stance machine; chapter 8, section 1.

Not described yet

These names appear in the data or in a tool's key list, but no source describes them well enough for an entry.

  • keys (blow)

Gates of Hell only

The Gates of Hell notes in this book have not been tested in a running game. Check them in your own game before you depend on them.

These keys, tags and names of this page's area exist only in Gates of Hell (GoH). This game does not know them: remove or replace them when you port a GoH soldier, then read game.log. The steps of a port are in Bring a unit from Gates of Hell; how the two games differ for soldiers is summed up in chapter 8.

no_inventory (breed)

Where: {breed}, after hero. Type: flag.

Values: present or absent.

Does: the soldier starts with an empty box of size zero. Armour pieces of the breed are still put on.

Limits: this game does not know the key and the breed fails to load; remove it when you port.

Form:

{no_inventory}

No stock Gates of Hell file uses it.

See: breed; inventory (breed); chapter 8, section 7.

field_icon (breed)

Where: {breed}, between portrait and icon. Type: text, a picture name.

Values: the name of an interface picture.

Does: gives the soldier a second icon that the interface can show; where GoH shows it is not confirmed.

Limits: remove it when you port.

Example:

{portrait ger_engineer}
{field_icon "ger_miner_ap"}
{icon tech}

See: breed; chapter 8, section 6.

Medic, Personage, Fortification and Mechanic (ability)

Where: a breed's {perks}, by the kind's name in lower case; Gates of Hell data keeps them in shared perk presets that its breeds include. Type: ability kind.

Values: Medic takes two plain numbers, a rate (5 when absent) and a veterancy (0); Personage one whole number (0 when absent); Fortification an optional factor (Gates of Hell data writes it bare); Mechanic the word veterancy (or vet) or the word factor, then a number.

Does: Medic lets the soldier heal others, and a medic goes to wounded friends on his own. Personage marks a hero, who is knocked out before he dies. Fortification scales how fast he builds field works. Mechanic sets how fast he repairs; any soldier who can repair may repair, and the perk only makes it faster.

Limits: this game knows the four names but does nothing with them.

Example:

{"medic" 10.0}
{"personage" 0}
{fortification}
{mechanic factor 1.0}

See: ability block; chapter 8, section 5.

Barricade (ability)

Where: a breed's {perks}, written barricade. Type: ability kind.

Values: {"fortifications" "name"} rows, one per field work, and {factor}.

Does: lets the soldier build the listed field works; a factor of 0 forbids building them.

Limits: unknown to this game.

Example:

{barricade
  {"fortifications" "foxhole"}
  {"fortifications" "medic_rally"}
}

See: ability block; Fortification.

Resources and Resources_Regeneration (ability)

Where: set/ability/*.set, as blocks {resources ...} and {resources_regeneration ...} with levels named by percent; a breed's {perks} picks a level. Type: ability kind.

Values: a factor per level.

Does: scale the size and the refill rate of a unit's own stock of resources, a GoH unit property ({Resources {max} {current} {income}}, 100, 100 and 0 when absent, refilled every 0.3 seconds by income per second).

Limits: unknown to this game, and so is the stock.

Example:

{resources
  {level "10%" 0.1}
  {level "1000%" 10.0}
}
{"resources" "1000%"}
{"resources_regeneration" "0%"}

See: ability block.

weapon_sway_control (ability)

Where: set/ability/*.set. Type: ability kind, one plain number.

Values: a factor.

Does: multiplies the sway of the soldier's weapon skill, for a gun in his hands and for a crew gun he works.

Limits: unknown to this game.

No stock Gates of Hell file uses it.

See: recoil, zoom_recoil and sway (skill).

recoil, zoom_recoil and sway (skill)

Where: a posture block (stand, squat, crawl, cover, vehicle, default) of a weapon skill level.

Type: number, a factor.

Values: 1 when absent.

Does: recoil scales how far the gun kicks with each shot, zoom_recoil does the same while the player aims down the sights, and sway scales how much the gun swings. The game's difficulty setting adds its own recoil factor. The kick is held for a moment, then the gun returns in a straight line. For a crew gun the game takes the best recoil and the smallest sway among the crewmen in working seats whose skill matches the gun. Computer soldiers do not feel the kick.

Limits: this game reads only accuracy and aim_range here and ignores the other three without a message.

Example:

{level "lvl_1"
  {stand
    {accuracy 0.65}
    {recoil 1.00}
    {zoom_recoil 1.25}
    {sway 0.90}
  }
}

See: stand, squat, crawl, cover, vehicle; default (skill); weapon_sway_control.

Damage, DamageTPC and DamageBlast

Where: the vitality block. Type: Damage and DamageTPC a list of {"volume" factor}; DamageBlast a number.

Values: each factor 1 when absent.

Does: Damage multiplies the damage of a hit on that volume of the body, for example more for the head and less for an arm. DamageTPC is used instead when the attacker is under direct control; it starts as a copy of Damage and its own entries replace those. DamageBlast multiplies all blast damage.

Limits: this game logs unexpected token for all three.

Example:

{Damage
  {"head" 1.3}
  {"face" 1.3}
  {"body" 1.0}
  {"hand1r" 0.80}
}
{DamageBlast 1.00}

See: Health (vitality); chapter 8, section 2.

bolt_action

Where: {tags} of a weapon item. Type: tag.

Values: the word bolt_action.

Does: the soldier works the bolt after each shot. Standing he plays stand_bolt_rifle_up (stand_bolt_rifle_open_up when the magazine is empty) with stand_bolt_rifle_down for the legs; crouching squat_bolt_rifle (squat_bolt_rifle_open). The stance data needs the states bolt, squat_bolt and stand_bolt.

Limits: unknown tag here; the rifle fires without the bolt animation.

Example:

{tags "weapon" "rifle" "bolt_action"}

See: weapon mode tags; State.

shortsmg

Where: {tags} of a weapon item. Type: tag, a weapon class.

Values: the word shortsmg; it wins over smg when both are present.

Does: gives the weapon its own poses and fire animations, among them pose_stand_fire_gun_short_up, stand_fire_gun_short_up, pose_squat_fire_gun_short, squat_fire_gun_short and walk_normal_gun_short_up. Lying, it uses the ordinary gun pose.

Limits: a weapon with this tag and no such animations plays nothing. This game does not know the class.

Example:

{tags "weapon" "shortsmg"}

See: weapon mode tags.

shoot_walking_manual and shoot_walking_ai

Where: {tags} of a weapon item. Type: tag.

Values: the two words.

Does: allow firing while walking, by who controls the soldier: shoot_walking_manual under direct control, shoot_walking when the player gives orders, shoot_walking_ai for computer soldiers.

Limits: a weapon carried over with only shoot_walking cannot be fired while walking under direct control or by computer soldiers in GoH.

Example:

{tags "weapon" "pistol" "shoot_walking" "shoot_walking_ai"}

See: weapon mode tags; tag (state).

no-fire (state tag)

Where: {tag} of a stance state. Type: tag.

Values: the word no-fire.

Does: the soldier cannot fire while in that state.

Limits: in this game the tag is only a name for fromTagged.

Example:

{tag "no-fire"}

See: tag (state); State.

lie_self-treatment animations

Where: the soldier's animation set. Type: animation names.

Values: lie_self-treatment_head_begin, lie_self-treatment_head, lie_self-treatment_head_end, and the same three for hand and for leg.

Does: a lying soldier bandages himself with these. This game has only the squat_self-treatment_* set.

Limits: a GoH soldier needs all nine in his animation set.

Example:

lie_self-treatment_leg_begin

See: Morale and self-healing; State.

select_idle (effect)

Where: the soldier's interaction script, as the handler {on "select_idle" ...}. Type: effect name.

Values: a handler that picks idle animations with set_idle_animation.

Does: when present, it picks the idle animations instead of the game. Without it only a standing soldier idles; with empty hands or a small item he plays stand_idle_empty most of the time.

Limits: this game picks idles on its own and has no such effect.

Example:

{on "select_idle"
  ...
  else squatting
    ("select_idle_empty_or_gun" probability(0.5) no_gun("idle_crouch_empty") with_gun("idle_crouch_gun"))
  ...
}

See: State; chapter 16, animations.

Reference 6: Weapons and Ammunition

This page lists every key of a weapon and its ammunition: timing, flight and aim, the damage and penetration numbers, bursts, spreading, the special aimed shot, ammunition and its traces, the damage effects of explosions and fire, thrown items, ballistic curves, and the {weaponry} block that mounts weapons on a unit. At the end, a short section shows step by step how the game decides whether a shot goes through armour. Chapter 9 explains how these pieces work together (Weapons, ammunition and damage); this page gives the facts for each key.

The job from start to end is Change a gun or its ammunition. In the ARSENAL window the Balance page shows each buy-panel unit's main gun with the columns "Gun", "Calibre mm", "Pen 100 m", "Damage", "Reload s" and "Range m"; a reload change there is written into the gun file, so every unit that carries the same gun changes with it. The Armor section of the Models page fires a chosen gun and shell at a unit (see The armour table on the Models page). The armour side of each test is in Reference 7; Gates of Hell weapon keys are listed at the end of this page under Gates of Hell only.

How to read an entry. "Where" names the file kind and the block the key is written in. "Type" gives the kind of value and its unit. "Values" gives what the game accepts and, when it is known, the value used when the key is absent. "Limits" lists what fails silently, crashes or is ignored. Keys are not case-sensitive: ProjectileDamage and projectileDamage are the same key. Where the same key name appears in two blocks, the heading adds the block in brackets.

A few words used throughout:

  • Stuff is anything a soldier or vehicle can hold: weapons, ammunition, grenades, tools. Each stuff file under set/stuff/ starts with its type word. The types on this page are weapon_bullet (guns that fire projectiles), weapon_flame (flame throwers), weapon_bombing (bomb drops), weapon_throwing (throwing), bullet (ammunition) and item (anything else, including grenades).
  • A pattern file (.pattern) holds shared keys that many stuff files start from; a .presets file holds macros that stuff files call with ("name" args ...).
  • Penetration ("pen") is how many millimetres of steel a shot goes through. Energy is a number that starts at 1 when the shell leaves the barrel and falls as it flies and as it passes through plates.

Work in your own mod folder. Text data files use CRLF line endings, string values are read as UTF-8, identifiers are ASCII, and old cp1251 bytes in vanilla ; comments should be kept as they are.

Weapon: timing, range and aim

These keys sit at the top level of a weapon_bullet stuff file or its pattern. Most of them may also be written inside a {parameters} block to give one ammunition type its own value.

rechargeTime

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: number, seconds.

Values: 0 or more; 0 when absent. Vanilla rifles use 3 (a new clip); vanilla guns mostly 2 to 12.

Does: the time to reload once the magazine is empty: for a rifle a new clip, for a gun that holds one shell the next shell.

Limits: a soldier's veterancy weapon_reload shortens it for soldiers only; guns and vehicles are sped up by their crew's skill instead.

Example:

{rechargeTime 5}
{parameters "apcr" {rechargeTime 6}}

See: recoveryTime; Reference 5, weapon_reload.

recoveryTime

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: number, seconds.

Values: 0 or more; 0 when absent. Vanilla rifles use 2.4 (the bolt); self-loading rifles 0.35 to 0.6.

Does: the pause after each shot before the next one, such as working a bolt. For a flame thrower it is how long one burst burns.

Limits: veterancy and crew skill do not change it; only rechargeTime is sped up.

Example:

{recoveryTime 2.4}

See: rechargeTime.

range

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: two numbers, metres.

Values: an effective range and a longest range. Vanilla rifles use 65 70, pistols 35 40, machine guns 75 80.

Does: how far the weapon is used. The first number is where the unit opens fire on its own; the second is the farthest the player can order a shot.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{range 65 70}
{parameters "fg" {range 120 130}}

See: aimRange; maxRange.

aimRange

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: number, metres.

Values: 0 when absent. Vanilla flame throwers use 20, mortars and rocket launchers 110 to 130.

Does: the range the unit aims at when it picks a target for this weapon (unconfirmed).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{aimRange 20}
{maxRange 25}

See: range.

maxRange

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: number, metres.

Values: no limit when absent. Vanilla flame throwers use 25 to 35.

Does: the absolute farthest a shot can be fired.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{maxRange 35}

Gates of Hell: a shot also needs at least MinRange, and under direct control the farthest range is not tested unless UnlimitedRangeTPC is off (see Gates of Hell only).

See: range.

speed

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: number, game speed units.

Values: positive. Vanilla gun presets write it as half the muzzle speed in metres per second.

Does: how fast the projectile flies.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{speed 380}

See: gravity.

gravity

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: number, a factor.

Values: 0 or more (negative values are raised to 0); 1.0 when absent. Vanilla rocket launchers use 0, long-range gun presets use 1.5.

Does: how strongly the projectile drops in flight.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{gravity 0}

Gates of Hell: past FalloffMeter the shell's gravity grows with FalloffStrength (see Gates of Hell only), so long-range rounds dive.

See: speed, reactive, Chapter 9, section 4.

AimingTolerance

Where: weapon stuff file. Type: number, degrees.

Values: 10 when absent. Vanilla rifles use 1, guns 2, rocket launchers 3.

Does: how far off the target the barrel may point and still fire.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{AimingTolerance 2}

See: SpreadTolerance.

SpreadTolerance

Where: weapon stuff file. Type: number.

Values: 0 or more (negative values are raised to 0); 0 when absent. Vanilla long-range gun presets use 0.4.

Does: how much of the spread the unit tolerates before it waits to fire (unconfirmed).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{SpreadTolerance 0.4}

See: AimingTolerance.

RelaxationTime

Where: weapon stuff file. Type: number, seconds.

Values: vanilla guns use 0.5, long-range presets 0.4.

Does: the settling time of the gun after it stops turning (unconfirmed).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{RelaxationTime 0.5}

See: AimingTolerance.

LockFireDistanceTime

Where: weapon stuff file. Type: number, seconds.

Values: 0 when absent. Vanilla stuff files do not set it.

Does: how long the fire distance stays locked after a shot (unconfirmed).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{LockFireDistanceTime 1}

See: range.

aimType

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters} (whole weapon). Type: word.

Values: direct, curved, adaptive; direct when absent.

Does: how the weapon aims. direct shoots flat, curved lobs over obstacles like a mortar or flare gun, adaptive picks between the two like a howitzer.

Limits: any other word logs Unknown aim type.

Gates of Hell: knows a fourth word, nocurve. This game logs Unknown aim type for it; drop it when you bring a weapon over.

Example:

{aimtype adaptive}

See: curve.

ZeroingAccuracy

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters} (whole weapon). Type: list of numbers.

Values: any count of factors. The first sight setting is always 1.0 and the listed numbers are for the settings after it. Vanilla long-range gun presets use 0.8 0.6.

Does: multiplies the spread for each sight setting, so later settings can be less accurate.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{ZeroingAccuracy 0.8 0.6}

See: Spreading.

reloadAnimBonus

Where: weapon stuff file. Type: number.

Values: vanilla bullet weapons use 0.5.

Does: a bonus applied to the reload animation of soldiers (unconfirmed).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{reloadAnimBonus 0.5}

See: rechargeTime.

automatic, automatic_ai

Where: weapon stuff file. Type: flag.

Values: present or absent.

Does: automatic makes the weapon fire bursts; automatic_ai does the same only when the computer controls it.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{Automatic}

See: burst.

ammoLocked

Where: weapon stuff file. Type: flag.

Values: present or absent.

Does: the ammunition cannot be taken out or swapped; vanilla single-shot launchers such as the panzerfaust use it.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{ammoLocked}

See: filling.

reactive

Where: weapon stuff file. Type: true or false.

Values: a flag; vanilla rocket launchers write it.

Does: marks a rocket weapon. Its shell flies with no gravity and a slight wobble, and its motor burns for 1.05 to 1.4 times the aim range.

Limits: gravity is ignored when reactive is on.

Example:

{reactive}

See: gravity, Chapter 9, section 1.

calibre

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters} (whole weapon). Type: number, millimetres.

Values: 0 when absent, in which case the game takes it from a bulletNN filling name. Vanilla rifles use 9.72 or 7.62, rocket launchers 50.

Does: the bore of the weapon. It decides how much a thin plate counts against a big shell (overmatch).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{calibre 7.62}

See: How penetration is worked out.

DisableRicochet

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters} (whole weapon). Type: flag.

Values: present or absent; ricochets allowed when absent.

Does: the weapon's shots never bounce off armour.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{DisableRicochet}

See: RicochetEnergyDamping.

TraceFreq

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: number, whole.

Values: 1 when absent; 0 turns tracers off.

Does: how often a shot shows a tracer: every shot at 1, every second shot at 2.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{traceFreq 0}

See: trace.

foresight

Where: weapon stuff file, or a weapon place in {weaponry}. Type: text.

Values: a foresight name; vanilla uses names such as "Foresight3" and "foresight5".

Does: picks the sight view used when the player aims the weapon directly.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{foresight "Foresight3"}

See: Weaponry.

Weapon: sounds, cursors and animations

fireSound

Where: weapon stuff file. Type: text, a sound name.

Values: a sound under sound/weapon/shot/.

Does: the sound of a shot.

Limits: a name that does not exist logs unknown sound file and the weapon fires in silence.

Gates of Hell: adds FireSoundClose (played instead when the shot comes from the unit the player controls directly) and ClickSound (a dry-fire click). See Gates of Hell only.

Example:

{fireSound "pistol/silent/welrod"}

See: reloadSound.

reloadSound

Where: weapon stuff file. Type: text, a sound name.

Values: a sound under sound/weapon/reload/.

Does: the sound of reloading.

Limits: a missing name logs unknown sound file and the reload is silent.

Example:

{reloadSound "rifle_bolt_five"}

See: fireSound.

cursor, cursorReloading

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: text, a cursor name.

Values: a cursor in interface/cursor.

Does: the mouse cursor shown when the player aims this weapon, and while it reloads.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{cursor "cannon_on_fg"}
{cursorReloading "cannon_reload_fg"}

See: crosshair, crosshairReloading.

crosshair, crosshairReloading

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: text.

Values: a cursor name. Vanilla stuff files do not set it.

Does: the crosshair in direct control, and while reloading.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{crosshair "cross_gun"}

See: cursor, cursorReloading.

states

Where: weapon stuff file. Type: block.

Values: {prepare}, {unprepare}, {reload}, {unload}, {fire}, {aim}, {can_aim}, each with a state name.

Does: the stance machine states a soldier uses to get the weapon ready, put it away, reload, unload, fire and aim.

Limits: any other key inside {states} is an error.

Example:

{states
  {reload "reload-bazooka"}
}

See: Reference 5, Stance machine.

Weapon: per-ammunition blocks

parameters

Where: weapon stuff file. Type: block with ammunition tags.

Values: {parameters "tags" ...} with any of the keys this page marks "top level or {parameters}".

Does: gives one kind of ammunition its own values, for example longer range for high explosive or a different damage table for APCR (armour-piercing composite rigid) shot. The block applies when the loaded ammunition carries all its tags.

Limits: blocks with the same tags are merged. Tags must match whole words: apc does not match apcbc. A top-level key written after a {parameters} block also overwrites that key in every block that still had the default value, so put top-level keys first.

Example:

{parameters "fg" {range 120 130}}
{parameters "apcr" {range 110 120}}

See: projectileDamageTable.

Weapon: damage and penetration

These keys sit in the weapon file (not in the ammunition file), at the top level or in {parameters}.

projectileDamage

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: number, millimetres.

Values: 0 when absent. Vanilla rifles use 5, rocket launchers 200, the 100 mm gun 171.

Does: penetration of the shot at the muzzle when there is no projectileDamageTable. When only one of projectileDamage and healthDamage is set, the other is filled from it (1 penetration energy equals 0.025 health).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{projectileDamage 200}

See: projectileDamageTable.

projectileDamageTable

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: block of {distance pen} pairs, metres and millimetres.

Values: pairs in rising distance. Between pairs the value is drawn as a straight line; before the first pair and after the last one it stays at that pair's value.

Does: penetration by distance. The game multiplies it by the shell's energy left at that point.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{projectileDamageTable {10 171} {50 160} {175 0}}

See: How penetration is worked out.

projectileDamageClip

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: number, millimetres.

Values: no limit when absent. Vanilla pistols use 3, rifles 5, shotguns 8.

Does: caps the penetration value.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{ProjectileDamageClip 5}

See: projectileDamage.

projectileDamageThreshold

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: number, a factor.

Values: unset when absent; when set it is never below 1. Vanilla gun presets use 1.10 to 1.30 by calibre, rifles 1.5.

Does: sets the threshold at which this shell damages an armour area: the plate's effective thickness divided by this number. A plate's own pierce threshold (value or koef) comes first; this key is used when the plate has none, and without either the threshold is two thirds of the effective thickness. The threshold decides only whether the area takes damage, not whether the shell passes.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{projectileDamageThreshold 1.15}

Gates of Hell: the value has no floor of 1; the fallback is still two thirds of the effective thickness.

See: How penetration is worked out, threshold in Reference 7.

healthDamage

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: number.

Values: 0 when absent. Vanilla rifles use 200, machine guns 135, pistols 137.5, shotguns 500.

Does: the damage to soldiers and other soft targets. When it is absent it is worked out from projectileDamage.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{healthDamage 200}

See: healthDamageClip.

healthDamageClip

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: number.

Values: no limit when absent.

Does: caps the damage to soldiers.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{healthDamage 500}
{HealthDamageClip 500}

See: healthDamage.

RicochetDamageClip

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: number.

Values: 0 when absent. Vanilla stuff files do not set it.

Does: caps the damage a ricochet can do (unconfirmed).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{RicochetDamageClip 10}

See: RicochetEnergyDamping.

RicochetEnergyDamping

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: block of {angle factor} pairs, degrees.

Values: vanilla guns use {0 1} {20 1} {30 0.8} {45 0.4} {60 0}.

Does: how much energy a ricochet keeps, by the angle at which it hit.

Limits: ricochets happen only after a failed penetration, at most twice per shell, and never for shells with the fg or no_ricochet tag or from a weapon with DisableRicochet.

Example:

{RicochetEnergyDamping {0 1} {30 0.8} {60 0}}

See: How penetration is worked out.

OvermatchDamping

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: block of {angle factor} pairs, degrees.

Values: vanilla guns use {0 1} {30 1.1} {55 1.15} {60 1.45} {70 4} {90 6}.

Does: scales how much a thin plate counts against this shell at each angle. The factor multiplies the ratio of plate thickness to calibre.

Limits: past the table's last angle the factor is 1. The result (ratio times factor) is kept between 0.2 and 1.0.

Example:

{OvermatchDamping {0 1} {60 1.45} {90 6}}

Gates of Hell: three more overmatch tables can stand in for this one: OvermatchCalibre, OvermatchFixed and OvermatchSlope (see Gates of Hell only). The first of them that has entries wins, in the order Calibre, Fixed, Slope, Damping. Data that has only OvermatchDamping gives the same result in both games.

See: calibre, How penetration is worked out, thickness (area), Chapter 9, section 5.

curve

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: text, a curve name.

Values: a curve from set/ballistics.set: vanilla has linear, cumulative, bullet, gun_std, gun_light, gun_medium, gun_heavy. Without the key the game uses a built-in curve that is not in set/ballistics.set: factor 1.2 at distance 0, 0.9 at half the range, 0.7 at the full range and 0 at twice the range.

Does: how the shell's energy falls with distance. The distance is measured in parts of the weapon's range.

Limits: an unknown name stops the game at load with Unknown curve.

Example:

{curve "gun_std"}

See: Ballistic curves.

bullet_view

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}. Type: text, an entity name, with an optional {tail}.

Values: an entity drawn as the flying shell.

Does: overrides the look of the shell in flight for this weapon.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{bullet_view "shell_ap_600" {tail "shell_tail" "root"}}

See: view (ammunition).

Weapon: bursts

burst

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters} (whole weapon). Type: block.

Values: {min}, {noaiming}, {short}, {long}, {rangeKoef}.

Does: how an automatic weapon fires its bursts.

Limits: any other key inside {burst} is an error.

Example:

{burst {short 7 0.5} {long 30 5}}

See: automatic, automatic_ai.

min (burst)

Where: {burst}. Type: number, rounds.

Values: 0 when absent. Vanilla howitzers use 6.

Does: the fewest rounds in a burst.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{burst {min 6} {noaiming}}

See: burst.

noaiming

Where: {burst}. Type: flag.

Values: present or absent.

Does: the weapon does not re-aim between the rounds of a burst.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{burst {min 6} {noaiming}}

See: burst.

short, long

Where: {burst}. Type: two numbers, rounds and deviation.

Values: a count and a random spread around it. Vanilla machine guns use short 7 0.5 and long 30 5; autocannons short 3 1 and long 5 1.

Does: the length of short and long bursts.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{short 5 0.3} {long 8 0.7}

See: rangeKoef.

rangeKoef

Where: {burst}. Type: number, a fraction of range.

Values: 0.33 when absent.

Does: the share of the weapon's range inside which long bursts are used instead of short ones (unconfirmed).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{rangeKoef 0.5}

See: short, long.

Spreading

Spreading is the circle around the aim point in which shots land. All its keys sit inside the {spreading} block of the weapon file (or of the spreading preset the weapon calls), after the block's optional first number, or inside the {spreading} block of a thrown item's {throw}. Written at the top level of a weapon file they are not spreading keys.

spreading

Where: weapon stuff file, top level or {parameters}; also {throw}. Type: number or block.

Values: in vanilla gun patterns a number (1), in thrown items a number (0.2 for anti-tank grenades, 0.5 for knives).

Does: the block that holds the keys below. A first number in it is the spread radius at full range in metres, the same as SpreadRadius. The spread radius is divided by the shooter's skill accuracy (or the unit's ManualAccuracy), then by the motion factor, multiplied by the zeroing factor, divided by the burst accuracy and changed by crew skill.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{spreading 1
  {SpreadPower 1}
  {BurstAccuracy 100 98 95 92}
}

Gates of Hell: a weapon with unlimited ammunition never spreads. The motion factor can be scaled per weapon with AccuracyByMotionK, and a weapon under direct control can have Recoil and SwayParams (see Gates of Hell only).

See: SpreadRadius; Reference 5, accuracy; Chapter 9, section 3.

SpreadRadius

Where: inside the {spreading} block of a weapon stuff file. Type: number, metres.

Values: 0 when absent. Vanilla anti-tank rifles use 0.5, rocket artillery 8 to 18.

Does: the spread circle at full range. Without a table, the circle grows in a straight line with distance.

Limits: RadiusTable overrides it.

Example:

{spreading {SpreadRadius 0.5}}

See: RadiusTable.

RadiusTable

Where: inside the {spreading} block of a weapon stuff file or its spreading preset. Type: block of {distance radius} pairs, metres.

Values: vanilla rifles use {0 0} {10 0.5} {25 1.0} {60 1.25}; machine guns {15 0.6} {40 1.2} {80 2.5}; sniper rifles {30 0.6} {60 1.1} {90 2.0}.

Does: the spread radius by distance. It wins over RadiusFunction and SpreadRadius.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{spreading {radiusTable {0 0} {10 0.5} {25 1} {60 1.25}}}

See: RadiusFunction.

RadiusFunction

Where: inside the {spreading} block of a weapon stuff file or of a thrown item. Type: list of x y number pairs.

Values: pairs of distance share and radius factor. Vanilla knife throws use 0 0 0.7 0.2 1 1 1.5 3 3 10.

Does: a curve of the spread radius by distance, multiplied by SpreadRadius.

Limits: RadiusTable overrides it.

Example:

{spreading {radiusFunction 0 0 0.7 0.2 1 1}}

See: RadiusTable.

SpreadXYRatio

Where: inside the {spreading} block of a weapon stuff file. Type: number.

Values: 1 when absent; vanilla's largest gun uses 5.

Does: stretches the spread circle into an ellipse, longer along the line of fire.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{spreading {SpreadXYRatio 5}}

See: SpreadYadjust.

SpreadYadjust

Where: inside the {spreading} block of a weapon stuff file. Type: number, degrees.

Values: 0 when absent; vanilla howitzers use 0.5.

Does: tilts the spread in height.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{spreading {SpreadYadjust 0.5}}

See: SpreadXYRatio.

SpreadPower

Where: inside the {spreading} block of a weapon stuff file. Type: number.

Values: 1 when absent; vanilla's largest gun uses 10.

Does: shapes how shots are scattered inside the circle: higher values pull more shots towards the centre (unconfirmed).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{spreading {SpreadPower 10}}

See: SpreadRadius.

BurstAccuracy

Where: inside the {spreading} block of a weapon stuff file. Type: list of percentages.

Values: one value per round in a burst. Vanilla rifles use 100 98 95 92; autocannons 100 90 85 80 75 65 55.

Does: the spread grows with each round: the radius is divided by this percentage.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{spreading {BurstAccuracy 100 90 85 80}}

See: BurstRecoveryTime.

BurstRecoveryTime

Where: inside the {spreading} block of a weapon stuff file. Type: number, seconds.

Values: 0 when absent; vanilla autocannons use 0.5.

Does: how long after a burst the accuracy returns to the first value.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{spreading {BurstRecoveryTime 0.5}}

See: BurstAccuracy.

BurstSpreadCount, BurstSpreadDelta, BurstSpreadWidth

Where: inside the {spreading} block of a weapon stuff file. Type: numbers.

Values: any.

Does: nothing; they are read but no part of the game uses them.

Limits: ignored.

Example:

{spreading {BurstSpreadCount 3}}

See: BurstAccuracy.

Special aimed shot

special

Where: weapon stuff file. Type: block.

Values: {mode}, {PrepareTime}, {PrepareCursor}, {accuracy}, {damage}, {throw_off}, {throw_off_always}.

Does: the weapon's special shot, such as a sniper's aimed shot. A soldier needs the matching special-attack ability to use it.

Limits: throw_off_always is not copied when another weapon starts from this one.

Example:

{special {mode aim} {PrepareTime 3.5} {PrepareCursor "aimed_shot"}
  {accuracy 2.5} {damage 2.5} {throw_off}}

Gates of Hell: {special} also takes sway (a factor on the aim sway while aiming through the scope, 1 when absent) and PrepareCursorScene (see PrepareCursor).

See: Reference 5, specialattack.

mode (special)

Where: {special}. Type: word.

Values: aim or detonate.

Does: aim makes the special an aimed shot; detonate makes it a remote detonation.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{mode aim}

See: special.

PrepareTime

Where: {special}. Type: number, seconds.

Values: vanilla sniper rifles use 3.5.

Does: how long the soldier aims before the special shot.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{PrepareTime 3.5}

See: PrepareCursor.

PrepareCursor

Where: {special}. Type: text, a cursor name.

Values: a cursor in interface/cursor.

Does: the cursor shown while the special shot is chosen.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{PrepareCursor "aimed_shot"}

Gates of Hell: PrepareCursorScene adds a second cursor picture, drawn in the scene over the target while PrepareTime runs; PrepareCursor stays at the mouse.

See: PrepareTime.

accuracy (special)

Where: {special}. Type: number, a factor.

Values: vanilla sniper rifles use 2.5.

Does: divides the spread of the special shot.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{accuracy 2.5}

See: spreading.

damage (special)

Where: {special}. Type: one or two numbers.

Values: a factor and an optional deviation. Vanilla sniper rifles use 2.5.

Does: replaces the curve's distance factor for the special shot with this value.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{damage 2.5}

See: curve.

throw_off, throw_off_always

Where: {special}. Type: flag.

Values: present or absent.

Does: throw_off lets the special shot knock the target off his feet; throw_off_always does it on every shot (vanilla shotguns use it).

Limits: throw_off_always is not copied by from.

Example:

{special {throw_off_always}}

See: Reference 5, explosive.

Filling

filling

Where: weapon stuff file; {weapon} line of a weapon place. Type: tags and an optional number.

Values: ammunition tags and a count; a weapon with a magazine writes its size, a gun writes the shell family ("bullet100").

Does: says which ammunition the weapon takes and how much one load holds. A gun's calibre comes from a bulletNN name when calibre is not set.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{filling "ammo mgun" 100}

See: calibre; Reference 5, filled.

fillingVisible

Where: weapon stuff file. Type: text.

Values: a name; vanilla rocket launchers write "rocket".

Does: shows the loaded round on the weapon model (unconfirmed).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{fillingVisible "rocket"}

See: filling.

Ammunition

These keys sit in a bullet stuff file or in a shell .pattern or .presets file.

view (ammunition)

Where: bullet stuff file. Type: text, an entity name, with an optional {tail "entity" "bone"}.

Values: an entity drawn as the flying round, and a trail effect fixed to a bone.

Does: the look of the round in flight.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{view "katusha_ammo" {tail "rocket_smoke" "tail"}}

See: bullet_view.

detonationThickness

Where: bullet stuff file or shell pattern. Type: number, millimetres.

Values: no detonation when absent. Vanilla high-explosive shells use 2, rockets 1.

Does: a plate at least this thick stops the round and sets it off.

Limits: a round stopped this way sends no pierce event, so scripts that react to penetration do not run.

Example:

{detonationThickness 2}

See: How penetration is worked out.

applyProjectile

Where: bullet stuff file. Type: true or false.

Values: present or absent.

Does: a round that explodes also deals its penetration hit (vanilla rockets use it).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{applyProjectile}

See: detonationThickness.

cumulative (ammunition)

Where: bullet stuff file. Type: number, metres.

Values: vanilla rocket ammunition uses 0.7.

Does: how far the shaped-charge jet of a HEAT (high-explosive anti-tank) round reaches past the point of impact.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{cumulative 0.7}

See: cumulative (effect).

trace

Where: bullet stuff file. Type: block.

Values: {view sprite {Light} {ScaleY}} and {length}.

Does: the tracer drawn behind the round.

Limits: any other key inside {trace} is an error.

Gates of Hell: {trace} can start with a list of tags, (Trace "tag1 tag2" ...), one tracer look per tag. Using the same View texture twice in one trace breaks the rest of the block with Block terminator expected!.

Example:

{trace {view "/texture/fx/trace" {Light 8} {ScaleY 0.35}} {length 12}}

See: TraceFreq.

length (trace)

Where: {trace}. Type: number, metres.

Values: vanilla shell presets use 12 times a factor.

Does: the length of the tracer.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{length 12}

See: trace.

possibleDamageRadius

Where: bullet stuff file or thrown item. Type: number, metres.

Values: vanilla rocket ammunition uses 4.

Does: the radius the computer's soldiers try to stay out of when the round is coming.

Limits: it does not change the damage; only the explosion's {damage} blocks do.

Example:

{possibleDamageRadius 4}

See: blastwave.

tag (ammunition)

Where: bullet stuff file. Type: text.

Values: words such as "ammo shell ap itemin2hands", "bullet stackable pierce", fg, no_ricochet.

Does: tags pick which weapon {parameters} block applies and turn some behaviour on. fg and no_ricochet stop the round from bouncing.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{tag "bullet stackable pierce"}

See: parameters.

Damage effects

Explosions and fire are {damage ...} blocks in a stuff file. The game knows blastwave, fire, flash and cumulative.

damage

Where: stuff file. Type: block with an effect name.

Values: {damage blastwave ...}, {damage add blastwave ...}, {damage fire ...}, {damage flash ...}, {damage cumulative ...}.

Does: adds an effect that happens when the round explodes or hits. add adds another layer; without add, a blastwave replaces the first layer the pattern gave. A second blast wave (damage add blastwave) is an explosion of its own at the same point, after the first: it runs its own blast_hit event and can hit each part once more.

Limits: projective and health log Unsupported damage effect; any other unknown name logs Unknown damage effect type. A number written straight after damage stops the game at load.

Example:

{damage blastwave {energy 1} {area 1 4}}
{damage add blastwave {energy 3.3} {area 4 5}}

See: blastwave, Chapter 6, section 4, Chapter 9, section 8.

blastwave

Where: {damage}. Type: block.

Values: {energy} and {area} only.

Does: a blast. Inside the inner radius it hits with full energy; between the inner and outer radius it falls in a straight line to nothing. Distance is measured to the point where the blast enters a hit volume. Armour takes 5 times the energy, soldiers under computer control 200 times, soldiers under the player's control a smaller factor. The wave travels at 15 metres per second. A soldier's pose shields him: crouching by 1.15, lying by 1.25, in cover by 1.5, lying ready by 1.75, ready in cover by 2.0.

Limits: the total explosive amount used by the game is the sum of all layers. Crew seated inside a vehicle are never hurt by a blast through the vehicle; only the vehicle's scripts hurt them. A blast meets plates without slope, calibre or overmatch (see blast in Reference 7).

Example:

{damage blastwave {energy 8} {area 0.2 0.4}}
{damage add blastwave {energy 2} {area 0.5 6}}

Gates of Hell: the energy factors (5 for armour, 0.025 health per unit of energy) are read from /set/damage.set, and every soldier, computer controlled or not, takes blast damage from the blast_to_health_scale table of that file times 125 times a difficulty factor. A volume keeps only as much blast energy as its threshold and passes the rest on. The block also takes ground_interaction_radius (see Gates of Hell only).

See: area; Reference 5, explosive; Chapter 9, section 8.

energy

Where: {damage blastwave}. Type: number.

Values: positive. Vanilla shell presets scale it with the calibre argument.

Does: the strength of the blast.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{energy 1}

See: blastwave.

area

Where: {damage blastwave}. Type: two numbers, metres.

Values: inner radius and outer radius; the outer must not be smaller.

Does: full energy inside the first number, falling to nothing at the second.

Limits: an outer radius smaller than the inner logs r1 must be >= r0.

Example:

{area 0.5 6}

See: blastwave.

fire

Where: {damage}. Type: block.

Values: {radius m}, {heating}, {time s}, {follow uid}.

Does: sets things on fire in a radius for a time. Vanilla rockets use radius 5, heating 0.8, time 3; the largest gun uses radius 20, heating 4, time 4.

Limits: any other key is an error. Each step, every unit within the radius gains heat: the step length times heating divided by the unit's inflammation_time (a fifth of that for an ally; none for a unit that cannot be hurt or already burns). Above 1 the unit catches fire: its burn reaction runs, then burn_volume for each of its volumes the fire reaches.

Example:

{damage fire {radius 5} {heating 0.8} {time 3}}

Gates of Hell: heat does not add up across a battle: a unit cools from 0.2 s after the last heat. Water puts a fire out only when the whole fire sphere is under the surface.

See: Reference 5, fire, inflammation_time, Chapter 9, section 9.

flash

Where: {damage}. Type: block.

Values: {radius near far}, {duration near far}.

Does: a blinding flash. No vanilla item uses it.

Limits: it blinds soldiers within reach only. A soldier on a seat is skipped, and vehicles and their crews are not touched.

Example:

{damage flash {radius 5 15} {duration 2 4}}

See: blastwave.

cumulative (effect)

Where: {damage}. Type: block.

Values: {distance m}, {damage mm}. Vanilla anti-tank grenades use {damage 75} {distance 0.3}.

Does: a shaped charge. It fires a second, invisible projectile of calibre 120 with a straight-line energy curve, with the given penetration and reach. The new projectile starts at the burst point and flies on along the shell's path. Its stuff is cumulative_charge (vanilla tank scripts test for it), its aim range is distance and its penetration is damage. It is a new shot, so it meets the same vehicle again with its own bullet_hit, pierce and break_armor events.

Limits: in vanilla only the anti-tank grenades use it, no gun shell.

Example:

{damage cumulative {damage 75} {distance 0.3}}

See: cumulative (ammunition), Chapter 9, section 8.

Thrown items

throw

Where: grenade or thrown stuff file. Type: block.

Values: {range}, {startAngle}, {spreading}, {constantSpeed}.

Does: how the item is thrown.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{throw {range 10} {startAngle 90} {spreading 0.2} {constantSpeed 10.5}}

See: startAngle.

startAngle

Where: {throw}. Type: number, degrees.

Values: held between 10 and 80. Vanilla knives write 8 and anti-tank grenades 90, which the game raises to 10 and lowers to 80.

Does: the angle of the throw above the ground.

Limits: values outside 10 to 80 are changed without a warning.

Example:

{startAngle 30}

See: throw.

constantSpeed

Where: {throw}. Type: number.

Values: vanilla anti-tank grenades use 10.5, knives 15.

Does: throws at this fixed speed instead of a speed worked out from the distance (unconfirmed).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{constantSpeed 15}

See: throw.

range (throw)

Where: {throw}. Type: number, metres.

Values: vanilla anti-tank grenades use 10, Molotov cocktails 14, knives 20.

Does: the farthest the item can be thrown.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{range 14}

Gates of Hell: without the key the range is 1 model unit (5 cm); in this game it is 0.

See: throw.

Ballistic curves

curve block

Where: set/ballistics.set. Type: block with a name and {x y} pairs.

Values: x is the distance as a share of the weapon's range, y is the energy factor. Vanilla gun_std is {0.1 1} {0.5 0.7} {1 0.4} {2 0.2} {4 0}; gun_heavy is {0.1 1} {0.6 0.7} {1 0.3} {2.5 0}. The built-in curve used when a weapon names none runs 1.2 at 0, 0.9 at 0.5, 0.7 at 1 and 0 at 2.

Does: makes a curve that weapons pick with their curve key.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{"gun_std" {0.1 1} {0.5 0.7} {1 0.4} {2 0.2} {4 0}}

See: curve.

damping

Where: set/ballistics.set. Type: block of pairs.

Values: vanilla {0 1} to {10 0}.

Does: nothing; the block is never read.

Limits: ignored.

Example:

{damping {0 1} {10 0}}

See: curve block.

Weaponry

The {weaponry} block in a unit .def or its class .ext file mounts weapons on the unit.

weaponry

Where: unit .def or class .ext. Type: block.

Values: {place}, {state}, {current}, {ManualAccuracy}, {RestoreIKTime}.

Does: lists the unit's weapon places. The first place is the basic one.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{weaponry
  {place "gun" {weapon "75mm_kwk40(L48)" filling "ammo bullet75 ap" 1}}
}

Gates of Hell: the block takes more words, ManualAccuracyZoom, TpcInstantAiming, AnimatedAiming, UseLookatAiming, AimingReferenceBone and Sealed, and a place takes AI_In_Manual, AimBone, Bullets and Sealable. This game does not read them; drop them when you bring a unit over.

See: place, Chapter 9, section 1, Change a gun or its ammunition.

place

Where: {weaponry}. Type: block with a name.

Values: the keys in this section from type to AccuracyByMotion.

Does: one weapon mount, such as the main gun, a coaxial machine gun or an anti-aircraft gun.

Limits: two weapons on one place log HolderWeapon: set user ... ignored; the second is not used.

Example:

{place "mgun2" {type "mgun_coaxial"} {weapon "mg34" filled} {basic}}

See: weapon (place).

current, number

Where: {weaponry}. Type: text or whole number.

Values: {current "place"} names the active place. {number i} gives it by index.

Does: the place selected when the unit is created or loaded.

Limits: {number} is old: it logs Current weapon place with index is obsolete, resave.

Example:

{current "gun"}

See: place.

state (weaponry)

Where: {weaponry}. Type: block, optional name.

Values: written by the game.

Does: the saved state of the weaponry.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{state "gun"}

See: weaponry.

ManualAccuracy

Where: {weaponry}. Type: number, a factor.

Values: 1.0 when absent.

Does: divides the spread of shots under direct control.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{ManualAccuracy 1.5}

See: spreading.

RestoreIKTime

Where: {weaponry}. Type: number, whole.

Values: 0 when absent. Vanilla tanks use 4, guns and armoured cars 10. The unit is not documented (unconfirmed).

Does: the delay before a turret or gun that has stopped aiming turns back to its rest position.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{RestoreIKTime 4}

See: RestoreIKAfterAim.

type (place)

Where: {place}. Type: text.

Values: a place type, such as "mgun_aa" or "mgun_coaxial".

Does: the kind of mount, used by the interface and the bots.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{type "mgun_aa"}

See: place.

weapon (place)

Where: {place}. Type: text, a weapon name, then optional filled or filling.

Values: a weapon stuff name.

Does: the weapon on this mount and its first load.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{weapon "mg34" filled}

See: filling.

ammo (place)

Where: {place}. Type: block.

Values: recovering, loading, reload, written by the game.

Does: the saved reloading state of the mount.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{ammo {reload}}

See: place.

gunner, charger, shooter

Where: {place}. Type: text, a crew role.

Values: a crew place name; gunner and charger by default.

Does: who aims (gunner), who loads (charger) and who fires (shooter) this mount.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{gunner "gunner2"} {charger "gunner2"}

See: place.

basic

Where: {place}. Type: flag.

Values: present or absent; the first place is basic when no place says so.

Does: marks the mount as the unit's main weapon.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{basic}

See: place.

Barrels

Where: {place}. Type: number, whole.

Values: 1 when absent.

Does: how many barrels the mount fires from.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{Barrels 2}

See: place.

LinkBone

Where: {place}. Type: text, a bone name.

Values: a bone of the unit's model.

Does: the bone the mount turns with.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{LinkBone "mgun1_rot"}

See: LinkAnimation.

LinkAnimation

Where: {place}. Type: text.

Values: an animation name or "off".

Does: the animation played with the mount.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{LinkAnimation "off"}

See: LinkBone.

Rotate

Where: {place}. Type: flag.

Values: present or absent.

Does: the mount turns (unconfirmed).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{Rotate}

See: place.

RestoreIKAfterAim

Where: {place}. Type: flag.

Values: present or absent.

Does: the mount returns to its rest position after aiming, after RestoreIKTime.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{RestoreIKAfterAim}

See: RestoreIKTime.

SequentialAim

Where: {place}. Type: number, whole.

Values: on when absent.

Does: the mount turns and then raises its barrel one after the other instead of both at once (unconfirmed).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{SequentialAim 0}

Gates of Hell: off when absent. A turret brought over that should aim one axis after the other must set it.

See: place.

StationaryFiring

Where: {place}. Type: flag.

Values: present or absent.

Does: the mount fires only while the unit stands still.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{StationaryFiring}

See: AccuracyByMotion.

AccuracyByMotion

Where: {place}, usually through a preset. Type: block.

Values: {maxlinearspeed}, {bylinearspeed}, {maxangularspeed}, {byangularspeed}, {disordertime}, {ordertime}. Vanilla presets: low 20 0.4 4 0.6 1.5 1.5, medium 21 0.55 4 0.65, high 22 0.7 4 0.7, machine gun 16 0.5 4 0.8 1.2 2.0 in the order above.

Does: lowers accuracy while the unit moves or turns.

Limits: any other key inside is an error.

Example:

{AccuracyByMotion {maxlinearspeed 21} {bylinearspeed 0.55}
  {maxangularspeed 4} {byangularspeed 0.65}}

Gates of Hell: the weapon can scale this penalty with AccuracyByMotionK: the spread is divided by (motion factor - 1) * K + 1, so K 0 removes the motion penalty for that weapon.

See: spreading.

maxlinearspeed, bylinearspeed

Where: {AccuracyByMotion}. Type: km/h and a factor.

Values: maxlinearspeed 0 when absent; bylinearspeed 1 when absent and at most 1.

Does: at maxlinearspeed and above, accuracy is multiplied by bylinearspeed.

Limits: a bylinearspeed above 1 logs Accuracy must be <= 1.

Example:

{maxlinearspeed 20} {bylinearspeed 0.4}

See: AccuracyByMotion.

maxangularspeed, byangularspeed

Where: {AccuracyByMotion}. Type: degrees per second and a factor.

Values: vanilla uses 4 and 0.6 to 0.8.

Does: at this turning speed and above, accuracy is multiplied by byangularspeed.

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{maxangularspeed 4} {byangularspeed 0.6}

See: AccuracyByMotion.

disordertime, ordertime

Where: {AccuracyByMotion}. Type: seconds.

Values: 1 when absent.

Does: how long accuracy takes to fall when motion starts (disordertime) and to come back when it stops (ordertime).

Limits: none recorded.

Example:

{disordertime 1.5} {ordertime 1.5}

See: AccuracyByMotion.

How penetration is worked out

This is the order the game follows when a shell hits a plate. There is no dice roll: the same shot at the same plate gives the same result every time.

  1. Penetration at this distance. The game reads projectileDamageTable at the distance flown (or uses projectileDamage) and multiplies it by the energy the shell has left, which the curve lowers with distance.
  2. Angle. The plate's slope factor is one divided by the cosine of the hit angle, and never more than 10.
  3. Overmatch. A plate that is thin compared with the shell's calibre counts for less of its slope: the game works out the ratio of thickness to calibre, multiplies it by the OvermatchDamping factor for that angle, and holds the result between 0.2 and 1. The effective thickness is ((slope - 1) x ratio + 1) x thickness.
